00 · The Method

How to use thisDon't read for completion. Read for one application, then drill it.

Each book is a card — tap to open. Tick a Capture when the idea is in your own words; tick a Drill when you've actually done it in your week. The bars only count when you do the work.

Library 01

Get Seen & BelievedPositioning · story · presence · brand — your distribution layer.

The sharpest thesis in Europe earns nothing if no decision-maker hears it. These four make people lean in and believe.

1
Start With WhySimon Sinek · L1 · Positioning
0/8▶
The one ideaPeople don't buy what you do — they buy why you do it. Lead with conviction, not credentials.
Author & why it matters

Simon Sinek — British-American author and former ad strategist; his 2009 TED talk is among the most-watched ever. His work sits where anthropology meets leadership: why some people command loyalty others can't buy.

For you: you sell trust before you sell a structure. In long, illiquid, high-stakes project finance, people back a financier they believe in.

The people & the dates (references)

Company: Nvidia (founded 1993 by Jensen Huang, Chris Malachowsky, Curtis Priem). Theme: the enabler/arms-dealer of the AI boom — GPUs + CUDA; the picks-and-shovels of the compute gold rush.

Capture the ideas

Run the drills

How to drillWrite your Why in one sentence. Test it against skeptics. Iterate weekly until it's yours.
2
The Storyteller's SecretCarmine Gallo · L1 · Story
0/8▶
The one ideaFacts inform; stories move. Wrap your data in narrative or it won't stick.
Author & why it matters

Carmine Gallo — former CNN and CBS journalist turned communications coach; author of Talk Like TED. He reverse-engineers what makes audiences remember and act.

For you: your edge is an abstract intersection thesis that's easy to glaze over. Story makes it felt in seven minutes.

The people & the dates (references)

Company: Motorola Solutions (the enterprise/public-safety radio business that split from Motorola Mobility in 2011; Mobility was later sold to Google then Lenovo). The boring, indispensable mission-critical-comms moat.

Capture the ideas

Run the drills

How to drillBuild a story bank of 5–7 tagged stories. Rehearse one aloud daily until it's a 90-second reflex.
3
Speak Like a CEOSuzanne Bates · L1 · Presence
0/8▶
The one ideaExecutive presence — the ability to inspire confidence — is learned, not born.
Author & why it matters

Suzanne Bates — former award-winning TV news anchor who founded Bates Communications and coaches executives on presence and influence.

For you: you're moving from "skilled operator" to "principal people back." That transition is won on presence — sounding like the person in charge.

Capture the ideas

Run the drills

How to drillOne presence habit per week — pace, headlines, hedges. Record yourself. The camera is the coach.
4
The Gary Vee CollectionGary Vaynerchuk · L1 · Brand
0/8▶
The one ideaGive relentless value in public; monetize the attention later.
Author & why it matters

Gary Vaynerchuk — Belarusian-American entrepreneur who grew his family's wine business through early online video, then founded VaynerMedia. The loudest evangelist for personal brand.

For you: you're building authority before you have a company. Attention is the asset, and you can compound it now, for free, in public.

Capture the ideas

Run the drills

How to drillOne platform (LinkedIn). Post 3×/week for 8 weeks, documenting real analysis. Track which posts pull senior people in your domain.

Library 02

Decide Where to WinStrategy · moat · structured problem-solving.

Zero to One asks "what's the secret?" The rest give you the tools to map and defend it.

5
Zero to OnePeter Thiel · L2 · Moat
Keystone0/14▶
The one questionWhat important truth do very few people agree with you on?
Author & why it matters

Peter Thiel co-founded PayPal, was Facebook's first outside investor, co-founded Palantir, and runs Founders Fund. Blake Masters was his Stanford student; the book grew from his class notes.

For you: his whole worldview is building something singular and defensible rather than competing on the same field as everyone else — exactly your play across three fields most keep separate. You uploaded this book twice. That's a signal.

Capture the ideas

Run the drills

How to drillOne idea per day for 9 days — don't binge. Keep a "my contrarian secret v1, v2, v3…" doc. Graduation: state in one sentence the valuable thing nobody else builds that you do.
6
Blue Ocean StrategyKim & Mauborgne · L2 · Market space
0/9▶
The one ideaStop competing in the red ocean. Create uncontested space where competition is irrelevant.
Author & why it matters

W. Chan Kim & Renée Mauborgne — INSEAD professors who studied 150+ strategic moves across decades.

For you: your intersection is a blue ocean. Most players sit in one ocean — pure energy, pure AI-infra, pure banking. This is the toolkit to own the space between.

Capture the ideas

Run the drills

How to drillBuild your Strategy Canvas + ERRC grid in one sitting — a one-page picture of how you'll be uncontested, not just better.
7
CEO ExcellenceDewar, Keller & Malhotra · L2 · Owner mindset
0/9▶
The one ideaSix responsibilities define the best CEOs — and your attention is the scarce resource to allocate.
Author & why it matters

Carolyn Dewar, Scott Keller & Vikram Malhotra — senior McKinsey partners who interviewed ~67 of the world's highest-performing CEOs.

For you: the literal field manual for thinking like an owner, not an employee.

Capture the ideas

Run the drills

How to drillPick your weakest of the six (likely "do only what only you can do") and apply it for two weeks before the rest.
8
The McKinsey MindRasiel & Friga · L2 · Problem-solving
0/9▶
The one ideaSolve fact-based and hypothesis-driven; structure rigorously; communicate top-down.
Author & why it matters

Ethan Rasiel & Paul Friga distilled McKinsey's problem-solving and communication methods into a practical playbook.

For you: deal analysis rewards structure. This makes your judgment sharp and credible — and stops you boiling the ocean.

Capture the ideas

Run the drills

How to drillRun a real problem: hypothesis → MECE breakdown → the 3 decisive facts → 30-second answer-first summary. That sequence is the whole method.

Library 03

Run YourselfMindset · focus · emotional intelligence — the operating system.

The best strategy fails if the operator running it is distracted, defensive, and reactive. This is what prevents that.

9
MindsetCarol S. Dweck · L3 · Mindset
0/8▶
The one ideaAbilities are developed through effort, not fixed at birth. The growth view wins over time.
Author & why it matters

Carol Dweck — Stanford psychologist whose research produced the fixed-vs-growth mindset distinction.

For you: at 40, switching into building something new, the real risk isn't the market — it's the quiet belief that this is "too late." That belief kills second acts.

Capture the ideas

Run the drills

How to drillTally fixed vs growth self-talk for a week. Graduation: setbacks make you curious, not defensive.
10
Deep WorkCal Newport · L3 · Focus
0/8▶
The one ideaFocused, undistracted, demanding effort is the rare superpower of this economy.
Author & why it matters

Cal Newport — Georgetown computer-science professor who argues deep focus is becoming both rare and valuable.

For you: your edge is judgment at a complex intersection, built only in long uninterrupted blocks — your unfair advantage over busier, shallower competitors.

Capture the ideas

Run the drills

How to drillOne 90-minute deep block daily for two weeks — same time, phone elsewhere. Log what you produced. It will outproduce most "busy" competitors.
11
Emotional Intelligence 2.0Bradberry & Greaves · L3 · EQ
0/8▶
The one ideaEQ is four trainable skills — and unlike IQ, you can raise it.
Author & why it matters

Travis Bradberry & Jean Greaves — co-founders of TalentSmart, builders of a widely used EQ assessment.

For you: deals are decided in rooms full of egos, fear, and competing incentives. Reading the room and managing yourself converts a thesis into a signed mandate.

The people & the dates (references)

Company: Amazon Web Services (AWS) (launched 2006; architect Andy Jassy, later Amazon CEO; founder Jeff Bezos). The toll on the internet — own the indispensable infrastructure layer.

Capture the ideas

Run the drills

How to drillPick ONE skill (start with self-management). Two strategies, daily, for three weeks. EQ improves through repetition, not insight.
27
The Marshmallow TestWalter Mischel · L3 · Self-control
0/7▶
The one ideaSelf-control — the ability to delay gratification — predicts success, and it's a skill you can train.
Author & why it matters

Walter Mischel — Austrian-born American psychologist who ran the famous Stanford "marshmallow" experiments on delayed gratification.

For you: building compounds slowly. The ability to forgo the quick win for the bigger later payoff is a core founder muscle — and, crucially, trainable.

Capture the ideas

Run the drills

How to drillDon't rely on willpower — design distance from temptation and pre-load "if-then" plans. Self-control is strategy, not strength.

Library 04

Keep & Compound MoneyCash discipline · tax structure · debt.

A financier who structures other people's capital brilliantly but runs his own loosely is a contradiction. Close it.

Caveat: two of these are written for the US system — the principles travel, the specifics don't. You're in France with cross-border considerations. Treat them as frameworks to discuss with a French expert-comptable / fiscaliste. Not tax or financial advice.

12
Profit FirstMike Michalowicz · L4 · Cash
0/8▶
The one ideaFlip the formula: Sales − Profit = Expenses. Take profit first.
Author & why it matters

Mike Michalowicz — serial entrepreneur who writes practical cash systems for owners.

For you: with lumpy deal-fee income, "I'll take profit if anything's left" means there's never anything left. A system fixes it, not willpower.

Capture the ideas

Run the drills

How to drillRun it on personal income now: savings off the top, separate accounts, fixed rhythm. Install the habit before you have an entity.
13
Tax-Free WealthTom Wheelwright · L4 · Tax (mindset only)
0/8▶
The one ideaThe tax code is a roadmap of incentives. Align with what the law rewards and keep more, legally.
Author & why it matters

Tom Wheelwright — CPA and longtime advisor who frames the tax code as incentives for behaviors governments want.

For you: employee→owner changes your tax situation structurally. The transferable lesson is the mindset; the US specifics are not your law — verify everything with a French professional.

The people & the dates (references)

Company: Microsoft and Copilot (CEO Satya Nadella; the OpenAI partnership led by Sam Altman). Distribution as the weapon — bundling AI into an installed base.

Capture the ideas

Run the drills

How to drillDrill the mindset, not US specifics: every big financial decision gets "what does the law here reward, and how should this be structured?" — with a qualified French pro.
14
The Total Money MakeoverDave Ramsey · L4 · Stability
0/8▶
The one ideaBuild wealth through a fixed sequence of steps. Behavior beats math.
Author & why it matters

Dave Ramsey — US personal-finance figure known for a strict, behavior-first path out of debt.

For you: the entrepreneurial leap is far less terrifying from stability. A clean personal balance sheet buys the runway and nerve to make bold bets instead of desperate ones.

Capture the ideas

Run the drills

How to drillMap onto the sequence: buffer → kill bad debt → full fund → invest. Knowing the math isn't living it. The drill is consistency.

Library 05

Lead & Build the TeamLeadership levels · habits · choosing the right people.

You can't build at the intersection alone. These three are how you grow influence and pick the few collaborators who multiply you.

15
The 5 Levels of LeadershipJohn C. Maxwell · L5 · Influence
0/8▶
The one ideaLeadership isn't a title — it's five ascending levels you climb separately with each person.
Author & why it matters

John C. Maxwell — American leadership author and speaker (The 21 Irrefutable Laws of Leadership) who has trained millions of leaders worldwide.

For you: moving from operator to principal who leads a team and a network, this is the map of how influence actually grows — and why a title alone earns you nothing.

Capture the ideas

Run the drills

How to drillYou're on different levels with different people. Climb deliberately — relationship, then results, then developing others.
16
H3 LeadershipBrad Lomenick · L5 · Habits
0/7▶
The one ideaLead from three habits held in tension — Humble, Hungry, Hustle.
Author & why it matters

Brad Lomenick — American leadership expert who led Catalyst, a major leadership movement, for over a decade.

For you: a practical, balanced habit-set for the kind of leader backers and partners actually trust.

Capture the ideas

Run the drills

How to drillStrong leaders run all three at once. Find the one you're short on and train it deliberately.
17
The Ideal Team PlayerPatrick Lencioni · L5 · People
0/7▶
The one ideaThe best team players — and partners — are Humble, Hungry, and Smart (people-smart). All three.
Author & why it matters

Patrick Lencioni — American consultant and founder of The Table Group; author of The Five Dysfunctions of a Team.

For you: your leverage comes from a small network of collaborators — this is your screen for choosing them, and a mirror for yourself.

Capture the ideas

Run the drills

How to drillHumble + Hungry + Smart. Hire, partner, and become all three — one missing virtue is a predictable failure mode.

Library 06

Endure & BuildMeaning · resistance · failure · grit — what building actually takes.

Strategy is the easy part. These six are about the years of uncertainty, setbacks, and grind between the idea and the win — and what carries you through them.

18
Man's Search for MeaningViktor Frankl · L6 · Meaning
0/7▶
The one ideaHe who has a why to live can bear almost any how. Meaning is what lets you endure.
Author & why it matters

Viktor Frankl — Austrian psychiatrist and Holocaust survivor who founded logotherapy. He observed that those with a sense of meaning were the likeliest to survive the camps.

For you: building is a long road through uncertainty and hardship; a clear why is what sustains you when results lag far behind effort.

Capture the ideas

Run the drills

How to drillAnchor the build to a meaning bigger than the outcome. That anchor is what carries you through the years results take to arrive.
19
The War of ArtSteven Pressfield · L6 · Resistance
0/7▶
The one ideaAn invisible force — Resistance — stops you doing your real work. Beat it by turning pro.
Author & why it matters

Steven Pressfield — American novelist (Gates of Fire) who wrote the definitive book on creative Resistance.

For you: building authority means shipping work daily against fear and procrastination — exactly what Resistance attacks hardest.

The people & the dates (references)

Houses & people: Gucci within Kering (controlled by the Pinault family, François-Henri Pinault). The perishable luxury brand; the dependence on a single star creative director.

Capture the ideas

Run the drills

How to drillResistance is loudest around what matters most. Treat it as a compass — then sit down and do the work daily.
20
Failing ForwardJohn C. Maxwell · L6 · Failure
0/7▶
The one ideaAchievers aren't people who don't fail — they're people who respond to failure differently.
Author & why it matters

John C. Maxwell — leadership author who reframes failure as the price and feedback of progress.

For you: a venture at a new intersection guarantees failures; what you do with them decides whether they compound into expertise or stop you cold.

Capture the ideas

Run the drills

How to drillFail more, but fail forward — every setback debriefed becomes a step instead of a wall.
21
Sometimes You Win, Sometimes You LearnJohn C. Maxwell · L6 · Learning from loss
0/7▶
The one ideaThere's no losing if you learn — losses are the best teacher when you let them be.
Author & why it matters

John C. Maxwell, with a foreword by legendary coach John Wooden. The book lays out the qualities that turn losses into learning.

For you: the discipline of converting every setback in the build into compounding judgment.

Capture the ideas

Run the drills

How to drillWin or learn, never just lose. Debrief every setback with humility and honesty until the lesson is explicit.
22
Grinding It OutRay Kroc · L6 · Persistence
0/7▶
The one ideaPersistence and relentless execution — not genius — built McDonald's. Kroc went all-in at 52.
Author & why it matters

Ray Kroc — the salesman who turned a single California burger stand into a global empire, told in his own autobiography.

For you: you're 40 and "starting over" — Kroc started later. Proof that a repeatable system plus persistence beats early brilliance.

Capture the ideas

Run the drills

How to drillBuild a standard, make it repeatable, and out-persist everyone. Late starts win when the system and the grind are relentless.
23
Connect the DotsRashmi Bansal · L6 · Resourcefulness
0/7▶
The one ideaYou don't need elite pedigree to build something great — passion, instinct, and resourcefulness connect the dots.
Author & why it matters

Rashmi Bansal — Indian author and entrepreneur who profiled self-made founders who succeeded without elite business-school credentials.

For you: validation that an unconventional path — an energy-finance veteran crossing into AI infrastructure — is an edge, not a liability.

Capture the ideas

Run the drills

How to drillYour scattered experience is the moat. Connect the dots into one story, then test the idea cheaply and fast.

Library 07

Execute & ClosePriorities · recall · persuasion · negotiation — turning intent into done.

Strategy and grit mean nothing without execution in the room. These three sharpen what you do daily and how you close.

24

0/7▶
The one ideaEat your biggest, ugliest frog first — do your most important, most-dreaded task before anything else.
Author & why it matters

Brian Tracy — Canadian-American productivity author and speaker.

For you: with a sprawling agenda across three domains, doing the one high-leverage task first beats a day of busywork.

Capture the ideas

Run the drills

How to drillOne frog, eaten first, every morning. Importance is defined by consequences — start there and don't switch.

Author & why it matters

Dominic O'Brien — British eight-time World Memory Champion who built the techniques he teaches.

For you: recalling a counterpart's name, a deal's terms, and your three points without glancing at notes reads as command and presence.

Capture the ideas

Run the drills

0/8▶

Author & why it matters

Chris Voss — former lead FBI international hostage negotiator, with co-author Tahl Raz; founder of The Black Swan Group.

For you: project finance is one long negotiation; these tools convert a strong thesis into signed terms.

Capture the ideas

Run the drills

Author & why it matters

Daniel Pink — American author (Drive) who reframes selling as "moving others," backed by social science.

For you: raising capital, winning mandates, recruiting partners — all are "non-sales selling." This modernizes how you do it.

The people & the dates (references)

Owner: LVMH, controlled by Bernard Arnault — the house-of-brands empire built by acquisition (Louis Vuitton, Dior, Moët Hennessy, Tiffany, etc.).

Capture the ideas

Run the drills

How to drillSelling is serving — attune, stay buoyant, bring clarity. Find the problem worth solving and frame the pitch for the other side.

InfluenceRobert Cialdini · L7 · Persuasion
0/8▶
The one ideaPeople say yes for seven predictable, largely automatic reasons. Know them to persuade ethically — and to defend yourself.
Author & why it matters

Robert Cialdini — American social psychologist, the most-cited authority on persuasion, who went undercover for years to study compliance. (You uploaded the French edition, Influence et manipulation.)

For you: deals are decided by these triggers; using them with integrity, and spotting them used on you, is a direct edge.

Capture the ideas

Run the drills

How to drillSeven reasons people say yes. Use them with integrity to persuade, and recognize them instantly when they're aimed at you.

Library 08

Founders' Field NotesEight lives that built iconic companies — mined for what transfers.

Don't read these for the stories. Read them for the moves — the decisions, the grit, and the timing behind companies that started exactly where you are: with nothing but conviction.

30
Shoe DogPhil Knight · L8 · Nike
0/7▶
The one ideaNike was built on a "crazy idea," relentless cash-flow survival, and refusing to quit — not on a master plan.
Author & why it matters

Phil Knight — co-founder of Nike, who started by importing Japanese running shoes from the trunk of his car. His memoir is unusually candid about the near-death cash crises.

The Case Files ▶Real companies — history, failures, and the lessons that transfer. Video deep-dives.

Books give you the frameworks; these give you the reps in the wild — real companies that nearly died, bet everything, and either compounded or collapsed. Each case is summarised, mined for entrepreneur and investor lessons, and tied back to your own intersection. Starting with Sébastien Koubar's channel.

01
Nvidia — 30 Days from Bankruptcy to $5 TrillionSébastien Koubar · Video case · Semiconductors → AI
▶ Video0/14▶
The one ideaSurvive the near-death moment with brutal cash discipline — then bet the company on a technology the world won't understand for another decade, and become the layer everyone else has to buy from.
The story (in brief)

Founded in 1993 by Jensen Huang, Chris Malachowsky and Curtis Priem, Nvidia's first chip — the NV1 (1995) — bet on curved surfaces and bundled-in audio just as Microsoft's DirectX made triangles the industry standard. It flopped: most units were returned, its big partner Sega walked, and the company was left with roughly 30 days of cash. Jensen cut every cost — office lights off, his own bills unpaid — to make payroll, while Intel earned billions a quarter.

Cornered, they bet everything on one last chip, the RIVA 128 (1997). With no money to iterate, they verified the design in simulation and shipped without the usual physical test cycles. It worked — ~1 million units fast — and saved the company. The GeForce 256 (1999) became the first "GPU," pioneering massively parallel processing. Then in 2006 Jensen poured all profits into CUDA: software turning graphics chips into general-purpose parallel computers — for a market that did not yet exist. It sat largely unused for ~6 years.

In 2012, AlexNet (Krizhevsky, Sutskever, Hinton) trained a neural network on Nvidia GPUs via CUDA and crushed the ImageNet contest — proving GPUs were the engine of modern AI. Google, Tesla, Meta and OpenAI all built on Nvidia + CUDA. A near-bankrupt gaming-chip maker became the backbone of the AI era.

Where it stands

From about $345 billion when ChatGPT launched in late 2022, Nvidia became the first-ever $4 trillion company in 2025 and the world's most valuable, hovering near $4.5–5 trillion into 2026 — roughly a 13× in three years. (Figures move; the trajectory is the point.)

▶ Original video ↗

The people & the dates (references)

Company: Nvidia (founded 1993 by Jensen Huang, Chris Malachowsky, Curtis Priem). Theme: the enabler/arms-dealer of the AI boom — GPUs + CUDA; the picks-and-shovels of the compute gold rush.

Capture the lessons

Run the drills

Beyond the video — added insight

NV1's deeper failure was over-integration (graphics + audio + ports) plus betting on quadratic texture mapping — technical elegance that fit no ecosystem. Elegance that ignores the standard is worthless.

RIVA 128 wasn't luck. Having no money for silicon re-spins forced Nvidia to pioneer emulation-based verification — a process innovation that became a permanent speed edge (a relentless ~6-month release cadence rivals couldn't match). Constraint became capability.

CUDA was a loss-leader platform — free and subsidised for years — the same playbook as Amazon's AWS, Apple's App Store, and Adobe: give the tool away, own the ecosystem, monetise the lock-in.

Why AI made GPUs the chokepoint: neural networks are massively parallel matrix math — exactly what GPUs do — and transformers (2017) plus scaling laws turned raw compute into the scarce input. Nvidia sat on the exact bottleneck.

Your intersection, one layer down: AI data centres are now increasingly power-constrained, not chip-constrained — training clusters draw hundreds of megawatts, and grid interconnection, transformers and cooling are the new bottleneck. Nvidia's story is about to re-run in energy — which is precisely your blue ocean.

The risk nobody prices at the top: customer concentration (a few hyperscalers), cyclicality (remember the crypto-demand whiplash), and the fact that the same hindsight bias that once hid the opportunity now hides the risk.

Make it click — similar plays

TSMC — the ultimate picks-and-shovels: nearly everyone's advanced chips, one foundry, the enabling layer few notice. ARM — licenses the architecture; an ecosystem moat like CUDA. AWS — Amazon bet on infrastructure years before demand; it became the profit engine.

Counter-examples that sharpen the lesson: 3dfx was the gaming-GPU king, bet wrong, went bankrupt, and was absorbed by Nvidia in 2000. Intel — the giant in this very story, earning billions a quarter — missed mobile and was late to AI/GPU: dominance is not durability. Kodak, Nokia, BlackBerry — incumbents that missed the shift entirely.

Your version: in energy × AI, who is the "Nvidia / TSMC"? The bottleneck enabler — power interconnection, grid capacity, SST transformers, cooling. Financing that chokepoint is the uncontested space.

How to drillSurvive, align with the standard, then build the platform beneath the next wave — and be the layer everyone must buy from. For you: find the financeable bottleneck in AI-infra power, and own it before it's obvious.
02
Motorola — Left for Dead, Now Worth $70B+Sébastien Koubar · Video case · Mobile → Public safety
▶ Video0/14▶
The one ideaAccept that a business can die so the company can live. Split, shed, reinvent — and remember the real gold may be hiding in the half everyone ignored.
The story (in brief)

Motorola didn't just join the tech age — it built it. Its comms gear carried Apollo 11's words from the Moon (1969); its engineer Martin Cooper made the first handheld mobile call in 1973 (phoning his rival at Bell Labs to gloat); its 68000 processor powered the first Macintosh, the Sega Genesis and 1980s arcades; and its DynaTAC 8000X (1983) was the first commercial mobile phone. In 2004 the razor-thin RAZR V3 sold 130M+ units and became a Hollywood icon.

Then success became the trap. The RAZR was so profitable that Motorola stopped innovating and just re-coloured it. Samsung, Nokia and BlackBerry closed in — and in 2007 the iPhone changed the game from hardware to software. Motorola's mobile arm lost $1.2B in a single quarter and 40% of its market share by 2009. In 2011 the company split in two; Google bought Motorola Mobility for $12.5B — mainly for its 17,000 patents to protect Android — then sold the husk to Lenovo for $2.9B in 2014. The public buried Motorola.

But two comebacks were underway. Motorola Solutions, the forgotten half, pivoted under CEO Greg Brown to public safety — radios, cameras and AI software for police, fire and 911 centres — and became a hidden giant equipping nearly every US/EU emergency service. And Motorola Mobility under Lenovo clawed back through survive → stabilize → reinvent: the cheap-but-indestructible Moto G cash cow, the foldable Razr's genuinely useful outer screen, and dominance in overlooked geographies (No. 1 in Brazil), grabbing US shelf space when LG quit in 2021 — reaching No. 3 in US smartphone sales by 2025.

Where it stands

Motorola Solutions trades around $70–80 billion with revenue guided near $12.7 billion for 2026, growing ~7–8% a year — quietly one of the market's most durable compounders. Motorola Mobility, once written off, is a top-three US smartphone seller. Two survivors from one "corpse."

▶ Original video ↗

The people & the dates (references)

Company: Motorola Solutions (the enterprise/public-safety radio business that split from Motorola Mobility in 2011; Mobility was later sold to Google then Lenovo). The boring, indispensable mission-critical-comms moat.

Capture the lessons

Run the drills

Beyond the video — added insight

A third Motorola child the video skips: Motorola was once a semiconductor powerhouse (that 68000 chip). It spun the chip unit off as Freescale in 2004, later absorbed into NXP — today a leader in automotive and edge chips. The invention DNA outlived the brand in three directions, not two.

Why the public-safety moat is deeper than "radios": government procurement means multi-year contracts, certification barriers, interoperability standards (P25) and recurring cloud/software revenue. It behaves like a near-utility — which is exactly why it compounds so steadily.

The accurate Axon comparison: the video says Motorola Solutions is "10× bigger than Axon." It isn't — it's roughly 2× by market cap and ~4× by revenue. But Axon grows far faster and trades far richer. The real lesson is the trade-off, not the size: durable-and-cheap versus fast-and-expensive.

Lenovo ran a private-equity playbook inside a company: buy a distressed asset cheap, cut hard, refocus, then grow. That sequence is a repeatable value-creation template.

Your intersection: Motorola Solutions is the shape of the opportunity you keep circling — a boring, mission-critical, high-switching-cost, long-cycle niche. Grid interconnection, transformers and power infrastructure for AI have exactly that profile. This case is a template for the durable niche you should be hunting and financing.

Make it click — similar plays

Reinventors who cannibalised themselves: IBM (sold its PC business — to Lenovo too — and pivoted to services and software), Netflix (killed its own DVD cash cow for streaming), Fujifilm (turned film chemistry into healthcare and materials and survived the digital shock).

Parallel split-and-pivot: Nokia sold handsets to Microsoft and reinvented as a telecom-network-equipment company — Motorola Solutions' twin.

Counter-examples that make it bite: Kodak (invented digital, refused to cannibalise film, died), BlackBerry (clung to the keyboard), Nokia's handset unit (missed the software shift). Same shock, opposite endings.

Your version: in energy × AI, the unglamorous power bottleneck is the "Motorola Solutions" of the space — the hidden giant nobody's watching.

How to drillNever coast on a hit, amputate what's dying, and hunt value in the boring, essential, sticky half no one is watching. For you: the durable niche beats the glamorous one — find yours in AI-infra power.
03
EssilorLuxottica — The Invisible Eyewear MonopolySébastien Koubar · Video case · Vertical integration & moat
▶ Video0/14▶
The one ideaDon't compete on the product — privatise the entire infrastructure around it. Own the factories, the shelves, and the payers, and every "choice" the customer makes still ends in your pocket.
The story (in brief)

A €350 pair of glasses costs roughly €5–20 to make. You don't pay for craftsmanship — you pay a monopoly. Whether the frame says Ray-Ban, Chanel, Prada, Versace, Oakley, Ferrari or Burberry, there's a ~90% chance one company made it: EssilorLuxottica, formed by merging Italy's frame-maker Luxottica with France's lens giant Essilor.

It owns the whole chain — 150+ brands (owned and licensed), the lens labs (Essilor, Varilux), the shops (Sunglass Hut, LensCrafters, Target Optical, GrandVision) and even vision insurance (EyeMed in the US). Luxury houses like Prada make nothing; they license their logo for a royalty and let Essilor design, manufacture, distribute and price. Margins run near 1,000%.

Competition is impossible by design: a new entrant must buy lenses from Essilor (paying its rival on day one) and get shelf space in stores Luxottica owns — which it can deny, undercut, or simply buy out. It controls demand too: owning EyeMed (and, in France, leaning on care networks like Santéclair) funnels reimbursed customers to its own brands and stores. When Oakley refused to sell in the early 2000s, Luxottica pulled it from Sunglass Hut's shelves, collapsed its revenue, and bought it cheap in 2007. Today it's extending the moat into tech — the Ray-Ban Meta smart glasses sold 7M+ pairs in 2025.

Where it stands

~$32B revenue (2025), ~200,000 employees, market cap around €75–90B. The stock compounded ~2,500% from 2000–2025 on a ~12% revenue CAGR — yet it has fallen roughly 40–50% over the past year (from ~€320 to ~€160–190), partly on fears that AI smart glasses invite Big-Tech competition. A fortress moat is not a floor under the share price.

▶ Original video ↗

Capture the lessons

Run the drills

Beyond the video — added insight

The regulatory paradox: how does a ~90%-share giant avoid being broken up? Because "global eyewear" is framed as a fragmented market (its share of the whole is ~15%), and antitrust hunts horizontal concentration in one product — vertical control across the chain slips through. Owning every link is harder to attack than owning one link completely.

GrandVision (2021): it bought Europe's largest optical retailer, adding thousands of stores after a heavily scrutinised deal — deepening the distribution stranglehold the video describes.

The founder: Luxottica was built by Leonardo Del Vecchio, who grew up in an orphanage — a rags-to-riches empire, now controlled by the family holding Delfin after his death in 2022.

The frenemy move: partnering with Meta on Ray-Ban Meta means allying with the very Big-Tech player that could one day disintermediate it — and Meta has taken a stake in EssilorLuxottica. Keep-your-enemies-closer, as moat insurance.

Why the stock corrected: a rich valuation unwinding plus the AI-smart-glasses narrative cutting both ways — the same product is both the moat's extension and its biggest disruption risk.

Your intersection: this is vertical integration and choke-point control in their purest form. In energy-infra finance, the equivalent moat isn't the "frame" (the deal) — it's owning the scarce link (interconnection rights, structuring relationships, off-take) and the demand funnel. Don't compete on the product; become the toll-collector on infrastructure everyone must cross.

Make it click — similar plays

Apple App Store — owns the channel, takes a toll, holds life-or-death over developers (the video's own analogy). Live Nation / Ticketmaster — venues + ticketing + promotion = the eyewear model for live events. De Beers — controlled diamond supply and manufactured demand ("diamonds are forever") to hold prices. BYD — vertical integration pushed even further in EVs (mines → batteries → cars).

The pattern to hunt: the hidden giant behind familiar brands — YKK (zippers), TSMC (chips), Luxottica (glasses). The risk: monopolies eventually invite regulation (Standard Oil was broken up), and even fortresses get repriced — as the −50% shows.

How to drillOwn the infrastructure and the demand funnel, and the channel becomes your weapon — you set the price and erase all comparison. For you: stop competing on the deal; own the choke point everyone must pass through. And never confuse a great business with a great entry price.
04
Anthropic vs OpenAI — Winning by Refusing to RaceSébastien Koubar · Video case · AI & strategy
▶ Video0/14▶
The one ideaDon't beat the leader at the leader's game — change the scoreboard. While everyone raced on speed and virality, Anthropic bet the opposite: that reliability and trust, sold to enterprises, would be the real weapon.
The story (in brief)

In 2020, Dario Amodei — then VP of research at OpenAI — saw the "scaling laws" up close: pour in more model size, data and compute and intelligence rises exponentially, with no clear ceiling. That both thrilled and frightened him. Late in 2020 he and a small group (including his sister Daniela) left to found Anthropic, raising ~$124M from backers who also took the risk seriously.

OpenAI had everything — the best product, top talent, a billion-dollar Microsoft cheque. Anthropic had a whiteboard. Its contrarian bet: while the whole industry screamed "ship faster, scale faster," Amodei concluded that once companies hand their code, data and decisions to AI, they won't want the flashiest model — they'll want the most trustworthy one. So Anthropic went enterprise, not consumer; built for document-handling, data security and above all coding; registered as a Public Benefit Corporation with a Long-Term Benefit Trust that can legally put mission over profit; and invented Constitutional AI — training the model against a written rulebook it critiques itself against, instead of relying on armies of human raters (RLHF).

Claude stayed invisible through 2023, then Claude 3 Opus (March 2024) was briefly considered the smartest model in the world, Claude 3.5 Sonnet (June 2024) became developers' favourite for coding, and Claude Code (2025) hit ~$1B annualized within months. Revenue went vertical.

Full disclosure: Claude — the assistant compiling this tracker — is Anthropic's model, trained with the Constitutional AI method described here. I've kept this factual and even-handed; OpenAI's consumer-first bet is equally legitimate and still leads by a wide margin on users and mindshare.

Where it stands

Anthropic reached roughly a $30B annualized run rate by ~April 2026, overtaking OpenAI (~$25B) — despite ~30M weekly Claude users versus ChatGPT's ~800M+. About 80% of revenue is enterprise, from 300,000+ business customers, with 1,000+ paying over $1M/year. It was valued ~$183B in 2025, with 2026 raises reported to push it far higher. Two caveats the video glosses: "run rate" is annualized from the current pace (not booked annual revenue), and neither company is profitable yet. (The video's "$47B" is higher than I can confirm; ~$30B run rate is the well-sourced figure.)

▶ Original video ↗

Capture the lessons

Run the drills

Beyond the video — added insight

This is textbook disruption theory (Christensen): Anthropic didn't out-OpenAI OpenAI — it competed on a different value dimension (enterprise trust and coding) where the incumbent was weak. Changing the scoreboard beats winning the incumbent's game.

The coding wedge is the real engine: Claude Code was a specific beachhead that developers adopted, then expanded from — exactly Zero to One's "dominate a small market first, then widen." Not a broad launch; a sharp wedge.

Governance as go-to-market: Wall Street dislikes mission-locked structures, but for safety-conscious enterprises and governments, the PBC + Trust is a trust signal — values doubling as a sales advantage.

RLHF vs Constitutional AI, honestly: human-rating is slow, costly, inherits raters' biases, and rewards sycophancy; a written constitution scales, is auditable, and can prioritise honesty over flattery. It's a genuine methodological fork, not just branding.

The risk the video skips: enterprise concentration (1,000 clients driving huge revenue), no profitability yet (Anthropic reportedly targeting breakeven ~2028, OpenAI ~2030), and total dependence on Nvidia compute and — your thesis again — power. Every dollar of this AI revenue rests on data-centre capacity the grid can barely supply.

Your intersection: "trust, reliability, compliance" for institutional and government capital is precisely an enterprise-grade, high-value, sticky, mission-aligned wedge — your Anthropic-style move against commodity brokers racing on fee.

Make it click — similar plays

AWS — Amazon monetised the unglamorous layer while others chased the shiny app (the video's own parallel). Salesforce & enterprise SaaS — land-and-expand, high switching costs, high contract value: the playbook Anthropic runs. Slack vs Teams, Dropbox — the consumer-viral-vs-enterprise-monetised tension in miniature.

The pattern: when a giant owns the mass market, the durable challenger often wins the professional market underneath it. The caution: plenty of "safer / higher-quality" challengers still lost to the faster, cheaper incumbent — and the whole AI-revenue boom carries real bubble risk given the cash burn.

Your version: don't fight the big banks for mass mandates; own the trusted, specialised, high-value corner of energy-infra finance they can't be bothered to serve well.

How to drillChange the scoreboard instead of racing on the incumbent's axis. Pick the profitable, sticky, high-trust niche; make your constraint your method; lock in with switching costs. For you: be the reliable specialist institutional capital trusts — not the cheapest broker in the crowd.
05
Japan — The Superpower That Stalled for 30 YearsSébastien Koubar · Video case · Macro, bubbles & risk
▶ Video0/14▶
The one ideaThe crash didn't kill Japan — the response did. Cheap money built twin bubbles, and then a refusal to let failures fail turned one crash into thirty years of zombie stagnation.
The story (in brief)

In the 1980s Japan was unstoppable: average income leapt from ~$500 (1960s) to ~$25,000 (1980), six of the world's ten biggest companies were Japanese, it took 23% of the US car market and overtook the US in semiconductors, and its land was famously valued at ~4× all of America's. It was closing on the US in GDP. The roots were Cold-War: the US had rebuilt Japan as a capitalist bulwark against communism — injecting capital, transferring steel and electronics know-how, and opening its market.

In 1985 the Plaza Accord pushed the yen from ~260 to ~130 per dollar, halving Japan's export edge overnight. Japan responded by offshoring production (hollowing out its industrial jobs) and slashing rates from 5% to 2.5%. But the cheap money didn't go into R&D — it flooded stocks and real estate. The Nikkei ran from ~6,000 to ~39,000 (1989); land rose 200–300%. Companies became traders — at one point ~30% of Toyota's profit came from financial trading, not cars — and borrowed against inflated shares to buy yet more land (Sony bought Columbia Pictures for ~$4.8B with near-free money).

Then the central bank panicked and hiked from 2.5% to 6%. Asset values fell 50–70%; debt-laden firms were insolvent; the Nikkei took 34 years to recover. The fatal error came next: instead of letting failures fail (as the US does), Japan kept insolvent firms alive with drip-feed loans — creating "zombie companies" (~30% of firms by the early 2000s) that didn't hire, invest or innovate. A decade-long freeze on graduate hiring created a "lost generation," now ~50, under-skilled and often unmarried — feeding a demographic collapse (births ~700k vs ~2M in the 1970s) and, by 2025, thousands of closures, some purely from labour shortage.

Where it stands

The Nikkei finally reclaimed its 1989 high in February 2024 — 34 years later. In dollar terms Japan's GDP is lower than in 1995, average wages have barely moved since then, and depopulation now closes schools and shutters firms for lack of workers. Markets can recover; a lost generation cannot.

▶ Original video ↗

Capture the lessons

Run the drills

Beyond the video — added insight

A fairer read than "the American scam": the Plaza Accord was a coordinated G5 agreement (US, Japan, West Germany, France, UK), and the real damage was largely self-inflicted — Japan's central bank kept rates too low for too long, then hiked too hard. The bubble was Japan's own policy error as much as anyone's arm-twisting.

The true mechanism — a "balance-sheet recession": after the crash, companies spent a generation paying down debt instead of investing, no matter how low rates fell (economist Richard Koo's famous diagnosis). That, plus zombie lending, is why cheap money never restarted growth.

The deflation trap: once prices and wages fall and people expect them to keep falling, they defer spending — a self-reinforcing stagnation that took Japan 30 years and enormous money-printing to fight.

A doom loop, not just a downturn: the lost generation → collapsed family formation → a shrinking workforce → the 2025 labour-shortage bankruptcies. Policy errors hardened into demography, which is far harder to reverse than a market crash.

The live parallel: read today's AI-capex boom through this lens — is the borrowing funding productive capacity, or a bubble detached from profit (see Case 04's "no profit yet")? And is the decade of near-zero rates still hiding zombies now that rates have risen?

Your intersection: project finance is the most rate-, currency- and duration-exposed craft there is — 20–30-year assets, cross-border (EUR/TND) cash flows, single-counterparty off-takes. This is the case most directly about your job. The discipline "never depend on one thing, and let zombies die" is your risk framework, not just history.

Make it click — similar plays

2008 US crisis — the opposite path: forced failures (Lehman) + bank recapitalisation + fast rate cuts → recovery in ~5–6 years, not 34. The contrast is the lesson. Dot-com 2000 — the same "new paradigm, prices only rise" psychology. China's property bubble (Evergrande) — cheap credit → real-estate mania → zombie developers → the same forbearance dilemma, live.

The pattern to distrust: the "unstoppable rising power" — 1980s books literally predicted Japan would rule the world. Treat every inevitable-winner consensus with suspicion. And globally: a decade of near-zero rates kept countless zombie firms alive; higher rates since 2022 are the reckoning.

Your version: never build a plan whose survival hinges on one currency, one rate regime or one partner — and never be the financier who keeps a zombie project on life support.

How to drillDiversify ruthlessly, respect that recoveries can take decades, and let failures fail so capital flows to the living. For you: stress-test every deal against a rate and currency shock, and never let one country, partner or zombie project hold your whole future.
06
Gillette — Telling Your Customers They're the ProblemSébastien Koubar · Video case · Brand, positioning & the customer
▶ Video0/14▶
The one ideaYou can challenge society, but the moment your message reads as "you, my customer, are the problem," your customers stop being customers. Know who actually pays you — and never build a strategy to please people who applaud but don't buy.
The story (in brief)

For a century Gillette sold not razors but a model of manhood. Founded in 1901 by King Camp Gillette, it invented "razor and blades" — cheap handle, expensive locked-in refills (the ancestor of subscription) — and got the US Army to hand a Gillette to every WWI soldier, turning shaving into a national daily ritual. Its 1989 slogan, "The Best a Man Can Get," crowned decades of associating shaving with success and confidence. By the early 2000s it held ~70% of the global market at 80%+ gross margins; P&G bought it in 2005 for ~$57B.

By 2018 the fortress was bleeding: share fell from ~70% to ~54% in three years. Beards were back, shaving frequency dropped, and two direct-to-consumer disruptors — Dollar Shave Club (viral 2012) and Harry's (2013) — offered cheap, transparent, subscription blades. Gillette's 2017 price cut just shredded its own margins. So in January 2019 it swung for cultural relevance: a "We Believe: The Best Men Can Be" ad on toxic masculinity, made by a feminist-campaign director, aimed at its all-male base — and implying those customers were part of the problem.

The backlash was instant: hundreds of thousands of dislikes within days, #BoycottGillette, men filming themselves binning razors. Gillette disabled comments, then pulled the video. A post-campaign study found 77% called the message "positive" but only 34% said it made them want to buy Gillette — and 51% of the audience reached was female (a men's-razor message to people who don't buy men's razors). Grooming sales fell ~$352M in a year; by 2020 Gillette had quietly reverted to reassuring, product-focused ads.

Where it stands

P&G took an ~$8B writedown on Gillette in July 2019 and a further ~$1.3B in December 2023 — but, importantly, those impairments were driven mainly by currency and a structurally shrinking shaving market, not chiefly the ad (see below). P&G, diversified across dozens of brands, recovered strongly and remains a dividend staple. Gillette still leads its category — at a lower share, in a smaller market.

▶ Original video ↗

Capture the lessons

Run the drills

Beyond the video — added insight

The $8B was mostly FX and market decline, not the ad: P&G attributed the impairment chiefly to currency headwinds and a structurally shrinking blades market (beards, less-frequent shaving, DTC price competition). The ad did real reputational and sales damage, but "$9.3B evaporated because of the commercial" confuses correlation with cause — a lesson in reading a number's true drivers.

The root cause was the innovator's dilemma: Gillette kept moving up-market — more blades, higher prices, 80% margins — over-serving customers who just wanted a cheap, decent shave. That opened the low end for DSC and Harry's to attack from below. The activism ad was a symptom of a brand out of touch with its market, not the disease.

The disruptor cashed out: Unilever bought Dollar Shave Club for ~$1B in 2016 — the model won even where the specific company later plateaued.

When brand-activism actually works: only when it's (a) authentic to the brand's history, (b) attached to an identity/public product, and (c) aligned with the base rather than splitting it. Nike/Kaepernick fit all three; Gillette fit none.

Your intersection: in trust-based institutional finance your "brand" is congruence and reliability. Don't chase trendy positioning that fits neither your service nor your client — and build for your real buyers (LPs, developers, lenders), not for LinkedIn applause. The vanity-metric trap maps straight onto your content plan: measure "senior people in my domain engaged," not likes.

Make it click — similar plays

Nike / Kaepernick (2018) — activism done right: base-aligned, identity product. The control case. Bud Light (2023) — the same mechanism, bigger: alienating the core customer with a values signal that didn't fit the base, and a far worse sales collapse. Patagonia — activism that works because it's congruent with a 40-year environmental identity.

The classics: New Coke (1985) — ignore who actually buys and loves your product at your peril. Porsche / Jaguar — brands that nearly lost everything by abandoning their fundamentals.

Your version: your brand is trust with a specific professional buyer — never trade it for cultural trendiness that fits neither your product nor your client.

How to drillServe the buyer, not the applause; make sure any bold message fits what you sell and never blames the people who pay you; and measure the metric that converts, not the one that trends. For you: guard congruence and reliability above all — that's your brand.

BYD — From Phone Batteries to Tesla's NightmareSébastien Koubar · Video case · Vertical integration & cost
▶ Video0/14▶
The one ideaBuild a boring cash machine first, turn every constraint into a cost advantage, and integrate the whole chain until price itself becomes a weapon. Glory is downstream of cash flow and cost control.
The story (in brief)

BYD was a joke — ugly cars, no pedigree. Its founder, Wang Chuanfu, was a chemist and ex-government worker with no auto or tech background who started in 1995 with a ~$300k loan from his cousin. In 2021 Tesla sold ~1M cars ($53B) to BYD's ~590k ($33B). By 2024 BYD's revenue (~$108B) had passed Tesla's (~$97B), and in 2025 it overtook Tesla as the world's largest pure-EV maker.

The playbook was contrarian from day one. As Japanese giants moved from nickel to lithium phone batteries, Wang built nickel capacity — to serve the clients (IBM and others) they were abandoning. With no money to automate like the Japanese, he did the opposite: cheap manual labour split into hundreds of simple micro-tasks, and he reverse-engineered not just the batteries but the machines that made them. His masterstroke of frugal innovation: instead of a costly full clean room, a small sealed glove-box around each battery ("shoes, not carpet") — cutting production cost 70–80%, five times cheaper than Japan, and infinitely scalable. By 2000, Motorola and Nokia signed on and BYD became the world's #1 nickel-battery maker.

Knowing lithium would win, Wang bought a bankrupt state carmaker in 2003 (the stock fell 20%); the BYD F3 (2005) was a $10k Corolla clone. In 2008 Charlie Munger sent Buffett in — Wang drank battery electrolyte to prove it was safe — and Berkshire took 10% for $230M (now up ~30×). BYD stayed a China-only story until Covid, when it pivoted its engineers to become the world's biggest mask maker in two weeks and turned a $643M profit while every rival bled. Then came total vertical integration (~90% in-house, own lithium mines and chips), the safer-and-cheaper LFP Blade Battery (so good Tesla became a customer), poached European designers, and a 2024 "forced deflation" price war — a €9,000 Seagull — to purge weaker rivals.

Where it stands

In 2025 BYD overtook Tesla as the world's largest pure-EV maker — ~2.26M battery-electric cars vs Tesla's ~1.64M — and ~4.55M total New Energy Vehicles including hybrids, while Tesla logged a second straight annual decline. BYD now localises production in Hungary, Turkey and Brazil to sidestep EU tariffs, and runs its own fleet of car-carrier ships to cut logistics costs ~30%.

▶ Original video ↗

Capture the lessons

Run the drills

Beyond the video — added insight

Subsidy honesty: the video calls critics "jealous," but Chinese state support — subsidies, cheap credit, a vast protected home market, industrial policy — was a real and material tailwind. The mature read is that BYD is both heavily state-backed and operationally excellent; don't let either fact cancel the other.

The recurring killer — low-end disruption: BYD attacked from the cheap, good-enough bottom exactly as Dollar Shave Club did to Gillette (Case 06) and Samsung did to Toshiba (Case 05). Across your case files, disruption almost always comes from below, not above.

The Blade Battery was a Blue Ocean call: choosing cheaper, safer, lower-density LFP over "best-spec" NMC redefined the axis of competition to safety + cost, not maximum range — the same "differentiate on the ignored dimension" move as Anthropic (Case 04).

The risk the video underplays: BYD's greatest strength (Chinese scale + state backing) is also its biggest vulnerability — EU/US tariffs, data-security scrutiny, US-China tensions, and a domestic price war so brutal that Chinese regulators are now pressing BYD to ease it.

Your intersection — directly: BYD is an energy + manufacturing + capital vertical-integration machine, and batteries, minerals, grid and power are your energy-transition domain. China's grip on the battery and mineral supply chain is a live project-finance and energy-security theme. "Own or finance the bottleneck (batteries, minerals, chips, power)" is your thesis restated in steel.

Make it click — similar plays

EssilorLuxottica (Case 03) — vertical integration in eyewear; BYD is the same idea in cars and energy, pushed further (from mines to its own cargo ships). Amazon — AWS, warehouses, its own delivery fleet and planes: integration as a cost-and-control moat (BYD buying ships mirrors Amazon buying planes). Ford's River Rouge / Standard Oil — the historical extremes of owning everything.

The caution: vertical integration is capital-heavy and can backfire when it just adds complexity rather than lowering cost or securing a genuine bottleneck. Tesla is vertically integrated too — BYD just did it cheaper.

Your version: the durable positions in energy-transition finance sit around the vertically integrated bottlenecks — batteries, minerals, grid, power — where China already leads. Financing the Western, African and MENA response to that is a real, open opportunity.

How to drillMaster a cash-generating core before the glamour play, make your constraints into cost advantages, integrate the chain, and only then wield price as a weapon. For you: own or finance the energy bottleneck — batteries, minerals, grid — before the West realises how far behind it is.

The Seed Oligopoly — The Business That Privatised LifeSébastien Koubar · Video case · Moats, IP & recurring revenue
▶ Video0/14▶
The one ideaTake something that reproduces for free forever, wrap it in patents, biology and contracts so it must be re-bought every year — then consolidate the market to four players and price to the customer's upside. Recurring revenue + IP moat + pricing power is the anatomy of a fortress.
The story (in brief)

For 10,000 years farmers saved their best seeds and replanted them — free, infinite, autonomous. Then in 1930 the US Plant Patent Act (backed by Thomas Edison) let people patent living plants for the first time, turning a freely-copyable good into intellectual property. The 1960s Green Revolution — Norman Borlaug's high-yield wheat and rice — tripled output and is credited with saving ~1 billion from famine, but it standardised agriculture (the world lost ~75% of its crop diversity) and made crops dependent on chemical fertiliser and pesticide.

Enter the chemical giants (Bayer, BASF, Monsanto), which bought up hundreds of family seed firms and engineered seeds to work only with their fertiliser and pesticide — total vertical dependence. Then came the biotech lock: F1 hybrids, whose perfect first generation produces unstable, near-useless offspring, so farmers must repurchase every year. And the legal lock: Technology Use Agreements that forbid seed-saving and let companies send inspectors to DNA-test crops. Monsanto sued hundreds of farmers. Nature's free, infinite reproduction became a subscription — "Seed as a Service."

Twenty years of mergers left the "Big Four": Bayer (bought Monsanto for ~$63B), Corteva (Dow + DuPont), Syngenta (Novartis + AstraZeneca ag, now owned by state-owned ChemChina) and BASF. Together they control 60%+ of the world's seeds and 70%+ of pesticides.

Where it stands

Eat anything made of corn or soy, or wear cotton, and there's a ~2-in-3 chance it traces to one of four companies. Their moat rests on three pillars: recurring revenue (trapped repurchasing), sky-high barriers (billions in R&D plus a patent-lawyer army), and pricing power — they even index seed prices to grain prices, so when farmers earn more, the seed firm takes its cut. As a backstop against genetic catastrophe, Norway's Svalbard Global Seed Vault (2008) stores millions of seed samples in the permafrost — natural varieties only.

▶ Original video ↗

Capture the lessons

Run the drills

Beyond the video — added insight

The genuine other side: the video frames this as "the heist that privatised life," but the Green Revolution is one of history's great humanitarian achievements, hybrids give farmers real yield security, and decades of R&D by hundreds of scientists genuinely need IP incentives to happen. "Innovation that fed an exploding planet" is as true as "corporations captured the food supply." Hold both.

The real systemic cost: monoculture. Losing ~75% of crop diversity means a single new pathogen hitting a globally uniform crop is a food-security tail risk — exactly the genetic-uniformity trap behind the Irish Potato Famine. Svalbard is the civilisation-level backup.

The M&A cautionary tale: Bayer paid ~$63B for Monsanto, then absorbed tens of billions in Roundup/glyphosate cancer litigation that gutted its market value — the textbook case of buying a liability you didn't fully price. Due diligence is about the downside, not the synergy deck.

The geopolitics: state-owned ChemChina owning Syngenta means China controls a slice of the world's seeds and agrochemicals — the same supply-chain-security theme as BYD and batteries (Case 07), one field over.

Your intersection: the seed model — an essential input, sold on recurring contracts, with indexed pricing and high barriers — is exactly how good energy-infra deals are structured (PPAs, off-take, availability payments, escalators). Agriculture, water and energy are the three great resource-security plays; this is the moat blueprint for the one you already work in.

Make it click — similar plays

Gillette razor-and-blades (Case 06) — the original "cheap base, locked-in refills," here applied to the food supply. Adobe / Microsoft — turning a one-time software sale into an annual subscription: "Seed as a Service" made literal. EssilorLuxottica (Case 03) — a hidden oligopoly on an everyday essential. Printer ink, Nespresso pods, insulin — engineered consumable lock-in.

The risk: moats built on public resentment invite regulation — the peasant-seed and open-source-seed movements, and antitrust scrutiny, are the counter-pressure (just as Standard Oil and EssilorLuxottica drew it).

Your version: build or finance the recurring, contracted, indexed position around an essential input — energy, grid, water. That's seed-company economics applied to your domain.

How to drillConvert one-time sales into recurring, contracted revenue; defend it with IP and layered lock-in; price to your customer's value. For you: structure your work as reusable, recurring, indexed positions around essential inputs — not one-off deals you have to win again from zero every time.

Dubai — The City That Wins by Letting Everything Pass ThroughSébastien Koubar · Video case · Hubs, leverage & reinvention
▶ Video0/14▶
The one ideaWith no oil, water or fertile land, Dubai got rich on a single insight: never win by producing — win by removing all friction so the world routes its trade, capital and people through you. Be the conduit and take a cut of everything that passes.
The story (in brief)

Dubai began in 1833 when a branch of the Bani Yas broke from Abu Dhabi and settled a poor fishing creek. Under British maritime dominance, its rulers chose submission over resistance and bought stability. The turning point came in 1894, when Maktoum bin Hasher abolished all customs duties — and merchants, especially Persians, flooded in. Pearls made the town rich until ~1930, when Japan's Mikimoto invented the cultured pearl and the market collapsed overnight, triggering a ruined-merchant reform movement (the Majlis) that the ruling family crushed by 1939. Lesson burned into the city's DNA: power is not shared.

Then its neighbours struck oil — and Dubai found almost none. That "curse" was its salvation: unable to live off a petro-rent, the Maktoums had to build a real economy. Sheikh Rashid (from 1958) borrowed £400,000 from Kuwait to dredge the silting Creek — a bet-the-emirate gamble that worked — turned India's 1962 gold-import ban into a booming re-export (smuggling) trade, found modest offshore oil in 1966, and treated it not as a foundation but as a cash cow to build fast. After Britain withdrew, Rashid and Abu Dhabi's Sheikh Zayed formed the UAE in 1971.

Rashid built infrastructure ahead of need — Port Rashid, the World Trade Center, and the vast Jebel Ali port and free zone (1985: 100% foreign ownership, zero tax, zero duties). His son MBR then went for myth: borrow massively, build a global icon, inflate property on the buzz, borrow again — the Burj Al Arab, the Palm (sold before a grain of sand was laid), the DIFC with its own common-law courts. In 2008 the model imploded: Dubai World couldn't repay ~$26B, and Abu Dhabi's $10B rescue came with a message — the Burj Dubai reopened as the Burj Khalifa.

Where it stands

Oil is now ~1% of Dubai's GDP; the money comes from trade and logistics (ports and airport), tourism, financial services, real estate and wealth services. Post-2008 it repositioned from "mythical city" to "stable haven in an unstable world" — zero tax, geopolitical neutrality and few questions on the origin of funds, making it the sanctuary of choice for capital fleeing sanctions, instability or taxes. Dubai is, in effect, a company that mirrors the world's disorder in real time.

▶ Original video ↗

Capture the lessons

Run the drills

Beyond the video — added insight

On the "massacres": the 1833 founding is more accurately a secession — a Bani Yas branch broke away from Abu Dhabi after a succession dispute; the "Red Wedding" framing is dramatisation. The 1938–39 crushing of the Dubai Reform Movement (the Majlis) is the better-documented act of repression. One embellished, one grounded.

The dark side the video soft-pedals: the icons were built largely by migrant labour under the kafala sponsorship system with few rights; there is near-total absence of political freedom; and Dubai's "no questions asked" money has made it a hub for illicit finance — it was on the FATF money-laundering "grey list" (2022–2024). The haven that profits from instability also shelters sanctioned and illicit wealth. Real, and worth naming.

The genuine achievement: turning a pearling village with no oil, water or arable land into a top global hub in ~50 years is a real feat of vision and institution-building (free zones, ports, aviation). Both the achievement and its costs are true.

The missing pillar — Emirates Airline: Dubai built a global carrier to make itself the world's connecting point (an 8-hour flight reaches two-thirds of humanity). Geography turned into a conduit, on purpose.

Your intersection — directly: the Gulf is the epicentre of your work — energy, infrastructure, project finance, sovereign capital, and now hundreds of billions flowing into AI-data-centre and power megaprojects. The "frictionless hub / build-ahead-of-demand / sovereign-backed project finance" model is your actual playing field, and as a French-Tunisian financier you are a natural bridge between Europe, MENA and Africa. Dubai is your choke-point thesis, incarnated as a city.

Make it click — similar plays

Singapore — the other great conduit city-state: no resources, got rich by removing friction (free port, rule of law, low tax) and building ahead of demand. MBR explicitly wanted to rival it. Hong Kong — the gateway/entrepôt model. Switzerland — the neutral wealth haven that profited from others' instability, and faced the same reputational reckoning as its secrecy eroded.

The pattern and the risk: conduit and haven models are immensely lucrative but face regulatory reckonings, and leverage-fuelled property booms crash (see Japan, Case 05, and 2008). Concentration in one city or one model is fragile.

Your version: position as the trusted bridge/conduit for energy-infrastructure capital flowing into MENA — the frictionless, reliable channel institutional money routes through.

How to drillRemove friction until the world routes through you, build the capacity before the demand arrives, and use leverage boldly but know who backstops you. For you: the Gulf energy-infra corridor is where your intersection is richest — be the trusted conduit into it, not a one-off dealmaker at its edge.

Spotify — The Innovator Who Doesn't Own the ResourceSébastien Koubar · Video case · Value chains & who captures value
▶ Video0/14▶
The one ideaWhoever controls the essential resource dictates the terms — and the innovator pays the bill. Spotify built the product that saved the music industry and still hands ~70% of every euro to the people who own the catalogue.
The story (in brief)

Around 2000, piracy (Napster, Kazaa, Pirate Bay) halved music revenue in a decade. Daniel Ek — a young Swedish millionaire who still pirated music — realised piracy was an experience problem, not a price problem: beat "free" by being better, not just legal. With Martin Lorentzon he built instant streaming using the peer-to-peer architecture of Pirate Bay itself (near-zero infrastructure cost, kept until 2014) — pirate tech, legalised. But the app was empty.

To fill it he needed the Big Three — Universal, Sony, Warner (~80% of all music). After two years of relentless, humiliating pitching and rejection, he won them over by selling fear (the industry was dying; a free-but-legal option could kill piracy). The labels said yes — with a devil's pact: free equity stakes (they'd later sell ~$1B of Spotify shares around the 2018 listing) and a huge cut of every stream (~70% today). Holding no leverage — because whoever owns the content owns the power — Ek said yes instantly, condemning Spotify to 15 years of losses.

It worked: Sweden became the first country to reverse piracy, and Spotify swept the world. But the economics stayed broken — of ~11 million artists, only a small fraction earned even $1,000 in a year, as label advances, recoupment and producer cuts siphon the artist's slice. Then came loss-leader rivals (Apple, Amazon, Google, for whom music just sells iPhones, Prime and data) and Apple's 30% App Store toll on top of the 70% to labels. Spotify's escape was to change what it sells — podcasts and audiobooks it controls — and a clever audiobook "bundle" reclassification that trimmed its music-royalty rate. In 2024 it turned its first-ever annual profit.

Where it stands

700M+ monthly users, ~€16B revenue, and — after 16 years — profitable for the first time in 2024, once non-music passed ~20% of listening and Ek reframed Spotify as "an audio company, not a music app." The stock, flat-to-down for years post-listing, roughly 10×'d off its lows once the market understood the pivot. Whether the hybrid model is durable is still unproven — the royalty share only fell from ~74% to ~70%.

▶ Original video ↗

Capture the lessons

Run the drills

Beyond the video — added insight & update

The prediction came true: the video (mid-2025) said the labels were "in talks" to settle with AI-music startups Suno and Udio. They did — Universal settled with Udio (Oct 2025, partnering on a new platform), and Warner settled with Suno (Nov 2025) in a licensing deal reportedly worth ~$2.45B, even selling its Songkick platform to Suno. Same Spotify playbook, run again: sue the innovator, then take equity, royalties and a licensing cut. Sony is still litigating, independent artists were left out (a two-tier outcome), and the "fair use for AI training" question was sidestepped, not decided.

The template for the AI age: every content industry will run this move against AI — control the training data (the base resource), litigate, then license and take a cut. It's the seed / Luxottica / Spotify logic applied to AI, and it ties directly to Case 04: whoever owns the corpus has leverage over the labs.

Fair to Spotify: it's largely the legacy label contract structure (advances, recoupment, producer cuts) that starves artists, not Spotify's payout rate — Spotify pays out ~70%. And the audiobook-bundle reclassification is a genuinely clever use of a contract's own definitions, like BYD's frugal engineering applied to law.

The risk: the pivot may be too little, too late — royalties only fell ~74%→70%, infinite-money rivals persist, and one profitable year is not a durable business.

Your intersection — the cautionary mirror: Spotify is what every other case warns against — the brilliant innovator who does not own the choke point, and so builds enormous value while capturing almost none of it. In project finance the "labels" are whoever controls the scarce input — the capital, the interconnection rights, the asset, the off-take. Be that, negotiate from strength, or you're Spotify: beloved, huge, and barely solvent.

Make it click — similar plays

The seed oligopoly (Case 08) & EssilorLuxottica (Case 03) — the same "control the base resource, collect the rent" logic; Spotify is the victim's-eye view of it. Netflix vs the studios — Netflix escaped Spotify's fate by producing its own content (owning the resource) instead of only licensing it — the exact route Spotify is now copying with podcasts and audiobooks. Epic vs Apple — the innovator versus the 30% gatekeeper.

The next arena: AI training data — the Suno/Udio settlements are the opening move of the same game, industry-wide.

Your version: don't be the Spotify of energy-infra finance — doing all the structuring work while whoever owns the scarce input takes the lion's share. Own or lock up the scarce input, or sign only from strength.

How to drillOwn the scarce resource or negotiate only from strength — and if the core game is rigged against you, change what you sell toward what you control. For you: this is the inverse of every other case — proof that building brilliant value means nothing if you don't own the choke point.

Amazon / AWS — The Hidden Empire Running the InternetSébastien Koubar · Video case · Infrastructure, lock-in & cross-subsidy
▶ Video0/14▶
The one ideaAmazon's real business isn't retail — it's the invisible infrastructure ~30% of the internet runs on. An internal cost-cutting fix became the world's most profitable toll booth, and the money printer that funds everything else.
The story (in brief)

On 20 October 2025, three words broke the internet: US-EAST-1. A DNS failure at AWS's DynamoDB API cascaded into EC2 and Lambda, taking down ~78 services for seven-plus hours — Snapchat, Ring, Fortnite, Alexa, banks, crypto exchanges, even Nintendo Switch Online. The world glimpsed how much runs on one company's infrastructure: Netflix, Spotify, Uber, Airbnb, Zoom, the CIA, NASA — all on Amazon Web Services.

AWS was an accident. In the early 2000s Amazon.com's infrastructure was a decentralised mess; Bezos imposed an efficiency rule — teams stop buying their own servers and instead expose and rent computing to each other via APIs. Without meaning to, they built the world's most standardised data centre. The insight followed: if we can rent internally, why not rent to the world? AWS launched in 2006 with a radical model — sell computing as a metered utility (pay-as-you-go), not fixed servers — destroying the traditional data-centre business and creating the first commercial cloud.

Bezos then priced deliberately low to keep rivals out; by the time Google Cloud (2008) and Azure (2010) arrived, AWS had a two-year head start and took most of the market. It layered on lock-in — 200+ proprietary services, a certified-partner ecosystem — so leaving costs years and millions (Netflix took 7 years to migrate on, and now spends ~$1M/day). The result is a money printer: in 2024, retail did ~$530B at ~5.5% margin while AWS did ~$108B at ~37% margin — roughly 60% of all Amazon's profit — funding everything from Alexa to international expansion.

Where it stands

AWS is the cloud leader (~30% share) and the profit engine of a ~$640B company. Its dominance is now a regulatory subject: the EU's DORA (Digital Operational Resilience Act, in force from January 2025) forces financial firms to manage exactly the cloud-concentration risk the us-east-1 outages exposed. An idea born to cut Amazon's own costs is now infrastructure that governments treat as systemically critical.

▶ Original video ↗

The people & the dates (references)

Company: Amazon Web Services (AWS) (launched 2006; architect Andy Jassy, later Amazon CEO; founder Jeff Bezos). The toll on the internet — own the indispensable infrastructure layer.

Capture the lessons

Run the drills

Beyond the video — added insight & corrections

Why us-east-1 specifically: it's AWS's oldest, largest, default region (Northern Virginia's "Data Center Alley"), so a disproportionate share of services and global control-plane functions route through it — making it a single point of failure even for apps hosted elsewhere. That's the crux of the systemic risk.

Correction — Blue Origin: it's Bezos's personal space company, funded largely by selling his own Amazon shares (~$1B/year), not an AWS-funded project. The video conflates them.

Nuance — the "AWS spies on customers" claim: AWS contractually and technically isolates customer data, and there's little evidence it mines hosted data to compete. The real, documented data-advantage scandal is Amazon's retail marketplace using third-party seller data to launch rival products (an EU antitrust case). The genuine AWS conflict is structural, not data theft: it profits from hosting rivals it also competes with.

The management gem — the 2002 API mandate: Bezos ordered every team to expose its functionality via APIs, no exceptions — forcing a modularity that accidentally created a $100B+ sellable platform. Architecture decisions create optionality.

Your intersection — the punchline: AWS is compute, and compute is now bottlenecked by power. Data centres are the fastest-growing electricity load on Earth, and Amazon is pouring tens of billions into energy (including nuclear and SMR deals) to feed them. The hidden empire now runs on an energy-and-grid bottleneck that people like you finance. The cloud's next constraint is your speciality.

Make it click — similar plays

Nvidia (Case 01) — the chips beneath the cloud; AWS is the service layer above them (and buys Nvidia's chips). Two floors of the same "own the AI/internet infrastructure" stack. Stripe, Shopify, Slack — internal tools turned into platforms, the same origin as AWS. Electric utilities — the original metered-essential model AWS copied.

The pattern, now proven five times: Nvidia, Luxottica, the seed giants, BYD and AWS all win the same way — own the boring, essential layer everyone must pass through. It is the single most repeated lesson in this entire library. The risk: concentration invites antitrust and resilience regulation (DORA), and single-point-of-failure fragility is now a board-level concern.

Your version: AWS's constraint is power — be the one who finances the energy layer beneath the cloud.

How to drillTurn your own internal fix into a metered utility, price to own the market, and lock clients in three ways — then let the profit engine fund your next bets. For you: own or finance the enabling layer, and notice that the cloud's next bottleneck (power) is exactly your field.
