BIC — Own the Machine, Not the ProductVideo case · Vertical know-how, commodity-vs-desire & double-voting control
▶ Video0/14▶
The one ideaBIC's treasure was never the pen, the lighter or the razor — it was the machine and the know-how that stamps out perfection millions of times, kept entirely in-house for 75 years. Own the capability that makes the thing, protect it, and never mistake it for the thing itself.
The story (in brief)

The BIC Cristal is the best-selling pen in history — and sits in New York's MoMA. But BIC is also lighters and razors: one French company, ~€2B revenue, 27 million products sold a day in 160 countries. Marcel Bich invented none of the three — he bought the ballpoint patent — but in 1950 he built the machine. The real feat is that machine: a 1mm tungsten-carbide ball polished to near-diamond hardness that must roll >2km without leaking or drying (a watchmaking problem, solved with watchmaking precision, over a 9-day production cycle). Every detail is engineered — the hexagon stops it rolling off the table, the transparent body shows the ink, the tiny body hole balances air pressure, and the famous cap hole exists so a swallowed cap doesn't suffocate a child (a BIC first, now a world safety norm). Umberto Eco called it "achieved socialism": the exact same pen for the boss and the worker.

BIC owns 20+ factories and makes >90% of what it sells in its own walls — pens in France, lighters at Redon, razors in France. That's the moat: rivals outsourced production abroad to cut cost, including machine-setting (the heart of the craft) — and the foreign factory that learns to set your machines learns your trade, then does it cheaper without you. BIC kept the mold, the machine and the settings in-house, transmitted worker to worker. The second pillar is trust: you grab the BIC over the cheaper generic without thinking, certain it won't disappoint (50+ quality controls per lighter; up to 3,000 lights). It wins not by selling dear but by selling colossally — the machine must never stop.

The one time the machine jammed is the key lesson. In 1988, at its peak, BIC launched a perfume — same recipe (cheap, sold at tobacconists between the cigarettes and gas lighters). It flopped and was pulled by 1991, at a loss of hundreds of millions of francs. Why, when the method won everywhere else? Because a perfume isn't a commodity — its value is the dream it carries, and a machine, however perfect, can't manufacture desire. It makes utility, flawlessly.

Where it stands

All three markets are shrinking (BIC says so in its own filings): writing (screens replace paper), tobacco (French cigarette deliveries −24% from 2021-2024, so fewer lighters), and single-use plastic (banned product by product). To escape, BIC bought "desire" businesses — temporary tattoos (Inkbox, ~$65M), Tattly, premium hairbrushes (Tangle Teezer, ~€200M) — but in late 2025 shut its whole tattoo branch: 37 years after the perfume, the identical lesson. The hairbrush survives — because it's a tool, the machine's natural terrain. So BIC did its most lucid thing: it started making razor blades for its competitors — selling the machine itself. Per the video (2025 events around my cutoff): the family named a non-family, Dutch CEO (Rob Versloot) in 2025, and JAB's Olivier Goudet (ex-AB InBev, one of the world's most feared consumer-goods acquirers) built to ~10% of the capital.

▶ Original video ↗

Capture the lessons

Run the drills

Beyond the video — added insight

The governance gem — double-voting rights: France's droit de vote double (from the 1933 law, and since the 2014 Loi Florange the default for registered shares held >2 years unless the bylaws opt out) is a powerful, France-specific control tool. It's why founding families across the CAC 40 keep control with minority capital — and why, as a French value investor, you must read the voting structure, not just the cap table: "takeover optionality" may be legally impossible, and minority holders have less power than their capital suggests. It's the same end as Samsung's cross-shareholding (Case 16) and Leclerc's association (Case 22) — three different legal machines for control without full ownership.

The profound, twice-proven lesson — commodity vs desire: the same capability that makes BIC unbeatable at utility makes it incapable at desire (perfume 1988, tattoos 2025). It's the exact inverse of Gucci (Case 19: a desire brand that can't do commodity) and the same as Dell (Case 17: "value that doesn't fit in Excel"). Your greatest strength defines the game you can win and the one you can't — know both, and don't spend 37 years repeating the same category error.

The lucid endgame — sell the machine: making blades for competitors is the AWS move (Case 11) — when your product markets decline, monetise the actual asset (the capability) directly. The recognition that the treasure was never the product. And keeping the core in-house is the positive proof of the lesson Toys "R" Us (Case 12) failed: don't hand a partner the know-how that lets them replace you.

The Gillette cross-link (Case 06): BIC beat Gillette in lighters — for Gillette a side-business, for BIC vital ("a hobby vs survival") — then challenged it in razors on its home turf. A focused challenger for whom the fight is existential beats a giant for whom it's a side-project.

Your intersection: a French company; the double-voting-rights rule is a direct home-market value-investing and control-structuring tool; "own/sell the machine not the product" reframes your real asset as the structuring capability and network (productisable, not just sold deal by deal); and "know what your capability can and can't make" is a self-knowledge check for your own moves.

Make it click — similar plays

Gillette (Case 06) — the rival BIC beat in lighters and challenged in razors; the focused-challenger-vs-side-project-giant lesson. AWS (Case 11) — sell your internal capability as a service (BIC's blades-for-competitors). Toys "R" Us (Case 12) — the outsourcing-teaches-your-competitor mistake BIC refused to make.

The self-knowledge pair: Gucci (Case 19) and Dell (Case 17) — commodity-vs-desire and "value not in Excel"; know what your capability can and can't do. The control machines: Samsung (Case 16) and Leclerc (Case 22) — control without full ownership, via cross-shareholding, an association, and here double-voting rights.

Your version: own and never outsource your real machine (your structuring know-how), don't chase "desire" games your capability can't win, consider productising your competency — and, as a French investor, always read the double-voting structure before valuing control.

How to drillOwn and guard the machine, not the product; win on reliability and volume; refuse the games your capability can't win; and — as a French investor — read the voting structure before the cap table. For you: your machine is your structuring know-how, and control ≠ ownership is a home-market rule you can use.

BlaBlaCar — 12 Years to the First EuroVideo case · Obsession, trust-as-product & platform vs operator economics
▶ Video0/14▶
The one ideaBlaBlaCar never sold transport — it sold trust between strangers. It took 12 years and six failed models to monetise that, and the moment it extended into a business where trust was worthless (the bus), it bled hundreds of millions. Know what you're really selling, and never extend past where your moat applies.
The story (in brief)

BlaBlaCar is the world's biggest carpooling community — 100M+ members, 20+ countries, ~$2B valuation, a signup every two seconds at its peak. But it took 12 years to earn its first euro, losing money every single year, testing six business models that all failed. The idea seemed doomed: paying to pre-book a seat in a stranger's car, when carpooling carried the grim reputation of hitchhiking. Founder Frédéric Mazzella (ENS, then Stanford, where he saw carpool lanes make sharing a privilege) had his flash on a packed 2003 Christmas trip — hundreds of cars, each with one driver and three empty seats: the seats home existed, just not in the trains where he was looking.

Then a decade of walls. He bought covoiturage.fr (2006), took on €70k of personal debt (repaid only in 2013), drew no salary until 2009, and tried everything — parking terminals, radio read-outs, corporate subscriptions, white-label — while the site stayed entirely free, taking not a cent on trips. The corporate model's flaw: the companies bought it but the employees had to use it (misaligned). Six ways to make money, six failures — and the one he never dared (charging for the trip) was the answer. The unlock came from a mundane moment: co-founder Francis Nappez waited half an hour for a no-show passenger who'd simply fallen asleep. The insight: a free reservation commits no one. Requiring pre-payment (2011) cut no-shows from ~35% to ~3% — he thought he was forcing payment; he was making the service reliable. The commission followed (from ~8-12% in 2014 to ~20-30% today) — money that falls without the company running a single vehicle.

Where it stands

After a cash-burning global land-grab ($300M raised, spent on headcount, acquisitions and ads; retreats from the US, UK, India where the savings were too small or payment stayed cash-only), BlaBlaCar finally turned profitable in September 2018 — exactly 12 years in. Then it made its costliest bet: buying SNCF's loss-making bus subsidiary (Ouibus, carrying ~€165M of accumulated losses — more than the ~€101M BlaBlaCar raised to buy it) to become the platform for all ground travel. Rebranded BlaBlaBus, it owned no buses (contractors drove) — same model — but with a fatal difference: a carpool seat costs no one anything, while a bus runs its fuel, tolls and driver whether full or empty. For the first time, it had to pay to fill the vehicle. Per the video (2026, around my cutoff): despite a record 2025 (~€115M revenue, 6M passengers), on 21 April 2026 BlaBlaCar shut the bus business — the seventh failure, now in the hundreds of millions. Meanwhile the carpool core broke records (the busiest Easter in three years). Trust never faltered; the bus, where no one trusts anyone, was doomed from the start.

▶ Original video ↗

Capture the lessons

Run the drills

Beyond the video — added insight

The business-model gem — zero marginal cost: the difference between carpooling and the bus is the difference between a matching platform (inventory that costs no one anything → commission is near-free money, huge upside operating leverage) and an operator (real marginal cost per seat → fill the vehicle or bleed). BlaBlaCar's genius and its bus disaster are the same lesson from both sides. When you evaluate any "platform," the first question is whether it truly bears no marginal cost — many "platforms" secretly subsidise their inventory (drivers, couriers, buses) and are really capital-heavy operators in a platform costume.

Trust as the compounding moat — your positioning: BlaBlaCar's only real, un-copyable asset was mass trust between strangers — which is why investors funded 12 profitless years, why the carpool core never faltered, and why the bus (where trust is irrelevant) was doomed. It's the Anthropic thesis (Case 04) in a marketplace: trust is the weapon — slow to build, un-copyable, and the thing that survives every downturn. For a "trusted specialist," this is the whole game, and the reminder that trust, once built, outlasts every failed side-bet.

"Don't extend past your moat" unifies the recent cases: BIC (Case 26, the machine can't make desire), Decathlon (Case 21, silence becomes invisibility where the model can't deploy), Gucci (Case 19, drifting from heritage), and now BlaBlaCar (trust is worthless in a bus). Your moat has a domain — extend inside it, not outside it.

The endurance capstone: this is the real-world exemplar of your Endure & Build library (Frankl, Pressfield, Maxwell) — 12 years, six failed models, personal debt, no salary; and the unlock came from a mundane operational moment (a no-show), not a grand strategy.

Your intersection: platform-vs-operator economics is a precise underwriting distinction for a financier; trust-as-the-real-product is your exact positioning; the endurance maps to long-horizon project finance; and "test whether your moat and unit economics travel before you extend" is a discipline for both your investing and your own career moves.

Make it click — similar plays

Anthropic (Case 04) — trust as the weapon, the same thesis in AI. Airbnb / Uber / eBay — trust-between-strangers marketplaces (ratings turn strangers into transactions), and the platform-vs-operator and take-rate-creep dynamics. BIC (Case 26), Decathlon (Case 21), Gucci (Case 19) — don't extend where your capability or moat doesn't apply.

The finance echoes: Auchan (Case 23) — operating leverage, here inverted (the bus's real marginal cost vs the carpool's zero); the Endure & Build books — BlaBlaCar as the grit exemplar; Doctolib (the video's teaser) — the marketplace take-rate/monopoly endgame that drew regulators.

Your version: build the trust that compounds, sell the zero-marginal-cost match, and never extend into a "bus" where your real asset is worthless and the economics don't hold.

How to drillOutlast failure while you search for the model, sell the trust (not the surface), find the inventory that costs no one anything, and never extend past where your moat and unit economics hold. For you: trust is your product, platform-vs-operator is your underwriting lens, and endurance is the long game of your profession.

LVMH — The Most Beautiful Casino in the WorldVideo case · The aspirational pyramid & a three-key luxury-investing framework
▶ Video0/14▶
The one ideaLuxury's real customer isn't the billionaire — it's the aspirational middle class putting half a month's wage into a bag. That engine made LVMH the most resilient machine in modern capitalism for 30 years, and its slowdown now is the reason the model is cracking. Read the tickets, not the runway.
The story (in brief)

LVMH is the world's biggest luxury empire — ~€86B revenue, 75 maisons, Bernard Arnault at times the richest person alive. Yet the client who really runs the machine earns €2,500-5,000 a month. The model is a three-tier pyramid: at the top, haute couture and high jewelry — a small share of volume, but "advertising disguised as products" that creates the aura (an €80,000 Dior runway dress no one buys, so millions buy the Dior perfume); in the middle, leather goods and iconic bags (€1,000-3,000) — the economic heart, with margins of 60-80% (a €1,500 bag can cost ~€300 to make); at the bottom, perfume and cosmetics — the entry drug. Make the image pay for the product, and the product pay for the dream. It's a casino: the VIP high-rollers are the vitrine, but the revenue comes from thousands at the slot machines. And it runs an escalator — perfume at 20, bag at 30, clothing at 40, watch at 50: LVMH sells a trajectory of social ascension, not objects.

For ~20 years it worked flawlessly — prices rose faster than inflation and demand still followed — because of a colossal external fuel: 1B+ people joining the global middle class from 1995-2015, above all in China (~30-40% of world luxury). Arnault's insight was to make luxury an integrated industry: control the brands, the distribution, the pricing and above all the narrative; orchestrate scarcity; raise prices to maintain the signal. But the fuel is now failing. China's "common prosperity" politics discourage ostentation, and its property crisis (~70% of household wealth is in real estate) has gutted the wealth-effect. And in the West, status is reconfiguring: "quiet luxury" makes visible logos vulgar (the real rich wear brands only insiders recognize), while the "dupe" makes copies a proud act. From below the logo is cheapened; from above ostentation is rejected — and both attack the psychological core of a logo-driven model.

Where it stands

LVMH stock fell ~30% from its peak in 2024-2025, with disappointing results for the first time in over a decade — while Hermès barely moved. That's no accident: Hermès is the anti-LVMH — one house, one family for six generations, one iconic product (the Birkin), and a philosophy of refusing to sell (you can't buy a Birkin even with the money; you need a purchase history and the house's permission). Vuitton sells to those who want to become rich; Hermès sells to those who already are. So when the desire for ascension weakens, the middle class tightens, and the dupe ridicules logos, aspirational luxury suffers and exclusive luxury resists — the fashionable restaurant empties, the unmarked private club keeps its waiting list. LVMH will adapt the way Arnault always does — by buying (note it already owns Loro Piana, the quintessential quiet-luxury brand, so he saw the shift coming).

The finance gem — a framework that generalises: the three keys work far beyond luxury. (1) Segment any sector into sub-models that react differently to the same shock (aspirational vs exclusive; mass vs premium; cyclical vs defensive; volume vs scarcity). (2) Read the client/revenue mix as the early signal — a mix-shift down the pyramid flags purchasing-power stress before it hits headline revenue. (3) Use a relative-value spread between two players in the same sector as a sentiment compass — the market re-rating one model vs another. That's a repeatable value-investing method for reading any consumer or cyclical sector. (Not financial advice — a reading grid, as the video itself frames it.)

The Hermès-LVMH pair sharpens Case 19: aspirational (logo, desire-to-rise, middle-class-dependent, dupe-able, cyclical) vs exclusive (scarcity, belonging, refuse-to-sell, family-controlled, resilient). Hermès is the definitive "own the scarcity, say no to the customer" moat — the ultimate pricing power. For your positioning, it's the clearest statement of the target: be the private club with a waiting list, not the fashionable restaurant.

Status is a rented cultural meaning: quiet luxury and the dupe prove a moat built on visible signaling can be dissolved by a shift in what people want to signal — a cultural risk, not an economic one (Gen Z will decide if the logo means success or ringardise). A brand moat is only as durable as the meaning it rents.

Arnault's tell: already owning Loro Piana, the quintessential quiet-luxury house, shows the master anticipates the shift and adapts by buying the new game rather than defending the old — the anti-Auchan, anti-Gucci move.

Your intersection: the three-key framework is a direct, repeatable value-investing tool (segment / mix / spread) — the sharpest upgrade to your analytical kit in this library; aspirational-vs-exclusive is your positioning north star (be the Hermès); and the concentration (China/middle-class) and operating-leverage (pricing-volume) lessons recur from your other cases.

Hermès — the exclusive/scarcity/refuse-to-sell exemplar. EssilorLuxottica (Case 03) — own the chain and orchestrate the market; here plus the narrative and the pricing.

Marie Blachère — The Greengrocer Who Took the Throne of BreadVideo case · Loss-leader traffic, total ownership & the handshake that broke
▶ Video0/14▶
The one ideaA greengrocer took the throne of bread by asking the wrong question on purpose — not "how do I make good bread?" but "how do I sell bread like vegetables?" The bread is bait sold at a loss; the money is what you grab inside; and the un-copyable moat is that one man owns 100% of it.
The story (in brief)

Marie Blachère is France's #1 bakery — 830+ shops, ~€1.1B revenue, 12,000 staff, a baguette every 6 seconds — and ranks #3 in French quick-service by revenue, behind McDonald's (~€6B) and Burger King, ahead of KFC and Subway. Yet its baguette is sold at a loss (under €1, half-price at close) and its founder never baked one in his life. Bernard Blachère spent 20 years as a primeur (greengrocer), and the primeur thinks in volume, rotation and price — not craft. When he opened his first bakery (2004, named after his daughter Marie), it was a disaster, because he'd asked the artisan's question ("how to make good bread"). The unlock came when he flipped it to the primeur's question ("how to sell bread like tomatoes"). His signature "la Marie" baguette came with market-stall mechanics no baker dared: buy 3 get the 4th free, and everything half-price in the last half-hour — the tomato-seller emptying his crate before noon, and discounting rather than throwing away.

The real machine is a gas station: bread is the fuel (sold near cost, earns nothing) whose only job is to pull people in; the money is the sandwich, pizza slice, coffee and cookie they grab inside (non-bread ≈ a third of sales). You come for a €0.71 baguette and leave with a €12 ticket. And the un-copyable part isn't the promos (anyone can copy those) — it's ownership. Most big bread chains (Paul) franchise: grow on others' capital, split the margin. Blachère does the inverse — barely ~5% franchised, and he owns ~100% of the group himself. Every cent of margin stays in the group, there's no stock-market pressure, and he decides in the morning and signs in the afternoon while rivals spend six months convincing banks and franchisees. A new shop every ~6 days.

Where it stands

The French eat a seventh of the bread they did post-war, yet Blachère booms — because he stopped being a bakery and became a QSR (a bakery on the façade, fast-food in the numbers). One caveat on the narrative: the bread is genuinely baked on-site, but much of the viennoiserie arrives frozen from an industrial supplier — artisanal in the discourse, industrial in the wings; the edifice balances on customers believing the "artisanal" story. And the French cluster now converges: the 2008 handshake with Grand Frais ("you do bread, I do fresh" — 9 of 10 Grand Frais have a Marie Blachère next door) is breaking. Per the video (2026 events around my cutoff): Blachère quietly built France's #2 fresh chain (~265 stores, ~€300M) competing with his partner Grand Frais (#1), and then took Carrefour's fruit-and-veg aisles (target ~200 aisles at ~10% royalty) — going to work for Grand Frais's biggest rival. And Grand Frais itself was bought by US fund Apollo (~€4B, Case 25) — and a fund won't honour an old French handshake. The primeur who ran Carrefour-linked fresh aisles in the 1990s is back at the heart of Carrefour 40 years later. The one fault line: Blachère is ~70, owns everything, and has no known succession plan.

Your entire positioning — energy × AI-infrastructure × project finance — IS a cross-industry arbitrage: applying project-finance structuring logic to the AI-power frontier that neither pure energy nor pure AI people think in. For a dealmaker that's a real underwriting principle — assess who might own your counterparty tomorrow, and formalise what matters. It also completes Case 25's Apollo story from the other side: the fund's consolidate-and-simplify reflex now threatens even the handshake partnerships.

The 100%-ownership moat is the full statement of the control theme: full ownership buys speed, full margin capture and freedom from quarterly pressure — but concentrates everything, including succession risk, in one person. The strength and the fragility are the same fact (as with Auchan, Case 23, and Samsung, Case 16).

Held fairly: the chain's scale pressures artisans (4 in 10 gone in 40 years; a 2023 protective bill) — and it also bakes real bread on-site with French flour and ranks well on health among chains. The portrait is grey, not black.

Vinted — The Closet Was Just the PrototypeVideo case · Fee incidence, network effects & narrative vs mechanism
▶ Video0/14▶
The one ideaVinted nearly died charging sellers — then it made selling free, moved a tiny fee to the buyer, and became a machine. It was never really about ecology; it's a transaction loop where the money never leaves. And the closet was just the prototype for an everything-resale infrastructure.
The story (in brief)

Vinted has 23M+ French members (1 in 3 people, more than Netflix in France) and the slogan everyone knows: "you don't wear it, sell it on Vinted." It began in 2008 in Vilnius, when 21-year-old Milda Mikutė, packing boxes, found 100+ garments (some with tags still on) and told a developer friend her idea — a platform where each woman puts her closet online. Renamed Vinted (vintage + wanted), it grew across Europe and hit France in 2013, where word-of-mouth among women 20-35 made it the #1 country in two years. But growth nearly killed it: chasing the US, it opened offices in San Francisco, LA, Paris and London, tried the UK five times and failed five times, and its 20-30% seller commission strangled supply (sell a €20 jean, €6 gone before you pack it → sellers don't return → a death spiral). By 2016, months from bankruptcy and under €10M revenue, founder Milda stepped down after burnout.

The savior was Thomas Plantenga — a Dutchman with a background in fluid dynamics who thinks of users "circulating in a platform like a fluid in the blood." He cut ~40% of staff, closed the foreign offices, and made the radical move: he eliminated the seller commission — selling became free — and shifted a tiny fee to the buyer (~5% + €0.70 "Buyer Protection"). His logic: supply drives demand, so if listing costs nothing, people list everything; more supply → buyers find what they want → they return → they become sellers. Five cents per euro sounds like nothing, but across ~2.2 items exchanged per second it's ~€1.1B revenue (2025), ~€11B of goods, +47% in a year, 26 countries.

Where it stands

The loop has an engine and a blind spot. The engine: your sale proceeds land in a Vinted wallet (like casino chips you leave on the table), and notifications trigger impulse buys — you thought you were emptying your closet; you're recharging Vinted's circuit. The blind spot: what circulates isn't vintage but fast fashion (~83M Zara items, ~76M H&M, ~39M Shein) — research (Journal of Cleaner Production, 2025) calls it the "circular rebound effect": resale substitutes only ~31% of new purchases; the other ~69% just stacks. It was never officially sold as ecological — the culture mis-heard a transaction machine. Downstream, Emmaüs says the good clothes now sell on Vinted while charity gets the unsellable rest (of 100 tonnes collected, ~40 now reach shops vs ~60 twenty years ago), draining a system that funds reinsertion work — and Vinted's answer was to offer Emmaüs a Pro account. And at €1.1B revenue it still had no age verification and under-invested in moderation, drawing regulators. Per the video (2025-26, around my cutoff): profit fell by design (€62M vs €77M) as Vinted reinvested in logistics, payments, a startup fund and acquisitions; it launched in the US (shipping some parcels by air) and BlackRock came in at an ~€8B valuation. Plantenga: "by year-end you'll be able to sell every object in your home."

Beyond the video — added insight

The finance gem — fee incidence: Vinted's entire turnaround was a change in who pays, not how much. Charging the seller 20-30% strangled the network-driving side (supply); moving a tiny fee to the buyer preserved supply and monetised volume. In any two-sided structure — a marketplace, a deal, a fee arrangement — the incidence of the charge can matter more than the rate. The elegant fix is often architectural, not incremental — a precise, transferable structuring principle.

Read the mechanism, not the narrative — your DD muscle: Vinted never officially sold ecology; the culture did, while the reality is a transaction machine where resale substitutes only ~31% of new purchases ("cleaning your room by pushing everything into the hallway"). Separating the story from the mechanism is the same discipline as reading Ireland's GNI* behind its GDP (Case 18) or LVMH's client-mix behind its revenue (Case 28). Don't buy the narrative; read what the machine does.

Every efficient system has an externality — systems thinking: the "free, green" loop presents a bill downstream — the good clothes leave Emmaüs, reinsertion work dries up, and the fast fashion it recirculates still ends in landfill, just later. It rhymes with Leclerc (Case 22): the low price is a bill presented to someone else down the chain. For a financier assessing a deal's true impact, trace the cost that lands off its own books.

The behavioural engine and the endgame: the closed-loop wallet (casino chips) plus impulse notifications is the LVMH-casino lesson (Case 28) in a resale app; and the closet → every object → logistics/payments expansion is the Amazon/AWS (Case 11) and Lidl-to-data-centre (Case 24) pattern — the boring, high-volume machine becoming category infrastructure.

Your intersection: fee-incidence/take-rate architecture is a precise structuring insight; read-the-mechanism-not-the-narrative is your investing DD and your integrity; the externalities lens is full-chain deal assessment; and the platform-becomes-infrastructure endgame ties to your AI-infra thesis. It also deepens the marketplace economics of BlaBlaCar (Case 27).

Make it click — similar plays

BlaBlaCar (Case 27) — the marketplace/network-effects and trust-between-strangers cousin, another French-market platform. Amazon / AWS (Case 11) & Lidl (Case 24) — the boring-machine-becomes-infrastructure endgame. LVMH (Case 28) — the casino/impulse behavioural engine (money stays on the table).

The critical-thinking echoes: Leclerc (Case 22) — the low price is a bill to someone else down the chain (externalities); Ireland (Case 18) — read the real metric behind the narrative. The marketplace family: eBay, Poshmark, Uber, Airbnb — fee-incidence and take-rate dynamics.

Your version: architect your fee incidence, ignite the flywheel's driving side, read the mechanism behind every narrative, trace the downstream externality, and watch for the boring machine quietly becoming infrastructure.

How to drillChange who pays (not how much), remove friction on the side that ignites the flywheel, win on velocity, and read the mechanism behind every mission narrative — tracing the externality to whoever pays downstream. For you: fee-incidence is your structuring, narrative-vs-mechanism is your due diligence.

Doctolib — The Free App That Became a MonopolyVideo case · Network-effect lock-in, acquire-to-kill & regulatory blowback
▶ Video0/14▶
The one ideaA service that's free, genuinely useful, and chosen willingly can still be a trap — for competitors, and eventually for the state. Doctolib became the reflex of 50 million people, and its genius (becoming irreplaceable) is now exactly what turns the government from customer into adversary.
The story (in brief)

Doctolib works — voted the most useful company in French daily life two years running, off-hours booking, and a ~75% cut in no-shows. But it's also, per a November 2025 competition ruling (which it is appealing), a monopoly: fined €4.6M for abuse of dominance, with seized internal documents stating the aim to "be an obligatory, strategic interface between doctor and patient, to lock in both." Founded in 2013 by six people with zero medical expertise (the idea came from co-founder Stève Abou Rjeily seeing a booking app in Korea; the marketplace muscle from Stanislas Niox-Chateau, ex-La Fourchette), it won not by code but by a ground war — hundreds of door-to-door salespeople with a "sales Bible," while the founder criss-crossed France in a Twingo hearing "no" a hundred times. The unlock argument was the no-show reminder. Then the network effect took, neighborhood by neighborhood.

Three moves built the moat. (1) Social lock-in: Doctolib auto-created a profile for every French doctor from public registry data — appearing first on Google, hard to remove, reappearing when deleted — so patients expected their doctor there and doctors subscribed because they couldn't reach patients otherwise ("the trap is social, not technical"). (2) The anchor institution: the 2016 AP-HP contract (Europe's biggest hospital group) delivered in one signature as many doctors as three years of door-to-door, and its ecosystem pulled city doctors in. (3) Acquire-to-kill: it bought its #1 rival MonDocteur (~€45M, below the merger-notification threshold) — the seized docs show the goal was its disappearance, plus intent to raise prices 10-20%; and it kept exclusivity clauses (barring doctors from rival platforms) for five years after its own lawyers warned they were illegal, because the monopoly gain dwarfed a fine that might come in five years (and was ~1.3% of revenue).

Where it stands

With rivals dead or marginalised (70-90% booking share) and no investor willing to fund a competitor in a locked market, prices climbed (€109 → €149/month, up to ~37%, no customer flight) — golden handcuffs: the service is so essential that price stopped mattering. Then Covid super-charged it: teleconsultations went 1,000 → 100,000/day, and the 2021 vaccination campaign anchored it into 50M lives (926,000 bookings in one evening after the pass-sanitaire announcement). Doctolib "lost money" on vaccination but gained irreplaceable anchoring — becoming a verb like Google, and a system the strained public sector can't replace overnight. Now the paradox bites (2025-26 events, per the video, around my cutoff): the more indispensable Doctolib became, the more the state moved to impose its own public alternative (Mon Espace Santé, made mandatory by law with fines — censored by the Conseil constitutionnel on procedure, not substance; and a January 2026 doctors' strike). And ~90M Europeans' health data sits on AWS, theoretically reachable via the US Cloud Act. Its greatest strength — being irreplaceable — is what could cost it its freedom.

This closes the BlaBlaCar loop and completes the French-platform trilogy: BlaBlaCar's video teased Doctolib, "the free platform that quietly became a health monopoly." Together BlaBlaCar (Case 27, trust + the bus limit), Vinted (Case 30, fee-incidence + the rebound externality) and Doctolib (monopoly foreclosure + state blowback) are one lesson on network effects, the "free" model, and where each lands.

The regulatory-blowback paradox — the sharpest, and most yours: Doctolib's genius (become irreplaceable, essential infrastructure) is exactly what turned the state from customer into adversary — because a private monopoly on critical national infrastructure is intolerable to a government, which then builds and legally imposes a public alternative. "Moats invite regulation" escalated: when your moat becomes critical infrastructure (health, energy, payments, data), the state isn't just a regulator — it's a permanent, potentially existential stakeholder that can legislate you out. For an energy/infra financier, this is a core risk: the more essential the asset, the more the state owns its fate. (It's the inverse of Lidl/Schwarz's sovereign-cloud bet, Case 24 — there a private player builds infrastructure the state wants; here one holds infrastructure the state wants back.)

The rational-lawbreaking calculus, held evenhandedly: the economics genuinely favoured keeping illegal clauses (gain ≫ a slow, cheap fine), and the ~1.3%-of-revenue penalty "proved" the calculus in narrow financial terms — but it's illegal, it drew the state's existential counterattack, and it's the reputational/regulatory tail an investor must price. The lesson isn't "break the law"; it's that weak, slow enforcement creates a real incentive to — and therefore a real risk in — businesses that do.

Data sovereignty is your AI-infra thesis: ~90M Europeans' health data on AWS, reachable via the Cloud Act, is the exact gap sovereign-infrastructure plays (Schwarz Digits, Case 24; and AWS itself, Case 11) aim at. Where data and compute live is geopolitical — and adjacent to your energy-for-AI-infrastructure work.

Your intersection: social lock-in, acquire-to-kill foreclosure, the regulatory-tail risk (a financier's due diligence), golden-handcuffs pricing power, the state-as-existential-stakeholder paradox (core to energy/infra), and data sovereignty (Cloud Act) — this case sits squarely in your professional environment.

Maison du Monde — Seized Through Its Debt, Not Its SharesVideo case · Distressed debt, loan-to-own & why debt is the control key
▶ Video0/14▶
The one ideaTwo London funds took 95% of a €947M company in six weeks without buying a single share. They bought its debt — at 7 cents on the euro. Because when a company falls, power stops belonging to those who own its equity and passes to whoever owns its debt.
The story (in brief)

Xavier Marie, a former door-to-door encyclopedia salesman ("you never sell an object, you sell what people imagine holding it"), rebuilt a dead Asian-imports wholesaler into Maison du Monde in the 1990s. His innovation was the store as a decor — scented candles, warm light, whole reconstituted rooms, chairs with first names; you came for a €12 photo frame and left with the imagined life around it (it even opened hotels you could sleep in). It passed €1B in sales, took French PE money (2008, €435M), was bought by Bain Capital (2013, €680M), and IPO'd in Paris. Covid then produced a freak record — a whole country redecorating at once — pushing sales to €1.31B in 2021. That summit is what killed it: the group cut its costume (warehouses, offices, teams) to a one-time peak, and when normal returned — inflation, a frozen housing market (furniture is an "event industry" chained to home sales), Temu-style platforms and second-hand — sales fell four straight years to €947M, with a €52M warehouse written down as built for volumes that no longer exist.

The stock slid, and two kinds of investor arrived: Gabriel Naouri (son of Casino's Jean-Charles Naouri) via Majorelle, backed by Apollo, and Swiss Teleios — "smart money" convinced it was buying a trough. It was a trap. As sales fell, the company drew ever more on its revolving credit facility (the corporate overdraft: €90M end-2024 → €196M a year later); "health was no longer measured, it was negotiated." Then the cruel twist: by spring 2026 the stores were recovering (traffic +2%, brand score up, sales stabilising) — and it was seized anyway, because the debt moved faster than the turnaround.

Where it stands

Per the video (2026 events around my cutoff): after a cold "financial-partner discussions failed" notice and a postponed annual report, the stock hit 44 centimes (−98% from 2021) and the company asked the exchange to suspend its own share. In the discreet conciliation antechamber (behind closed doors, at the commercial court), two distressed-retail funds — Alteri and Aeneas — bought €210M of Maison du Monde's debt from the banks at ~7 cents on the euro (the banks rationally took 7 cents now over a likely zero in bankruptcy). Then loan-to-own: a coup d'accordéon wiped the old shares, new shares (reserved for the funds, at 28 centimes) were issued and paid for by offsetting the discounted debt, and the crown jewels — brand, stocks, fonds de commerce, the French subsidiary's shares — were placed in a fiducie (security trust) as collateral. Existing shareholders, including Naouri, voted for their own dilution because 4.78% of something beats 100% of nothing. The irony: the exact creditors-turn-debt-into-capital procedure that undid the father's Casino empire now took the son's stake. Alteri's record (Bensons for Beds / Harveys — one saved debt-free, one liquidated) shows the endgame is to cut, not keep.

▶ Original video ↗

Capture the lessons

Run the drills

Beyond the video — added insight

This is the most professionally on-point case in the file: every mechanic — distressed-debt buying at a discount, loan-to-own, the coup d'accordéon, debt-to-equity by compensation, the fiducie-sûreté, conciliation, the RCF as the pressure point — is your daily structuring and credit vocabulary. The single most important truth it teaches governs your whole discipline: in distress, control follows the debt, not the equity. A financier who reads the capital structure's seniority sees the endgame that the equity market (watching sales and stores) never does.

The profound counterintuitive lesson: the business was recovering and was seized anyway, because the balance sheet's clock (the RCF draw-down, the maturity wall) ran faster than the operational turnaround. A company doesn't die when the P&L turns; it dies when it can't roll or service its debt — "health is negotiated, not measured." Underwrite the clock and the security package, not just the earnings line.

Distressed investing, elegantly and brutally: the banks' rational choice to take 7 cents now over a likely zero, and the funds' conversion of that discounted debt into 95% control, is the whole logic of loan-to-own. And a caution: "smart money" equity (Naouri, Teleios) bought a value trap — even professionals mistake a maturity-wall trap for a trough. The Bic contrast (Case 26) is exact: a controlling family with double-voting rights could have blocked the dilution — ownership structure is protection, and its absence is the vulnerability the creditors exploited.

The Casino/Naouri irony deepens the theme: the same creditors-turn-debt-into-capital procedure that took the father's Casino empire now took the son's Maison du Monde stake — the law of the capital structure playing out across French retail (it also shadowed Auchan, Case 23). And the cost-base-for-a-peak trap rhymes with Auchan and the LVMH pricing-volume loop (Case 28).

Your intersection: this case is your job — debt-is-control, the maturity wall, the security package/fiducie, distressed-debt pricing, loan-to-own, conciliation, the RCF — your structuring and credit craft told as the fall of a French retailer. It upgrades both your investing (don't buy a value trap; check seniority) and your structuring (the security package is the endgame; underwrite the clock).

Toys "R" Us (Case 12), Picard (Case 20), Dell (Case 17) — leverage and the intent of the debt-holder (extraction vs transformation vs, here, loan-to-own seizure). Grand Frais/Apollo (Case 25) & Marie Blachère (Case 29) — fund control of French retail, here via debt not equity.

Your version: read the capital structure's seniority, underwrite the maturity wall and the security package, price distressed debt on the recovery-vs-zero calculus — and remember that in distress, whoever owns the debt owns the company.

Celio — The Survivor of a Devastated SectorVideo case · Timeless over trend, weakness-as-weapon & hunting the ruins
▶ Video0/14▶
The one ideaWhile every fashion brand around it died against Zara and Shein, the most banal brand of all — a menswear-basics chain — not only survived but earns more than before the crisis. It sold what never goes out of fashion because it was never in it, turned its banality into its flag, and bought its dead rivals' names for a handful of euros.
The story (in brief)

Celio grew to ~1,600 stores in 50 countries. Then in three years the sector around it collapsed — Camaïeu, Naf Naf, Kookaï, Pimkie, San Marina, Jennifer all liquidated or gone — and only the most banal one stayed standing, earning more than before: €680M+. Its founder, Maurice Grossman, learned survival as a 12-year-old in 1942, escaping (from a hospital bed) the roundup that took his whole family — a survival instinct he built into the company. A men's tailor after the war, he and his sons Marc and Laurent turned one disturbingly simple idea into a method: sell clothes like a supermarket — the same pull in 15 colours piled on a table, self-service, no advice, basics, cheap. The plain t-shirt built the empire.

The power of the basic: while others chase the trend, Celio sells the navy pull that never dates — because it was never in fashion to begin with; it's everywhere and invisible. But a giant of ~1,600 rents survives only if customers keep entering — the rent falls whether you sell 1,000 t-shirts or zero. So March 2020 nearly killed it: all stores shut, ~€100M of sales gone in two months, a state-loan refusal, and the last resort — sauvegarde (court protection from creditors). ~100 stores closed. And on 14 February 2021, as his sons fought to save the company, Maurice Grossman died — the man who survived everything, gone as his work fought not to.

Where it stands

The turnaround man, Sébastien Bismuth, didn't start with clothes — he dug the archives and found a forgotten slogan: "la mode, je m'en fous" (fashion, I don't care). In an age of curated perfection, being "a normal guy" had become a compliment — so Celio stopped being ashamed of its banality and made it the flag ("Be normal," with the un-polished Benoît Paire as ambassador): ~+15% sales. The t-shirt didn't change; the story did (self-service stores, YouTuber collabs, a mate's voice). Then it hunted the ruins: it bought the dead Camaïeu name at auction for ~€1.8M (not the stores, staff or debts — just the name) and used it as a Trojan horse into womenswear (~1/3 of sales in mixed shops), later replacing it with "Celio Woman." Per the video (2026, around my cutoff): a "missing L" stunt earned tens of millions of views for the price of a few unscrewed letters. In France it closed ~4 in 10 stores (478 → ~290) yet earns more — fewer but the right stores, higher margins. The honest footnote: the "normal Frenchman" brand makes ~70% in Bangladesh, with documented labour and dye concerns — grey, not black.

The finance gem — a durability screen: the dead were all women's-fashion brands (trend, 3-6-month collections) — the exact terrain Zara and Shein dominate; the survivors sell men's basics that don't date because they never tried to. For a value/quality investor, that's a screen: prefer businesses selling the timeless (immune to the fashion cycle and to fast-fashion's speed) over those whose product expires each season. It's the definitive statement of the thread through Gucci (Case 19), LVMH (Case 28) and BIC (Case 26) — and note the ultimate winners aren't "fashion" at all but functional basics (Intersport, Decathlon).

Turn weakness into weapon — the positioning gem: Celio's banality was its shame, then its flag. The defect you can't hide is often the positioning nobody else can own — and in a culture of curated perfection, "normal / honest / un-flashy" became the differentiator. It's the inverse of Gucci uprooting its identity: Celio leaned into its true one.

Ownership-resilience is now a five-case pattern: BIC, Picard, Auchan, Maison du Monde and Celio — family/patient capital survives black years; fund/quarterly capital cuts and sells at the first stumble (Camaïeu). Who owns a business predicts how it behaves in a crisis; patient ownership is a moat downturns can't easily break.

Hunt in the ruins — counter-cyclical distressed M&A, your craft: buy the dead rival's name (€1.8M) and best stores cheap in the very downturn that killed them. It pairs with Maison du Monde (Case 32): there a fund buys the debt to seize; here a survivor buys the assets to consolidate. And the free-attention marketing and change-the-packaging-not-the-product reinvention are the Decathlon (Case 21) and Lidl (Case 24) lessons applied.

Your intersection: the timeless-vs-trend durability screen (your investing), family-control resilience (your ownership lens), hunt-in-the-ruins distressed M&A (your craft), fewer-but-better cost discipline — and the positioning lessons (turn weakness into weapon, free attention, be the trusted un-flashy substance). A strong consumer-durability capstone.

Decathlon (Case 21) / Intersport — functional basics as the ultimate winners, and free-attention marketing. BIC (Case 26), Picard (Case 20), Auchan (Case 23), Maison du Monde (Case 32) — family/patient control as resilience vs the fund countdown.

The tactics: Picard (Case 20) & Marie Blachère (Case 29) — the brand name as a cheap, powerful asset; Maison du Monde (Case 32) — the distressed side (fund buys the debt to seize; here the survivor buys the assets to consolidate); Lidl (Case 24) — change the story, keep the engine.

Your version: own the timeless not the trend, keep patient control, hunt distressed assets in the downturn, rationalise to the profitable core, and turn your plainness into the trusted-substance positioning no flashier rival can claim.

Club Med — Fired at the Summit, Owned in ShanghaiVideo case · Dilution & lost control, the up-market pivot & financialisation
▶ Video0/14▶
The one ideaThe man who ran one of the finest turnarounds in French economic history was fired months later — not for failing, but for succeeding so well that his brand became worth taking. Because Club Med never had the means of its ambitions, so at every crisis it called someone richer — and each rescue took a piece of the keys.
The story (in brief)

Club Med was founded in 1950 on a Mallorca beach by Gérard Blitz — a Belgian water-polo champion and resistance member who, at the Liberation, helped camp survivors return to life and wanted "something profitable that didn't betray his need for sharing." His rule changed everything: here money doesn't exist — you pay once in advance, and on-site there's no cash (a bead necklace buys your drink), no social class, everyone on "tu." A beautiful utopia — and, unseen, a formidable cash machine: the money comes in before the client arrives. But it never earned fast enough for its dreams, and that is the mechanism that pilots the whole story: it will never have the means of its ambitions, so every time it wants to grow — or just survive — it must call someone richer. First in 1961 (12 villages, 45,000 members, yet near bankruptcy): Rothschild writes the cheque and leaves with a third. Then American Express (1968), then Agnelli/Fiat (1970s) — at the height of its glory the founders were no longer masters of their house.

Gilbert Trigano (the tent supplier turned boss) built the GO culture, the tridents, the mini-club, the global brand, even a 1984 NYSE listing; Les Bronzés (1978) mocked it — and became its best free advertising while dating it for 30 years. But by the late 1980s the all-inclusive idea was copied everywhere: Club Med was stuck in the middle — too expensive for the cheap-seekers, not refined enough for the luxury-seekers. It discounted to fill villages, recovered one year — and broke the only thing it had left, its reputation ("saved the year, condemned the decade"). Blitz died (1990), a plane crash killed ~30 vacationers (1992), the Triganos were ejected (1997), and a string of failed bets (OYYO, Club Med World) left a giant on the ground.

Where it stands

In 2002 Henri Giscard d'Estaing made the bet everyone judged insane: out of the middle, go up — turn the "tanning factory" into a luxury brand. Brutal surgery (~85 villages closed, the rest renovated, only the wealthiest targeted), an "Exclusive Collection," and a secret weapon — all-inclusive ski (filling the winter, drawing foreigners). It took ~20 years — and €1B+ of works the club didn't have, which is what handed control to Shanghai: after the longest takeover battle in Paris history (20 months, Fosun vs Bonomi, ~€500M → ~€1B), Fosun won and delisted it in 2015. Under the Chinese flag it soared — 2024 record results (~€2B revenue), villages ~100% up-market, the brand desirable again. But (per the video, 2022-25 events around my cutoff) the success was French and the power was in Shanghai: Fosun, crushed by ~€20B+ of debt since the pandemic, turned its now-profitable Club Med into a liquidity source — pushed the French out of management, and prepared to sell/list it (Hong Kong, not Giscard's preferred Paris) to lighten the parent's debt. Giscard, discovering his replacement had been recruited behind his back, was fired at the summit and is contesting it. The flag stayed tricolor; the cash register isn't.

Beyond the video — added insight & correction

Correction: the "€2 billion" is Club Med's record revenue, not net profit (which is far smaller) — "record results, ~€2B revenue" is the accurate framing.

The finance gem — dilution equals loss of control: Club Med "never had the means of its ambitions," so it called a richer saviour at every crisis (Rothschild 1961 → Amex 1968 → Agnelli 1970s → Fosun 2015), and each rescue took a piece of the keys until the founders were minority and ejected. It's the single most important governance truth for a founder or financier: growth funded by dilution eventually transfers control, and the day it goes wrong — or right enough to be worth taking — whoever holds the shares decides. It's exactly why BIC's double-voting defence (Case 26) matters, and it rhymes with Maison du Monde (Case 32): equity dilution and debt are two roads to the same place — someone else holds the keys.

The positioning masterstroke — go up, not down: the definitive answer to the Dell (Case 17) / Gucci (Case 19) "stuck in the middle" trap. The instinct is to discount (destroying the brand); Giscard went up, betting on fewer clients paying much more — and it worked, but required €1B+ of capital he didn't have, which is what cost him control. The pivot that saved the brand demanded the capital that ended its independence.

The financialisation endgame ties the French cluster together: Fosun, drowning in debt, turns its profitable Club Med into a liquidity source — develop, turn around, sell/list once it's worth gold. The beloved brand becomes a pure asset whose fate is decided abroad — the same "who really owns the cash flow and logic" theme as Picard (Case 20), Grand Frais/Apollo (Case 25) and Maison du Monde (Case 32). The profound closing insight: a brand can keep its name, flag and accent while silently changing owner and, above all, logic.

Your intersection: the dilution/loss-of-control and financialisation lessons are your capital-structure and PE world; the negative-working-capital cash machine is your structuring; the up-market-out-of-the-middle is positioning; and "look past the flag to who owns the cash flow and where it lists" is a governance/sovereignty due-diligence lens (rhyming with the data-sovereignty of Doctolib and Lidl). It caps the cluster's ownership-and-control thread.

Make it click — similar plays

Dell (Case 17) & Gucci (Case 19) — "stuck in the middle" and the timeless/luxury positioning; Club Med's up-market pivot is the escape. BIC (Case 26) — the double-voting control defence Club Med's founders lacked. Maison du Monde (Case 32) & Auchan-Casino (Case 23) — control via debt; Club Med is the equity-dilution road to the same place.

The endgame: Picard (Case 20) & Grand Frais/Apollo (Case 25) — the financialisation / "who really owns it" logic; Doctolib (Case 31) — success and indispensability invite the taker (the state there, the owner here); Dell (Case 17), Amazon, Vinted (Case 30) — negative working capital / prepaid cash machine.

Your version: guard control before you raise, engineer negative working capital, escape the middle by going up not down, and always look past the flag to who owns the cash flow and where it will list.

How to drillFund the operation with customers' money, escape the middle by going up, and — above all — guard control before you raise, because every rescue takes a piece of the keys. For you: dilution-is-control and the financialisation endgame are your capital-structure world, told as the fall of France's happiest brand.

Subway — The Chain That Sold Stores, Not SandwichesVideo case · Franchise incentives, cannibalisation & the fund's right-sizing
▶ Video0/14▶
The one ideaThe moment Subway stopped selling sandwiches and started selling franchises, its real customer became the person who signs a store — not the person who eats. Because HQ took 8% of every franchisee's revenue (not profit), "opening = winning" regardless of whether anyone made money — and that one design choice explains the whole collapse.
The story (in brief)

Subway grew to ~44,000 restaurants in 100+ countries — more US outlets than McDonald's — then began emptying: a store closing every 12 hours in the US, the network falling below 19,000 for the first time in 20 years. It began in 1965 in Bridgeport, Connecticut: Fred DeLuca, a 17-year-old who wanted to be a doctor but couldn't afford college, took a $1,000 cheque from family friend Peter Buck (a nuclear physicist) to open a sandwich shop (the parent is still called "Doctor's Associates"). The appeal was watching your sandwich made fresh. By 1974, stuck at 16 shops and unable to keep up, they made the decision that changed everything, silently: stop opening stores themselves and sell them — the franchise. From then, Subway earned money by selling stores, and its real customer was the franchisee.

The entry ticket was tiny (~$15,000 vs ~$45,000 at McDonald's), so anyone — many immigrants with their savings — could become a boss; in exchange, 8% of everything they took in went to HQ, whether the store made or lost money. The machine flew (1,100 openings in 1993 alone), passing McDonald's in count (US 2002, world 2011) — but each Subway sold ~3x less, because each opening was just an entry fee plus an 8% tap. DeLuca believed more Subways in a neighbourhood meant more sales for all, and imposed it: no reserved territory — HQ could open a second store across from yours. On the ground, the two shops just split the same customers (mortal for the franchisee, identical cheque for HQ). By 1998 Subway had ~160 lawsuits pending, more than its seven biggest rivals combined.

Where it stands

The 2008 "$5 Footlong" (a franchisee's idea) made ~$4B in year one — but as beef, cheese, rent and wages rose, the price couldn't, so franchisees sold more and earned less, and the "fresh" brand became "the cheap-sandwich brand." Blows piled up: founder DeLuca died (2015); its longtime spokesperson was convicted that year of serious crimes involving minors and Subway cut ties within hours — a whole "health" pillar resting on one man, gone; "Subwaygate" (a footlong measuring 28cm), a yoga-mat bread additive, a disputed chicken-DNA claim (Subway sued for $210M), and an Irish ruling that its bread had too much sugar to legally be "bread." Behind the scenes, "development agents" who were themselves franchisees policed, resold and reclaimed rivals' stores using a 3,000-rule manual and forced arbitration. Per the video (recent events around my cutoff): a US Subway now takes ~$450k/year (rivals do $1M+), franchisees often earn less than their own employees, ~8,000 US signs went dark in a decade — while ~4 in 10 openings are now abroad (a 4,000-store China deal). And in 2023 Roark Capital (which also owns Arby's, Dunkin' and rival Jimmy John's) bought Subway for ~$9.5B and drove record profit by "right-sizing" — closing 700+ stores a year. In France, Subway handed development to the fund McWin, targeting 600 new stores.

Beyond the video — added insight & corrections

Corrections: the per-store figure is ~$450k/year (the transcript's "4,500€" is a garble), vs rivals ~$1M+; the Canadian "half-soy chicken" claim was disputed (Subway sued for $210M) — treat as contested; the 2023-25 items (Roark, McWin, China) are recent, around my cutoff.

The incentive gem — a royalty on gross: because HQ took 8% of sales, not profit, the parent's interest was store count and gross volume, and it was structurally indifferent to whether any franchisee made money — "opening is winning." That one design choice explains the cannibalisation (two small stores pay the same or more than one big one), the grow-at-all-costs obsession, and franchisees earning less than their own employees. For a structurer, it's the sharpest illustration that incidence and base of a fee (gross vs profit, who bears it) determine behaviour — align the fee with your partner's profit or the model cannibalises itself. It pairs with Marie Blachère (Case 29): Blachère kept ~95% company-owned to capture margin; Subway franchised for growth and misaligned everyone.

The loss-leader-promise trap: the $5 footlong was a brilliant demand tactic that became a prison — a price the customer got hooked on, that couldn't rise as costs did, and that the franchisee (not HQ, still taking its 8%) had to absorb — and it repriced the brand down-market for good (fresh → cheap). Two lessons: a fixed price promise is a liability once costs move, and discounting can move you down-market permanently (Club Med, Case 34; Gucci, Case 19).

Governance and jurisdiction: oversight delegated to people who directly compete with those they oversee — armed with an un-passable rulebook and mandatory arbitration that removes the courts — is a self-dealing red flag. And the French franchisees' win (annulling the New-York-under-Dutch-law clauses) is the "where a dispute is heard decides your protection" lesson — the theme of Leclerc/Eurelec (Case 22), Doctolib (Case 31) and BIC's French-law protections (Case 26); for a cross-border structurer, governing law and forum are never boilerplate.

The financialisation endgame: Roark completes the thread across the file — for a fund, unit count is nothing, profit-per-unit is everything, so it pilots a "fall" (record profit while closing 700+/year) that's really a sort. Same logic as Apollo/Grand Frais (Case 25), Picard's dividend recap (Case 20), Maison du Monde's loan-to-own (Case 32) and Fosun/Club Med (Case 34) — and the caution that the engine (multiply, squeeze, then a fund optimises) is now arriving in France via McWin: a shiny new opening isn't brand health, it can be the front end of the same multiply-cannibalise-close machine.

The closing lesson & your intersection: Subway spent 50 years asking how many stores it could open, never how many it could keep alive — the vanity metric vs the real one (Rovio, Case 14; the "read the real number" thread of Ireland's GNI*, LVMH's mix, Grand Frais's velocity). For you: royalty-on-gross-vs-profit incentive design, per-unit viability over vanity count, the loss-leader-promise liability, conflict-of-interest and jurisdiction diligence, and the PE right-sizing lens — an incentives-and-financialisation case squarely in your craft.

SFR / Patrick Drahi — Buy a Giant With Its Own MoneyVideo case · The LBO, ring-fencing the crown jewel & consolidation's bill
▶ Video0/14▶
The one ideaA man who didn't have €13B bought a giant with the giant's own money — by loading the acquisition debt inside SFR, so your monthly plan repaid his loan. Then, when the debt crushed it, he ring-fenced the best asset beyond his creditors and forced them to erase €8.6B. In leverage, control follows the assets and the debt — not the equity or the operations.
The story (in brief)

In 2011 a French mobile plan cost €60-80/month and felt normal — three operators had shared a fat oligopoly for 20 years (French plans among Europe's most expensive). Then on 10 January 2012 Xavier Niel unveiled Free Mobile: €2 and €19.99 plans, a third of rivals' prices, calling the incumbents' customers "pigeons." The market flipped in 24 hours; SFR's margins collapsed and its owner Vivendi decided to sell. Two men bid: Martin Bouygues (an industrial merger, state-backed, €15B cash) and an unknown — Patrick Drahi, who owned Numericable, a cable operator 10× smaller than SFR. Drahi had spent the 1990s buying small rural cable networks nobody wanted with one repeated move: borrow, buy, cut costs, repay a little, restart bigger; by 2001 his Luxembourg holding Altice spanned four continents, cemented by one thing — debt. In April 2014 Altice bought 80% of SFR for ~€13.4B (with a public promise: no social plan for 3 years).

He didn't have the €13B. Like buying a flat with the flat as collateral, he borrowed against SFR and installed the debt inside SFR — so from that day the plan revenues of 20M subscribers serviced the debt of a man who'd bought the company with money he didn't have. "Monsieur 30%" (his cost-cutting nickname) then ran the extraction: the 3-year promise carried a buried escape clause he could trigger himself, and in 2016 he cut ~5,000 jobs (a third of staff) as "voluntary departures"; he offshored customer service to a Moroccan call-centre he owned (44h/week, ~€400/month, 10× cheaper), leaving <40 people for 20M subscribers; between 2014-2022 SFR went from 15,000 to under 7,000 staff. SFR fell to last in customer satisfaction and bled 1.3M customers a year. Yet he also modernised — 4G first in France, rural fibre, the low-cost Red brand — because he did both: a little gas, a lot of loan (~€10B of interest since 2014, ~€500 per subscriber). "Worth more on paper, less at the end of the line."

Where it stands

By 2023-24, ~€24B of debt strangled SFR as rates rose (each point ≈ €250M/year), amid a Portugal corruption scandal (co-founder Armando Pereira arrested; a French inquiry opened) and a hack that leaked 450,000 internal documents. Drahi's endgame was pure structuring: he moved €3.8B of asset-sale cash to Luxembourg, placed SFR's crown-jewel fibre network (XpFibre) in a fiducie (a bank-held legal safe) beyond creditors' reach, and told them "erase a third of the debt or get nothing." It worked — Altice's debt fell from €24.1B to €15.5B (~€8.6B erased forever, validated Aug 2025, the biggest private-debt renegotiation in French history); in exchange the creditors (BlackRock, PIMCO, Fidelity, Elliott) took ~45% of the equity, and then pushed for a sale. Per the video (the 2025-26 breakup, around my cutoff): in April 2026 SFR was carved up and sold to its three rivals for ~€20.35B — Bouygues (the 2014 loser) taking the biggest piece (42%, the enterprise business + rural network), Free 31%, Orange 27% — with 8,000-12,000 more jobs at risk (a 4th social plan in 12 years). And the last bill is yours: France goes from four operators to three for the first time since 2012, and (as Austria's 2012 "4-to-3" showed) prices rise. The disruptor Niel, who broke prices, buys a third of the carcass — the consolidator now, and the pigeon is us again.

The people & the dates (references)

Capture the lessons

Beyond the video — added insight

With Maison du Monde (Case 32), the two most on-point cases in this library — from opposite ends: there, creditors used the security package to seize a company; here, a financier weaponised the same structures to strip his creditors — loading the debt inside the target, moving the fibre into a fiducie and the cash to Luxembourg, then forcing an €8.6B write-off by controlling the collateral. Both teach one law of leveraged finance: control follows the assets and the debt, not the equity or the operations.

The LBO's real consequence: because SFR's own revenues (~€10B of interest) serviced Drahi's acquisition debt, the customers and staff effectively paid for the purchase — "worth more on paper, less at the end of the line." The value extracted was transferred, not created. For a financier, it's the sharpest illustration that a leveraged buyout can enrich the acquirer while hollowing the operating business — and why the interest burden, not the valuation, is the number to watch.

The lender's lesson from the ring-fencing: your recovery depends entirely on whether the borrower can move the assets away from you. The fibre-in-a-fiducie and cash-to-Luxembourg are the mirror of Maison du Monde: there the security package trapped the company for creditors; here it let the borrower escape them. The covenants against asset transfers and the security package are the deal — everything else is commentary.

The market-structure lesson is your infrastructure world: "4 to 3 raises prices" is evidence-based (Austria 2012, measured by the European Commission), and it rhymes with Doctolib (Case 31, monopoly → price rises). Energy and telecom are both concentrated, regulated and essential — the same dynamics you underwrite. And the profound cycle irony: Niel, who broke prices to liberate the market in 2012, becomes the consolidator who buys into the re-concentration that may close the cheap-price era. Disruption and consolidation are phases of the same cycle.

Your intersection: the LBO-debt-on-target, the fiducie ring-fencing, the forced haircut, the debt-to-equity, "read the escape clause," the invest-vs-extract nuance, and the consolidation-price economics — this case is your profession, and with Case 32 forms a two-part masterclass in leveraged finance and restructuring from both sides.

Make it click — similar plays

Maison du Monde (Case 32) — the other pole: creditors seize via the security package; here the borrower strips them with it. Toys "R" Us (Case 12), Picard (Case 20), Dell (Case 17) — the LBO/leverage family (extraction vs transformation vs debt-on-target). Club Med (Case 34) — dilution/foreign-owner loss of control (the equity road to the same place).

The market & the funds: Doctolib (Case 31) — consolidation/monopoly raises prices; Grand Frais/Apollo (Case 25) & Subway/Roark (Case 35) — the financialisation endgame; Mulliez (Cases 21-23), Leclerc (Case 22), Schwarz (Case 24) — opaque, concentrated control structures (11 people ran Altice's four continents).

Your version: know where the debt sits and whose cash flow serves it, read every guarantee's escape clause, watch for (or protect) the ring-fenced crown jewel, and price the consumer-and-regulatory cost of consolidation in the essential sectors you finance.

Conforama — The Pawn Nobody Played for ItselfVideo case · A profitable company as an asset, the cash-siphon & the €6.5B fraud
▶ Video0/14▶
The one ideaConforama wasn't killed by IKEA, Amazon or e-commerce — it was everyone's pawn, played by no one for itself. Across six owners it was moved, kept "in a drawer," drained as a cash machine, and finally propped up by €6.5B of invented profits. The moment you're profitable without control, you're an asset to be used, not a business to be built.
The people & the dates (references) — four owners, 60 years, one pawn

The founders (1967): Pierre and Guy Sordoyer (with Jean Molle, Jacques Ragageot) — merchants, not heirs or financiers — launched flat-pack, self-service, bargain furniture ("sell furniture like supermarket tins"), first store at Saint-Priest (near Lyon), Dec 1967. A refused franchise birthed the rival: in 1967 a Le Havre entrepreneur, André Venturini, asked to open a Conforama franchise, was told no, and opened his own discount store — But — launching a 53-year war on the same turf, same customers, same weekend promos (But buys Conforama in the end). Owner 2 — the Willot brothers: four Roubaix industrialists (textile/distribution — the Boussac/Dior group, the US "Korvette" chain) whose empire (Agache-Willot) collapsed into a 1981 bankruptcy, trial and conviction; Conforama kept trading, "more solid than its owners." Owner 3 — François Pinault (1991): a Breton who left school at 16 for the family timber business and built PPR by serial acquisition "à coup de reprise, pas de diplôme"; he ran Conforama as a real business (Spain/Portugal/Italy/Switzerland, >200 stores, revenue toward €3bn) for ~20 years — its "golden age" — but his real prize was luxury (by 2005 luxury was ~17% of PPR revenue, ~35% of profit), and in 2018 Conforama was the asset he’d cash to build Kering (Cases 19/28 — the dépôt-de-bilan-to-LVMH-rival arc). Owner 4 — Steinhoff / Markus Jooste (2011): the South African accountant (racing stables) whose Steinhoff International bought Conforama (~€1.2bn) as a listed-group showpiece. The fraud (Dec 2017): Jooste quit on 5 Dec 2017; the accounts couldn’t be certified, the share fell ~60% in a day (~€14bn vaporised), and PwC later found ~€6.5bn of fabricated transactions (2014-2017) — phantom purchases, Excel-only subsidiaries, profits "written in pen." It spread into every unit: Conforama France accumulated ~€500m of losses from 2011 as the parent "pumped the till" to patch its own holes (French suppliers unpaid while cash flowed to South Africa). Jooste died in 2024 amid prosecution. The end (2020): COVID closures (Mar 2020), banks dragging their feet, cessation de paiement — and in July 2020 the historic rival But/Mobilux bought Conforama France. Today: it survived everything; ownership went Lyonnais → Parisian → Breton → South African → Austrian/American; by 2025 French furniture fell ~10%, a Chinese platform took ~9 points of décor share in a year, Amazon locked e-commerce, and But/Conforama CEO Alexandre Palk pledged 15-20% of revenue into AI/online. The sign-off: "Conforama never held the keys to its own destiny" — and Arnault and Pinault, whose Gucci-vs-LVMH Notre-Dame-donation war explains how French luxury was built, only ever crossed paths around Conforama.

The story (in brief)

Four Lyon merchants founded Conforama in 1967 — furniture sold like canned goods (self-service, flat-pack, slashed prices), slogan "the country where life is cheaper." It grew fast and profitably — and that was the trap: by 1976 the founders were already out, because to a financier a profitable company isn't an enterprise, it's an asset. It passed through the Willot conglomerate (which collapsed in 1981), then to Bernard Arnault, who bought the whole ruined lot (textiles, Conforama, Le Bon Marché) in 1984 for one thing inside the box: Dior — and kept Conforama seven years "in a drawer," undirected, while it began losing ground. In 1991 he sold it to François Pinault, a true merchant who actually grew it (200+ stores, ~€3B) — until IKEA overtook it (2005-2008) while Pinault looked elsewhere (Gucci, Saint Laurent, ~€8.6B into luxury). His son renamed PPR "Kering," and in that house discount furniture was "the grease stain on the evening gown," so in 2011 he sold Conforama at its peak — into the worst possible hands.

The buyer was Steinhoff International, run by South African accountant Marcus Jooste, whose talent was acquisition, not accounting. Steinhoff piled up chains (Mattress Firm, Poundland, Pepkor, and Conforama for €1.2B) to become world #2 in furniture. Because it was listed and its valuation rested on market confidence, it needed its subsidiaries to look flourishing — hence a Ligue 1 title sponsorship (€25M, on every jersey before 121M viewers) and a giant warehouse. But behind the facade the walls were cardboard: on 5 December 2017 Jooste walked out, the accounts couldn't be certified, the stock lost 60% in a day (~€14B gone), and PwC found Steinhoff had fabricated €6.5B of transactions that never happened — phantom purchases, subsidiaries that existed only in Excel, profits written in pen. And the fraud had drained its subsidiaries: Steinhoff pumped Conforama's till to plug its own holes (~€500M of French losses) while the stores stayed full on Saturdays. The €25M naming had been paid with fictitious profits.

Where it stands

Conforama went under judicial surveillance; Steinhoff's €316M "rescue" mostly repaid debt and funded the very layoffs the looting caused; asset fire-sales (Spain/Portugal, Showroomprivé at half price) repaid creditors, not the business; the 2019 social plan cut ~1,900 of 9,000 jobs. Steinhoff — worth ~€20B at its peak — was liquidated to zero in 2023; and in March 2024, the day before he was to surrender, Marcus Jooste died by suicide — a stark reminder that fraud of this scale destroys companies, jobs and lives, not just accounts. In 2020, drained and in cessation de paiement, Conforama was bought by its 53-year rival But (founded in 1967 by an entrepreneur Conforama had refused a franchise) — merged into But Conforama Holding: 500 stores, ~€4.6B combined revenue, >25% of the French furniture market, ahead of IKEA. Per the video (2025 items around my cutoff): the true owners now are an Austrian furniture group (XXXLutz) and a New York fund — Conforama no longer has a single shareholder from the country of its slogan. The question is no longer "will it survive?" (it survived everything) but "how long before the new owner decides French discount furniture isn't its business?"

The capstone of the ownership/financialisation thread: across the French cluster (Picard, Grand Frais/Apollo, Maison du Monde, Club Med, Subway, SFR), Conforama is the purest case of a company that was never a business to its owners, only an asset — moved, drawered, drained, defrauded and merged, across six owners "everyone's pawn, played by no one for itself." The central lesson: the moment you're profitable, a financier sees an asset, not an enterprise — and profitability without control is a target, not a fortress.

It closes the SFR loop and is its twin: that video's teaser was this story (the man who died on a South African beach). And Steinhoff draining Conforama's till is the near-exact twin of Altice pumping SFR (Case 36) — the parent bleeding the healthy subsidiary — except here the parent's whole engine was accounting fraud.

The new lesson — verify the numbers: €6.5B of profits "written in pen," hidden inside a sprawl of 40 brands in 30 countries controlled by essentially one man. Fraud lives in complexity and opacity; the harder a structure is to audit, the more the numbers demand verification. And the facade point — spending on visible flourish (the naming, the warehouse) funded by fictitious profits — is the darkest version of the "read the real number, not the show" thread (Ireland's GNI*, LVMH's mix, Rovio's downloads, Subway's store count). Steinhoff is Europe/Africa's Enron or Wirecard.

The bonus tie to LVMH and Kering: Arnault (Case 28) and Pinault (Case 19) both used Conforama as a means — Arnault to reach Dior, Pinault as a cash-generating asset he shed to chase luxury ("the grease stain on the evening gown"). A profitable, un-glamorous cash generator is often the funding source, or the discard, for an owner chasing a more prestigious game.

Your intersection: this is your investing worldview at its starkest (profitable = an asset to be moved, not protected), plus the governance/credit red flags you diligence — the subsidiary-as-ATM cash-siphon (the SFR twin), the facade-funded-by-fraud, accounting fraud hiding in complexity, and rescue-money-follows-the-debt. And "survival ≠ control" is the thesis of your whole French cluster: a company that doesn't control its own capital structure and ownership controls nothing.

Make it click — similar plays

The thread & the frauds: Maison du Monde (Case 32), Grand Frais/Apollo (Case 25), Picard (Case 20), Club Med (Case 34), Subway (Case 35) — the financialisation / "who really owns it" thread Conforama caps; Enron / Wirecard — the great accounting frauds (profits written in pen, hidden in complexity); and the "read the real number, not the show" thread (Ireland, Case 18; LVMH, Case 28; Rovio, Case 14; Subway, Case 35).

Your version: never mistake profitability for control, trace the cash between parent and subsidiary, treat opacity as a red flag not a strength — and remember that who owns you, and whether you own your own capital structure, decides everything.
