GoPro — The Camera That Thought It Was AppleVideo case · The monoproduct in a niche, the identity delusion & the squeeze from above and beside
▶ Video0/14▶
The one ideaGoPro went from "the Apple of cameras" to near-oblivion — the stock from $94 to under $1.30 in a decade, losing millions a month. It sold a lifestyle brilliantly and mistook that for a moat; convinced it was a tech giant, it spent like a media empire and forgot the one thing it actually was: a very good camera in a niche that saturates.
The story (in brief)

It began in 2002 when Nick Woodman, a Californian surfer on a trip to Indonesia, wanted to film his own sessions and, finding no camera that could, jury-rigged a small, rugged one you strap to your wrist — the first GoPro. As the concept improved and YouTube exploded, skaters, riders, divers and base-jumpers all adopted it to film their exploits; it became not a camera but a symbol of freedom, adventure and adrenaline — a small object that made you the hero of your own story. And the strategy was brilliant: GoPro didn't sell a product, it sold a lifestyle, flooding social media with viral footage and partnering with Red Bull and the X Games until everyone wanted one, even weekend cyclists. Revenue rocketed from $240M (2011) to $1.6B (2015); the 2014 IPO sent the valuation past $11B. "The Apple of the action camera." The coronation — and the summit. The higher you climb, the more the fall can hurt.

Nothing is more dangerous than a company that believes it's unstoppable. High on its success, GoPro decided it was more than a camera-maker — a lifestyle brand, a tech giant, a future Apple — and spent accordingly: it doubled headcount after the IPO, the CEO took a ~$285M package (the highest-paid in the US at the time), and the real money-burn was the plan to become a media company — poaching an ex-HBO/Hulu executive, launching streaming channels on Xbox and Roku, producing original content. A total flop, shut down in 2017 after billions, the first in a long series — because behind the inspiring storytelling there was still just a camera. A very good one, but serving an ultra-specific market (athletes, creators, adventurers) that saturates fast, because a GoPro doesn't break, doesn't age quickly, and once you own one you don't buy another every year. Worse, the company couldn't diversify — no new flagship, no breakthrough, no ecosystem, just iterative Hero 5, Hero 6 with minor changes and no more "wow." GoPro lived in a bubble where it thought it was Apple while remaining a monoproduct in a niche.

Where it lands

Its second bet, in 2016, was drones. The idea dated to 2014, when GoPro approached DJI for a partnership — DJI builds the drones, GoPro the onboard cameras, together they'd dominate — but GoPro reportedly demanded two-thirds of the profits, DJI walked, and GoPro went it alone with the Karma (2016). Bugs, instability, crashes; every Karma was recalled just 16 days after launch — a financial disaster and a reputational blow. A second attempt also failed, and the drone division closed in 2018. Beyond the money lost, the real damage was that GoPro slashed R&D on its core product — the camera — at the exact moment that was the nerve of the war: smartphones were integrating ever-better cameras, cheap accessories (stabilisers, waterproof cases) were everywhere, and direct competition arrived. In 2017 Insta360 shipped a 4K 360° action cam, and for the first time GoPro went from leader to follower — its me-too Fusion was better quality but $300 dearer and worse for social sharing. DJI, meanwhile, integrated smartphones into its ecosystem and focused on what its cameras add over a phone. GoPro never adapted to the smartphone-centred world. It has since steadied revenue and margins — going direct-to-consumer (often cheaper than retail, without the distributor's cut) and launching GoPro Plus (cloud, discounts, tools, $50/yr, a free year with any camera) — and in 2021, after five years of losses, posted a $371M profit, tripling the stock from $4 to $13. But 2023-24 brought heavy losses again: sales still slipping, operating costs still rising, and though units and subscribers grew, ferocious price competition forced GoPro to slash prices. It's now a niche brand for a handful of enthusiasts where it dreamed of a global creation ecosystem — still ~700 employees keeping the machine running, but the magic is gone, because it never reinvented the product, only iterated in a market that moved on.

Capture the lessons

Beyond the video — added insight

The identity-delusion is the gem, and the spine of the whole story: GoPro thought it was Apple when it was a monoproduct in a niche, and that self-image licensed everything fatal — the ~$285M pay, the doubled headcount, the media empire, the drone adventure. It's the inverse of the return-to-source discipline (Porsche 56, Nike 58): those recovered by remembering what they were; GoPro fell by forgetting. Diagnose what you are, coldly, before you spend like what you wish you were — the honest one-sentence self-diagnosis is a survival tool.

The pincer is the sharp investing structure: a single product squeezed from above by the smartphone (the free substitute that keeps getting better — the Apple/commoditisation thread, Cases 41 and 60) and from beside by a cheaper, sharper rival (Insta360, DJI) has nowhere to stand. It's the durable-monoproduct trap: the very durability that made the product great (doesn't break, doesn't age) caps the market, and with no ecosystem there's no second leg to stand on when the pincer closes.

The failed-diversification-that-starves-the-core rhymes with HTC (61): both had a hit, both chased away from it (HTC into the low end and acquisitions, GoPro into media and drones), both cut discipline on the core, both went from leader to follower — and the first me-too product (HTC's flood, GoPro's Fusion) marks the date the moat broke. Adjacent bets are only safe once the core is defended and funded; the new frontier financed by starving the old loses both.

The 2021-profit-then-relapse is a clean investing lesson for your value screen: distinguish a margin fix (direct-to-consumer, a subscription — real, but operational) from a demand fix (a revived product moat — durable); GoPro's recovery was the former, so the relapse followed. And growing units with widening losses is a pricing-power failure — read the price line, not the unit line. The DJI-deal greed (demanding two-thirds) is the deal-discipline lesson: overreaching for the split can forfeit the deal, exactly the negotiation trap you underwrite in project finance — take the smaller share of the bigger outcome.

Your intersection: the identity-delusion (diagnose what you are before you spend) and iteration-without-reinvention are your management-and-strategy radar; the pincer, the margin-fix-vs-demand-fix, the price-line and the me-too-as-moat-signal are your value-investing craft; the durable-product demand ceiling is a sizing discipline; and the DJI-deal greed is your deal-table discipline. It's the monoproduct-in-a-niche cautionary — the camera that believed the story it sold.

Make it click — similar plays

HTC (Case 61) — the sibling: a hit squandered by chasing away from the core (media/drones ≈ low-end/acquisitions), leader-to-follower, the me-too product as the moat's death date. Apple (Cases 41 & 60) — the smartphone as the commoditising force from above, and the identity/promise questions. Porsche (Case 56) & Nike (Case 58) — the inverse: return-to-source by remembering what you are (GoPro forgot).

The niche & the fad: Holy (Case 59) — the saturation ceiling and niche-to-mass question; Angry Birds/Rovio (Case 14) — the one-hit-wonder that couldn't follow up; Wish (the video's teaser) — another billion-dollar collapse. Your version: diagnose what you actually are before you spend, find the repurchase engine, defend and fund the core before any adjacent bet, and read the pincer and the price line — because a lifestyle amplifies a great product, it doesn't replace one.

The Economics of Formula 1 — The Money Isn't in the RaceVideo case · The toll-booth owner, the loss-making teams & the franchise moat
▶ Video0/14▶
The one ideaA single F1 car costs as much to build as a luxury villa, and drivers crash them into walls at 300km/h every weekend; teams spend $400M+ a year knowing they'll probably never win. It looks like a billionaires' Squid Game — until you follow the money and see the real business isn't the race. It's the toll booth that owns the sport, the B2B deals in the VIP suites, and a franchise value that only goes up.
The story (in brief)

The 1996 Monaco Grand Prix made the risk vivid: after a storm, chaos — by lap one three cars were out, five laps later eight, and only three of the field finished all 75 laps, while team owners and sponsors watched their investments explode into the walls from yachts in the harbour. So at what point does an investment doing 300km/h become a good financial decision? Follow the money. It starts with the Formula One Group, the listed company behind the entire sport, which in 2024 generated $3.65B in revenue (the sport's operator, not the teams) from four sources: broadcasting rights (~33%, ~$1.2B — the biggest), Grand Prix hosting fees (~29% — circuits and countries pay $15-50M a year for the privilege), sponsors (~20% — Pirelli, Rolex, Aramco), and extras (~18% — tickets, hospitality, merch licensing). The operator keeps most of it but redistributes ~38% (~$1.2B) to the ten teams under the Concorde Agreement (binding the operator, the teams and the FIA — F1's FIFA). And it's not an even split: the money is allocated by end-of-season performance and by how long a team has been in F1, so the oldest and biggest — Ferrari, with the largest longevity bonus, and Mercedes — can draw $150M+, while the smallest teams get $60-70M.

That sounds like a lot until you see the cost of running a team. Before 2021 there was no spending limit: Ferrari, Mercedes and Red Bull poured in unlimited sums ($400-500M a year) to crush the field — a chasm between rich and small, predictable races, teams condemned to stagnate. The money went into the car above all (hundreds of engineers spending millions to claw a tiny optimisation, every part a purpose-built prototype), plus labour (sometimes 1,200+ staff), global logistics, and drivers (from ~$500k to $60M for Hamilton or Verstappen). In 2021 F1 finally imposed a budget cap — $145M, cut to $135M now — but with a loophole: it excludes driver salaries, top management and marketing, so it rebalanced things a little but didn't stop the biggest teams from legally continuing to dominate.

Where it lands

How do small teams compete? Like any small business — by being creative. Haas entered with a completely different model: instead of building the car itself, it bought everything it legally could from Ferrari (engine, suspension, gearbox), starting with just ~250 employees, a fraction of the giants. But not any billionaire can join: to enter the club of ten you first pay an "anti-dilution tax" to compensate the existing teams for their diluted share of the prize pot — set at $450M for Cadillac's 2026 entry, split among the other ten — then build the infrastructure (factory, offices, simulators, a wind tunnel: $100-200M), design and build the first car ($100-150M), and cover two years of operating costs before you've warmed a tyre. Half a billion to a billion dollars before you race. It's the world's most expensive and most vicious private club, where each new application raises the entry ticket — a system that's no longer about sport but about protecting a franchise. And how do teams make money? The prize money isn't enough; the real ticket is sponsors, priced by logo size and count (Oracle pays Red Bull ~$100M a year to be title sponsor and put its name in "Oracle Red Bull Racing"; good placements run $10-30M; mini-stickers $500k). But the true value is hidden backstage in the Paddock Club, F1's luxury hospitality — where sponsors bring clients to dazzle them, sign contracts and network; billion-dollar handshakes happen there every race weekend. It's pure B2B marketing, and seen that way, $50M to put your logo on a car that might hit a wall is worth it.

Are sponsors enough to make teams profitable? Historically, no — most run at a loss, kept afloat by wealthy owners or carmakers who treat it as a giant marketing expense. Ferrari doesn't care whether its F1 division is profitable — it's a colossal advertisement for the brand; if it profits, bonus (and it does). Same for Mercedes (€97M profit in 2023) and McLaren (€15M). But the real story is valuation: since Liberty Media bought the Formula One Group in 2017, audiences exploded worldwide — thanks to Netflix's Drive to Survive and, more recently, the Brad Pitt film — turning F1 into a mass sport. In 2024 the average team is worth $2.3B (Ferrari $4.8B, Mercedes $3.9B); Williams, bought by Dorilton Capital in 2020 for $180M, is now worth $1.24B — a 600% return in under five years, the best financial decision of the decade, and exactly why the club is so closed and the entry ticket so high. Liberty Media itself bought the Formula One Group for $4.6B in 2017; it's now valued around $33B — a ~7x. The paradox: what draws the fans — the race — is often just the pretext. The real business plays out elsewhere: the VIP suites, the sponsorship contracts, the data centres, the many-zero industrial deals.

Beyond the video — added insight

The own-the-platform lesson is the gem, and it's the toll-booth thread at its purest: Liberty Media 7x'd its money owning the sport ($4.6B → ~$33B) while most teams lose money racing in it — the same structure as AWS (Case 11, the toll on the internet), Nvidia (Case 01, the enabling layer), and Le Bon Coin (Case 53, own the marketplace). The P&L-vs-valuation distinction is a clean investing lesson for your value screen: most teams lose money yet are worth billions because the return is appreciation and strategic value, not annual profit (Williams: 600% in five years). It pairs with the "loss as marketing budget" insight (Ferrari) — a rich parent running an operation for brand-building means "unprofitable" misreads the purpose. Underwrite the asset's value and what its spending buys, not just whether it clears a profit — directly relevant to how you'd value a strategic asset held for reasons beyond its own P&L.

The franchise-scarcity moat and the entry ticket are the sharp structural lesson: a closed club of ten that charges a rising anti-dilution tax ($450M for Cadillac) to enter is a self-reinforcing moat — the more valuable the franchise, the higher the price to join, the more valuable it becomes. It's the scarcity/pricing-power thread (Hermès 19, Le Bon Coin's captive audience 53) applied to membership itself; the value is the closed door.

The read-the-exclusions and read-the-split lessons are your diligence and deal craft: a budget cap that excludes driver pay, management and marketing barely binds (the biggest kept dominating "legally"), and Concorde money split by performance-and-longevity rewards incumbency — so the formula, not the pool, is the business model. For a project financier, it's the reminder that a covenant, cap or waterfall is only as real as its carve-outs, and that who the allocation rules favour matters more than the headline number. And the Haas asset-light model is the "rent the incumbent's scale, compete on what's left" lesson (the counterpoint to vertical integration, echoing Holy 59).

Your intersection: own-the-platform/toll-booth and forward-integration are your infrastructure/capture-the-economics thesis; P&L-vs-valuation and loss-as-marketing are your value-investing and strategic-asset lens; the franchise-scarcity moat and the entry ticket are your durability screen; read-the-exclusions and read-the-split are your project-finance covenant-and-waterfall craft; and the demand catalyst (Drive to Survive) is the re-rating lesson. A league-economics case that maps cleanly onto who captures the economics of any complex, multi-party venture — exactly your world.

China & the Conquest of the Oceans — Who Builds the Ships Controls the TradeVideo case · The 30-year state-industrial playbook, maritime sovereignty & strategic dependence
▶ Video0/14▶
The one ideaOne number says everything: ~50% of all the world's ships — cargo, tankers, container vessels — now come out of Chinese shipyards. Thirty years ago China couldn't build a modern ship. Behind every vessel is not just steel but power, commerce and strategic dominance: whoever controls the shipyards controls the fleet, and whoever controls the fleet has leverage over the trade of every nation.
A note on framing

A resource-and-geopolitics case, presented factually and neutrally; I extract the industrial-strategy and investing lessons and don't take a side on any sovereignty dispute. The Trump/Panama-Canal material is presented as reported political claims, around my cutoff, not as established fact.

The story (in brief)

We think of economic dominance as metals, militaries, technology or energy — and forget ships. Yet 90% of world trade goes by sea: your phone, clothes, food and computer almost certainly travelled on a cargo ship, and those ships must be designed, built and maintained in shipyards. So whoever controls the shipyards controls the global fleet, and controlling the fleet is leverage over every country's trade. It's no accident that the US became the top power by building thousands of Liberty Ships in WWII, that Japan built its 1960s economic miracle around shipbuilding, or that South Korea reached the G20 on giants like Hyundai Heavy Industries. The recipe is always the same: guarantee your exports can leave without depending on third parties, capture the value on international maritime contracts, become indispensable to the world's shipowners, and — in a crisis — retain the capacity to build a military fleet at speed.

That is exactly what China wanted — but in 1990 it was nonexistent in the industry: no know-how, no serious infrastructure, no reputation, with the orders going to Japan and South Korea. In that context the government set a simple objective — become the world's number one in shipbuilding — via a formidable 30-year industrial plan: massive subsidies for state shipyards; mergers of state groups into giants (in 2019 CSSC and CSIC merged into the world's largest shipbuilder, under direct Party control); ultra-privileged credit for Chinese shipowners (a state bank offers a rock-bottom loan to buy a container ship — on condition it's built in China); and sometimes a legal obligation to use a Chinese yard for national fleets. China first built itself a captive domestic market where buying foreign ships made no sense, then used it as a springboard to conquer the world. It worked: 5% of global ship production in 2003, past Japan by 2010, past South Korea by 2020, and ~50% today — alone. And not just volume but a move up-market: from basic rusty cargo ships to ultra-technological LNG carriers, giant container ships, latest-generation naval vessels and even cruise liners — cheaper and faster than the competition.

Where it lands

The West, meanwhile, simply gave up — yards closing one after another, not for lack of need but for lack of investment, vision and political will. Rather than compete on cargo and container ships, the few surviving European yards retreated to the high end (cruise liners, ferries, luxury yachts), and even European shipowners with deep maritime histories — Maersk, CMA CGM — now order in China because they can't do otherwise. The US is more extreme: it builds almost no civil cargo ships, and its merchant fleet depends nearly 100% on Asia, including for repairs and spare parts. The West has become strategically dependent on China for something as vital as its own seaborne trade — many ships used by Western firms are now financed, insured or even registered via China-linked structures. In a war, a geopolitical tension or a simple logistics rupture, the impact would be immediate: blocked ports, halted supply chains, a paralysed world economy (recall the panic when the Ever Given blocked the Suez Canal for seven days — experts estimated $9B a day in cost). And China doesn't stop at building ships: through COSCO and other state groups it increasingly controls the ports they pass through — terminals at Piraeus, Antwerp, Djibouti, Haifa, Valencia, even a 14% stake in the Port of Seattle. From building the vessels to running the ports, Beijing is gradually locking up the world's trade routes — a rope Trump said he felt around the neck when he claimed the Panama Canal was China-controlled and hinted at taking it back by force: two visions of power, the American exercised through bombs, the Chinese through economics. And the next step is already launched — heavy investment in autonomous ships, hydrogen and even nuclear propulsion, with one goal: not to catch up with the West but to overtake it for good. (The video links this to China's quiet 2015 purchase of Club Med — Case 34 — as another piece of empire-building.)

Ceding the boring volume layer looks like smart specialisation until you've surrendered the lever.

It's the counter-model to the financialisation/short-termism thread (Boeing-style, Apple buybacks 41): patient, coordinated capital vs. harvest-now capital.

The vertical-control-of-the-whole-route and strategic-dependence-tail lessons are your risk and value-chain craft: owning both ships and ports locks the entire route (the deepest moat owns every link — the vertical-integration spine, BYD 43, Luxottica 03, applied to trade infrastructure), and concentration in a vital invisible layer is a latent systemic risk (Ever Given, ~$9B/day) — price the fragility of the chokepoint, not just the efficiency of the chain. And the reinvest-into-the-next-frontier lesson (autonomous, hydrogen, nuclear ships) is the compounder discipline: the durable winner buys the next lead before securing the last.

Wish — The Machine That Lost More the More It SoldVideo case · Negative operating leverage, loyalty-to-price & the trust the growth never bought
▶ Video0/14▶
The one ideaWish IPO'd at $17B in 2020 — the world's most-downloaded shopping app, the third-biggest e-commerce site in the US, a founder who'd turned down $10B from Bezos. Three years later the stock was down 99% and it sold for $173M. The fatal flaw was hidden in plain sight: a model that lost more money the more it sold, built on customers who were never loyal to Wish — only to the price.
The story (in brief)

Wish came from the vision of Piotr Szulczewski, an ex-Google ad-optimisation engineer who in 2010 wanted to build the "Google Ads of shopping": a marketplace where products aren't searched for but discovered by chance, pushed by an algorithm watching your browsing habits. You open the app and the algorithm serves what you didn't know you wanted — dozens of cheap, colourful, often useless but addictive objects, designed like a mobile game, each scroll a little dopamine hit, prices ridiculously low, the interface optimised for impulse buying, and aggressive Facebook ads on top. It worked: in a few years Wish became an e-commerce giant without owning a single warehouse or holding any stock, because everything shipped directly from small sellers in China via the heavily subsidised ePacket system. That's the key — Wish broke prices by breaking the logistics chain: no stock, no intermediary, factory-direct delivery, and, crucially, no quality filter. By 2016 the success was global and Szulczewski was invited to a confidential meeting with Jeff Bezos at Amazon HQ (NDAs, lawyers — a clear takeover intent, rumoured at $10B); Bezos was his idol, the perfect opportunity — and he refused, telling Bezos he had no intention of selling. Alibaba offered the same $10B; he refused again, though Wish was then valued at ~$3B. His vision: Wish would do $100B in revenue, a quarter of Walmart's sales. Revenue kept climbing — $1.9B by 2019, valuation $8.7B, 400M+ users, the most-downloaded shopping app in the world — and the 2020 IPO raised $1B+ at a $14B valuation. Szulczewski was on top of the world, and about to come crashing down.

The flaw was in the engine itself. The absurd ads (a bin-bag as underwear, a USB pregnancy test) went viral because the algorithm matched products to browsing habits — but browsing habits mean everything and nothing. See an ad for a motorcycle helmet for chickens and you'll stop scrolling and click, even with no bike and no chicken; to the algorithm you've ticked every box, so it pushes the ad harder. Wish's campaigns were perfectly optimised to generate traffic and clicks — but not sales. And Wish spent enormously — $1B+ a year, the biggest spender on Facebook and Instagram — while never being profitable. Not startup-not-profitable: in 2024 its net margin was −174%, meaning it spent $2.74 for every $1 of revenue. The maths are terrible — the more it sold, the more it lost: negative operating leverage, every new user nudging it closer to bankruptcy.

Where it lands

Then Covid hit — e-commerce boomed, seemingly good for Wish, but in fact catastrophic: every brand poured its ad budget into online, competitors copied Wish's one strategy and bid on the same keywords, and since ads are an auction, ad costs spiked — devastating for a company running millions of ads that couldn't turn a profit even when marketing was controlled. 2020 was its biggest sales year ($2.5B) and its biggest loss ($745M); in 2021, ten years in, revenue fell for the first time. And a deeper problem surfaced: customers were never loyal to Wish, only to the bargains and the absurd prices — and loyalty built on price is no loyalty, because the moment something is cheaper or less painful elsewhere (Amazon's experience and speed, then Shein and Temu), they leave. Worse, Wish was full of scams — $1 TVs, a dress order arriving as a tablecloth, a drone order arriving as an empty box, products that never came or came three months late, broken, or unrelated to the order — because Wish never controlled its sellers: anyone could sell anything, no quality control, no tracking, no after-sales, a three-month wait even to open a dispute. You can scam a customer once, maybe twice; by the third time they never come back. A 2022 reorganisation (new Google execs, a rebrand, new categories, actual customer support) was too little, too late — the reputation was already set — just as Temu arrived on Wish's exact positioning, backed by Chinese giant Pinduoduo ($170B market cap), with more money, more trust, direct access to Chinese suppliers without the scams, and two Super Bowl ads five months after launch. Wish couldn't respond: mass layoffs, the stock down 99%, monthly active users from 107M (2020) to under 12M (2022), a 89% collapse. Szulczewski resigned under pressure, and in February 2024 the parent (ContextLogic) sold Wish for $173M to Singapore's Qoo10 — nothing beside the $10B offer years earlier (though the timing was right: Qoo10 itself went bankrupt in late 2024).

▶ Original video ↗

The people & the dates (references)

Company: Wish (ContextLogic, founded 2010 by ex-Google/Yahoo engineers Piotr Szulczewski and Danny Zhang; IPO Dec 2020). Theme: negative operating leverage — it lost more the more it sold; demand rented from the ad auction; no lock-in. The blitzscaling failure (vs Uber 97).

Capture the lessons

Run the drills

Beyond the video — added insight

Wish is the dark mirror of Holy (Case 59): both are ad-driven, asset-light, China-sourced consumer plays — but Holy engineered positive unit economics (lose on the first order, profit on retention, two-thirds repeat) while Wish ran negative operating leverage (spend $2.74 per $1, no retention because loyalty was to price). Read them as a pair: the same asset-light, ad-fuelled shape can be a compounding machine or a bankruptcy machine, and the entire difference is the sign on the unit economics and whether anything but price binds the customer. It's the CAC/retention lesson (59) shown from the failure side.

The trust-as-the-product failure connects to Kape (57) and Duolingo (54): Wish cut the quality filter to break the price and filled the gap with scams, destroying the trust the business ran on — "scam a customer three times and they're gone." Trust is the real product in a marketplace, slow to build and instant to lose; the growth that ignores the customer experience borrows against a debt that comes due (and a late rebrand can't repay it). The corner you cut for the low price is often the corner the customer needed.

The demand-is-rented and single-imitable-strategy lessons are your investing craft: Wish rented its entire demand from ad auctions it didn't control (so competitors could bid up its costs and Covid crushed its ROI), and its one strategy had no defensible edge, so a better-funded, more-trusted copy (Temu, Pinduoduo-backed) ran the same play cleanly and killed it. Underwrite whether demand is owned or rented, and what stops a richer copy — the moat questions Wish flunked.

The refused-$10B lesson is the nuanced one for your value lens: a founder betting vision over a huge cheque is only vindicated if the underlying economics can actually reach the vision (Snapchat could; Wish's negative-leverage engine never could). A visionary revenue target on a broken model is just a bigger eventual loss — and the top line is the most misleading number, since Wish's biggest sales year was its biggest loss. Read the margin and the unit economics before the revenue and before the founder's story.

Your intersection: negative-operating-leverage and top-line-is-misleading are your value-investing red flags (read the sign and the margin before the growth); loyalty-to-price and trust-as-the-product are your moat/durability lens; demand-is-rented and single-imitable-strategy are your competitive-moat craft; and the refused-exit is the vision-vs-economics discipline. Groupon — The Fastest-Growing Startup That Burned Its Own MarketVideo case · No moat, the merchant-poisoning model & the gross-vs-net accounting trick
▶ Video0/14▶
The one ideaGroupon was the fastest-growing startup in history — 35 countries and $100M/month before it was two, an offer to be bought by Google for $6B, a $13B IPO. Then, almost nothing. It had no barrier to entry, a model that quietly bled the very merchants it depended on, and a top line inflated by an accounting trick the SEC forced it to unwind. It didn't just fall — it burned its own market to grow.
The story (in brief)

In 2008 Chicago, Andrew Mason launched "The Point," a site to organise collective social action — you only act if enough people commit together. He noticed the "group deal" logic worked far better for saving money than saving the planet, so he pivoted, and the pivot became Groupon ("group" + "coupon"): a merchant offers an irresistible deal conditional on enough people buying it — more buyers, better for everyone. It was natural viral marketing, every customer an ambassador, and it offered something new: free advertising where the merchant only pays if the customer shows up. No newspaper page, no flyers, no mistargeted Facebook campaign — the customer comes first, the bill comes after — a breath of fresh air for small merchants fighting to survive after the 2008 crisis. It went viral instantly: a Thai restaurant offers −70%, 1,200 customers in two days; a half-price massage, sold out in hours. Users signed up not to miss deals; merchants queued to reach the homepage. By 2010 Groupon was the fastest-growing startup in history — under two years old, in 35 countries, 10M+ active users, $100M+ a month in revenue. The press called it "the Groupon effect," a tsunami on local commerce; analysts declared traditional marketing dead; Google offered $6B to buy it — refused.

But the model was about to crack. Its core flaw: no barrier to entry — any coder could clone a local Groupon in three weeks, and that's exactly what happened: 200+ copycats in the US, 100 in China, 500+ worldwide. Groupon burned cash buying local clones fast (CityDeal in Europe, Beeconomic in Singapore, ClanDescuento in Latin America, Spreets in Australia) — good short-term, but done in a rush, so it woke up with dozens of teams, incompatible product cultures and badly integrated systems, 10,000+ employees worldwide, often very young and untrained, armies of salespeople cold-calling thousands of small shops with no follow-up, no retention strategy, just filling the deal pipeline. And then the model itself broke, when the merchants realised the maths didn't work.

Where it lands

Groupon needs two things: customers who buy deals, and merchants willing to slash prices. Take a €50 restaurant menu at −50% (€25); Groupon takes ~50% commission, so the merchant nets €12.50 — a loss, accepted in the hope that new customers either return at full price or spend more than the offer. Spoiler: almost never. Groupon customers come for one thing — the discount — and don't return; worse, they often leave bad reviews if the experience isn't perfect, feeling like "full customers" despite the rebate. So merchants lost money and gradually deserted the platform — and with fewer merchants you can't sustain thousands of salespeople, so in 2015 came the first layoffs (1,100 people; 10,000 posts cut between 2015 and 2024), an infernal cycle: fewer salespeople, fewer deals, fewer sales. Revenue went from $14M (2009) to a $3.2B peak (2014), then fell inexorably to under $500M by 2024 — helped down by Facebook Marketplace (2015), Google Offers, and merchants building their own promo channels. And there was a scandal: at its 2011 peak Groupon IPO'd at $13B ($520/share, the biggest tech IPO since Google), but within a year the stock had fallen 90%+ to $58 — because to impress Wall Street Groupon had booked the total deal value as revenue when it only kept the 40-50% commission (a €100 massage booked as €100 of revenue when it earned €40). When the SEC dug in, Groupon had to restate, the stock cratered, and the board fired founder-CEO Andrew Mason, who wrote with irony: "I've decided I want to spend more time with my family. Just kidding — I was fired." The deeper truth: Groupon forgot that a pizzeria, a hairdresser or a yoga studio isn't a startup — it's a fragile small business with thin margins, and a flood of −50% customers isn't an opportunity but a tidal wave that destroys its balance. Growing at all costs, Groupon grilled its own market: merchants tested it and left, customers learned to wait for promos, the brand lost all credibility. It's still online — but an empty shopping mall no one talks about. (The video's next stop: WeWork.)

The people & the dates (references)

Capture the lessons

Run the drills

Beyond the video — added insight

The no-barrier-to-entry lesson pairs Groupon with Wish (66), HTC (61) and GoPro (63): a single, imitable strategy with no defensible edge is a lead you hold only until someone copies it — 500+ Groupon clones, Temu copying Wish, everyone copying HTC. Being first and fastest-growing is worthless without a moat; the durable question is never "how good is the idea" but "what stops the next person doing it too." Groupon is the purest version — a model so copyable it was cloned in three weeks.

The merchant-poisoning model is the misaligned-incentive lesson (Subway 35) at its sharpest: a platform that needs its partner to lose money on every transaction is mining a finite seam, not building a market — merchants tested it once and left. It pairs with the loyalty-to-price failure (Wish 66): the discount attracts the least loyal customer, so neither side of the marketplace forms a lasting bond. A two-sided platform only compounds if both sides win repeatedly.

The gross-vs-net accounting trick is a clean, important investing lesson for your value screen: Groupon booked the whole deal as revenue while keeping a 40-50% commission (agent vs principal), and the SEC restatement — not a sales miss — cratered the stock. It's the gross-vs-net thread (Holy's margin 59, the F1 pool-vs-take 64) turned into an outright red flag: whenever a platform takes a cut, check whether it books the gross transaction or its net take, and treat an aggressive method plus a too-good top line as the story itself. The stock fell 90% while revenue "grew" — proof that how revenue is recognised can matter more than that it grew.

The scorched-market and doom-loop lessons round it out: growth that consumes its own resource (merchant goodwill, willingness to pay full price) leaves nothing to harvest — grow at the rate the market can bear — and a sales force scaled to boom-time demand becomes a spiral in reverse (fewer merchants → fewer reps → fewer deals). And the refused-$6B-exit is the vision-vs-economics discipline (Wish's refused $10B, 66): a refusal is only wise if the model is defensible; with no moat, the buyout was the peak.

Your intersection: no-barrier-to-entry and the panic-acquisition mess are your moat-and-M&A radar; the merchant-poisoning model and loyalty-to-price are your two-sided-platform and incentive-alignment lens; the gross-vs-net trick and revenue-recognition red flag are your value-investing accounting craft (agent vs principal — a genuinely useful diligence check); the scorched-market and cost-base-in-reverse are your durability and operating-leverage screen; and the refused exit is the vision-vs-economics discipline. The fastest-growing-startup-with-no-moat cautionary, and the accounting-red-flag case of the file.

Make it click — similar plays

The no-moat / copyable-strategy: Wish (Case 66) — the imitable model killed by a richer copy; HTC (Case 61) & GoPro (Case 63) — first and fastest, no defence. Subway (Case 35) — the misaligned incentive that bleeds the franchisee/merchant. Holy (Case 59) & F1 (Case 64) — the gross-vs-net / take-rate distinction (here turned into a fraud red flag).

The trust & the exit: Wish (Case 66) — loyalty-to-price and the refused billion-dollar exit; Kape (Case 57) — the accounting/ownership you must read behind the story. Your version: name the barrier to entry or admit there isn't one, check both sides of the transaction make money, ask whether growth builds or burns the market, and read agent-vs-principal in the revenue — because the fastest-growing company with no moat is just the fastest to the copy.

How to drillName the barrier to entry or admit there isn't one, check both sides of the transaction actually make money, ask whether growth builds or burns the market, and read agent-vs-principal in how revenue is booked — because the fastest-growing startup with no moat, on a model that bleeds its own partners, is just the fastest to the cliff. Souk Al-Manakh — The Anatomy of a Speculative BubbleVideo case · Kuwait 1982 — the casino of checks that didn't exist, leverage & moral hazard
▶ Video0/14▶
▶ Watch the film: Madoff: The Monster of Wall Street (2023, doc) — the Ponzi, the trust, the run at the first default.
The one ideaThe biggest, most forgotten crash in modern finance had no listed stocks. In 1982 an unofficial Kuwaiti market run out of an air-conditioned building peaked at a $45B capitalisation — bigger than the country's GDP, the third-largest exchange on Earth — with 95% of trades paid in postdated checks: money that didn't exist yet. One bounced check brought the whole thing down. It's the timeless anatomy of a bubble.
A note on framing

A historical finance case, presented factually; I extract the bubble-mechanics and investing lessons and omit the video's sponsor segment. Link to confirm: the URL provided points to another case (the shipbuilding video) — send the correct one and I'll patch it in.

The story (in brief)

1970s-80s Kuwait: one of the smallest Arab countries (about the size of Île-de-France) and one of the richest, sitting on vast oil reserves. The 1973 oil shock sent the barrel from $3 to $12, then to $35 by 1980 after the Iranian revolution — Kuwait's oil revenues rose eightfold between 1973 and 1980, and the economy was flooded with cash that, as in every euphoria, sought a way to reproduce itself. But the official stock exchange (opened 1977) was small and heavily regulated — licences, few listed firms, thin volumes — too slow for a young, ambitious population. So a parallel market emerged: the Souk Al-Manakh, once a camel market in central Kuwait City, then a shopping centre, gradually taken over by traders. An informal OTC venue with no formal authority, where people traded shares of non-listed (often Gulf offshore) companies hand-to-hand, on paper, paid with postdated checks — a culturally accepted practice. Everyone played along, paying with promises, and as long as prices rose no one asked questions. Between 1979 and 1982 transactions exploded: shares changed hands dozens of times a day, companies with no revenue, no employees and no products rose 10x, 50x, 100x in months, and paper "startups" were minted by the chain — 2,000+ unlisted companies trading at the souk against a dozen on the official exchange. The car parks filled with Porsches and Rolls-Royces, some traders arrived by helicopter, and 17-year-olds were millionaires. At its peak the souk's capitalisation hit ~$45B while Kuwait's GDP was under $30B — the third-largest stock market in the world, behind only the US and Japan — with 95% of transactions based on postdated checks dated 30, 60 or 90 days out: pay later, with the gains you'll have made by then. Which is no longer investment. It's a casino.

Where it lands

For three years it ran — until a morning in August 1982 when an investor deposited a check and it bounced for insufficient funds: the first and only one so far, but enough. In a system built purely on trust, the smallest default is a panic signal, and within hours the word spread — "someone didn't pay." Buyers doubted, sellers refused new deals, prices stopped rising, and within days the market seized; everyone rushed to cash their checks and all were refused. The system collapsed instantly — one of the largest crashes in history with no listed stocks, estimated at ~$250B in today's money, the Lehman Brothers of the Arab world, except with no formal institution to blame. The government ordered the souk closed immediately — but the real crisis was only starting, because Kuwait's commercial banks were exposed: the postdated checks circulating at the souk had been pledged as bank collateral, loans granted against them, credit lines flowing through the economy into houses, cars and consumer goods. Now those checks were worth zero, the banks held mountains of unrecoverable debt, and all but one prepared to declare bankruptcy. So in September 1982 the Emir made a historic decision: the state would assume all the debts of the Souk Al-Manakh — the Treasury would repay the losses — because letting the banking system collapse meant a collapse of confidence, bank runs, an unprecedented social crisis in a rentier state, and regional contagion across the Gulf. Kuwait recapitalised the banks, settled the checks, bought the bad debt, and avoided public trials that would have exposed the fraud (IMF estimate: ~KD 6bn, ~$22B of the era, probably understated as the state kept paying for years). No one was ever judged — "to preserve the country's image." The intervention likely averted a systemic crisis, but planted moral hazard — the knowledge that risk-takers would be rescued — and the same recipe has rhymed ever since: subprime 2007, Dubai 2008, the Saudi crash 2006, crypto and SPACs. Believe prices always rise, confuse wealth with speculation, look away while everyone wins, intervene when everyone loses. History doesn't repeat, but it rhymes — and sometimes very expensively. (The video's next stop: Nauru, the resource-curse — Case 62's cousin.)

The people & the dates (references)

Event: the Souk Al-Manakh unofficial stock market crash, Kuwait, 1982 — speculation financed by postdated checks; trust broke at the first default, triggering a chain-reaction collapse of ~$90bn+ in claims. The moral-hazard/trust-breaks gene.

Capture the lessons

Run the drills

Beyond the video — added insight

The file's first pure speculative-bubble case — a gift for your money cluster: the timeless anatomy of a mania — excess liquidity seeking yield, price divorced from fundamentals, leverage as the transmission channel, trust that breaks at the first default, liquidity that vanishes on the first doubt, and a bailout that plants the next crisis. It's the greater-fool / speculation-vs-investment distinction (your value-investing bedrock) at its most extreme, and the Gulf/MENA setting makes it a piece of financial history from your own region — the "Lehman of the Arab world."

The speculation-vs-investment distinction is the gem and your discipline's foundation: paying with money that doesn't exist yet, on the assumption the next buyer pays more, is a bet on a greater fool, not an investment with a margin of safety — the line the whole value tradition draws between price paid and value received, illustrated at its purest.

The leverage-is-the-transmission-channel lesson is the sharp macro/risk one, and directly your world: the Souk looked contained (unlisted paper, no formal exchange), but the postdated checks pledged as bank collateral wired it straight into the banking system — exactly the subprime mechanism (collateralised bad paper flowing through the banks). The risk that matters is never the asset alone; it's how the asset connects to leverage and the financial plumbing. For a financier who lives in structures, covenants and collateral, the damage is in the linkages.

The trust-breaks and liquidity-vanishes lessons are your risk radar (the bank-run dynamic, tied to the digital-euro confidence lesson 50): a confidence-based system holds until the first crack then collapses in hours, and liquidity is a fair-weather friend that disappears exactly when needed. And the moral-hazard / bailout lesson is the macro thread (the Fed put, US macro 15): the rescue that prevents systemic collapse removes the consequence of risk and seeds the next bubble — price the moral hazard, not just the rescue. The excess-liquidity-seeks-yield and history-rhymes lessons are your macro pattern-recognition — a wall of money chasing too few real assets is the precondition of every bubble (relevant to your rates/OAT thinking), and the recipe never changes.

Your intersection: speculation-vs-investment and price-vs-fundamental are your value-investing bedrock; leverage-as-transmission and read-the-plumbing are your risk/structuring craft (the project-finance collateral lens); trust-breaks and liquidity-vanishes are your risk radar; excess-liquidity and moral-hazard are your macro threads (rates, the Fed put); and history-rhymes is your epistemic discipline. The money cluster's bubble-anatomy capstone — and a piece of your own region's financial history.

Club Med & Fosun — Selling an Asset, or Ceding a Symbol?Video case · The soft-power acquisition, the bidding war & Made-for-China — companion to Case 34
▶ Video0/14▶
The one ideaYou think you booked a week of French sunshine and all-inclusive relaxation. In fact you've entered the largest tourism-seduction operation China ever ran. Club Med is no longer French-owned — the resort design is thought in Shanghai, the strategy piloted from Fosun, and the next openings target where Beijing wants to shine. The question under every cross-border deal: are you selling an asset, or ceding a symbol?
A note on framing (and a companion)

This is the soft-power companion to Case 34 ("Club Med — Fired at the Summit, Owned in Shanghai"): Case 34 covers the dilution mechanics (selling shares = ceding control); this one covers the symbol-vs-asset thesis, the 19-month bidding war and the Made-for-China reorientation. Read the pair together. China and the geopolitics are presented neutrally; the "geopolitical instrument" framing is the video's thesis, and the turnaround is credited honestly — this is a business/M&A case, not a nationalist one.

The story (in brief)

Club Med began in 1950 when Gérard Blitz — a Belgian judoka and Holocaust survivor — opened a village of military tents on Majorca: all-inclusive, barefoot, egalitarian, cheap, built for sport, dancing and meeting people, under the slogan "the point of life is to be happy; the time to do it is now." It invented democratic tourism decades before low-cost and Airbnb, exploded through the 1960s (100+ villages in 40 countries), and in 1963 Gilbert Trigano industrialised it, inventing the GO ("Gentil Organisateur") and GM ("Gentil Membre") to erase the line between staff and guests — a temporary egalitarian tribe where everyone, even the CEO, is on first-name terms. At its 1980s apogee: a million clients a year, 26,000 seasonal staff, revenue over a billion francs, its own airline and the Club Med 2 cruise ship — a listed Paris company and a jewel of French soft power. But from the 2000s the magic faded: mass tourism and low-cost squeezed it, and Club Med was stuck between two worlds — not luxe enough for the grand hotels, too dear for the middle class. In 2010 CEO Henri Giscard d'Estaing (son of the former president) began a premium "all-inclusive upscale" pivot, closing unprofitable villages — but it needed fresh capital. Enter China.

The timing was perfect: China's outbound tourists went from 4M (2000) to 57M (2010) to 155M (2019), and they wanted a Western, all-inclusive, prestigious experience — above all "made in France," synonymous with luxury and art de vivre. Fosun, a conglomerate worth $100B+ founded by Guo Guangchang ("the Warren Buffett of China," owner of Lanvin, insurance, later Wolverhampton FC), bought 7% of Club Med in 2010, built up, and in May 2013 launched a friendly takeover at €17.50 a share to delist and own it outright. Then, in summer 2014, the Italian fund Investindustrial (Andrea Bonomi, ex-Ducati and Aston Martin) surprised everyone, judging the price too low and the Fosun alliance dangerous for Club Med's French identity, and launched a hostile counter-bid at €21, then €22, then €23 — igniting a war. The duel ran 19 months, escalating before the AMF, the longest takeover battle in Paris Bourse history, and it stopped being about economics and became about ideology. In January 2015 Fosun won at €24.60 a share — valuing Club Med at €939M, 40% above its opening bid. Club Med delisted and became a private, Chinese-owned subsidiary. The strategy was explicit: Made in France, but Made for China.

Where it lands

It began at once — Club Med everywhere in China overnight via Alipay, WeChat campaigns and partner agencies, the target shifting from French baby-boomers to young, urban, tech-savvy Chinese families chasing premium, "instagrammable" tourism. By 2016 it was profitable again; Fosun opened villages for Chinese tourists in China, Thailand, the Maldives, Morocco and Japan. The business core inverted: 70% European clients before the deal; within five years China became Club Med's #2 market, behind France but ahead of Italy and Brazil. On the scoreboard the bet worked beautifully — a company many thought finished became a cash machine, with record 2023 revenue of €2.06B (+17%), 90%+ occupancy on some destinations, and rising revenue per client. But something quieter changed. The HQ is officially still Paris (rue de Cambrai), yet the real power sits in Shanghai, at Fosun Tourism Group's Asian HQ: the big strategic orientations, the village openings, the marketing priorities are decided there. Asia went from 7% of clients (2014) to ~25% (2023); the Guilin village became a best-seller; campaigns run primarily in Mandarin. Internally, employees describe (anonymously) a "soft asiatisation" — centralised HR, Fosun-style financial reporting, heavier commercial pressure, an obsession with digital and e-commerce KPIs — and a hiring shift toward "multicultural globetrotters" over French-tourism experts. And capital followed the owner: the French mountains (Serre-Chevalier, La Plagne) saw development frozen or slowed while Fosun concentrated on Beijing's strategic destinations — Thailand, Bali, and China's own ski resorts, booming after the 2022 Beijing Olympics. Club Med isn't a Party annex; it wasn't sold off or destroyed — it was revived. But it changed camps, discreetly. Can you still call it a "national jewel" when the key decisions are made abroad? Chinese money is silent but everywhere — luxury real estate, vineyards, football clubs, Parisian palaces, fashion houses — and each time the question is the same: are you selling an asset, or ceding a symbol?

▶ Original video ↗

The people & the dates (references)

The deal: China's Fosun (Guo Guangchang) won Club Med after a ~19-month bidding war (concluded 2015) — the symbol-vs-asset, Made-for-China pivot.

Capture the lessons

Run the drills

Beyond the video — added insight

The companion to Case 34: that card covers the dilution mechanics (selling shares = ceding control, the prepaid model); this one covers the soft-power / symbol-vs-asset thesis, the 19-month OPA war and the Made-for-China reorientation. Read them together — the mechanics of how control was lost (34) and what the new owner did with it and why it matters (69).

The flip side of the sovereignty thread: where BYD (43) and shipbuilding (65) show China building industrial dominance from scratch, Club Med shows China acquiring an established Western symbol — the two routes of strategic capital (build the champion or buy it), and "Chinese money is silent but everywhere." For your sovereignty radar, dominance is acquired as often as it's built, and the acquisition route is quieter and easier to miss.

The symbol-vs-asset question is the gem, and directly your M&A/diligence world: every cross-border deal is at once an asset sale, a control transfer, and a redirection of strategic priorities — Club Med was revived (the turnaround was real) but its decisions moved to Shanghai and its capital to Beijing's destinations. Underwrite what control and direction transfer with the shares, not just the price and the P&L — Case 34's loss-of-control sharpened to the level of national symbols.

Keep-the-badge and provenance-premium are your brand/luxury lens: "made in France" was the very thing that made Club Med valuable to a Chinese buyer selling to Chinese consumers — country-of-origin is a durable, transferable intangible that lives in the customer's mind, not the cap table (the LVMH/luxury provenance thread, 28); the label stays, the substance reorients to the owner's market. And where-decisions-are-made and capital-follows-the-owner are your control/governance craft: ownership relocates power quietly (follow the decision-flow, not the org chart) and capital flows to the owner's priorities (frozen French Alps vs funded Chinese ski resorts).

Your intersection: symbol-vs-asset and asset+control+direction are your M&A/diligence craft; acquire-vs-build is the flip side of your sovereignty thread; keep-the-badge and provenance-premium are your brand/luxury lens; where-decisions-are-made and capital-follows-the-owner are your control/governance radar (Case 34's dilution sharpened); and capital-need-as-a-door is the financing-side warning. WeWork — The $47B Cult That Was a Real-Estate CompanyVideo case · Tech valuation on a sublet business, the founder-guru & the maturity mismatch
▶ Video0/14▶
▶ Watch the film: WeCrashed (2022, series) — this case, dramatized: the cult valuation, the real-estate reality, the unchecked founder.
The one ideaA charismatic founder with messianic hair promised to "reinvent work" and was valued at $47B — nearly as much as Airbnb or SpaceX. Then the IPO filing forced the numbers into daylight, and the world saw the truth: a classic office-sublet business dressed as tech, run by a guru with no checks, on a model that lost $5M a day. It's the definitive case of an era where the PowerPoint was worth more than the balance sheet.
The story (in brief)

In 2010 New York, Israeli entrepreneur Adam Neumann — fresh off failing to sell children's shoes with built-in heels, but overflowing with charisma and an obsessive need to leave a mark — launched WeWork with Miguel McKelvey. The mechanics were unremarkable: lease a floor long-term, divide it, sublet the spaces short-term to freelancers and startups. But Adam saw much bigger. WeWork wasn't an office-rental company — it was a philosophy, a culture, a lifestyle. He didn't sell square metres, he sold meaning: not offices but "inspiring communities," not a lease but "joining a tribe" of entrepreneurs and dreamers, colourful walls, free coffee, boozy afterworks. He sold himself as a visionary — "reinventing work," "professional spirituality," "curing modern loneliness through architecture," a better world built on WiFi and design sofas. And it worked: investors adored it, media raved, WeWork became the coolest startup going. Behind the scenes the model stayed basic — lease long, renovate tastefully, sublet short at higher prices — pure real estate. But Neumann sold it as tech, wielding "disruption," "scalability," "space-optimisation algorithms," comparing WeWork to Uber and Amazon, and everyone believed him. SoftBank smelled "the next Google" and poured in billions; the valuation soared to $47B by 2019. WeWork was everywhere — New York, London, Paris, Shanghai — opening sometimes 10+ buildings a month, each time repeating: "we're not a real-estate company, we're a technology company redefining how people work." Awash in investor cash, Neumann bought private jets, invested in a spiritual school, rented a luxury yacht as a "mobile office," and spun ever-vaguer visions: WeGrow (a Montessori school), WeLive (upscale co-living), maybe one day WeBank, rebranding the whole thing "The We Company" — a religion, an empire. An empire that wasn't profitable, and nowhere near it. But nobody looked at the numbers, because Adam was selling a dream — one he sustained right up to the 2019 IPO announcement.

Where it lands

To go public, WeWork had to file the S-1 — a public dissection: numbers, governance, strategy, in black and white. The shock: colossal losses — in 2018, $1.9B lost on just $1.8B of revenue, worsening yearly, $5M burned a day. Why? Because the model was unbalanced: sign 15-20-year leases with landlords, sublet short-term to startups — so in any downturn or vacancy, the charges explode while revenue collapses. An ultra-fragile model with disastrous cashflow, dependent on infinite growth in a world of low rates and tech euphoria. But the real shock was Neumann himself: the S-1 revealed a string of self-dealing — he'd bought buildings personally then leased them to WeWork, collecting the rent into his own company; he'd trademarked the word "We" through a company he wholly owned, then sold it to WeWork for $5.9M; and a multiple-class share structure gave him 60%+ of the voting rights — nobody could fire him or challenge him, king of his empire — all before the megalomania (drinking in meetings, cannabis on the company jet, firing staff to Alicia Keys' "Empire State of Mind"). When the media pounced (WSJ, Bloomberg, Forbes), it was carnage: the IPO was suspended, the valuation fell from $47B to $15B to under $8B in weeks, and Neumann was pushed out — with a $1.7B golden parachute, part-funded by SoftBank. The man who burned billions left rich while everyone else sank. SoftBank (Masayoshi Son, who'd put in $10B+ via the $100B Vision Fund) couldn't let it die — a personal and strategic disavowal — so it injected $3B more, took control, installed a corporate real-estate CEO, and tried to renegotiate leases, close sites and cut staff. But the long-term contracts weighed like an anvil, the fundamentals didn't change, and Covid killed shared-space demand. A 2021 SPAC merger got it public at $9B (from a $500+ stock to under $8 two years later); in August 2023 WeWork warned it might go bankrupt, and did, three months later.

Dates: founded 2010; peak private valuation ~$47bn; the IPO prospectus (S-1) exposed the maturity mismatch and the IPO was pulled 2019, collapsing the valuation toward ~$8bn. (Dramatised in WeCrashed, 2022.)

Capture the lessons

Run the drills

Beyond the video — added insight

WeWork is the capstone of the failure shelf — it braids the whole thread: the real-estate-dressed-as-tech mislabel (the "thinks it's Apple" delusion of GoPro 63 and Wish 66), the founder-with-no-checks (the identity delusion of GoPro 63, the unaccountable control), the free-money bubble (the excess-liquidity precondition of Souk 68), the accounting reckoning (the top-line-vs-reality of Groupon 67 and Wish 66), and the repackaging that doesn't heal (the too-little-too-late of HTC 61). It's the era's defining "PowerPoint worth more than the balance sheet" case.

The maturity mismatch is the gem, and it's your project-finance world exactly: long liabilities (15-20-year leases) funding short revenues (month-to-month tenants) is a machine for turning a slowdown into a collapse — the same asset-liability mismatch that felled banks in every crisis (borrow short, lend long — WeWork ran it in reverse, commit long, earn short). For a financier who structures long-dated, contracted cashflows, it's the reminder that the tenor and the certainty of the two sides must match, and that a mismatch is fragility no story can paper over.

The tech-valuation-without-tech-ingredients lesson is your value-investing discipline: zero IP, zero network effect, zero owned property, zero competitive advantage, valued at 20x revenue like software — the label without the economics. A tech multiple requires tech economics; strip the story and name the actual business, and price it as what it is (the discipline Wish 66 and Groupon 67 also teach — read the model under the marketing).

The governance lessons are the sharpest for your underwriting: a founder with 60%+ voting control and no board is a guru not a CEO, and self-dealing in plain sight (buildings leased back, "We" trademarked and sold to itself) is the tell the whole thing is rotten — governance isn't bureaucracy, it's the brake. And read who gets paid in the bad outcome (Neumann's $1.7B parachute while everyone sank) — the incentive structure tells you whose interests the company serves. Plus the macro thread: free money is a drug (the Souk 68 / Fed-put lesson), and a marquee backer's conviction is not diligence (SoftBank's commitment bias made it the last to fold).

Your intersection: the maturity mismatch and the rate-dependence are your project-finance and risk craft (the asset-liability tenor match, the fragility of a model that needs the tailwind); the tech-valuation-without-ingredients and strip-the-story lessons are your value-investing discipline; the governance, self-dealing and founder-incentive lessons are your underwriting red flags; and free-money-is-a-drug plus marquee-backer-isn't-diligence are your macro and diligence radar. The definitive PowerPoint-over-balance-sheet cautionary — and a maturity-mismatch masterclass for a man who structures long-dated cashflows.

Intel — How the King of Chips Auto-DestructedVideo case · Missed transitions, the integration trap & the $100B bet to catch up
▶ Video0/14▶
The one ideaIntel once ruled processors absolutely — 90% of PCs, the server market, its own fabs. Then, resting on its laurels, it missed mobile, missed GPUs, botched its own manufacturing roadmap, and lost its biggest symbol (Apple) to a rival's chips. By 2021 the saviour-CEO bet $100B to catch up; four years later the stock had collapsed and he was fired. The story of how the king of chips auto-destructed — one missed transition at a time.
A note on framing

The supplied transcript cuts off mid-story (at the AMD/GlobalFoundries spin-off), so this card covers the four historical errors it lays out plus the documented outcome of the $100B IDM 2.0 bet; the 2024-25 specifics (Gelsinger's removal) are presented as widely reported, around my cutoff. Send the rest of the transcript and I'll extend the card.

The story (in brief)

On 23 March 2021, Intel's new CEO Pat Gelsinger took the stage to unveil a plan to save the company: IDM 2.0, an ultra-aggressive strategy built on $100B of investment to climb back to the top. There was a time Intel reigned unchallenged over processors — PCs, servers, data centres, it crushed all comers — but 2020 began the descent into hell: AMD stole its place in PCs and servers, Apple abandoned its chips, and TSMC and Samsung became the absolute masters of semiconductor production. Intel went from untouchable to a struggling player desperately trying to catch up. The board thought it had found a saviour in Gelsinger — but four years on, the stock had collapsed, the company was in flames, mass layoffs followed one another, and Gelsinger was fired.

The roots run deep. In the 2000s Intel was everywhere — 90% of PCs, dominant in servers with its Xeon chips — and its model looked perfect: it designed AND manufactured its own chips, an edge that let it dominate and set the rules. But resting on its laurels, it made four strategic errors. First, it completely missed the smartphone turn: when mobile exploded with the iPhone and Android, Intel refused to invest massively, thinking it a niche fad with margins too thin — and in 2007 it even turned down Steve Jobs' offer to supply the iPhone's processors, letting ARM come to dominate all of mobile (Intel later tried, with x86 phone chips built for performance, but ARM's lower-power architecture was simply far better suited to a phone, and Intel's attempt failed). Second, the manufacturing model: in the early 2010s Intel had a huge lead, but its transition to 10nm failed — chips meant for 2016 didn't ship until 2019, years late and already obsolete on arrival — which opened a boulevard for TSMC, which reached 7nm and 5nm well ahead and became the new technology leader. AMD, partnered with TSMC, launched Ryzen in 2017, far more competitive; and the worst blow came from Apple, which since 2005 had run every Mac on Intel but in 2020 switched entirely to its own Apple Silicon, made by TSMC — Intel losing one of its biggest customers, a symbol of its fall. Third, it underestimated GPUs, again dismissing them as a gaming niche while concentrating on CPUs — catastrophically wrong once crypto mining and AI arrived, leaving Nvidia the world leader with 88% of the GPU market (the same Nvidia Intel had refused to buy for $20B in 2005). Fourth, and beneath it all, Intel trapped itself in its old IDM 1.0 model — designing AND fabricating — while AMD, Apple, Nvidia and Qualcomm concentrated purely on design and outsourced production to TSMC or Samsung; Intel spent its resources on two fronts while its rivals poured everything into one. (Even AMD had once been an IDM and spun off its fabs in 2009 into GlobalFoundries.)

Where it lands

The pattern is a masterclass in how a dominant incumbent auto-destructs: a series of dismissed transitions (mobile, GPUs) rationalised as "niches," a technology lead squandered through an execution failure (the 10nm delay), and a business model — vertical integration — that flipped from Intel's greatest strength into its heaviest burden as the industry's economics changed. Where owning both design and fabrication once let Intel set the rules, it came to mean carrying the colossal cost and complexity of leading-edge fabs on two fronts, while focused rivals rented the world's best fab (TSMC) and put everything into design. Gelsinger's answer — $100B to rebuild manufacturing leadership and open Intel's fabs to outside customers (a foundry to rival TSMC) — was the right diagnosis of the strategic bind, but a staggeringly capital-intensive, multi-year bet against an entrenched leader, made from a position of weakness and a falling stock; it consumed cash, missed milestones, and ultimately cost Gelsinger his job. A cautionary tale about how the very integration that builds an empire can become the anchor that sinks it when the technology and the economics move.

The misses: rejected building the chip for Apple's iPhone (reportedly under then-CEO Paul Otellini); missed mobile and GPUs; the integration trap vs fabless designers and TSMC. Turnaround: the ~$100B comeback attempt (CEO Pat Gelsinger era).

The integration-trap is the gem, and the sharpest counterpoint in your whole file: your vertical-integration spine (BYD 43, Luxottica 03, Decathlon 21, shipbuilding 65) shows owning the chain as a moat — Intel is the case where that same integration inverts into an anchor when the economics change, because carrying leading-edge fabs on two fronts lost to focused rivals renting the world's best fab. The lesson isn't "integration bad" — it's that no moat is permanent, and the deepest, most capital-heavy one can flip into the heaviest burden when the industry's cost structure moves. Hold both cases side by side.

The serial-niche-dismissal is the Kodak/HTC missed-transition archetype with a cultural diagnosis: Intel dismissed mobile and GPUs on the same "small niche" logic and passed on Nvidia for $20B — one miss is luck, the same miss three times is a culture that can't see past its core (the optimizer's blindness of Apple/Cook 41, La Redoute 39). For your management assessment, the tell is repetition: underwrite whether a dominant firm can recognise a transition it isn't already winning.

The picks-and-shovels and missed-acquisition lessons are your investing craft: TSMC won regardless of who won the chip war (look one layer down for the indispensable supplier — the toll-booth thread, AWS 11, F1 64), and Intel's $20B "no" to Nvidia became an 88%-market loss (the cost of passing on the future is the position you forfeit, not the cheque you save). And the capital-allocation lesson is directly your world: a $100B turnaround launched from weakness against an entrenched, moving leader is among the hardest bets there is — the right diagnosis doesn't make a winnable plan, and catching a leader who keeps advancing is a low-odds use of capital.

The fallen-king cautionary — a moat that inverted.

Nauru — The Richest Country That Mined Itself to RuinVideo case · The resource curse, the missing sovereign fund & the one-asset economy
▶ Video0/14▶
The one ideaA 21km² Pacific island was, a few decades ago, the richest country on Earth per capita — GDP per head of ~$88,000 in today's money, double the US at the time — built on the purest phosphate ever found. It dug up its one asset, spent and squandered the proceeds, and when the phosphate ran out in 2003 the economy fell 90%. Today Nauru is poorer than before the phosphate was ever discovered. The textbook resource curse.
A note on framing

A resource/macro case, presented factually; I extract the capital-stewardship and investing lessons. The sensitive material (an SBF/FTX court detail, the vote-selling, the Australian refugee-processing centre) is stated soberly, and the geopolitics is presented neutrally without taking a side.

The story (in brief)

In 1899 a Pacific Islands Company employee in Sydney, Albert Ellis, noticed a strange rock used as a doorstop, was told it was fossilised wood from an island called Nauru, and had it analysed — it was phosphate, the purest ever found. Over millennia, migratory seabirds resting on the predator-free island had deposited vast quantities of guano that fossilised into rock ~90% pure phosphate covering 80% of Nauru — and the discovery landed exactly amid a global guano rush, because its nitrogen-phosphate mix made the best fertiliser of the age, contributing to half the world's food supply. Exploitation began immediately and was an environmental carnage: every tree razed, digging 30 metres down between coral pillars, 200,000 tonnes a year by the early 1920s. Control passed (after WWI) to a Britain/Australia/New Zealand consortium that sold the phosphate to itself below world prices, fuelling those countries' growth. By 1968, 35M+ tonnes had been extracted, with the Nauruans receiving royalties of just 9% of the revenue from their own resource — small, and on cut-price phosphate, but enough to give a few thousand people schools, a hospital and Western goods without working the mines themselves; the cost was that a third of the island was already environmentally dead. Riding the anti-colonial wave, Nauru gained independence in 1968, bought the mines from Australia, and created its own Nauru Phosphate Corporation — so now 100% of the profits (and risks) were the Nauruans'. With no long-term thinking, they doubled down on extraction, and by the 1980s Nauru was the richest country in the world per capita: 96% of the population employed by the government on huge salaries for doing nothing, free healthcare, electricity, rent and schools, everyone driving a Mercedes.

Where it lands

But the wealth was an illusion, because the island was tiny and phosphate is finite — the entire economy rested on a single commodity that would one day run out. The government knew it and tried to prepare for the post-phosphate era, but agriculture, fishing and tourism were impossible (the land and seabed were devastated) and industry unviable (too small, too remote), so it poured hundreds of millions into four bets: overseas luxury real estate, an airline (Air Nauru, seven planes), a cruise ship, and a London musical about Leonardo da Vinci. It reeked of disaster. The musical flopped and closed in a week; Air Nauru's mostly-empty flights lost, between 1975 and 1987, as much as 30% of the country's phosphate export revenue; the property was mismanaged (the Grand Pacific Hotel in Fiji bought, closed for renovations that never happened, sold at a loss). Revenues fell as spending rose to maintain the population, hundreds of millions were embezzled by politicians, and in 2003 the phosphate officially ran out: GDP fell 90%, unemployment hit 90%, foreign assets were seized by creditors. The crisis was environmental and health as much as economic — 80% of the island uninhabitable, nothing grows, the reefs barren, so the population lives on imported industrial food, driving an obesity and diabetes epidemic (90% obese, life expectancy ~60). Desperate, the government turned to unsavoury lines of business: for a time a no-regulation tax haven and money-laundering hub (until the US forced it to stop), selling passports, selling its UN votes, and — nearly 60% of national revenue now — hosting an Australian offshore centre for refugees Australia won't accept (officially a reception centre, in practice closer to detention, ironically named "the Pacific Solution"). Even Sam Bankman-Fried's FTX, a court document revealed, had explored buying Nauru outright — a tax haven with a bunker to survive an event killing "50 to 99.99% of the world's population" — because it had become the cheapest country on Earth to buy. The fatal error, in hindsight, was glaring: no sovereign wealth fund. Norway, which found North Sea oil in the 1960s, invested the proceeds into a fund now worth $1.3T+ that preserves the wealth for future generations; Botswana did the same with diamonds (the Pula Fund, ~$4B). Nauru's leaders spent the wealth on short-term consumption and risky bets instead, and by the time a fund was obviously needed, the wealth was already gone. This is the resource curse: the paradox where resource-rich countries grow more slowly than resource-poor ones, via two mechanisms — abundance breeds corruption, waste and power struggles; and "Dutch disease," where booming resource exports drive up the currency, making all other exports uncompetitive and hollowing out the rest of the economy.

▶ Original video ↗

The people & the dates (references)

Country: the island republic of Nauru — once among the richest per-capita nations on phosphate mining, then ruined (the resource curse / Dutch disease), contrasted with Norway's sovereign wealth fund. Windfall ≠ income.

Capture the lessons

Run the drills

Beyond the video — added insight

The resource-curse capstone of the money-and-sovereignty cluster: it completes the thread teased across Sand (62) and Souk (68) and pairs with the French state (44) — the definitive case of wealth that impoverishes. And it lands on your world twice: the sovereign-wealth-fund discipline (Norway vs Nauru) is your value-investing and capital-stewardship creed, and "a whole economy on one finite resource that will run out" is the energy-transition question in miniature — exactly the stewardship problem a nuclear/energy principal thinks about at national scale.

The windfall-is-not-income lesson is the gem, and it scales from a nation to a person: a one-time gain from a finite asset is the liquidation of capital, not a salary — Norway converted its oil into a machine that pays forever, Nauru spent its phosphate on Mercedes. For a value investor with lumpy income (deal fees, one-off gains), it's the personal discipline: decide what share of any windfall becomes a permanent income-producing endowment before you consume a euro of it. The sovereign fund is the idea; the habit is yours to run at your own scale.

The one-asset fragility and diversify-into-competence lessons are your investing and risk craft: concentration produces spectacular numbers up and total exposure down (the richer the single source makes you, the more completely its end ruins you), and Nauru's failure was not lack of awareness but diversifying into vanity ventures it couldn't operate (an airline, a musical) — diversification into things you can't run is just a faster loss. The value answer is a diversified, income-producing portfolio, not a scatter of trophy bets.

The build-at-the-peak and 100%-ownership lessons are your governance and timing discipline: the window to convert a boom into durable structure closes while the money flows (build the fund when rich, not when desperate), and full ownership removes the checks that restrain temptation (Nauru took 100% and doubled extraction with no plan) — the governance/counter-power thread (WeWork 70, BIC 26, Danone 38) applied to a nation. And the bottom-can-get-lower lesson (selling passports and votes to survive) is the preserve-the-base creed: a wrecked position strips away the ability to make good choices at all — protect the downside so you're never forced into ruinous ones.

Your intersection: windfall-is-not-income and convert-the-wasting-asset are your capital-stewardship creed (the personal sovereign-fund habit for lumpy income); one-asset fragility and diversify-into-competence are your concentration/risk and portfolio craft; build-at-the-peak, 100%-ownership-needs-governance and preserve-the-base are your timing, governance and margin-of-safety discipline; and the resource curse / Dutch disease is your macro literacy — and the energy-transition stewardship question writ small. The capstone of the resource-and-sovereignty thread.

Make it click — similar plays
