The governance & the base: WeWork (Case 70), BIC (Case 26), Danone (Case 38) — control with no counter-power; the FIRE / Real Estate cases (47, 48) — the preserve-the-base and margin-of-safety discipline.

The one-asset trap: GoPro (Case 63) — the monoproduct with a demand ceiling (the company-scale version of a one-resource economy). Your version: separate the windfall from the income, name your single-source dependence, diversify only into what you can manage, and build the durable structure at the peak — because a windfall from a finite asset is the liquidation of capital, and the discipline that feels unnecessary in the good years is the only thing that survives the bad.

How to drillSeparate the windfall from the income and convert the wasting asset into a permanent one, name your single-source dependence, diversify only into what you can manage, and build the durable structure (the fund, the governance) at the peak not the crisis — because a windfall from a finite asset is the liquidation of capital, not a salary. For you: the resource-curse capstone, and the sovereign-fund discipline at every scale.

Palantir — The Invisible Infrastructure of DecisionVideo case · Data-as-the-real-asset, the sovereignty question & "your weapon is software"
▶ Video0/14▶
▶ Watch the film: The Great Hack (2019, doc) — Cambridge Analytica; data as the real asset, and its dark side.
The one ideaThe software that helped track Osama bin Laden now runs the CIA, FBI and NSA — and a dozen European intelligence services, including France's DGSI — while quietly piloting Airbus, BP, Shell and Wall Street. Palantir's ambition is singular: become the invisible infrastructure that feeds the decision-making of the world's most powerful states and companies. Its business is one word — data — and its slogan is "your weapon is software."
A note on framing

An intelligence/data-infrastructure case, presented factually and soberly; the surveillance capabilities and the geopolitics (the bin Laden operation, the Ukraine targeting, the DGSI contract) are stated neutrally, without endorsement or a political verdict, and I extract the strategic and investing lessons. The card raises the sovereignty and civil-liberties questions the video itself poses rather than resolving them.

The story (in brief)

After 9/11, two adolescent friends set out to fight terrorism through technology without trampling civil liberties: Peter Thiel (PayPal co-founder) and Alex Karp (a philosophy PhD). In 2003 they founded Palantir — named for the seeing-stones of The Lord of the Rings — with a simple starting idea: detect unusual or suspicious patterns across vast databases. The technology traced back to PayPal, which was losing $10M a month to card fraud (so badly that Visa and Mastercard threatened to cut it off) until CTO Max Levchin built "IGOR," a program that scanned every transaction and flagged the dubious ones for manual review — solving the problem and even exposing two Russian cyber-criminals the FBI arrested. An improved, counter-terrorism-oriented IGOR became Palantir's first prototype — and instead of heading to Silicon Valley to raise money, the team went straight to Langley, to In-Q-Tel (the CIA's venture arm, which had also backed Google and Facebook), which invested $2M and connected them with analysts to turn the prototype into a real product. The CIA adopted it fast, and the "virus" spread: by 2013, 12+ agencies used it (FBI, NSA, Homeland Security, Treasury, the Marines, Air Force, Army), and by 2015 so did the Los Angeles and Chicago police. What Palantir actually does gravitates around one keyword — data: big-data management and analysis oriented to detecting and reducing risk, via two products. Gotham (the original, used by 40+ governments) ingests data from every conceivable source — emails, browsing history, social media, surveillance and drone footage, medical records, bank accounts, toll crossings, comms and GPS, police reports, even food deliveries — and does automatically, in minutes, the work of the movie detective's cork-board: a vast web of interconnected profiles with per-node risk analysis, criminal-activity detection, and even prediction of the likely scenario or an individual's presence at a given time and place. On the battlefield it coordinates every asset in a zone (units, drones, aircraft, tanks, danger points, likely enemy positions) — and Ukraine uses it now, with a "Skykit" letting a soldier connect to commercial satellites and "see" the enemy within two hours of an overflight; Karp has said Palantir is "responsible for most of the targeting in Ukraine." Palantir is redrawing how war is waged.

Where it lands

The bin Laden hunt is the emblem: for a decade the world's most-wanted man vanished into the mountains, and US intelligence had astronomical data but assembling the puzzle was a nightmare — too much information, too many sources, too much noise. Gotham centralised the wiretaps, interrogations, financial transactions and satellite imagery, and a name kept recurring on its relationship graphs: Abu Ahmed al-Kuwaiti, a trusted courier — and a courier has a weakness, he must move. The trail led to a strangely fortified compound in Abbottabad (no internet, no phone, walls twice as high as needed), the profile sharpened, and the evidence struck: the only person who justified such a setup was bin Laden himself. After the raid, the hard drives and notes seized were analysed with — of course — Palantir. Then a French footnote that "concerns us": after the 2015 attacks, France's DGSI signed a €10M contract with Palantir in 2016 (Thales bid and lost), assured as temporary until a French solution existed — and renewed it in 2019 because there still wasn't one, handing the nation's security data to a private American company. Because Palantir doesn't stop at governments: Foundry, its enterprise product, does the same for the giants — centralising the scattered data every company holds (Excel files, SQL databases, internal reports, IoT sensors, customer histories) into one interface and using AI to spot trends, anticipate risk and optimise decisions. Airbus tracks production and aircraft maintenance in real time; BP and Shell analyse billions of extraction data points to improve energy yield; Britain's NHS used it in Covid to manage medical stock, forecast hospital beds and distribute vaccines; Morgan Stanley and Credit Suisse use it to detect fraud and predict markets. With Gotham it influences modern wars, with Foundry it pilots great companies, and with AIP (its new AI) it wants to be the strategic brain of governments and multinationals alike — all built on our data. Beautiful and unsettling at once, because the line between assistance and total control is very thin: Palantir may have helped capture bin Laden, but the video's closing question is the one that matters — who watches the one who watches everyone?

▶ Original video ↗

The people & the dates (references)

Company: Palantir (co-founded 2003 by Peter Thiel, Alex Karp (CEO), Joe Lonsdale, Stephen Cohen, Nathan Gettings; named for Tolkien's seeing-stones). Facts: the integration/decision layer (Gotham, Foundry) for intelligence, defence and enterprise; data-as-the-real-asset and the "temporary" dependence that becomes permanent (the sovereignty thread).

Capture the lessons

Run the drills

Beyond the video — added insight

The capstone of the data-and-sovereignty thread, and it lands on your world directly: it completes the data-as-the-real-asset thread (Waze 51, Niantic 55, Kape 57 — even sharing the intelligence lineage, In-Q-Tel echoing the 8200 pedigree of Kape) and the sovereignty thread (digital euro 50, Doctolib 31, shipbuilding 65 — the DGSI dependence is the Doctolib/Cloud-Act question made explicit). And Foundry runs Airbus, BP and Shell — the exact industrial-and-energy operations you finance — so this is the software layer sitting on top of your sector's assets.

The integration-layer and invisible-infrastructure lessons are the gem, and your infrastructure thesis in software form: the value isn't the data (everyone has it) but the layer that connects it into a decision — the same "own the layer everything must pass through" logic as Nvidia (01), AWS (11) and the Sand/shipbuilding chokepoints (62, 65), now applied to decisions rather than compute or trade. The most durable position is the invisible, indispensable substrate beneath the decision; own the orchestration and the hardware (or the raw data) becomes your peripheral — "your weapon is software" is the value-migration thesis (BYD 43, Apple 60) at its most literal.

The temporary-dependence-becomes-permanent lesson is the sovereignty gem for a French principal: the DGSI's "temporary" Palantir contract renewed because no French alternative got built — the stopgap became the structure, and sovereignty was quietly ceded. It's the Doctolib/Cloud-Act and Lidl-sovereignty thread (31, 24) sharpened to national security: if a function is critical, build the capacity or stay captive, because a convenience dependence calcifies into a permanent one. For your energy/infrastructure world, it's the reminder that the software and data layer on top of strategic assets is itself a sovereignty question.

The moat and risk lessons are your value-investing craft: the deepest moat is switching-cost-plus-mission-criticality (depth of embedding, not brand — the sticky-infrastructure thread), a government/defence anchor is durable revenue and reputational/regulatory exposure at once, and the dual-use platform (Gotham + Foundry on one engine) doubles both the market and the concentration. And "who watches the watcher?" is a financial variable — a total-data-access model carries a regulatory tail that belongs in the valuation, not just the ethics discussion.

Your intersection: the integration-layer and invisible-infrastructure lessons are your infrastructure/chokepoint thesis in software; temporary-dependence-becomes-permanent and the DGSI case are your sovereignty radar (and directly a French-principal concern); the embedding-moat, government-anchor and dual-use lessons are your value-investing craft; "your weapon is software" is the value-migration thread; and the accountability-gap-as-risk is your regulatory-tail discipline. Mercedes EQ — Watching the Rival Instead of the CustomerVideo case · The copy-Tesla error, the residual doom loop & the return to heritage
▶ Video0/14▶
The one ideaMercedes unveiled a science-fiction electric S-Class concept the whole world coveted — a genuine Tesla-killer — then shipped a bland "egg" that looked worse than its combustion car, because it optimised for aerodynamic efficiency the buyer didn't care about. The world leader in luxury became the smallest EV player of all, from one fatal error: it watched its rivals so closely it forgot to watch its own customers.
A note on framing

The failure here is not "electric is bad" — BMW won on electric by doing the opposite (see below), and BYD (Case 43) wins on electric outright. Mercedes failed by copying the wrong things and forgetting who its customer is. EV-transition framing kept evenhanded; the 2022-25 figures are the video's account, around my cutoff.

The story (in brief)

At the 2019 Frankfurt motor show, the crowd had eyes for one car: Mercedes' Vision EQS concept — the first fully-electric S-Class, its most luxurious line — a Tesla-killer priced against the Model S Plaid, surreal, clean, with a dashboard spanning the full width, rounded corners flowing into the doors, continuous neon, the feeling of being enveloped as if at the helm of a yacht. Mercedes promised production soon and a car visually very close to the prototype; the world's rich and chancelleries readied their chequebooks. Then in April 2021 at the Shanghai show it revealed the final EQS — and it was a shock: nothing like the promised prototype, and just banal, even ugly, uglier than the combustion S. To cut drag and boost range, Mercedes had binned the car's aesthetics for efficiency. The problem: when someone spends €130,000 on a luxury car, the exterior look is probably the single most important thing — not the electrical efficiency, which they likely don't care about at all. Sales were terrible: 23,000 EQS in 2022, only 14,000 in 2023 (a 40% drop in year two), and buyers were destroyed on resale — luxury cars depreciate fast, but the EQS set records, resold at ~50% of sticker just one year in (€130k cars on Le Bon Coin under €70k; in the US, some from €40k — less than a fully-loaded Toyota Camry, for an S-Class). The EQ range became arguably the biggest flop in Mercedes history.

The roots trace to a leadership change. Dieter Zetsche — the iconic-moustached engineer who joined R&D in 1976, became CEO in 2006, dumped the money-pit Chrysler (which went bankrupt days after being cut loose), survived 2008, and made Mercedes the world's biggest premium carmaker by 2016 — retired in 2019. His successor, Ola Källenius, joined in 1993 with an accounting degree, and took over just as Tesla's Cybertruck and the EV boom exploded (Rivian was worth $150B at IPO, double Mercedes' market cap). Under enormous pressure to prove himself and keep Mercedes at the front, Källenius studied what the EV makers did — and they weren't just electrifying cars, they were modernising them (start/off buttons gone, giant-iPad dashboards, grille-less "this is electric" design, Rivian's light bar, Tesla's clean interior). So he plunged in, staking $60B and an all-electric-by-2030 headline. The mistake was fatal.

Where it lands

The 2021 EQ range (EQS, EQA, EQB, EQE saloon and SUV) all shared the same grille and bumper and all looked like an egg — catastrophic on the luxury models like the €220,000 EQS Maybach SUV, which looked like a slightly-better Toyota Corolla. The reason was an obsession with matching Tesla's and Lucid's aerodynamics to maximise range — but in copying its rivals, Mercedes forgot to observe its customers: people spending €100-200k aren't won by a good battery, they're won by opulence and extra comfort, especially in the rear (wealthy Chinese buyers love to sit in back with a chauffeur), which the egg didn't deliver. The contrast is instructive: GM understood the Hummer buyer perfectly and made its electric Hummer the most opulent 4x4 possible (so huge, at 4.5 tonnes, it's barely road-legal in Europe) — a niche, but a hit; Ford kept everything about its best-selling F-150 (America's top seller for 41 years) and just made it electric. Both embraced electric while knowing their customer cold. Mercedes did the reverse. Realising the EQ disaster before the electric G-Wagon (EQG) shipped in 2024, Mercedes reversed course — quietly, to avoid admitting failure and further crushing resale values: the EQG became the "G580 with EQ technology," the futuristic silver-and-black dropped for traditional colours, and customers offered the option to remove every trace of "electric" (a basic grille and bumper, the spare wheel back). Minor face-saving tweaks (fake traditional grilles, the bonnet star returning, better rear seats) hold the line until a new 2028 range with a silhouette aligned to Mercedes' traditional values. But the cost is heavy: auto-division profitability fell from 15% (Q1 2023) to 9% (Q1 2024), EV sales down 8%, and Mercedes abandoned its all-electric-by-2030 goal. Meanwhile BMW prospered — 15% of its 2023 sales electric (vs Mercedes 12%, Audi 9.4%) — by keeping its traditional aesthetic and building EVs on the same production lines as its combustion cars to cut costs. Where Mercedes radically innovated only to crawl back to its heritage, BMW started from its heritage and innovated gradually, acclimatising its customers. The error cost Mercedes ~10 years in a cut-throat market. And the tell, per the video: all was well under an engineer, and it all went wrong when an accountant with no real product knowledge took over — the same error, it argues, that Boeing made.

Read all three together: the transition punishes whoever misreads it (Porsche's pace, Mercedes' customer), and rewards whoever masters the value chain (BYD) or adapts pragmatically (BMW). And note the framing discipline — the failure is never "electric is bad" (BMW and BYD win on electric); it's execution, timing and customer-reading.

The watch-your-customer-not-your-competitor lesson is the gem, and a universal one for your desk: Mercedes studied Tesla so hard it optimised for a battery efficiency its €130k buyer doesn't care about, forgetting that in luxury the look is the product. It's the Nike optimizer error (58) — measuring the wrong thing — applied to competitive obsession: copying rivals is not serving customers, and the discipline (Ford's F-150, GM's Hummer) is to adopt the new tech in service of the brand's DNA, not at its expense. For an investor, it's a management-quality tell: does the company optimise for what the customer values or for what impresses engineers and mirrors competitors?

Underwrite the resale curve, because it's the market's real-time verdict on the product.

The engineer-vs-accountant and heritage-vs-leap lessons are your management-and-strategy radar: the video's tell (thrived under an engineer, stumbled under an accountant with no product feel — the Boeing parallel, and the Apple/Cook optimizer thread, 41) is the caution that in a design-led business, product intuition at the top matters as much as financial competence; and BMW's start-from-heritage-and-evolve beat Mercedes' leap-and-retreat, the cheaper pragmatic adaptation winning the transition over the grand expensive spectacle. Both are how you'd assess which carmaker (or any incumbent) navigates a disruption.

The German-EV trilogy's customer-blindness case.

Gold, the Dollar & the End of Bretton WoodsVideo case · Money as confidence, the weaponised dollar & why central banks are hoarding gold
▶ Video0/14▶
The one ideaFor a year, the world's central banks have been buying gold by the hundreds of tonnes — China 314, Poland 130, India 69 in 2023 alone — driving the price to records. The question worth a million euros: why, and what's being prepared under our noses? The answer runs through how the dollar conquered the world — and the first cracks in the confidence that holds it up.
A note on framing

A macro/money case, presented factually and neutrally; the geopolitics (the Ukraine-linked asset freeze, Taiwan) is stated without taking a side, and the closing allocation view is the video's sober counsel — deliberately the opposite of the "collapse-is-coming, buy gold now" sales pitch. Figures are the video's account, around my cutoff. Sponsor segment omitted.

The story (in brief)

Rewind to the 1940s. Two world wars had emptied the coffers of the old powers — Britain's debt-to-GDP went from 25% (1914) to 270% (1942), and France and the USSR were similar — while one country played arms-merchant first and entered late: the US. In WWI its exports leapt from $2.4B (1913) to $6.2B (1917) selling cotton, rubber, engines and arms to the warring rich; the same pattern repeated in WWII until Pearl Harbor. By 1945 the US held 75% of the world's gold reserves (up from 2,000 tonnes in 1910 to 20,000 in 1945) — the story of how it rose to the top of the world. Seizing the moment, it gathered 44 allied nations to sign the Bretton Woods accords (1944), building the post-war financial order: each currency pegged to the dollar, the dollar pegged to gold at $35 an ounce, and any nation holding dollars could redeem them for US gold. Why did they agree? Because a gold-backed reserve currency was the purest instrument of trust for world trade — if Indonesia took $1M from Pakistan it knew it could always convert to gold, whereas Pakistani rupees could be debased or distrusted overnight, and it would be left holding paper no one wanted. Bretton Woods also created the World Bank and the IMF, financing the reconstruction loans a ruined world urgently needed — largely funded by the US — cementing the dollar as the world reserve. That was step one.

Step two was oil. During WWII the Arab tribes of Saudi Arabia were racing camels, not yet knowing they sat on the world's largest reserves of black gold; the country, then poor and bombed by Italy, badly needed protection. In a famous 1945 meeting, Roosevelt and the Saudi king struck the deal that would change the dollar's destiny forever: the US would protect Saudi Arabia and arm it; in exchange, Saudi Arabia would sell its oil exclusively in dollars — the petrodollar. Step three was the collapse that, paradoxically, sealed the dollar's dominance. By the 1970s the US economy had weakened and its gold reserves had melted from 22,000 tonnes to 10,000 (Vietnam, debt, a rising gold price), so it could no longer honour Bretton Woods' convertibility. Nixon went on TV and "temporarily" suspended it — Bretton Woods was dead. Yet no one panicked or dumped dollars, because the dollar's value no longer rested on gold but on its utility: what it, and only it, could buy on the world market — oil, the century's most-demanded commodity, which the Saudis sold only in dollars. So every nation kept its dollars, and the status quo persists to this day, with the dollar still the reserve currency and most trade still dollar-denominated.

Where it lands

So why the sudden gold rush? Four reasons. First, the dollar was weaponised: on the first days of the Ukraine war the US froze $300B+ of Russian dollar assets in Western banks, as it froze $10B of Afghan assets (with $7B held in New York) when the Taliban took power in 2021 — and China, holding $800B and eyeing its own Taiwan scenario, started to sweat; its gold reserves were flat until the Russian invasion, then exploded. The confidence in the dollar is slowly eroding — the dollar's share of central-bank reserves fell from 75% (1966) to 59% (2022). Second, the US habit of printing money to infinity: $6T injected in 2020-21 (more than double France's GDP), which drove the post-pandemic inflation — and the very instrument 44 nations chose in 1944 as a safe haven is no longer one, so holders diversify into gold, which cannot be printed (all the gold ever mined fits in a 23-metre cube). Third, massive consumer demand in India and China: the Indian buyer's traditional love of gold plus rising wealth, and a Chinese investor trapped between a burst property bubble and a stock market that returned −2% over five years (vs the CAC 40's +31% and the S&P's +80%) — so, with real estate a terrible bet and stocks useless, only gold is left; Chinese consumers bought 824 tonnes in 2022, Indians 774, together more than the next ten countries combined. Fourth, investor sentiment: gold usually rises when a recession is expected, and it's rising now with no recession visible — meaning the market expects one. Should you buy? The video's honest counsel, against the doom-mongers and gold-sellers who profit from your panic: never react to a headline, invest steadily into a portfolio matched to your risk (100% equities, or 50/50 with property, or 50/30/20 equities/property/gold), and remember that gold is not an investment meant to grow your wealth — it's a placement meant to preserve it.

▶ Original video ↗

The people & the dates (references)

The pivots: President Richard Nixon ended dollar-gold convertibility (the "Nixon shock," 15 August 1971), ending Bretton Woods; the subsequent petrodollar arrangement with Saudi Arabia. Money as trust/utility; the weaponised dollar; gold preserves, doesn't grow.

The macro capstone of the money-and-sovereignty cluster: it completes the digital euro (Case 50, money as confidence/debt) and Souk (Case 68, the bubble and the trust that breaks) and joins the sovereignty thread (shipbuilding 65, Palantir 73) — the story of the reserve currency itself, and the first cracks in the confidence that holds it. For a value investor's macro radar, it's the foundational frame: what money actually is (trust and utility, not metal), and what the current gold rush is telling us about that trust eroding.

The money-is-trust and value-is-utility lessons are the gem, and your macro bedrock: Bretton Woods died in 1971 and the dollar didn't fall because its worth had migrated from gold to utility (the ticket to buy oil) — modern money is a shared belief in future usefulness, and the deepest question behind any currency or asset is "will others still trust this tomorrow?" It's the value-migration thesis (BYD 43, Apple 60, Palantir 73) applied to money itself: the anchor can vanish and the value persist, so long as the utility and the trust remain. The weaponised-dollar lesson is the sovereignty gem, and the driver of the gold rush: freezing Russian and Afghan dollar assets proved to every holder that reserves can be seized, so the biggest holders hedged into gold — power wielded coercively erodes the trust that created it, and accelerates the search for an alternative. It's the sovereignty thread's core (who controls the flow, who can cut you off — the Cloud-Act/Doctolib 31, the shipbuilding-dependence 65) applied to the ultimate flow: the dollar system. Read the de-dollarisation trend as a slow confidence erosion, not a sudden collapse (share of reserves 75%→59%, not zero).

The investing lessons are your value-and-allocation craft: gold preserves wealth, it doesn't grow it (match each asset to its job — the grows-vs-preserves distinction is the cleanest allocation lesson in the file), a big flow can be desperation as much as conviction (the Chinese no-alternatives rush — read the why behind the flow), a price move prices in an expectation not yet realised (gold rising before a visible recession — assets discount the future), and never react to a headline because the panic moment is when you're most manipulated (the pre-decided plan is the antidote — the anti-doom-seller discipline, echoing Kiyosaki 49 and the FIRE cases 47). And the merchant-of-war and turn-leverage-into-structure lessons are strategy: sell the picks and shovels (the toll-booth/enabler thread, Nvidia 01, AWS 11), and convert a peak of relative strength into rules that outlast it.

Your intersection: money-is-trust and value-is-utility are your macro bedrock (and your rates/OAT lens — currency as a confidence variable); the weaponised-dollar and de-dollarisation are your sovereignty radar; grows-vs-preserves, flow-as-desperation, price-discounts-the-future and never-react-to-a-headline are your value-investing and allocation discipline; and sell-the-tools plus turn-leverage-into-structure are strategy. The reserve-currency capstone of the money cluster — what money is, and what the gold rush says about the trust beneath it.

Your version: ask "will others still trust this tomorrow?" of any store of value, sort each holding into grows-vs-preserves, read a big flow as conviction or desperation, and pre-decide the plan so headlines can't move you — because money is trust, and the gold rush is the sound of that trust eroding.

Boeing — The Product Company That Became a Numbers CompanyVideo case · Product-vs-profit, the reverse-takeover culture flip & the certification shortcut
▶ Video0/14▶
▶ Watch the film: Downfall: The Case Against Boeing (2022, doc) — this case on screen: the engineer-vs-accountant culture flip.
The one ideaFor 90 years Boeing built the world's safest, most advanced aircraft, run by engineers obsessed with the best possible plane — even when that nearly bankrupted it. Then it made one fatal shift: from a company centred on the product to a company centred on the numbers. That single change — margins, profit and shareholders first — is the whole story of how the most revered name in aerospace ended up with a body count.
A note on framing

The video is explicit that it's a business-and-investing lesson, not a true-crime exposé, and so is this card. The two 737 MAX crashes and the two whistleblower deaths are stated soberly and factually, without speculation; the focus is the product-vs-numbers framework and its lessons. Figures are the video's account, around my cutoff.

The framework first (it's the point)

There are two ways to run a company: centred on the product, or centred on the numbers. "But aren't all companies driven by profit?" Yes and no. When Steve Jobs built Apple (1976-85) it was product-centred: he spent eight months on a polished plastic case when rivals shipped in wooden boxes, obsessed over the manual while competitors chased sales, and priced at double the market — decisions that would give any MBA a heart attack. In 2007, weeks before the iPhone launch with mass production ready, he told Tim Cook the prototype screen had scratched in his pocket and it had to be replaced — no matter that scratch-proof screens didn't yet exist; 50 days later Gorilla Glass was invented. Business logic said don't — the phones would have sold fine with plastic, and Gorilla Glass could have been next year's marketing hook. But Jobs thought product first, profit and shareholders second. A product company makes every decision to build the best product, even at the cost of profit and shareholder value; a numbers company does whatever raises sales, profit and shareholder value, and nothing else matters. Hold that distinction — it is the entire Boeing case.

The story (in brief)

Founded 1916, Boeing supplied WWI military aircraft, launched its first passenger transport (the Model 80) in 1933, and in 1958 became the first US company to launch a commercial jetliner (the 707). It was so far ahead that in the 1970s, when a DC-10 carried 220 passengers 6,100km, a Boeing 747 carried 460 passengers 15,000km — because it was run by engineers obsessed with the best possible plane, even at the risk of bankruptcy. In 1965, on $2B of revenue, Boeing bet 50% of it developing a single aircraft, the 747 — insane, because in aerospace there's no link between R&D spend and success, timelines run a decade, and break-even is brutally hard (the later 787 cost $32B to develop — twice LVMH's annual profit — and needed 1,100 sales just to break even, as many planes as the entire fleets of Air France, Lufthansa and British Airways combined). The 747 took 28 months and 4,500 full-time engineers, and they built it so well it stayed the world's largest airliner for 37 years (1970-2007). That was the product era, and the results followed: 1975-1995, the stock rose from $0.4 to $18 (+4,400%), revenue from $3.9B to $19.5B.

Then the shift. In 1996 the market was Boeing 54%, McDonnell Douglas 19%, Airbus 18%; to consolidate, Boeing bought McDonnell Douglas for $13B — the fatal error. McDonnell's CEO wrote a clause making himself CEO of the combined group, so the small acquired company's leadership took over the giant, and by tribalism McDonnell's numbers-first culture and engineers took the helm of Boeing's design and production. They broke with "Made in USA" for extreme outsourcing: the 787 was 65% built by 50+ suppliers across 135 factories worldwide (wings in Japan, rear fuselage in Italy) — chosen because it lifted sales (outsourcing to Japan brought orders from ANA and Japan Airlines), but it so complicated operations that the 787, meant to cost $20B, cost $32B; to cope, Boeing cut 53,000 staff (1999-2003). Worse, instead of developing better planes, from 2008-2010 it bought back $61B of its own shares (80% of the period's profit) to mechanically pump the stock, and in 2001 moved its HQ of 85 years away from its Seattle factory to Chicago for tax incentives — putting management 3,000km and two time zones from its engineers. Every ingredient of the disaster was now in place.

Where it lands

While Boeing spent $61B on buybacks, Airbus worked. In 2011, after 50 years of buying only Boeing, American Airlines ordered 200+ Airbus — the alarm bell. Boeing realised it was no longer first and had to respond — and instead of ending buybacks to fund a genuinely new plane ($20B), it took the shortcut: $2.5B to modify the existing 737 into the "737 MAX," fast, because Airbus was urgent. Here's why that was the last nail: every new aircraft must be certified airworthy (EASA in Europe, FAA in the US), which takes 5-9 years — too long. So Boeing dodged it by copying almost the entire 737 and "just" changing the engines, meaning crews would need no new training or simulator time, and since the 737 was already certified, the MAX sailed through fast. But the bigger engines had to be mounted further forward and higher, which lifted the nose in flight — so Boeing added MCAS, a system that automatically pushes the nose down if it rises too high. When the two MAX aircraft crashed, the nose rose naturally on takeoff, MCAS engaged and forced it down; the Lion Air black box showed the system activating 26 times over 10 minutes as the pilot fought to raise the nose, until he lost control. The terrible part: one button could have disabled it — but the pilots didn't know it existed, because Boeing hadn't disclosed MCAS, precisely to keep the certification fast. That is what a numbers company looks like: the obsessive chase for margins, profit and shareholders led Boeing to negative margins, no profit and shareholders abandoning ship — the stock down 50% over the five years since the first crash, 970 incidents in a decade, drowning in lawsuits, and two whistleblowers dead (John Barnett, a quality-control critic, found shot before an audience in March 2024; Joshua Dean, months later, to a rapid infection). The most revered company in the world, undone by leaders armed with accounting degrees. The lesson, for entrepreneur and investor alike: make sure a company is product-centred and led by people who know the product — it's no accident that Nvidia, Microsoft, Apple and Amazon are run by builders, not accountants.

▶ Original video ↗

The people & the dates (references)

The culture flip: the 1997 merger with McDonnell Douglas (CEO Harry Stonecipher era) that put finance over engineering; ~$61bn of buybacks. The disaster: the 737 MAX's MCAS software shortcut caused two crashes — Lion Air (Oct 2018) and Ethiopian Airlines (Mar 2019), 346 dead — and a worldwide grounding; CEO Dennis Muilenburg ousted. (Documentary: Downfall: The Case Against Boeing, 2022.)

Capture the lessons

Run the drills

Beyond the video — added insight

The capstone of the engineer-vs-accountant thread, and the framework the whole file has been circling: Boeing makes explicit the product-vs-numbers lens that runs through Apple/Cook (41, the optimizer who forgot to innovate), Nike (58, the optimizer measuring the wrong thing), Mercedes (74, the accountant CEO who forgot the customer) and Intel (71, the integrator that financial-engineered instead of executing). It's the master case: the orientation at the top — builder or bean-counter — is the deepest fact about a business, and it decides the fate.

The profit-is-a-result-not-a-goal lesson is the gem, and your value-investing bedrock: Boeing's product era produced the +4,400% stock, and its profit-first era produced negative margins — put the product first and the profit follows, invert the order and you lose both. For an investor it's a management-quality filter of the first order (Nvidia, Microsoft, Apple, Amazon run by builders), and it pairs with the sharp corollary that a rising stock can hide a rotting product for years — financial metrics lag product reality, and that gap is where the biggest losses are set up.

The financialisation lessons are your capital-allocation craft, and directly your world: $61B of buybacks instead of a new plane (eating the seed corn), extreme outsourcing chased for orders that blew the cost from $20B to $32B, and moving HQ 3,000km from the engineers — the same financial-engineering-over-building pattern as Intel (71) and the Apple-buyback thread (41). For a project financier and infrastructure principal, the standout is match-the-capital-style-to-the-industry: aerospace (like nuclear, like long-dated infrastructure) has decade-long timelines, no link between spend and success, and brutal break-evens, so it can only be run by patient, product-first capital — quarter-to-quarter financial optimisation is lethal in exactly the long-cycle, safety-critical industries you operate in.

The shortcut-around-scrutiny and culture-flip lessons are your diligence and M&A radar: the fatal flaw hid in the clever path that dodged re-certification (the proper, slow process exists for a reason, and speed bought by hiding something is a debt paid in disaster), and Boeing lost its soul not by being acquired but by letting the acquired company's culture take the controls (win the deal, lose the company — check whose culture will steer after any merger). And the who-leads-and-how-close-to-the-work lesson is a governance safeguard: distance between decision-makers and the product is a slow corruption of judgement.

Your intersection: product-vs-numbers and profit-is-a-result are your management-quality filter and value-investing bedrock (the thread's capstone); match-the-capital-to-the-industry and buybacks-vs-building are your capital-allocation craft (and a direct caution for long-cycle, safety-critical sectors like yours); the culture-flip and shortcut-around-scrutiny are your M&A and diligence radar; and stock-hides-a-rotting-product is your value-investing discipline. The master case of the engineer-vs-accountant thread — the deepest management lesson in the tracker.

Abercrombie & Fitch — The Phoenix That Killed Its Brand to Save ItVideo case · Aging up with the customer, the data-inventory engine & the tech-company turnaround
▶ Video0/14▶
The one ideaThe shirtless-model, sex-sells teen brand of the 2000s became "ringarde," lost its CEO to scandal, and flatlined for a decade. Then, in 2022, it made a move everyone ignored except Wall Street — and on 20 May 2023 the stock went 8x in a year, beating the S&P and even Nvidia. Its secret: it stopped being a clothing brand and became a technology company that happens to sell clothes — after deliberately destroying its own brand to rebuild it.
A note on framing

A turnaround case — one of the file's rare success stories — presented factually; figures are the video's account, around my cutoff. It's the bright mirror to the brand-dilution and optimizer failures (Nike 58, Gucci 19), and contains a sharp counter-example (Old Navy's sizing disaster) worth its own lesson.

The story (in brief)

A&F has always known how to transform radically — even after going bankrupt. It began in 1892 when David Abercrombie, an outdoorsman-engineer, made his own superior expedition gear; a wealthy client, Ezra Fitch, bought in, the firm became Abercrombie & Fitch (1904), and after the partners fell out Fitch took full control and made it the number-one address for New York's bourgeoisie outfitting for hunting and nature sports — luxury rifles, tents, boats; it kitted out Theodore Roosevelt's safaris and Richard Byrd's Antarctic expedition (and, grimly, sold Hemingway the gun he died by). But by the 1970s cheaper competition and fading ultra-luxury tastes caught up (it once sold a gold chess set for the equivalent of $140,000), and in 1976 it went bankrupt. A sporting-goods chain bought the name and customer list for $1.5M (1978), relaunched it as a mail-order hunting outfitter, then in 1988 offloaded it to The Limited (owner of Victoria's Secret), which abandoned the hunting theme for upscale young-adult clothing. In 1992 Mike Jeffries became CEO, took it independent and public, aimed it 100% at teenagers, and built the shirtless-models, sex-sells image — 20 golden years of relentless growth and international expansion (Canada 2005, Europe 2007, Asia 2009). Then, from 2012, the black period: the brand turned uncool, discrimination lawsuits piled up, Jeffries resigned, sales collapsed.

Where it lands

In 2017 Fran Horowitz became CEO with a secret, multi-part plan that bore fruit five years later: become a technology company first, that sells clothes second. But first she had to destroy the brand to rebuild it. Step one was a radical change of customer: no more shirtless models, no more teens on TikTok — A&F would age up with the customers who wore it in the 2000s and are now 25-40, the millennials, whose women are the biggest annual spenders on clothing (working, earning more, needing to look presentable). Changing the customer meant changing the product, so again she tore it down to zero: quality up, logos discreet or gone, sizing more inclusive — from low-rise sexy XS to minimalist, exacting, comfortable. Hugely risky, but a hit: search #abercrombie on TikTok now and it's women over 30 showing their hauls. With that done, the real catapult was technology. A&F uses AI and big-data analysis to make exactly the right quantity and sizes to minimise unsold stock — the nightmare of every brand — with a system that reads sales in real time and recommends what to produce next (notice smaller sizes selling this week, produce more slim fits next), cutting average inventory 30%. The sharp contrast: in 2022 Old Navy, in an inclusivity push, added sizes from XXXXS to super-XXXXL, guessed the mix wrong, drowned in unsold stock and frustrated customers, and its leadership was fired — the exact mistake A&F's data engine avoids. A&F went further digital, cutting floor space 25% (2017-2021) to save $230M a year in rent and pour it into online, now 50% of revenue (20 points above the industry) — which itself is a compounding edge, because more online sales means far more customer data and higher conversion. And it runs a different operating model from a Zara (one central collection shipped to every store): A&F uses AI to build different collections almost city by city — by weather, median age, median salary, customer data — run not by one HQ team but by many small, agile, independent teams per city and country. Wall Street understood instantly and rewarded the stock with one of the year's best performances, beating Nvidia — not on words but on results: 2023 revenue +16%, a record $500M profit, margins over 11%, debt sharply down. The phoenix that died several times and always rose stronger — a clothing brand that stopped selling clothes the old way in order to sell far more, by becoming a tech company.

It's the return-to-source discipline (Porsche 56, Nike 58) executed successfully, and the counter to WeWork (70): the "we're a tech company now" claim was real because the numbers moved with it (+16% revenue, record $500M profit, 11%+ margins). The destroy-to-rebuild and age-up-with-your-customer lessons are the gems, and a repositioning masterclass: a genuine turnaround is demolition before construction (the nerve to gut a recognisable brand), and following your loyal customers as they age and earn can beat endlessly re-recruiting a fickler younger cohort — the inverse of the strip-mine-the-brand error. And repositioning is a product rebuild, not a marketing repaint (change the customer, change the product); for your value-investing eye, it's the tell of a real vs cosmetic turnaround.

The inventory-as-the-edge and Old-Navy-counter-example lessons are your operational and diligence craft: the unglamorous back-office problem (unsold stock, the killer of apparel margins) is where the durable advantage lives, and A&F's real-time data engine cut inventory 30% while Old Navy's data-less good intention (mis-sized inclusivity) drowned it in unsold stock and fired its leadership — virtue without operational rigour is still a disaster, and execution, not intention, meets the customer. It's the data-vs-algorithm/data-vs-guess thread (La Redoute 39, Nike 58) shown from the winning side.

The operating-model-re-rating lesson is your value-investing gem: A&F earned a tech-company multiple (8x, beating Nvidia) because it operates like one — AI, big data, a compounding online data flywheel, city-by-city localisation — though it sells clothes; the market pays for how a business runs and compounds, not what it nominally makes. Judge the model, not the label — a "boring" category run with a genuinely superior operating model can earn a premium multiple (and the online-mix is a data-and-conversion flywheel, not merely a higher-margin channel). It pairs with demand-results-beneath-the-narrative: back the re-rating only when the fundamentals prove the story.

TSMC — The Company the World Would Go to War OverVideo case · The indispensable chokepoint, the silicon shield & the geopolitical tail
▶ Video0/14▶
The one ideaOne Taiwanese company is worth more to the world than ExxonMobil, Google or Microsoft — because the future runs through its hands. TSMC makes 54% of the world's semiconductors and virtually all the most advanced ones, the chips in your phone, your car, your hospital, the F-35, NASA's Mars rover and guided missiles. It's the picks-and-shovels supplier the whole chip war depends on — and the reason the West says it would go to nuclear war to defend Taiwan.
A note on framing

A geopolitics-and-strategy case, presented factually and neutrally; the Taiwan-China tensions and the invasion scenarios are stated as analysis, without taking a side on the sovereignty dispute or predicting outcomes. The Buffett exit and the fragility scenario are the video's account; figures are around my cutoff. Sponsor segment omitted.

The story (in brief)

TSMC (Taiwan Semiconductor Manufacturing Company) is the world's largest chipmaker and the only one producing the most advanced nodes — down to 3nm and 2nm, while rivals are only reaching 7nm and 5nm. Smaller chips mean more power in less space, which is why a pocket device now replaces a phone, camera, GPS, console and more; these micro-chips are the oil of the 21st century, and the US Commerce Secretary has said Chinese control of TSMC would be "absolutely devastating" for the world and US economies, which depend entirely on its chips. The China-Taiwan tension dates to the end of the Chinese civil war in 1949; China regards Taiwan as integral territory (as France regards Corsica, per the video's analogy) and, per a Chinese embassy note, sees reunification as inevitable and achievable only by force. Taiwan's defence — the "porcupine strategy" — aims to make any invasion so costly and difficult it deters China, backed by US-authorised arms sales that shift the economic cost of war onto the aggressor. And there's a deeper deterrent: TSMC itself, the "silicon shield." Its most advanced fabs are in Taiwan by law (national security forbids making cutting-edge chips abroad), so while it has plants in the US and China, China only ever gets chips one to three generations behind — and in 2020 TSMC cut off Huawei to comply with US sanctions, because defying them would have lost it access to Dutch ASML's chipmaking machines, ending its reign.

Why doesn't China — or anyone — just build its own leading-edge fabs? Because it costs too much and takes too long: even Apple, one of the world's largest companies, can't do it profitably, and if China or France started now, by the time the fab was ready (~8 years) TSMC would already be producing the next generation at 1nm and below. So to lead in semiconductors, China would need to take Taiwan — but force would destroy TSMC and its fabs, not necessarily on purpose, but because (as Ukraine and Gaza show) almost everything gets destroyed in war regardless of strategic value. The most troubling part: it might not be the Chinese who reduce the fabs to dust — since US military and space hardware (F-35s, Javelins, NASA's robots) is packed with TSMC chips, the Americans would have an interest in sabotaging or blowing up the fabs to keep the technology out of Chinese hands.

Where it lands

What would happen if TSMC's fabs went dark? A preview: early in the 2020 pandemic, the world's semiconductor fabs ran at 90% instead of 100% capacity — and that 10% drop caused the "chip shortage," hammering autos, graphics cards and consoles, forcing aggressive price rises that fed today's inflation; the world built 26% fewer cars in 2021, and 169+ industries were hit — all from a 10% shortfall. Now imagine the company that makes 54% of the market vanishing for weeks or months: every industry worldwide violently hit — no new phones, planes, medical devices or cars, AI stopped dead — global consumption cratering and prices soaring, a world depression that wouldn't recover for 10-15 years, making Covid and 2008 look like a stroll. Faced with this pessimistic but real scenario, the West responded: the US CHIPS Act (2022) and the European Chips Act subsidise fab construction on home soil (notably Germany) to reduce dependence on Taiwan — and tellingly, though the US has Intel and Germany has Infineon, much of the subsidy goes to TSMC, because without it the world stops and everyone knows it. A race against the clock has begun to be ready for the day China moves. Wall Street is preparing too: Warren Buffett bought 60M TSMC shares in summer 2022, then sold 85%+ within three months and exited completely in early 2023 — a startling reversal for a long-term investor, which he attributed to geopolitical tensions, saying TSMC is a well-run company but Berkshire had better places to deploy the capital and he never wanted to lose money for those who trust him (odd, given the risks existed when he bought, and that his huge Apple stake would be the first casualty if anything hit TSMC). Even so, the stock is at all-time highs on two things: the world's insatiable appetite for its products (the AI explosion) and simply excellent fundamentals — very high margins, growing sales, virtually no debt; without its inherent risk it would likely be a global top-10 company by market cap. Investing in it carries high risk but, for those who like a thrill and can exit before it's too late, an incredible opportunity.

The linchpin of your AI-hardware and sovereignty map: Intel (71) named TSMC as the supplier that won regardless of who won the chip war; this is its own card, and it completes the board — Nvidia (01) the enabling designer, Intel (71) the fallen integrator, the design champions (Apple, AMD, Qualcomm), and TSMC the indispensable fab beneath them all. It's the ultimate expression of the chokepoint/toll-booth thread (AWS 11, Sand 62, shipbuilding 65) and the sovereignty thread (Palantir 73, digital euro 50): the single physical node the entire modern economy and military run through.

The capital-and-time-wall moat is the gem, and your value-investing craft: TSMC's protection isn't a secret but a barrier so high even Apple won't attempt it, and a lead that compounds faster than an ~8-year fab build can catch — the most durable moat there is, because it deters even the richest rational challenger. And the small-disruption-cascades lesson (a 10% capacity drop hitting 169 industries) is the fragility principle at national/global scale, the exact strategic-dependence tail you map in shipbuilding (65) and Sand (62); for an infrastructure and energy financier, it's the reminder that a system's true fragility is set by its thinnest concentrated link.

The investing lessons are your value-and-risk discipline: a superb business and a superb investment diverge when the tail risk is existential (Buffett sold a wonderful, cheap company over a risk he couldn't diversify away — especially as his Apple stake shares the same fault line), the discount is the market pricing the tail (read it as an estimate of catastrophe, not a free bargain), and subsidies flow to the genuinely indispensable, not the domestic favourite (capability beats flag — underwrite who is truly irreplaceable, because that's where the money is forced to go). The Buffett exit is a masterclass in position-level vs portfolio-level risk and correlated tail exposure.

Your intersection: the supplier-more-powerful-than-its-customers and capital-and-time-wall lessons are your moat and chokepoint craft (the AI-hardware map's linchpin); the silicon-shield-both-ways and small-disruption-cascades lessons are your sovereignty and strategic-dependence radar (shipbuilding 65, Sand 62); and the business-quality-vs-existential-tail, discount-prices-the-tail and subsidies-follow-capability lessons are your value-investing and risk discipline (correlated tail exposure — a lesson for your own IBKR positioning). The single most critical node on the board.

The Streaming Trap — Diminishing Returns & the Road Back to TVVideo case · The law of diminishing returns, retention economics & Chesterton's Fence — companion to Case 42
▶ Video0/14▶
The one ideaEvery streaming platform faces a hidden problem that will only worsen until it kills them — and it isn't wokeness, prices or bad shows. It's a law of economics: each new title added to a vast catalogue adds less than the last, so every euro of content spend gets less profitable, until the platforms are forced back to the very thing they set out to disrupt — television, ads and all.
A note on framing (and a companion)

This is the diminishing-returns companion to Case 42 ("Netflix — The Empire That Predicted Its Own Disruption"): Case 42 covers the attention-ceiling and AI-disruption angle; this one covers the content diminishing-returns law, the retention economics, and the streaming-reverts-to-TV thesis via Paramount's collapse. Read the pair together. Figures are the video's account, around my cutoff.

The story (in brief)

Paramount ruled cinema from 1970-2000 (The Godfather, Apocalypse Now, Forrest Gump, Titanic); in 2021, mid-pandemic, the flailing conglomerate launched Paramount+ to become a tech company à la Netflix. By 2024 it passed 70M subscribers — yet the group was worse off than before: the worst credit rating (subprime-2008 level), a stock down 90% from its 2021 high, and a $500M streaming loss in a single quarter. How can an iconic brand with as many subscribers as France has people lose so much money? Because the streaming business model is broken and runs backwards. Every month, platforms face the near-impossible task of engaging and re-engaging tens of millions of subscribers, so to avoid mass cancellations they must offer a vast mix of content — the more there is for every taste, the more subscribers pass Netflix's internal watch-time target (say 20 hours/month), and once they do, retention rises (they stay another month). So content production is both the main growth engine and the main retention ingredient; underinvest and you enter a death spiral (fewer subscribers → less money → less investment → …), the fate of France's Salto.

Netflix, the undisputed leader, has the biggest catalogue (~2,400 series, 3x Paramount+, 5x Disney+), built with money: $18B on content in 2022, twice its 2019 spend. Spending that much, it isn't buying content — it's buying retention: 85% of new subscribers stay 6 months (vs 45% for Paramount+), and 98% monthly retention means the average subscriber stays 50 months (vs 16 for Paramount+, 12 for Apple TV+). At that rate Apple and Paramount must replace much or all of their base yearly — enormous marketing and production cost — and the more customers they have, the more expensive the churn.

Where it lands

Here's the law that kills them: not every new title adds equal value. When Stranger Things season 1 dropped in 2016, Netflix had fewer series, so a global hit was a big fish in a small pond and moved the financials hugely. Ten years and thousands of titles later, season 5 — even if it gets more views — is a big fish in an ocean, adding far less. This is the law of diminishing returns: each new title reduces the value of the next, so even as platforms spend more, each series brings fewer new subscribers or watch-hours, and every euro invested becomes less profitable. That leaves three options: implode (Salto, Paramount+); produce less content (but then fewer subscribers and no growth → implosion); or produce cheaper content — because a sci-fi film costs a fortune for average popularity while reality TV costs peanuts and is hugely popular, so it's more logical to make reality shows than Sci-Fi. Netflix has clearly chosen option three, pivoting hard into cheap documentaries and reality TV (non-fiction went from almost nothing in 2013 to the majority a decade later) — which is why its films and series feel increasingly mediocre. But that only delays the inevitable; diminishing returns slow, they don't stop, so platforms turn to price rises (Netflix's price doubled in a decade), and in early 2022 Netflix announced its first-ever subscriber drop — 200,000 lost on 221M (0.1%), a ridiculous number that still triggered a Wall Street earthquake: the stock instantly lost 70%+, evaporating $220B. To make the model durable, Netflix introduced ads on a cheaper plan — and ads, higher prices, mediocre content, bundled offers… remind you of anything? Television. The future of streaming is the past: a return to the fundamentals of TV, only with ads far better targeted thanks to our private data and viewing habits. Ten years of disruption and unprofitable platforms to arrive back where they started. It's Chesterton's Fence — before tearing down a fence you think is useless, understand why it was built; Hollywood cannibalised its own profitable cinema and pay-TV to reinvent a less profitable version of television. A bullet in its own foot.

▶ Original video ↗

Beyond the video — added insight

The companion to Case 42: that card covers Netflix's attention-ceiling and AI-disruption; this one covers the content diminishing-returns law, the retention economics and the streaming-reverts-to-TV thesis. Together they explain the whole streaming bind — a business that must spend ever more for ever less, priced for infinite growth, drifting back toward the television it set out to kill.

The diminishing-returns law is the gem, and a universal analytical tool for your desk: each new unit adds less than the last (Stranger Things S1 vs S5), so spend must rise just to stand still — the big-fish-small-pond insight applies to content, stores, ad spend, acquisitions, even your own portfolio's marginal position. It pairs with the you're-buying-retention lesson (the CAC/LTV thread of Holy 59 and Wish 66, at the subscription level): in recurring businesses the real purchase is the extra month, retention is the multiplier that makes spend compound or evaporate, and the winner of a capital war is whoever converts spend into retention (Netflix's 50 months vs rivals' 12), not whoever spends most.

Chesterton's Fence is the sharp mental model, and your diligence discipline: understand why the old system exists before tearing it down — streaming cannibalised profitable cinema and pay-TV to rebuild a less profitable television (ads, tiers, bundles), rediscovering the incumbent's logic the hard way. For a value investor and a financier, it's a caution against the "we'll disrupt this inefficient industry" thesis: the inefficiency is often load-bearing, and the disruptor's endgame is frequently to recreate what it destroyed.

The investing lessons are your value-and-risk craft: a 0.1% subscriber miss erasing $220B shows a stock priced for perpetual growth is fragile to the smallest crack (underwrite what the valuation assumes — the assumption is the risk, echoing the Boeing stock-hides-reality and WeWork story-vs-fundamentals threads), and a disruptor adopting the incumbent's monetisation (ads, tiers) signals the disruption has peaked and a re-rating from "disruptor" to "utility" is coming — a genuinely useful sell-signal to recognise.

Your intersection: diminishing-returns and buying-retention are your unit-economics and analytical craft (the CAC/LTV thread, Holy 59/Wish 66); when-every-option-is-bad-the-model-is-the-problem is your business-quality filter; Chesterton's Fence is your anti-disruption-hype diligence; and the growth-valuation-fragility and incumbent-monetisation-creep lessons are your value-investing and sell-discipline. The companion to Case 42 and a masterclass in the economics of subscription content.

Big Pharma — The Patent Clock & How to Invest in ItVideo case · The monopoly clock, the buy-the-biotech engine & reading a pharma stock
▶ Video0/14▶
The one ideaHalf of Americans regularly take a prescription drug and a fifth take five at once — the world is hooked on pills, and Big Pharma is hooked on that. It's a $1.2 trillion industry built on a strange clock: a drug costs ~$2.6B and a decade to develop, then earns a 20-year monopoly — and the day the patent expires, the revenue can evaporate 85% overnight. Understand that clock and you understand how to invest in the whole sector.
A note on framing

A sector-investing case (the file's second, after the video's insurance one), presented as the video does — with its "this is my view, not investment advice" caveat kept. Figures are the video's account (some, like the $2.6B development cost, come from a pharma-lobby-funded source it flags as possibly inflated); around my cutoff.

The story (in brief)

Pharma is a juicy business: a $1.2T industry, the Dow Jones pharma index up 300%+ since 2006 (beating the broad market), and with populations aging the drug market should grow ~5% a year. It offers investors capital gains, generous dividends (J&J, Merck, Pfizer), and defensive, non-cyclical exposure that holds up in downturns — but the risks are many. The economics start with brutal R&D: understanding a disease and finding the right molecule means testing 5,000-10,000 molecules on average, ~10 years and ~$500M just to reach a handful of candidates, then three clinical-trial phases (safety/dosing on a few volunteers ~1 year; efficacy on a few hundred ~2-3 years; long-term impact on thousands). 90% of drugs fail the trials, so counting the failures, a drug costs ~$2.6B to develop (per a lobby-funded estimate the video notes may be inflated to justify high prices) — and because nearly all the easy diseases already have drugs, new ones get ever harder and costlier.

The whole industry is controlled by patents: spend billions on a breakthrough and a rival could copy the formula, so labs patent to guarantee a ~20-year monopoly — the right to charge what they want (branded drugs average 28% margins) to recoup the cost and more. They sell to wholesalers, then pharmacists; and US pricing is radically different from the rest of the world — unregulated (the private sector sets prices) versus Europe's capped, reimbursable prices — which is why ~50% of global pharma revenue comes from the US, and why labs spend heavily (sometimes illegal bribery, more often intense marketing and gifts/speaking fees to doctors) to get their drug prescribed over a rival's. That aggression is driven by the clock: only 20 years to milk the cash cow before the patent expires and generics — which cost almost nothing to make, having no R&D to recoup — crash the branded price up to 85%. Pfizer's Lipitor earned $13B a year before expiry and $2B after.

Where it lands

To keep the cash flowing, labs have three growth ingredients: subsidies (governments offer grants, tax breaks and longer patents for "orphan drugs" for rare diseases no lab would otherwise touch); hard-to-copy drugs (biotech treatments hard to reproduce even after patent expiry — part of the current biotech buzz); and constant pipeline refill (the moment a drug is approved the 20-year timer starts, so the next blockbuster must already be in development — an endless cycle). And the future is a health revolution (nanorobots, smart toilets, AI medical advice), with the drug market projected to triple to $3.3T by 2060. To capitalise, Big Pharma increasingly buys the biotechs — innovative firms building living-organism treatments (enzymes, bacteria) that lack the experience to run trials and marketing, so when a big lab arrives with a cheque they say yes; Big Pharma bought $200B of startups in 2022 to outsource the research — not risk-free (Eli Lilly paid $1.6B for ARMO BioSciences in 2018, its pancreatic-cancer treatment failed trials, and the $1.6B vanished). To fund this, labs are shrinking to their core — Pfizer, GSK, Novartis and Sanofi spinning off their consumer/wellness segments (toothpaste, vitamins) to focus on oncology and immunology — a double-edged concentration (higher profit potential, higher risk if a rival's miracle drug beats you). The two big sector risks: a rival biotech beating you to a treatment you spent a decade on, and regulation (US prices average 56% higher than the rest of the world — a bonanza until a motivated president caps them, as China forced labs to cut prices 62% for reimbursement). The video's investing toolkit: decide the role you want pharma to play — defensive/non-cyclical protection, stable ~3.5% dividends (compare yield against balance-sheet health, especially debt-to-earnings), or growth (read the blockbusters, their patent-expiry dates, and above all the pipeline — the pillar on which a lab's success or failure is built — plus clinical-trial results, medical press and the PER as a confidence gauge). And a personal approach: plan entries around transitions — Pfizer, off its high, expects to lose $17B (2025-30) to patent cliffs and collapsing Covid-vaccine sales (the market panics), but also to add $25B+ by 2030 from new drugs and biotech buys; the revenue and the stock are falling now while the growth plans haven't yet borne fruit — and by the time they do, the attractive entry point will be gone.

Beyond the video — added insight

The file's second sector-investing case, and a how-to-read-a-sector toolkit: where most cases dissect one company, this (like the insurance video it references) teaches how to analyse and invest in a whole sector — a natural fit beside the compounders/serial-acquirer discussion and your value-investing craft. The transferable frame is: understand the sector's core economic clock (here the patent cycle), then choose the role (defensive/income/growth) and the metrics that role demands.

The patent-clock and pipeline-is-the-thesis lessons are the gems, and directly your value-investing craft: the business isn't the drug, it's the finite exclusivity window, so the patent cliff is a scheduled catastrophe (Lipitor $13B→$2B on a known date) and survival depends on the pipeline, not the current product. For a value investor it generalises to any moat with an expiry (a licence, a contract, a concession — directly your project-finance world, where a PPA or concession has a defined tenor and the value is the window): find the expiry date, read what refills the pipeline, and price the cliff years ahead. Read the clock, not the current sales.

The buy-the-biotech and concentration lessons are your M&A and risk craft: when innovation and commercialisation are different skills, acquiring the innovator beats building it ($200B in 2022) — but it's R&D risk transferred, not removed (Eli Lilly's $1.6B evaporated on a failed trial), the pharma version of the buy-vs-build and acquire-the-capability threads (Palantir 73, Intel 71). And the pure-play concentration trade (spinning off wellness to focus on oncology) is the specialisation-vs-diversification choice you've seen from both sides (the vertical-integration spine vs Holy's asset-light focus 59) — more profit, more fragility; know which you're buying.

The regulatory-tail and buy-the-transition lessons are your risk and entry-timing discipline: profit resting on the absence of regulation is borrowed (US pricing 56% higher until a president or a China-style 62% cut changes it — the price-the-political-tail lesson, echoing the weaponised-dollar 75 and the Ireland OECD-minimum threads), and the best entry is the trough between a visible priced-in decline and a not-yet-delivered recovery (buy when the bad news is priced and the good news isn't — the margin-of-safety and transition-timing craft, and a live example in Pfizer, which the memory notes you actually hold). And the 90%-failure lesson is the price-the-winners-to-cover-the-losers economics of any hit-driven business (the power-law thread, Zero to One and the serial-acquirer discussion).

Your intersection: the patent-clock, pipeline-is-the-thesis and expiry-on-any-monopoly lessons are your value-investing and project-finance craft (a moat with a tenor is a cliff — read the window); buy-the-biotech and the concentration trade are your M&A and risk lens; know-the-sector's-role and buy-the-transition are your allocation and entry-timing discipline; and price-the-regulatory-tail is your risk radar. The Insurance Business — Getting Paid to Borrow (Float)Video case · The float model, the "chaos pays" tailwinds & the four insurer ratios
▶ Video0/14▶
The one ideaIn 2001 Taco Bell painted a 150m² target in the Pacific and promised every American a free taco if the falling Russian Mir station hit it — then insured the $400M risk for a $4M premium. That stunt is the whole industry in miniature: insurers mostly lose money on insurance itself, and get rich on the mountain of cash they hold in between. The secret isn't the premium — it's being paid to borrow.
A note on framing

A sector-investing case (the sibling of Big Pharma, Case 80 — the video the pharma one referenced), presented as the video does, with its "not investment advice" spirit. The ransomware section is stated factually as a perverse-incentive lesson, not a how-to; figures are the video's account, around my cutoff.

The story (in brief)

The Taco Bell stunt shows how insurers think about risk. Say the insurer judged the chance of a hit at 1% and charged a $4M premium: it expects to pay out once in 100 times, so if 99 other firms had the same idea it could collect $4M from each — a $400M pool ready to pay the one claim, or a $400M profit if the station hits nothing (which it did; Taco Bell got a viral campaign for the price of a premium, the insurer kept the $4M). That's the model, and it's a $5.2 trillion industry that draws Musk and Buffett — many say Buffett wouldn't be where he is without insurance. There are three broad types (life, health, and property/casualty covering cars, homes, etc.), and the basic model is simple: sell a policy for a premium, absorb the risk, deduct operating costs and claims, keep the rest. But premiums are low because of competition, and claims can be enormous (a tsunami costs billions), so insurers fight to limit payouts (near-legal clauses to find an excuse not to pay, or reinsurance — insurance for insurers) — and the near-totality of insurers actually lose money on the insurance segment itself, paying more in claims and costs than premiums bring in.

So how do they make money? This is the key. An insurer collects premiums and waits for claims that may come in weeks, years, decades or never — so it sits on a vast mountain of cash (an estimated $8.5T in the US, €2,757B in France), and the real business is investing that cash. Insurers are allowed to invest it and do — bonds, real estate, equities: life insurers, being long-term with predictable liabilities, favour less-liquid, long-held assets (bonds, property); property/casualty insurers take more risk for more return because claims are unpredictable. In 2022 US property/casualty insurers ran a $24B underwriting loss ($752B premiums vs $775B claims, thanks largely to Hurricane Ian) — but their investments earned $71B, more than covering it, for a $38B net profit after tax. And 2022 was a bad year; usually the underwriting loss is smaller or there's a gain. On average since 2000, the insurance segment loses ~1% of premiums a year — meaning insurers are effectively borrowing money at a 1% interest rate to invest, a rate found nowhere else. And the best, like Buffett's Berkshire, average a gain rather than a loss on underwriting — so Buffett is literally paid to borrow money he then invests and keeps all the profit on.

Where it lands

The future favours insurers, because — in one phrase — the more chaos in the world, the more insurers earn. Three societal dangers pay them: climate change (more hurricanes, fires and floods cost billions now, but drive more demand for protection and thus higher premiums later); demographic aging (longer lives mean more and higher premiums, especially in emerging markets — behind the boom of China's Ping An, the world's largest insurer); and ransomware (governments and firms hold sensitive data, carry cyber-insurance, and in most cases the insurer tells the victim to pay the ransom with insurance money — because a 40-bitcoin ransom is cheaper than the hundreds of millions in data-loss costs, and, perversely, paying encourages more ransomware, which sells more cyber-insurance; financially, insurers benefit from cybercrime spreading). Technology, especially AI, will sacrifice some jobs (the risk inspector above all) for the good of the industry: startups like Lapetus (a selfie whose AI reads your BMI, skin and eyes to estimate your health and lifespan for fairer life/health premiums) and Aerobotics (drones and AI assessing crop health for farm insurance) mean better data and fairer, more individualised premiums instead of near-uniform pricing. And the investing toolkit: beyond the usual PER, yield and margins, insurers need four extra ratios. (1) Financial-strength rating (from S&P, Fitch, Moody's — AAA "extremely solid" to C/D "extremely fragile") — can it pay all claims without threatening its survival? (2) The cost of borrowing, i.e. the combined ratio: claims-plus-costs over premiums — 105% means it "borrowed" your money at a 5% cost, 95% means it was paid 5% to hold and invest it; the average is ~101%, and below 100% is excellent (Axa was 90% in H1 2023). (3) The annual return on the invested float — borrowing the money only helps if it earns a profit (a proxy is return on invested capital). (4) The price-to-book valuation — at or below 1 suggests undervaluation, at or above 2 overvaluation, best used to compare peers. And if you'd rather not stock-pick, there are insurance-sector ETFs, some PEA-eligible.

The sibling sector-toolkit to Big Pharma (80), and the one closest to your compounders discussion: float is the beating heart of the Buffett/Fairfax/Markel/Berkshire model you've studied — "getting paid to borrow money you invest and keep the profit on" is the compounding engine behind the serial-acquirer and insurance-float names, and this card gives you the exact four-ratio toolkit to analyse them. The float / paid-to-borrow lesson is the gem, and your value-investing bedrock: the visible business (policies) is a loss-leader for the hidden one (investing the held cash), and the best insurers borrow at a negative cost — the single most important idea in the sector, and the reason Buffett compounded as he did. It generalises to the find-the-hidden-engine discipline (the obvious business is often the front, not the profit — the F1 toll-booth 64, the "not a beverage company" of Holy 59): always ask whether the headline product earns the money or merely gathers it.

The combined-ratio-and-return-together lesson is your analytical craft: the two halves are one system — a great underwriter who invests badly, or a great investor overpaying for float, both fail — so you judge the discipline of the underwriting (combined ratio under 100%) and the skill of the investing (return on float) as a single machine. Paired with match-assets-to-liabilities (life vs P&C horizons), it's the asset-liability discipline that also underlies your project-finance world and applies to your own lumpy deal-fee income (match what you hold to when you'll owe it).

The disorder-is-the-tailwind and perverse-incentive lessons are your sector-and-risk radar: a protection business is structurally long on the world's problems worsening (climate, aging, cybercrime — a genuine long-run tailwind, and directly your climate/energy-transition world from the risk side), and the ransomware loop is the sharp caution about incentives where solving a problem quietly feeds it (the align-of-incentives thread, Subway 35, Kape 57). And better-data-means-fairer-pricing is the data-as-edge thread (Palantir 73, the A&F data engine 77) applied to risk: whoever prices risk most accurately wins.

Your intersection: float / paid-to-borrow and find-the-hidden-engine are your value-investing bedrock (the compounders/Buffett engine); combined-ratio-with-return and match-assets-to-liabilities are your analytical and project-finance craft (and your own capital discipline); disorder-is-the-tailwind is your sector radar (the climate/risk long tail); the perverse-incentive loop is your incentive-alignment diligence; and use-the-sector's-own-metrics is the how-to-read-a-sector discipline. The float-toolkit case — the engine behind the compounders you already track.

Your version: find the hidden engine, ask whether a sector profits from order or disorder, match assets to liabilities, and read the combined ratio and the float's return together — because in insurance the policy is the front and the float is the fortune.
