Beyond the video — the records-are-paid-later keystone, and the inverse of the toll shelf

Stellantis is the harvesting inversion of your toll keystone — where Kinder (116), Vinci (142) and CHEP (141) build durable, contracted, reinvested cash flow, Stellantis harvested the installed base (over-price, under-invest, defer the defect) to print a record, and paid for it with a €22bn loss. It's the engineer-vs-accountant thread (Boeing 76 — the numbers-company harvesting the product; the PureTech defect is Boeing's safety-shortcut gene in an engine), the German-EV trilogy's fourth member (Porsche 56 / Mercedes 74 / BYD 43 — the incumbent that mismanaged the transition and the pricing), and the Danone (38) governance lesson (a harvested champion, the State and employees as the pawns).

The records-are-paid-later and over-price-harvest lessons are the gems, and your value-investing craft: a best-ever profit built on price hikes and spending cuts is a bill deferred, not value created — so for any record result, ask what was sacrificed (the unsold inventory and halved share are the bill arriving), and separate price-driven margin (a one-off harvest) from cost/value-driven margin (durable). The deferred-investment and deferred-defect lessons (write-offs and recalls are the hidden liabilities surfacing — Benetton 90 / Boeing 76) are your quality-of-earnings diligence, and the follow-the-billions lesson (the EV-mandate scapegoat hid a management failure in US over-pricing) is the read-the-real-cause discipline (Turkey 88).

The exit-before-the-bill, insiders-warn-first and buy-at-the-record lessons are your governance and investor radar — and this one is literally your market (IBKR, a CAC 40 name, the French State involved): the CEO of the record left before the reckoning (the harvest-and-exit tell — Chesapeake 108), the dealer's letter warned weeks before the market (the insider signal — WorldCom 99 / Boeing 76), and the employees, the State and the pensioners who bought at the ~€14 record peak (locked 5 years) suffered the deepest loss below €4 (the buy-at-the-record / lock-in trap — Action 126). Decompose the profit and loss by region (the record and the reckoning were both mostly American — SEB 127 / Vinci 142 open-the-accounts), and watch who the faltering champion turns to for rescue (Dongfeng — the China-cluster 117-122 / sovereignty thread). Your intersection: records-are-paid-later and over-price-harvest are your value-investing lens (the harvest inversion of the toll keystone); deferred-investment, deferred-defect and follow-the-billions are your quality-of-earnings and read-the-real-cause craft; exit-before-the-bill, insiders-warn-first and decompose-by-region are your governance and diligence radar; and buy-at-the-record plus rescuer-reveals-the-weakness are your entry-timing and sovereignty read. The case that names the inverse of everything the toll keystone teaches — records are paid later.

Make it click — similar plays

The harvest inversion & the engineer-vs-accountant: Kinder (116), Vinci (142) & CHEP (141) — the durable reinvested toll (Stellantis is the harvested inverse); Boeing (76) — the numbers-company harvesting the product (and the safety/quality-shortcut, here the PureTech engine); Benetton (90) & GE (133) — deferred investment surfacing as write-offs. The auto trilogy & the governance: Porsche (56), Mercedes (74) & BYD (43) — the EV-transition/pricing mismanagement; Danone (38) — the harvested champion and the stakeholders; Chesapeake (108) — harvest-and-exit / pay the insiders. The entry timing & the rescuer: Action (126) — the buy-at-the-record / lock-in winner's-trap; the China cluster (117-122) & Dongfeng — the rescuer reveals the weakness. Your version: for any record ask what was sacrificed, separate price-driven from value-driven margin, follow the billions to the real cause, and watch who exits at the top and who warns from inside — because Stellantis printed €18.6bn by harvesting, and the records were paid two years later with a €22bn loss.

How to drillFor any record result ask what was sacrificed to produce it (a profit built on price hikes and spending cuts is a bill deferred), separate price-driven margin (a one-off harvest) from cost/value-driven margin, follow the billions to where they actually went rather than the easy scapegoat (the EV mandate hid US over-pricing and cancelled projects), and watch who exits at the top, who warns from inside, and the stakeholders who bought at the peak — because Stellantis printed a record €18.6bn in 2023 by harvesting the installed base, its CEO left before the bill, and two years later it lost €22bn. For you: the records-are-paid-later keystone — the inverse of everything the toll shelf teaches.

Starbucks — The App That Was a Bank and Killed the CaféVideo case · The float, the breakage & the error committed twice — records while the value died
▶ Video0/14▶
The one ideaStarbucks — 40,000+ stores, $37.2bn revenue, 89 countries, the world's #1 coffee — holds a place no one anywhere disputes, and yet in a single year its net profit halved (operating result ~$5.4bn → ~$2.9bn, ~−46%), footfall fell for months, and in China a rival born under ten years ago caught, passed and humbled it. It wasn't inflation, a fad, or a bad quarter. It was one error, committed twice, never truly acknowledged: it sacrificed the one thing that was its value — the place, the "third place" — to chase the numbers, while turning its app into a disguised bank. The app that captured the cash is the same app that silently destroyed the café.
A note on framing (source)

Video case (Thibaut Dcode, "La chute brutale de Starbucks," Sep 2026). Figures and framing are the video's own; the Freedom24 sponsor segment is omitted and the content kept factual/neutral. Filed in Consumer, Retail & Luxury; a keystone that unifies the records-are-paid-later / sacrifice-the-value gene (Stellantis 146, Nike 58), the float/breakage gene (Insurance 81, the own-the-float keystone Action 126 / CHEP 141), and the China-disruptor cluster (Luckin — 117-122).

The people & the dates (references)

The founders: founded 1971 in Seattle by three friends — Jerry Baldwin (English teacher), Zev Siegl (history teacher) and Gordon Bowker (writer) — a shop selling roasted beans and machines, no drinks; named after the first mate in Moby-Dick (nearly called "Pequod"/"Pod" after the ship); the siren logo. The visionary: Howard Schultz joined 1982 as marketing head; a 1983 Milan trade-show trip revealed the Italian espresso-bar "third place," his founding vision; the no-"small" sizing (tall, grande, venti = "20," 2011). Expansion: first store outside North America, Tokyo 1996 (200 queued despite a tea country); peak empire >$100bn; deliberate saturation/cannibalisation (two Starbucks a few steps apart to suffocate rivals). The 2008 reset: the machine seized, sales fell for the first time ever, the stock went ~$40 → <$10, Schultz returned and in Feb 2008 simultaneously closed 7,100 US stores for ~3h to retrain 135,000 employees on the espresso — a costly gesture that saved the brand. The second error: mobile order-ahead added 2015 (crowding destroyed the calm); the app as a bank (2018: 23.4m US app payers vs 22m Apple Pay); the 2018 sale of the brand's supermarket rights to Nestlé for a ~$7.17bn advance cheque. The float: ~$2bn held permanently on cards/apps; ~$187m of unclaimed "breakage" booked as profit in one year; in France ~€1bn of gift cards go unspent yearly (~1 in 5 expires), the card capped at €150. France: arrived 2004, ~260 stores, lost money for years (>€50m accumulated), invented the "blonde" (lighter) espresso. The rival: Luckin Coffee, founded 2017 in China by Jenny Qian (Qian Zhiya) — from car rental, never worked in coffee — app-only, no counter, ~30-second grab-and-go, ~9.9 yuan, the exact opposite of Schultz's Milan dream. (Added context: Luckin itself ran a ~$300m accounting fraud exposed 2020 and was delisted, yet recovered to overtake Starbucks in China.) Leadership chain: Schultz (×3 stints) → Kevin Johnson → Laxman Narasimhan (ousted 2024) → Brian Niccol (ex-Chipotle, "Back to Starbucks" turnaround from Sep 2024).

The error, committed twice

First error (2008): sacrifice the place for the pace. To grow faster, Schultz had opened stores everywhere and banalised the experience — so in 2008 sales fell for the first time in history and the stock collapsed. His famous rescue (closing 7,100 stores to retrain 135,000 baristas in one evening) was the admission: "to grow faster, Starbucks had sacrificed what made its value — the place." The lesson was learned, then forgotten. Second error (from 2015): the app killed the café. The genius of the Starbucks app — mobile order-ahead, 2015 — captured the cash and the data, and became a disguised bank: it holds ~$2bn of customers' money permanently (coffees charged but not yet served), so Starbucks runs thousands of shops on its clients' money, not its own — the float that funds the expansion without drowning in debt. And on that mountain of pre-paid money sits a silent profit: breakage — the gift-card and app balances never claimed (~1 in 5 cards expires; the law lets the merchant book it as pure profit — ~$187m in one year for Starbucks worldwide). The app even outgrew Apple Pay (23.4m vs 22m US users in 2018); and the cash-in-before-you-deliver reflex repeated when Starbucks sold its own name to Nestlé in 2018 for a ~$7.17bn advance. But — the fatal part — the same app silently destroyed the product it was serving: when millions order ahead from the couch and all arrive at once, the "third place" of calm becomes a chaotic pickup counter, and the premium ritual (the thing that justified paying $6 for a coffee) died. Schultz's Milan dream was engineered away in total silence, because the numbers stayed magnificent — until they didn't. And across the world, Luckin (2017, led by a car-rental executive who'd never worked in coffee) took Starbucks' own app-genius and pushed it to the extreme — no counter, no salon, ~30-second grab-and-go, half the price — and in China humbled the king. The records were paid later.

Capture the lessons

Beyond the video — the keystone that unifies three threads

Starbucks is a rare three-thread keystone. (1) It's the records-are-paid-later / sacrifice-the-value twin of Stellantis (146) — the app printed magnificent numbers while destroying the "third place" that was the entire source of the premium (and the 2008 close-7,100-stores reset is the honest anti-harvest, the inverse of Stellantis's exit-before-the-bill). (2) It's the float/breakage case — ~$2bn of customers' pre-paid money funding the stores (the negative-working-capital superpower of Insurance 81 / Action 126 / CHEP 141, the own-the-float keystone) plus ~$187m of breakage booked as free profit, "a bank disguised as a coffee card." (3) It's a China-disruptor case — Luckin (2017), led by a car-rental outsider, weaponised Starbucks' own app-genius to the extreme and humbled it (the outsider-disruptor of the 117-122 cluster).

The sacrifice-the-value and two-edged-success lessons are the gems: protect the intangible that justifies your price against the measurable pressure to scale (the records built by destroying your value are paid later — Stellantis 146 / Nike 58), and judge an innovation by its effect on the whole not the metric it optimises (the app captured the cash and killed the café — the optimise-the-wrong-variable gene, Mercedes 74). The repeated-error lesson (the same mistake in 2008 and 2015 is a cultural flaw, not an accident) and the magnificent-numbers-hide-the-rot lesson (SEB 127 diversification-as-anaesthetic, Stellantis 146) are your diligence discipline.

The float, breakage and cash-in-first lessons are your value-investing craft — directly the own-the-float keystone: pre-paid balances are an interest-free, recurring, self-funding float (run the business on the customer's money — Insurance 81 / Action 126 / CHEP 141), breakage is free high-margin profit (model the unclaimed rate), and the cash-in-before-you-deliver reflex is a powerful discipline with a sell-the-future caution (the Nestlé name sale — Kodak 95). And the outsider-sees-it lesson is your disruption radar (the Luckin/China-cluster weaponising-your-own-idea gene), while the honest-reset lesson is the anti-harvest mark of a true owner-operator. Your intersection: sacrifice-the-value and two-edged-success are your brand/moat and management lens (protect the intangible; judge the whole); float, breakage and cash-in-first are your float-keystone value-investing craft (the self-funding pool, the free profit, the advance); outsider-sees-it and over-expansion-banalises are your disruption radar (Luckin, saturation); and magnificent-numbers-hide-the-rot plus the-honest-reset are your diligence and owner-operator discipline. The café that became a bank and forgot it was a café.

Make it click — similar plays

The records / sacrifice-the-value & the honest reset: Stellantis (146) — records are paid later (Starbucks is its consumer twin; the 2008 reset is the anti-harvest); Nike (58) — strip-mining the icon / the algorithm optimises the past; Mercedes (74) — optimise the wrong variable. The float & breakage keystone: Insurance (81) — the float; Action (126) & CHEP (141) — negative working capital / own-the-float; the own-the-toll shelf (Kinder 116, Vinci 142). The disruptor & the dying core: the China cluster (117-122) & Luckin — the outsider weaponising your own idea; SEB (127) — diversification-as-anaesthetic / magnificent-numbers-hide-the-rot; Kodak (95) — sold the future. Your version: name and protect the intangible that justifies your price, judge every innovation by its effect on the whole, hunt the float and the breakage, and look past magnificent numbers to the health of the core — because Starbucks built a bank inside a coffee card, and in doing so killed the café that was its whole value.

How to drillName and protect the intangible that justifies your price against the scale/cash pressure (the records built by destroying your value are paid later), judge every innovation by its effect on the whole not the metric it optimises (the app captured the cash and killed the café), hunt the float (pre-paid balances funding the business on the customer's money) and the breakage (unclaimed balances = free profit), and look past magnificent numbers to the health of the core while valuing an honest costly reset — because Starbucks turned its app into a ~$2bn disguised bank, booked ~$187m of breakage as profit, and sacrificed the "third place" that was its whole value, committing the same error twice until Luckin humbled it. For you: the keystone that unifies records-are-paid-later, the float, and the China disruptor.

BCCI — The Bank Every Country FearedSébastien Koubar · Video case · The Third-World bank that became the world's laundromat — too criminal to fail
▶ Video0/14▶
The one ideaBCCI (Bank of Credit and Commerce International) began with one of the sharpest positionings in banking history — the first global bank for the people Western finance left at the door — and grew to ~$20bn of deposits, 70+ countries, ~1.3–1.4m clients and 14,000 staff in under twenty years. But it was a structure that could only survive by growing: losses were plugged with new deposits (a Ponzi), credibility was rented (straw-man shareholders, a Washington grandee), and growth was bought by opening the doors to cartels, dictators and spies. On 5 July 1991 regulators shut it in seven countries in a single morning. The victims were exactly the ordinary clients it had sworn to lift.
A note on framing (source)

Video case (Sébastien Koubar, "Pourquoi tous les pays ont peur de cette banque," Sep 2026). Figures and framing are the video's own; the sponsor segment is omitted and the content kept factual/neutral. Filed in Finance, Banking & Fraud; the keystone of the growth-as-oxygen / Ponzi gene (Wirecard 102, Parmalat 96, WeWork 70), the borrowed-credibility gene (Steinhoff 135) and the jurisdiction-arbitrage thread (Ireland 18, Dubai 09, Nauru 72).

The people & the dates (references)

The founder: Agha Hasan Abedi, a Pakistani banker who starts in Karachi, finds a classic career too small, and sees up close who traditional finance served (élites, empires, the West) and who it shut out (people like him). His talent: a hypnotic charisma — "a man able to walk into a room and convince anyone of anything." The capital: during a falconry hunt in the desert he befriends Sheikh Zayed, ruler of Abu Dhabi, newly rich from oil; in 1972, with $2.5m from the Sheikh, he founds BCCI. The structure: incorporated in Luxembourg, major operations run from London, the financial holding in the Cayman Islands — no single regulator sees the whole; a "spider's web" of Russian dolls, banks within the bank, secret rooms where money appears and disappears. The façade: rich Middle-Eastern personalities as "shareholders" — in reality straw men, lent the money by BCCI itself to buy its own shares, with BCCI paying the interest. The "Black Network": a private intelligence arm run from Karachi, reportedly ~1,500 agents (wiretaps, blackmail, bribery of officials, and per several reports, targeted killings), plus arms trafficking and gold smuggling. The clients: the Medellín cartel (Pablo Escobar), Panama's Manuel Noriega, Abu Nidal, Saddam Hussein — and the CIA (Central Intelligence Agency), which in Aug 1991 admitted extensive use of BCCI, including during the 1980s funding of the Afghan Mujahideen. The US capture: via straw-man Arab investors secretly financed by BCCI, it took control of First American Bankshares in Washington, fronted by Clark Clifford (former Secretary of Defense, adviser to Truman, Kennedy, Johnson and Carter) and his protégé, lawyer Robert Altman, who assured US regulators under oath that BCCI had no control. The sting: US undercover agent Robert Mazur, posing as a wealthy launderer, recorded 1,000+ hours via a brass eagle on his briefcase, reached BCCI's "Private Clients" department, and in 1988 closed the trap with a fake wedding in Tampa, Florida — the limousines drove the bankers to the FBI (Federal Bureau of Investigation) instead (filmed as The Infiltrator, 2016). The end: 5 July 1991, coordinated raids in seven countries (London, Luxembourg, Caymans, Abu Dhabi…); 1.4m clients — London shopkeepers, immigrant families, Bangladeshi villagers, African local authorities — lose more than $10bn. Abedi flees to Pakistan, is protected from extradition, and dies free in Karachi in 1995. The US Senate inquiry led by John Kerry concludes: too many people, in too many governments, knew — and looked away because the bank had become indispensable.

The mechanism — how a mission became a machine

1 · A real blue ocean. The founding insight was genuine: a large, unserved market (the Global South's savers, traders and diasporas) with a job-to-be-done no Western bank cared about — dignity, access, a banker who looked and spoke like them. That is why it grew faster than any bank in the world. 2 · Growth as the only oxygen. Bad loans and failed speculation left colossal losses; rather than recognise them, BCCI used new depositors' money to fill the holes left by old ones — the largest Ponzi of its era. A Ponzi has one survival condition: it must keep growing. 3 · The client who pays any price. To keep growing, BCCI opened its doors to the clients who pay most for absolute secrecy — criminals with mountains of cash they cannot use. Secrecy became the product. 4 · Regulatory arbitrage by design. Luxembourg charter, London operations, Cayman holding: each regulator saw a fragment, none saw the whole. 5 · Rented credibility. Straw-man shareholders and Clark Clifford's reputation made the edifice look respectable — a façade, not a foundation. 6 · Too criminal to fail. The same features that made it perfect for cartels (global, unsupervised, traceless) made it perfect for spies; once governments were clients, closing it meant exposing themselves. Mutual blackmail kept it alive — until a single undercover agent made it cheaper to defect than to protect.

Beyond the video — why this case is yours

BCCI is the dark twin of your own positioning. Look at the map: London, Luxembourg, Abu Dhabi, Karachi. Abedi's edge was standing between two worlds and speaking both languages — the Global South's trust and the West's financial plumbing. You stand on a similar bridge: France and Tunisia, French · Arabic · English, nuclear operations and project finance, Europe's capital and the energy-transition needs of North Africa and the Middle East. Underserved clients, a real job-to-be-done, a scarce translator between two systems — the same raw material.

The difference is the operating system. Abedi turned the bridge into a laundromat because his business needed growth to survive and credibility he didn't own. The clean version is the inverse on every axis: projects financed to European standards (bankable cash flow covering debt service from day one), credibility earned through delivered deals rather than borrowed names, structures built for transparency rather than for fragmentation, and clients chosen against red lines set in advance. The same bridge carries either a fortune or a crime scene; the steel is identical, only the load is different.

Make it click — similar plays

The growth-as-oxygen / Ponzi gene: Wirecard (102) — the cash that didn't exist; Parmalat (96) — the fictitious bank account; WeWork (70) — growth as the product. Borrowed credibility & fake equity: Steinhoff (135); Archegos (89) — hidden leverage. Jurisdiction arbitrage: Ireland (18), Dubai (09), Nauru (72); Dark Pools & HFT (145) — opacity as product. Banks that died of their own clients: Credit Suisse (139), Lehman Brothers (130), Silicon Valley Bank (85). On screen: The Infiltrator (2016) — the Mazur sting. Your version: keep Abedi's bridge, drop his engine — a bank-grade positioning for the underserved, run on cash flow, owned credibility and visible structures.

How to drillSteal the positioning, refuse the engine: write your own "only person who can" sentence on the same bridge Abedi stood on, then run the Ponzi test (cash from client #1, not #n+1), set your client red lines before you need a deal, and in every diligence trace the real equity, the consolidated view and the rented reputation — because BCCI had one of the best ideas in banking and died of a business that could only survive by growing, credibility it didn't own and clients it should never have taken. Too criminal to fail — until it wasn't.

Zara vs H&M (+ Shein & Uniqlo) — Why Paying More in Europe Beats Paying Less in AsiaSwapn · Video case · Fast fashion — the cost of the garment vs the cost of the wrong garment
▶ Video0/14▶
The one ideaH&M (Hennes & Mauritz) produces ~60% in Asia at a fraction of European labour cost; Zara makes about half its clothes close to home (Spain, Portugal, Morocco, Turkey) where wages are far higher. Logic says H&M should crush Zara on cost. The numbers say the opposite: Zara makes roughly three times the net margin on twice the sales. In fashion the expensive cost isn't the cost of making a garment — it's the cost of making the wrong garment: markdowns, dead stock, stores that age because there's no cash to renew them. Zara pays more per unit to buy speed, and speed converts forecasting risk into near-certainty.
A note on framing (source)

Video case (Grégoire, co-founder of Swapn, "Les secrets de la rentabilité de ZARA," Oct 2025), based on FY2024 annual reports; the sponsor segment is omitted. Comparison table adds the latest published figures (Inditex FY to Jan 2026, H&M FY to Nov 2025, Fast Retailing FY to Aug 2025, Shein 2025 per its Hong Kong IPO filing), converted approximately to euros. Filed in Consumer, Retail & Luxury; the keystone of the speed-beats-cost and inventory-turn genes (Starbucks 147, Camaïeu 94, La Redoute 39, Action 126).

The numbers the video uses (FY2024)

Sales: Inditex ~€35–38.6bn (Zara ~70% of it) vs H&M ~€19–20bn (−0.7%, near-stagnant). Gross margin: Zara/Inditex 57.8% vs H&M 50.8% — so production cost is not where the gap is. Net margin: Zara 15% (~€5.9bn) vs H&M 4.6% (~€880m) — on €100 of sales, Zara keeps 15, H&M barely 5. Stores: 5,563 vs ~4,250 — Zara sells far more per store. Inventory: H&M carries ~€3.7bn of stock, Zara ~€3.6bn — the same pile, but Zara sells twice as much, so its stock turns ~40% faster (stock/sales roughly 9% vs 18%). Cash: Zara ~€11.5bn vs H&M ~€2.8bn — 4× the war chest; Inditex invested ~€900m in 2024–25 in new automated logistics centres and grew selling space +2% while closing 386 small stores (bigger, more profitable flagships). H&M closed 116 stores (350 in the 2020 pandemic year) — by obligation, not choice, each closure costing lease-break fees and asset write-downs. Geography: ~70% of H&M sales in Europe (mature, stagnant, and the region hardest hit by 2020 lockdowns) vs a far more balanced Zara (~half Europe, rest Asia and the Americas). Speed: Zara renews collections every ~2 weeks and restocks 80% of stores every 4–5 days from its Spanish hub; H&M needs 1–2 months to make a piece. Founder Amancio Ortega became one of Europe's richest men.

The paradox, solved — four mechanisms

1 · Buy information, not labour. Producing near the market lets Zara design, cut and ship in weeks, so it commits only a small first batch, reads what actually sells, and re-orders the winners. H&M commits big volumes months ahead in Asia — a forecast bet. When the bet misses, the cheap garment becomes an expensive markdown. Zara's higher unit cost is an insurance premium against being wrong. 2 · Full-price sell-through. Scarcity ("if you don't take it now, it's gone in days") makes customers buy at full price and come back often to see what's new. Fewer, shallower markdowns protect the margin far more than cheaper sewing ever could. 3 · Inventory turn is the hidden engine. Stock that sleeps loses value (H&M famously even burned unsold clothes in a Danish power plant). Slow stock → less cash → no investment in stores and logistics → older stores → fewer sales → even slower stock: the vicious circle. Zara runs the virtuous version: fast stock → cash pile → automated logistics and flagships → more sales. A 40% slower turn, compounded season after season, ends at one-third of the margin. 4 · Geography and optionality. H&M's Europe concentration was a smart bet 15 years ago and is a weakness now; Zara's balanced footprint and €11bn of cash give it options (acquisitions, a digital-native brand, a model shift). The video's verdict: it isn't bad management at H&M — it's a structural gap that widens every season.

Stores~5,460, fewer & bigger flagships~4,200, shrinking under pressureNone — 100% onlineLarge stores, ~65% of Uniqlo sales abroad
Main weaknessOnline lag (click-and-collect); fast-fashion ESG critiqueSlow stock, Europe concentration, thin cashTariffs & end of de minimis duty exemptions (US May 2025, EU 2026); labour/ESG scrutinySlow to chase trends; Japan/China exposure

The pattern: the two highest-margin players solve the forecasting problem from opposite ends — Zara by being fast enough to fix its mistakes, Uniqlo by selling things that can't go out of fashion. Shein solves it with data and no stores, but its margin rode on duty-free parcels that governments are now closing. H&M is "stuck in the middle" (Michael Porter's term): neither the cheapest-and-fastest nor the timeless — it pays for the forecast risk and owns the slow stock.

Capture the lessons

Run the drills

Beyond the video — why this case is yours

This is your world in disguise. In nuclear and energy projects, the factory price of a component is rarely what sinks the budget; it's the cost of a late or wrong decision — rework, idle crews, schedule slip, interest during construction. A local supplier at +15% who can turn around a non-conformity in two weeks often beats a cheap far-away one who needs four months. Zara's lesson is the project-finance lesson: value time and information, not just unit price.

And it's a positioning lesson. Zara, Uniqlo and Shein each picked one clear way to beat the industry's central risk; H&M tried to be a bit of everything and ended in the middle. Your "only person who can" sentence needs the same clarity: one risk you kill better than anyone, in one market.

Make it click — similar plays

Speed, stock & full price: Starbucks (147) — don't sacrifice the value for volume; Action (126) — negative working capital; Decathlon (21) — vertical integration. The vicious circle in retail: Camaïeu (94), La Redoute (39), Celio (33), Toys "R" Us (12), Conforama (37). The digital-native disruptor: Wish (66), Vinted (30) — where the fast-fashion items end up. Rented edges: BCCI (148), Ireland (18). The companion: H&M — the iceberg (150), Uniqlo (151), Shein (152). Your version: price the cost of being wrong, buy speed when uncertainty is high, and pick one clean way to kill your market's central risk.

How to drillStop comparing unit costs and start comparing the cost of being wrong: Zara pays more in Europe to buy weeks of reaction time, sells most of its clothes at full price, turns its stock ~40% faster, and converts that speed into €11bn of cash and three times H&M's margin — while Uniqlo wins by selling what never expires and Shein by producing after the click. H&M carries the forecast risk unhedged. For you: value time and information, and choose one clear way to kill your market's central risk.

H&M — The Iceberg Behind the Fall of the Affordable-Fashion KingBaptiste GS · Video case · Companion to Zara (149) — squeezed by Zara, Uniqlo, Shein and the online shift at the same time
▶ Video0/14▶
The one ideaH&M (Hennes & Mauritz) looked "too big to fail": 4,300+ stores, the reference for affordable fashion, star collaborations (Karl Lagerfeld, Balmain). Yet from 2018 its sales began to fall for the first time in decades. No single blow did it. H&M was the leader of a position — "trendy and cheap" — that every rival attacked from a different side at once: Zara was faster, Uniqlo was more durable, Asos/Zalando and then Shein were more digital and cheaper. A business that is "a bit of everything" ends up being the best at nothing. That's the iceberg: the visible tip is store closures; the hidden mass is a position that quietly lost its reason to exist.
A note on framing (source)

Video case (Baptiste GS, "La vérité sombre derrière la chute d'H&M," Oct 2025). Figures and framing are the video's own, plus the latest published H&M results for context. Filed in Consumer, Retail & Luxury as the direct companion to Zara vs H&M (149): 149 explains the numbers (margins, inventory turn, cash); this card explains the story (positioning, competitors, digital, image).

The people & the dates (references)

Origins: founded in 1947 in Västerås, Sweden, by Erling Persson as a women's clothing shop called Hennes ("hers"); in 1968 he bought the hunting and fishing retailer Mauritz Widforss, which produced the name Hennes & Mauritz — H&M. France: first store on 25 February 1998, rue de Rivoli in Paris — an instant success; quickly a national network, 138 stores by 2010; the go-to store for men, women and children who wanted trends cheaply. Peak: 4,300+ stores worldwide by 2023; designer collaborations (Lagerfeld 2004, Balmain 2015) as brand events. The turn: 2018, first sales decline after decades of growth; late 2010s, the low-price fashion segment fills with aggressive rivals. 2020: pandemic, profits down more than 90% — the worst result in decades. 2021: announces closure of around 350 stores. Since: CEO Daniel Ervér from 2024; FY2025 (to Nov 2025) sales ~SEK 228bn (~€20bn), operating margin up to 8.1% from 7.4%, stock down 12% — early repair, but still about half Zara's profitability.

The iceberg — what's above and below the waterline

Above (visible): falling sales, hundreds of store closures, a fading image with younger shoppers. Below (causes):

1 · Attacked from every side. In the 2000s H&M owned "cheap and on-trend." By the late 2010s many big chains had moved into that very profitable segment, and H&M stopped being the most interesting option. 2 · Zara's urgency vs H&M's routine. Zara renews constantly and keeps some stock deliberately limited — "if you don't buy now it may be gone in four days" — playing on FOMO (fear of missing out), which brings customers back again and again. H&M stays on heavier seasonal cycles produced in Asia and Bangladesh; you find the same pieces week after week, so there's no urgency to buy and no reason to come back. 3 · Uniqlo on durability. Simple, well-made basics that last — the opposite end from H&M's trend churn. 4 · The digital gap. Asos and Zalando, born online, offer smooth apps, personal recommendations, free returns and live tracking; H&M's e-commerce existed but with less depth and a weaker experience. During lockdowns H&M was still seen as a store brand, exactly when buying moved to 100% digital platforms — hence the 2020 collapse and the 2021 closures. 5 · The perception trap. Its offer looked less attractive both in style and in price, and its renewal seemed slower even though it hadn't actually slowed — the market around it had sped up. 6 · Fast fashion's dark side. Pressure on costs, low-wage workshops, criticised working conditions, and a heavy environmental footprint (the video cites ~10% of global CO₂ for the fashion industry — estimates range widely, roughly 2–10%). Younger consumers increasingly care; H&M's Conscious lines (≥50% "more sustainable" materials) are a response, while Uniqlo and Patagonia sell timeless basics and "buy less, buy better."

Each rival chose one axis and went to the extreme. H&M sat in the middle of all four — Michael Porter's "stuck in the middle." For the full financial mechanics (gross vs net margin, inventory turn, cash), see Zara vs H&M (149).

Capture the lessons

Run the drills

Beyond the video — why this case is yours

H&M is the warning for a generalist profile. A senior project manager with nuclear, design and finance experience can drift into "a bit of everything": competent on many axes, extreme on none. Against specialists who each own one axis, the generalist loses everywhere at once. The fix is H&M's missing move: pick one axis — the intersection only you can cover — and push it to the extreme. That is exactly what your "I am the only person who can ___" sentence is for.

Make it click — similar plays

The companion: Zara vs H&M (149) — the margin and inventory mechanics behind this story. Uniqlo (151) — the durable alternative. Shein (152) — the ultra-fast rival. Stuck in the middle / slow incumbents: Camaïeu (94), La Redoute (39), Celio (33), Conforama (37), Toys "R" Us (12), Nokia (129), Kodak (95). The digital natives: Vinted (30), Wish (66), Netflix (42). Durable vs disposable: Uniqlo in 149; Starbucks (147) — don't sacrifice the core value. Your version: stop being good at everything; become the extreme on one axis that a client can't get anywhere else.

How to drillRead the iceberg, not the tip: H&M's store closures and 2020 collapse were symptoms; the cause was a "trendy and cheap" position that Zara (speed and scarcity), Uniqlo (durability) and Shein/Asos/Zalando (digital and price) each attacked from one side, while H&M stayed in the middle with no extreme. For you: draw your own "where I lose to each rival" table and choose the single axis you'll push to the limit.

Uniqlo — Winning Fast Fashion by Refusing to Be Fast FashionCorentin Mercadal · Video case · Engineered basics, giant volumes, few flagship stores — Europe's fastest-growing clothing brand
▶ Video0/14▶
The one ideaWhile the French buy fewer clothes than at any time in five years — Camaïeu liquidated, Esprit gone from Europe, H&M retreating — one Japanese brand grows 30–40% a year in Europe. Uniqlo doesn't play the trend game at all. It sells a small range of engineered basics (HeatTech, AIRism, Ultra Light Down, the €15 T-shirt) that come back season after season, slightly improved, and produces each model by the million. Huge volume spreads development and fabric costs to cents per piece, and products that never go out of fashion remove the markdown risk that kills its rivals. Zara beats fashion risk by being fast; Uniqlo beats it by making clothes that don't expire.
A note on framing (source)

Video case (Corentin Mercadal, "La stratégie cachée d'Uniqlo pour vous ruiner," Oct 2026); the sponsor segment is omitted. Figures are the video's own unless marked; group figures from Fast Retailing's FY2025 results. Filed in Consumer, Retail & Luxury as the third card of the fast-fashion trilogy with Zara vs H&M (149) and H&M — the iceberg (150).

The people & the dates (references)

Owner: Fast Retailing, led by founder Tadashi Yanai; group FY2025 (to Aug 2025) revenue ~¥3.4tn (~€19bn), operating margin ~16%, net profit ~¥433bn (~€2.4bn); ~65% of Uniqlo sales outside Japan. Network: 2,529 stores worldwide; ~900 in China but fewer than 100 in all of Europe (80 in Aug 2025, ~95 by May 2026), concentrated in France, the UK, Germany and Spain (only 4 in Italy, 2 in Poland). France: test store at La Défense end 2007; Paris Opéra flagship opened 1 October 2009 — 2,200 m² in an 1866 former theatre near the Palais Garnier and Galeries Lafayette, rebuilt in 2023 keeping the theatre staircase; Uniqlo's third-biggest store in the world after New York and Tokyo. France is its first European market, yet only ~30 stores after nearly 20 years (Zara has 104). Technology: in 2000 Yanai meets the leaders of Toray, the Japanese materials group that supplies carbon-fibre composites for the Boeing 787; the brief — warmth without three layers — produces HeatTech three years later (fibres that turn body moisture into heat and trap air) after 10,000+ fabric prototypes; then AIRism (soft, wicks sweat, dries fast) and Ultra Light Down (a fabric so tight it holds down without the usual inner envelope — lighter and thinner). Brand: Roger Federer signed in 2018, reportedly ~$300m over 10 years, designed to last beyond his playing career. Europe growth: 2025 European sales up by a third to ~€2.27bn — 13% of global sales but nearly a third of growth; under-30s now ~35% of European sales. France rank: only 47th in the Worldpanel barometer with 4.4m transactions (Kiabi has 10×), but transactions up 26% — while H&M grew 2% in 2025 and closed a net 152 stores. Ambition: ¥1,000bn of European sales within five years — double the 2026 target. Strain: on 11 July 2026 the CFDT union called a strike in a quarter of French stores over workload.

The mechanism — four engines

1 · Engineered basics, not trends. Uniqlo's product is the material: years of fabric R&D with Toray before a garment exists. A HeatTech top or Ultra Light Down jacket is bought for what it does, not because it's this month's look — so it can't go out of fashion, and nobody waits for the sale. 2 · Volume as a cost weapon. Many models are made ~1 million pieces at a time. Development (cut, fabric, samples, tests) is paid before the first sale: spend €1m on a product and sell 1m pieces, that's €1 per piece; sell 100m over the years, it's 10 cents. Because the same sweater, T-shirt and down jacket return each season with a better fabric or fit, one investment serves several product generations. Uniqlo also negotiates directly with fabric makers in huge quantities and has partners in Asia (China, Vietnam…) do the sewing. Result: premium-feeling quality at a €15 price. 3 · Few stores, each one a media outlet. Instead of saturating cities, Uniqlo opens big flagships in prime places: flagships make more than half its European profit. A tourist tries a sweater in Paris, learns their size, and keeps buying online at home. In Europe €1 in 5 is sold online, and when a store opens, online sales around it jump by double digits — the store is both a till and an advert. Federer and designer collaborations do the same job beyond the shops. 4 · Everyone improves the store. "Zen-in keiei" (management by everyone): staff flag promising products and feed field information back up, using software that spots missing sizes.

The risks the video flags: big series amplify good decisions and mistakes — Uniqlo has been stuck with winter and spring surplus sold off in promotions, while flying in missing products at extra cost. Store teams juggle restocking, click-and-collect and crowds of tourists; when staffing doesn't keep up, the workload becomes constant pressure (the 2026 French strike). And it has over-expanded before: in the UK in the early 2000s it multiplied stores before it had the recipe to run them well, and had to pull back. Accelerating now raises the same question.

H&M does neither; Shein's speed is real, but its margin depended on duty-free parcels that are now closing.

Capture the lessons

Run the drills

Beyond the video — why this case is yours

Uniqlo's play maps onto an expert's career. Most consultants chase each new theme (the "trend"): hydrogen this year, AI data centres the next. The Uniqlo version is a small number of durable, engineered offers built on a deep material edge — for you, nuclear-grade engineering judgment applied to energy and infrastructure finance — reused and improved with every mandate, so the cost of each new client falls while the quality rises. And the Toray lesson is direct: your differentiation is borrowed from an adjacent industry (nuclear) that pure financiers can't reach.

Make it click — similar plays

The trilogy: Zara vs H&M (149) — speed beats cost; H&M — the iceberg (150) — stuck in the middle. Shein (152) — the rented edge. Timeless beats trendy: Celio (33) — the survivor that sold what never dates; Action (126) — volume and low cost. Over-expansion: Starbucks (147) — saturation banalises; WeWork (70). Stores as media: Apple (41), Nike (58). Your version: a few durable, engineered offers, improved every year, built on a capability your competitors can't borrow.

How to drillDon't out-run the trend — make it irrelevant: Uniqlo sells a few engineered basics (HeatTech with Toray, AIRism, Ultra Light Down) made by the million and improved every season, so development costs fall to cents per piece and nothing goes out of fashion; it opens few, huge flagships that act as advertising for its online sales; and it grows 30–40% a year in Europe while the trend-chasers shrink. Its risks are the flip side: big series multiply mistakes, and expansion can outrun its teams. For you: build a few durable, improvable offers on a capability competitors can't copy.

Shein — The Ultra-Fast Fashion Machine and the Day France Closed the DoorB.A.M. + Ecotalk · Video cases · Produce after the click, ship by parcel — until regulation, scandal and the BHV bet broke the spell
▶ Video0/14▶
The one ideaShein built the most efficient fashion machine ever seen: it watches clicks and searches, makes a few hundred pieces of a new item through thousands of small Chinese workshops, scales only what sells, and ships each order as a cheap parcel straight to the buyer. In 2024 it had ~23 million customers in France and was the country's #1 seller of clothes. But the machine's cost advantage rested on things it didn't own: duty-free small parcels, permissive rules on advertising and marketplaces, workers paid by the piece, and the planet absorbing the waste. On 5 November 2025 — the very day it opened its first permanent store at the BHV in Paris — the French state moved to suspend its site. Within two months French spending on Shein fell 65%; within a year its IPO valued it at roughly a quarter of its peak. The model wasn't beaten by a better competitor; it was repriced by the rule-makers.
A note on framing (sources)

Two video cases: B.A.M. (Business Analyse & Marketing), "Comment l'État français a détruit Shein" (Oct 2026) — the regulatory and commercial collapse; and Ecotalk, "Shein : l'enfer derrière les T-shirts à 5 €" (May 2026) — the production model, working conditions, environment and a visit to the BHV. Figures and framing are the videos' own (several come from NGOs and panels, e.g. Public Eye, Joko, LSA, IFM); group financials from Shein's IPO filing. Sponsor segments omitted. Filed in Consumer, Retail & Luxury, fourth card of the fast-fashion set with Zara vs H&M (149), H&M (150) and Uniqlo (151).

How the machine works (Ecotalk)

Demand first, product second. Unlike Zara or H&M, Shein watches what is trending online — searches, clicks, baskets — then launches a new item in a small batch. If nobody buys, it moves on; if it sells, production restarts almost immediately. Workshops, not factories: no giant plants but a network of thousands of independent workshops — reportedly more than 10,000 manufacturers working directly or indirectly for Shein. Scale of choice: in 2022 Zara launched ~6,800 new products, H&M ~4,400, Shein more than 300,000 — the jump from fast fashion to "ultra-fast fashion." The selling engine: permanent discounts, promo codes, notifications and limited-time sales ("dark patterns") create urgency, so people buy because it's cheap and feels like a deal, not because they need it; many items are worn once or never. In 2025 one French person in three ordered at least once from Shein or Temu. The hidden costs: workers paid per piece; the NGO Public Eye documents 75–80-hour weeks with one day off a month, wages of 5,000–10,000 yuan a month reachable only with heavy overtime, and defects charged back to the subcontractor and so to the worker. Thousands of tonnes of clothes leave by air every day; the video says Shein's emissions nearly tripled in three years to about twice Nike's, and unworn clothes end up in open-air dumps abroad. It also cites design copying and a claim that 31% of items tested contained substances harmful to skin.

The collapse in France — a timeline (B.A.M.)

2024 — the golden age: ~23m French customers (Institut français de la mode), #1 in clothing sales; thousands of new items a day, an average item around €10. But "fake promotions" — crossed-out prices that were never real — were already drawing fines. The BHV bet: the BHV Marais, owned since 2023 by the Société des Grands Magasins (Frédéric Merlin), still made ~€300m in 2022 but was losing staff and shoppers. Merlin gave Shein 1,200 m² with 11 fitting rooms. On 10 Oct 2025 employees and Paris officials protested; on 23 Oct Disneyland Paris dropped its sponsorship of the store's Christmas displays. The scandal: early Nov 2025, Shein's marketplace (outside sellers listing their own products) was found selling illegal items — including child-like sex dolls, banned weapons and medicines. 5 Nov 2025, opening day at the BHV: the state launches a procedure to suspend the platform; Shein pulls the products and suspends its marketplace in France. Customs then inspect 320,474 Shein parcels at Roissy airport; the government first announced 80% non-compliant, corrected by customs at end-December to 25% (non-textile items, counterfeits, sub-standard toys, electrical goods without instructions). Customers leave: Joko (bank-transaction panel of 1.5m French people) shows spending at Shein −54% in Nov 2025 and −65% in Dec vs a year earlier, while Temu grows +91%. In Jan 2026 (LSA) the French spend €108m at Shein — half the year before — vs €239m at Temu, which passes it for the first time; Shein's share of low-price e-commerce falls from ~18% to ~9% and it drops out of the top 10 during the winter sales. The courts: 19 Dec 2025 the Paris court refuses to suspend the site (serious harm to public order, but suspension disproportionate once products were removed); 19 Mar 2026 the Court of Appeal also refuses a marketplace-only suspension, keeping just an age-check obligation for adult products (€10,000 per breach). Europe: 17 Feb 2026 the European Commission opens an investigation into illegal products, algorithm opacity and the site's addictive design. The BHV ends: Dior, Sandro, Guerlain (and per Ecotalk, Maje and Claudie Pierlot) leave; visiting five months in, Ecotalk finds a near-empty Saturday floor, black panels, and prices higher than on the app. On 16 Jun 2026 Merlin gives up running the store and the Shein partnership ends after seven months; he admits the Shein name may have become a handicap. Fines and taxes: 3 Jun 2026, consumer-fraud authorities fine two group companies €22m (blocked withdrawals, missing price/delivery information); French fines since July 2025 exceed €210m — yet €22m is less than a day of Shein's global sales. The real threat is the new rules: a French €2-per-item tax on small non-EU parcels (1 Mar–30 Jun 2026); from 1 Jul the EU ends the customs exemption under €150 and applies €3 per item category; and the anti-ultra-fast-fashion law bans advertising for such platforms, influencers included, from 1 Jan 2027 (legally fragile; the Commission has expressed reservations). The adaptation: Shein is building a giant warehouse (about 100 football pitches, still empty when visited by Yann Rivoallan, president of the French women's ready-to-wear federation) to ship in bulk and escape the per-parcel taxes; it absorbs the €3 duty while Temu passes it on.

Where it stands

Shein isn't dead: over the first nine months of 2026 it became France's #1 online fashion site by number of items bought (ahead of Vinted and Amazon, per IFM), with 15m monthly visitors in Q2 2026 (−7% year on year). But the IPO on 1 Sept 2026 in Hong Kong valued it around $26bn vs ~$100bn in 2022; its first results (28 Sept) showed European sales −14% in Q2 to just under $4bn and adjusted profit −67%. Group-wide: revenue $38.7bn (2024) → $41.8bn (2025), but net profit $3.37bn → $2.06bn (−39%), and a net loss in Q1 2026. Verdict (B.A.M.): Shein lost what made it strong — the image of a consequence-free bargain, its growth and its lead. Prices will rise (customs, the environmental penalty, a move up-market).

▶ Original video (B.A.M.) ↗

The key difference isn't speed or price — it's who owns the advantage. Zara's logistics and Uniqlo's fabrics belong to them. Shein's lowest-price edge relied largely on rules, tax gaps and costs borne by others; when France and the EU changed those, the advantage moved to whoever was next cheapest (Temu) or most trusted.

Capture the lessons

Run the drills

Beyond the videos — why this case is yours

This is regulatory risk, the daily bread of project finance. Many energy projects' returns rest on rules the developer doesn't control: feed-in tariffs, tax credits, capacity payments, grid codes, carbon prices. Spain's retroactive cuts to solar support in the 2010s did to some investors what the end of duty-free parcels did to Shein. A financier who can separate "owned" economics (resource quality, technology, cost of capital, contracts) from "rented" economics (policy support), and price the rented part properly, is valuable — and that's a natural strength for someone who has lived inside a regulated nuclear industry.

Make it click — similar plays

The fast-fashion set: Zara vs H&M (149), H&M (150), Uniqlo (151). Rented edges & regulatory repricing: BCCI (148), Ireland (18), Kape (57). Platforms that lost trust: Wish (66), Duolingo (54). Where the clothes go next: Vinted (30). Your version: keep Shein's "measure, then scale" discipline, but build the edge on things you own, and price every advantage that depends on a rule.

How to drillSeparate the brilliant from the borrowed: Shein's produce-after-the-click machine (300,000+ new items a year, micro-batches from 10,000+ workshops) is a genuine operational breakthrough, but its rock-bottom price also leaned on duty-free parcels, advertising freedom, piece-rate labour and a tolerant marketplace. When France and the EU changed the rules and a marketplace scandal hit on the day of its BHV launch, spending fell 65%, Temu overtook it, the BHV deal ended in seven months and its valuation fell from ~$100bn to ~$26bn. For you: mark every advantage "owned" or "rented," and price the rented ones as if they could vanish.

Nike — The Brutal Descent: How ~€200bn Evaporated and On Took the ShelfThibaut Dcode · Video case · Follow-up to Nike (58) — the round trip of going direct, and who filled the empty shelves
▶ Video0/14▶
The one ideaIn September 2020 a 60-year-old shopkeeper in New Jersey opened a letter: after 37 years, Nike — over half his store — was closing his account. No meeting, no call. Fourteen months later Nike hit its all-time high (~€245bn); today it's worth ~€46bn — less than Ferrari, which sells ~14,000 cars a year — and on 21 September 2026 it left the S&P 100 (the 100 biggest US companies) after ~18 years. Since then Nike has repaired almost everything: the CEO who made the big decisions left, the man who'd left came back, partners were re-signed, stores reinstated. Everything returned to its place — except the money. Some mistakes can be undone by a board; giving your shelf space to a competitor can't, because the competitor doesn't give it back.
A note on framing (source)

Video case (Thibaut Dcode, "La brutale descente aux enfers de Nike," Oct 2026); the NordVPN sponsor segment is omitted and figures are the video's own. This card is the follow-up to Nike — the strategic suicide of going direct (58): 58 explains the theory of the mistake; this card tells the full round trip (2017–2026), the numbers, and the challengers who took the space. Filed in Consumer, Retail & Luxury, next to the fast-fashion set (149–152).

The people & the dates (references)

The machine (1964–2019): Phil Knight, a young Portland accountant, has the idea at business school to import Japanese running shoes when everyone swears by German brands; with his former track coach Bill Bowerman, $500 each, he sells the first pairs from the trunk of his green Plymouth. For half a century the model is simple: design in Oregon, make in Asia, sit on shelves everywhere — neighbourhood shops, department stores, mall chains. 2019: ~€34bn of sales, ~€22bn of it through partner stores — twice its own channels; thousands of points of sale in the US alone, from the New Jersey shopkeeper to giants like Foot Locker. 2017 — the turn: CEO Mark Parker (a designer since the late 1970s) launches the "Consumer Direct Offense": not leave the shelves but sort hard — focus on ~40 big partners and build Nike's own site and stores. 2019: Nike leaves Amazon (it had joined in 2017 in exchange for Amazon fighting counterfeits — which now copy the whole shop: fake sites, fake promos, fake payment pages); in December it designs a boot for a 20-year-old forward with "93" stitched on the sole — Kylian Mbappé. Meanwhile in Zurich, three friends make an odd running shoe: On, ~€300m of sales — Nike is ~120× bigger. 13 Jan 2020: John Donahoe becomes CEO — ex-Bain, eBay, then a software company: a data-and-platform man, on Nike's board for five years, chosen to accelerate the digital turn; Parker stays executive chairman. A month earlier Elliott Hill, head of the commercial side (an intern in 1988), retired after 32 years. Spring 2020: 90% of Nike stores outside China closed ~8 weeks; 25 June: quarterly sales −38%. The plan: direct sales become the absolute priority; the 30% digital target is hit two years early and raised to 50%; 150–200 small app-connected Nike stores; and publicly, in writing, fewer partners. The logic: a retailer buys a pair at ~half price — its margin pays the window, the staff, the rent. CFO Matt Friend: a direct sale brings ~2× the revenue and ~2× the profit. Why leave half the cake to intermediaries when customers knock on your door? For ~18 months every number agreed.

The mechanism — how the bet turned

1 · The shelves empty… then refill with someone else. Whole chains were removed from the reseller list, leaving metres of empty shelf. Empty shelves don't stay empty: on 15 Sept 2021 On listed on Wall Street, its founder escorted by a hundred runners, and the stock jumped 46% on day one. Its prospectus showed more than 6 pairs in 10 sold through resellers, in ~8,000 stores — On boxes moved into the space Nike vacated. In sneaker shops, Nike's share of purchases slid from ~75% to ~60% in two years. 2 · Marketing moves from creating demand to harvesting it. Nike didn't cut advertising — 2021–2024 the budget rose from ~€2.7bn to ~€3.7bn — but it shifted from the great brand campaigns that built the legend to digital targeting, sponsored banners and links pushing traffic to the app. Less effective, but easier to measure. 3 · The classics are milked. In 2019 the Dunk was 0% of sales; Nike revived it in dozens of colours, made it the queen of lockdown and, with the Air Force 1 and Jordan 1, built "the biggest franchises in the industry" — vintage sold at high prices with little risk… until over-supply made the classics collapse. In one sentence: Nike went from creating demand to serving and retaining it. 4 · The reversal. 19 Sept 2024: Donahoe leaves; the new CEO is Elliott Hill — the 1988 intern who'd retired, back 4½ years later "to save what can be saved." December: sales −8% again; Friend admits Nike spent its time capturing demand and competing with its own partners instead of creating demand. Hill gives sales teams their voice back; Urban Outfitters returns; 200 women's corners open in former partners — the film rewound. Not enough: first full year (June 2025) sales −10%, US tariffs eat margins, China declines quarter after quarter. 5 · The verdict. March 2026: a court rejects almost all of a shareholder lawsuit — "a strategy that succeeds and then fails isn't fraud, it's business risk" (only a Sept 2023 "solid pipeline" claim survives). Summer 2026: Nike sells a bit more through partners than in 2019 (~€24bn), but total sales ~€40bn are far from the €44.5bn peak, and its customer base is more concentrated in a few big US retailers.

Who took the place
NikeOn (Zurich)Hoka (Deckers)
2019 → 2025/26 sales~€34bn → ~€40bn (peak €44.5bn)~€300m → ~€3bn (×11 in 6 years)Above €2bn
Channel betGo direct, cut partners (then reverse)6+ pairs in 10 through ~8,000 resellersRunning specialists & wholesale
MarketingShift to measurable digital adsProduct + athletes as shareholdersProduct-led, word of mouth among runners
StarsLost Mbappé after ~20 yearsFederer, then Mbappé (paid partly in equity); football boots from 2027—

On 18 Sept 2026, in its Zurich labs among robots that spray-form shoes, On announced its entry into football — the face of the conquest is Mbappé, whose Nike contract expired end of July. Not just paid: rewarded with shares, like Federer before him. The boy whose "93" boot opened this story closes it as a shareholder of the challenger. The open question is China, where Hill is cutting Chinese resellers' online shops while keeping their stores — a corrected version of the same bet.

Beyond the video — why this case is yours

In project finance, the shelf is the relationship. Banks, developers and EPC (engineering, procurement and construction) contractors who cut out advisers or partners to keep the margin often discover what the margin paid for — origination, local knowledge, trust. And the challenger lesson is your opening: large firms regularly abandon small or emerging-market mandates as "not worth it." That vacated shelf — mid-size energy and infrastructure deals in North Africa and the Middle East, for example — is exactly where an On-style newcomer can enter cheaply and keep the ground.

Make it click — similar plays

The winner's side: On (172). The mirror: Rolex (154) — the owner who can't panic. The first Nike card: Nike (58) — the theory of the mistake. Sacrificing the core: Starbucks (147) — the app killed the café; Stellantis (146). The fast-fashion set: Zara vs H&M (149), H&M (150), Uniqlo (151) — Federer, again, as a long-term ambassador. Incumbents who left the door open: Kodak (95), Nokia (129), Intel (71). Your version: never leave a position without asking who takes it, and look for the shelves the giants are abandoning.

How to drillSeparate reversible from irreversible: Nike could rehire Elliott Hill, re-sign Urban Outfitters and reopen partner corners, but it couldn't take back the shelves On and Hoka had filled, the Dunk it had over-milked, or Mbappé, now an On shareholder. Its direct-to-consumer bet (2× revenue per sale, 50% digital) forgot what the retailer's margin paid for and turned brand-building into measurable ad-harvesting — and ~€200bn of value evaporated. For you: before leaving any position, ask who takes it; and as a challenger, enter where the giants are leaving.

Rolex — The Company Owned by a Dead Man's SentenceThibaut Dcode · Video case · A foundation as sole shareholder, the power to say no, vertical integration and manufactured desire
▶ Video0/14▶
The one ideaRolex sells more than €10bn of watches a year — nearly a third of all Swiss watchmaking, more than its next five rivals combined, Cartier and Omega included. Yet nobody pockets the profits: no shareholder, no family, no hidden fund. All that money obeys one line written in 1945 by founder Hans Wilsdorf, who died in 1960. For 66 years the world's most desired watch has been carrying out a dead man's will. That should have frozen it in place; instead it became its greatest strength. Rolex can wait decades without reporting to anyone, say no to its own customers, and spend billions without asking permission. Its owner is a purpose, not a person — and a purpose never panics.
A note on framing (source)

Video case (Thibaut Dcode, "L'étrange vérité sur Rolex," Oct 2026); the Freedom24 sponsor segment is omitted and figures are the video's own (Rolex publishes no accounts, so sales figures are estimates). Filed in Consumer, Retail & Luxury. It's the mirror image of Nike (153): Nike's owners demanded a fast pivot; Rolex's owner can't demand anything.

The people & the dates (references)

The founder: Hans Wilsdorf, a Bavarian orphan, opens a small watch-import business at 24 with his brother-in-law. His bet: turn the wristwatch — then a fragile lady's jewel — into something that dethrones the pocket watch, the heavy, respectable object of the serious gentleman. Everyone thinks he's mad. He wants a short name pronounceable in every language and finds "Rolex"; nobody knows what it means — he took the secret to his grave. Proof 1 — precision: nobody believed a wristwatch could be as accurate as a big chronometer; in 1914 a Rolex wins a precision certificate from the Kew observatory in England, the same grade as marine chronometers. Proof 2 — the Oyster: a waterproof case. In 1927 swimmer Mercedes Gleitze, the first Englishwoman to swim the Channel, faces a rival claim that casts doubt on her feat and decides to swim again before witnesses. Wilsdorf gives her an Oyster to wear round her neck. After 10h24 in icy water she gives up — but the watch hasn't taken a drop and still keeps perfect time. Next day Wilsdorf buys a full page in the Daily Mail. Rolex doesn't sell the watch, or even the feat; it sells the proof and the desire that goes with it. WWII: British officers in German prison camps had everything confiscated; from neutral Geneva, Wilsdorf lets any prisoner order a Rolex by mail and pay only after the war, on simple word — sincere generosity and brilliant calculation in one gesture. 1945: the Hans Wilsdorf Foundation. 1960: an explorer cables Geneva that his watch came back from the deep ocean dive intact; six months later Wilsdorf dies. Normally predators circle. Instead the notary reveals what 1945 built: a "main morte" (mortmain, "dead hand") — property held by an entity that never dies, never inherits and never sells. Under Swiss law a foundation has no shareholder and no owner; its assets belong to a purpose, written in the statutes: the perpetuation of Rolex; charity comes only afterwards, and only with what's available. Nobody can buy Rolex, for the same reason nobody can buy a cathedral — the door Bernard Arnault never found simply doesn't exist.

The mechanism — four tests the "dead hand" passed (and one it can't)

1 · The quartz crisis — the power to say no. End of 1969: Seiko launches the first quartz watch — a battery and a vibrating crystal, more accurate than most mechanical watches at a fraction of the price. In 15 years Swiss watchmaking falls from ~1,600 manufacturers to ~600 and two jobs in three disappear. Rolex had the technology (its Oysterquartz) yet sold only ~25,000 in 25 years, then buried the range without a word. Why could it refuse almost alone? There was nobody to reassure. Everywhere else shareholders panicked and demanded the pivot to save the next balance sheet; at Rolex the only shareholder was a line that doesn't panic — it doesn't ask you to save the quarter, it asks you to last. CEO André Heiniger bet that people would come back to mechanical watches, not to read the time but for what they represent. History proved him right. Asked how the watch market was doing, he famously answered: no idea — Rolex isn't in the watch business, it's in the luxury business. Rivals cut prices to survive; Rolex held its line. 2 · Dependence — the hand closes. Rolex was then a constellation of ~30 sites and independent suppliers, each making one part of the watch. Its icon, the Daytona (soon legendary through Paul Newman), ran on an outside movement, Zenith's El Primero — the one saved by an employee, Charles Vermot, who had hidden its tooling in an attic during the quartz crisis. A sword of Damocles. CEO Patrick Heiniger closed the hand: over 12 years he regrouped 27 sites into four giant factories and bought the historic suppliers one by one — the 1839 bracelet maker Gay Frères, the dial makers, the crown makers. With the industry barely out of a 20-year crisis, it looked like folly; but again, no shareholder to doubt. 3 · An uncopyable machine. Every watch is tested individually to a precision twice as strict as official Swiss chronometer certification (within 2 seconds a day), and every case is dunked in a tank to check it's waterproof. To compete, a rival wouldn't need a factory but a whole industrial country — foundry, workshops, laboratories tuned to the millimetre over decades, almost like the most advanced chip fabs. Copyable in theory, impossible in economics. Right now Rolex is building a fifth giant factory in the canton of Fribourg — over €1bn, 2,000 jobs, opening 2029 — just as the rest of Swiss watchmaking freezes hiring. 4 · Scarcity as fuel. As long as demand exceeds supply the queue lengthens and desire rises; each watch becomes a privilege. Rolex's official version: production can't follow without sacrificing quality, there's no waiting list, retailers alone decide allocation. Manipulation or quality constraint? Either way, the wait isn't a production defect — it's the fuel. A new Rolex began to gain value: most models resold above shop price. A lucky buyer pays €10,000 and resells next day for €20,000 on the grey (second-hand) market — €10,000 of pure desire that Rolex never touches. Around it grew an entire industry: Chrono24 (an eBay for watches), auction houses (Phillips, Sotheby's, Christie's), even watch winders and safes costing up to €15,000. Then the hand reached further: Rolex says nothing changes and retailers still set prices; but many small resellers sitting on stock bought at the 2022 peak saw it melt. In December 2023 the French competition authority fined Rolex €91m for banning its jewellers from selling its watches online for more than ten years; its anti-counterfeiting defence was rejected.

Geneva. Rolex pays dividends like any company — to one shareholder, the foundation, which redistributes them in Wilsdorf's order: first Rolex's development, then the city. Locals call it "the foundation whose name one doesn't say"; for a long time it didn't even have a website. Per the video it spends the equivalent of ~€700m a year (works included), most of it in Geneva — over €1,300 per inhabitant of the canton every year: scholarships, associations, housing, people in need, bridges, the university, part of the city itself. The brand has also funded explorers and researchers since 1976. It gives massively and often silently.

5 · The one thing it can't own — desire. A will can own factories, shops and gold bars, but not the wish to own the watch. From 2022, when that desire looked like pure speculation, the bubble burst: the reference index of second-hand prices fell about 40% from its peak and Rolexes lost nearly 30% of resale value. The sign came from inside: Jean-Frédéric Dufour, who runs Rolex day to day under the foundation's authority, broke his silence to warn publicly that comparing watches to shares is dangerous. The company that spent a century turning its watches into treasure now has to ask people to stop seeing them as investments. The open question: is Wilsdorf's structure the secret of an uncopyable success — or an anomaly that may one day turn against it?

Capture the lessons

Run the drills

Beyond the video — why this case is yours

You live inside two of Rolex's lessons every day. First, patient ownership: nuclear programmes like EPR2 only exist because a long-horizon owner (largely the state, through EDF) can commit capital for 60+ years — infrastructure finance is the art of matching long assets with owners who won't panic. Second, critical supply: managing critical auxiliary equipment contracts is exactly the Daytona problem — a flagship that depends on one outside supplier carries a sword of Damocles. Rolex's answer (secure or own what is critical, even when it looks expensive) is a lesson you can apply now, and a story you can tell in any infrastructure-finance conversation.

Make it click — similar plays

The mirror: Nike (153) — shareholders cheering a fast, irreversible pivot. Long-horizon owners: Family Businesses & Principal-Agent (84), BIC (26) — the other discreet controlled empire the video recommends, LVMH (28) — the buyer who could never get in. Scarcity & desire: Zara (149) — engineered scarcity at the other end of the price scale; Starbucks (147). Disruption survived vs not: Kodak (95), Nokia (129). Your version: choose owners and partners whose horizon matches your assets, secure every critical dependency, and sell proof, not promises.

How to drillRead the owner before the strategy: Rolex's only shareholder is a foundation bound by one 1945 sentence — perpetuate Rolex — so it could refuse quartz while 1,000 Swiss manufacturers died, spend 12 years buying its suppliers, build a €1bn factory in a downturn, and fund a city. Its scarcity created a resale market worth more than the shop price (and a €91m fine for over-control), but the one thing a dead hand can't own is the desire of the living, as the post-2022 price fall showed. For you: match long assets with patient owners, secure every critical supplier, and prove rather than claim.

Basic-Fit vs Fitness Park — The Cash Machine of €25 SubscriptionsSwapn · Video case · Low-cost recurring revenue, fixed costs, ghost members — and owning every club vs franchising them
▶ Video0/14▶
The one ideaA Basic-Fit gym is a box of machines, a badge reader and almost no staff, selling a ~€25 monthly subscription. A mature club has ~3,283 members paying ~€23 a month on average, so it makes ~€906k of revenue a year at ~50% operating margin, and pays back its opening cost in about three years (~30% return on capital invested). The costs are almost all fixed, so every extra member is nearly pure profit, and members who pay but rarely come (the "ghost members") are a blessing, not a problem. And unlike most chains, Basic-Fit doesn't franchise: it owns every club and keeps every euro. Its French rival Fitness Park made the opposite choice — franchise — and both work. The question is who funds the clubs and who keeps the profit.
A note on framing (source)

Video case (Swapn, "Les secrets de la rentabilité de Basic-Fit (machine à cash ?)," May 2025), based on Basic-Fit's 247-page 2024 annual report; the per-club figures are the video's own estimates. Fitness Park figures come from press reports (late 2025–2026), added for the comparison. Filed in Consumer, Retail & Luxury; the subscription/fixed-cost companion to Starbucks (147, the float) and Action (126).

The numbers (Basic-Fit, 2024, per the video)

Network: ~1,500 clubs in Europe, 800+ in France; listed in Amsterdam (a Dutch company), so it must publish annual accounts, a management report and quarterly revenue. No franchise: an integrated network — every club belongs to Basic-Fit, every euro of revenue and profit goes up to the holding company and is reinvested in new clubs. Pricing: €24.99/month in France today (older subscriptions at €19.90 still exist), with upsells — Premium €29.99, Ultimate €34.99, personal coaching — lifting the average basket to a little over €23/month (France 2024 revenue ~€559.7m ÷ the clubs and members). Growth: a cluster strategy — several clubs in the same city where the population is large, to become the unavoidable leader fast; 77 openings in France in 2024, potentially ~1,200 clubs in the medium term. The model: open 24/7 with as few employees as possible, to cut costs and automate. In Spain, Belgium and Germany some clubs have no staff at all — a badge reader and an emergency call button; in France the law requires staff for the 24/7 format. Unit economics of a mature club (open 24+ months): ~3,283 members × ~€23 × 12 ≈ €906k revenue; ~50% operating margin ≈ €453k a year; opening cost (fit-out, machines, badge readers…) paid back in about 3 years; ~30% return on capital invested. Members stay ~23 months on average, so revenue is recurring and predictable. Unlike McDonald's, which runs on staff, a gym runs on fixed costs with very few variable ones. Marketing, purchasing and project structuring are centralised at head office, so Basic-Fit opens clubs much faster than an independent could.

Why it's a cash machine — four mechanisms

1 · Fixed costs + recurring revenue = operating leverage. Rent, machines and electricity are paid whether there are 1,000 or 3,000 members. Once break-even is passed, each extra subscription drops almost entirely to profit. 2 · Ghost members. Many people subscribe and come rarely. They pay full price, cost almost nothing (no wear, no crowding) and make room for more members per club. The business is priced so the casual majority finances the regulars. 3 · Clustering. Several clubs in one city share marketing, let members use any club, and leave no room for a competitor — local density is the moat. 4 · Integrated ownership. Owning every club keeps 100% of the margin and allows central control of speed and standards, but it means Basic-Fit funds every opening itself (equity and debt). The video's lesson: the most profitable model isn't always the one you see; a €20 subscription, replicated as fast as possible, is the real power.

The trade-off in one line: Basic-Fit keeps all the profit but must find all the capital; Fitness Park grows with other people's capital but shares the profit. Ownership wins when returns are high and money is cheap; franchising wins when capital is scarce or speed matters more than margin. The same choice exists in energy: own the assets (an IPP, independent power producer) or license and operate them for others.

Capture the lessons

Run the drills

Beyond the video — why this case is yours

A gym is a small infrastructure project. High upfront capex, low running costs, long-lived recurring revenue, a payback period and a return on capital — exactly how you'd read a solar farm or a data centre. And the Basic-Fit vs Fitness Park choice is the developer's classic dilemma: own the assets on your balance sheet (keep all the returns, carry all the financing) or structure them for others and earn fees. For someone moving from engineering into project finance, being fluent in both sides of that choice is a real edge.

Make it click — similar plays

Recurring cash & float: Starbucks (147) — pre-paid balances and breakage; The Insurance Business (81). Low cost done right: Action (126), Lidl (24), Uniqlo (151). The companion: Fitness Park — a franchisee's real accounts (156), On Air (157). Own vs franchise: Subway (35), O'Tacos (144), McDonald's via The Founder (Library 10). Your version: prove one unit, then decide whose capital multiplies it.

How to drillRead the unit, then the ownership: a mature Basic-Fit club turns ~3,283 members at ~€23/month into ~€906k of revenue at ~50% margin, pays back in ~3 years, and is made richer by members who rarely come; clustering and centralisation let it multiply fast. Basic-Fit owns every club and keeps every euro; Fitness Park franchises, growing with others' capital and attracting private equity. For you: model one unit, then choose whose balance sheet carries the rest.
