Fitness Park — The Real Profitability of a FranchiseeSwapn · Video case · Companion to Basic-Fit (155) — the brochure promise vs a real club's accounts
▶ Video0/14▶
The one ideaFitness Park's website promises franchisees a return on investment in 12 months and 35% margins. The real accounts of an established club tell a more nuanced story: about €1.15m of revenue and a 13.3% net margin — solid, but earned only by controlling rent and payroll every month. Badly run, the same €1.2m club (with €400k of your own money in it) falls to a 7% operating margin instead of 25%: "not the Eldorado any more, just a well-paid job with an enormous risk." A franchise sells you a proven formula, not a passive income. The franchisor collects its royalties on revenue whether you make a profit or not.
A note on framing (source)

Video case (Swapn, "La vraie rentabilité d'un franchisé Fitness Park en 15 min," Feb 2026), based on the published accounts of a real franchisee and of the franchisor; figures are the video's own. Direct companion to Basic-Fit vs Fitness Park (155): 155 compares the two models from the top; this card opens the books of one franchised club.

The network and the promise

Network (per the video): ~400 clubs in France, ~1.4m members, ~100 new clubs a year; a 35-year-old brand and the European leader in fitness franchising. Unlike Basic-Fit, which owns all its clubs, Fitness Park chose franchising to grow faster without tying up billions. Why franchise rather than go independent: a recognised brand with a real community, 35 years of know-how packaged into a turnkey concept, marketing tools, a purchasing centre that negotiates equipment, and operational support — you buy a tested formula instead of building from zero. What a franchisee actually owns: the company and its legal structure, the business goodwill (contracts, member base), the fit-out and equipment depending on the set-up — but usually not the walls. Clubs rent premises on 10-, 15- or 20-year leases, and rent becomes one of the biggest charges and a key risk. Entry ticket: about €1.2m of investment, with a minimum personal contribution of €400k; the rest is a bank loan. Recurring royalties: 8.2% of revenue excluding VAT (an operating royalty plus a communication royalty), fixed and non-negotiable — on the network's average revenue of ~€1.1m, about €90k a year paid to the franchisor. The promise: return on investment in 12 months (the Observatoire de la Franchise found 18 months) and a 35% EBITDA margin (operating cash profit) once the club is established.

A real club opened up — Rennes

Swapn pulled the published accounts of Rennes Fitness Développement (RFD), an established franchisee, for the year ended 31 August 2024 — a mature club, several years old, representative of the model once stabilised. Revenue: ~€1.15m, in line with the network average (~€1.1m). Merchandise sold in the club (protein bars, shakers, drinks) is marginal. Taxes: corporate tax €25,984 (2.3% of revenue) and other taxes €64,324 (5.6%). Result: a 13.3% net margin — roughly €150k of net profit. Solid, and enough to develop calmly, but it's the margin of a mature club with a well-negotiated lease and optimised staffing. The big lesson: external charges, especially rent, are decisive — if that line slips by 5 or 10 points, the whole profitability collapses.

Who really wins — the franchisor

Fitness Park Développement (the franchisor, not to be confused with the Rennes franchisee) makes about €66m of revenue from two activities: royalties and entry fees (services billed to franchisees) and the sale of merchandise to franchisees. Its income is a percentage of franchisees' revenue, not their profit: it earns as long as the clubs sell, while the franchisee carries the lease, the staff, the debt and the margin risk. That's why the network grows — and why the franchisees who execute well do well too, but those who don't carry the loss alone.

Day-to-day reality and the three levers

The daily job: staff turnover is high, so you recruit again and again; machines break down and must be repaired fast or members leave for the competition; cleanliness is the number-one criterion in customer reviews — dirty changing rooms or showers show immediately; seasonal peaks (January resolutions, September back-to-school) then keeping momentum the rest of the year; long opening hours (generally 6:00–23:00, 7 days a week) — even if you're not there, everything must run. Financial risks: energy-price inflation hits external charges directly; aggressive local competition (a Basic-Fit opens next door, an independent cuts prices); and churn — the rate at which members cancel — to watch permanently, because if people leave faster than they arrive, revenue erodes. It's not an investment where you put money in and wait for dividends; it's a job of execution, permanent optimisation and presence on the ground, at least in the first years.

Lever 1 — the lease. Rent is the single biggest determinant of a club's profitability; negotiate it like your life depends on it, because you'll pay it for 10–20 years. Lever 2 — payroll. The best clubs spend about 14–15% of revenue on staff, the weaker ones about 20%: a permanent trade-off between full-time and part-time, peak and off-peak hours — where operating experience makes the difference. Lever 3 — scale. Going from one to three clubs pools fixed costs (accounting, energy contracts, maintenance, insurance at bigger volumes, purchasing, marketing across territories), so profit per club rises mechanically. The best performers become mini-holdings; Fitness Park actively encourages multi-franchisees because they've proven themselves and reach break-even faster. But scale amplifies what works and what doesn't: a club with a catastrophic lease or badly sized payroll, copied twice, just multiplies the problem. Master one club first.

Capture the lessons

Run the drills

Beyond the video — why this case is yours

This is project finance at the scale of a gym. €1.2m of capex, a third equity and two thirds bank debt, a 10–20-year fixed commitment (the lease, like a land lease or a long-term O&M contract), a promoter's model (the brochure) and a lender's reality (the accounts). Your job as a financier is exactly what Swapn did here: take the sponsor's promised returns, open the real numbers, and stress the two or three lines that decide everything. It's a good practice case before you do it on energy assets.

Make it click — similar plays

The companion: Basic-Fit vs Fitness Park (155) — owning vs franchising; On Air (157) — the leaner rival built by ex-Fitness Park franchisees. Franchise economics: Subway (35), O'Tacos (144), McDonald's via The Founder (Library 10). Fixed costs & leverage: WeWork (70) — long leases, short revenue. Your version: read the accounts, not the brochure, and negotiate the long fixed commitment as if your margin depends on it — because it does.

How to drillPromise vs proof: Fitness Park advertises 12-month payback and 35% margins; a real mature Rennes club makes ~€1.15m revenue and 13.3% net, after ~8.2% royalties, rent and payroll. Three levers decide everything — the lease, payroll (14–15% vs 20% of revenue) and multi-club scale — and a badly run €1.2m club with €400k of your money falls to 7%. The franchisor, paid on revenue, wins either way. For you: model the downside, negotiate the long fixed costs hardest, and read real accounts before believing any promise.

On Air Fitness — The Insiders Who Left Fitness Park and Did It BetterSwapn · Video case · Third card of the gym set (155–157) — experience as marketing, a 13-person HQ, and profits that depend on growth
▶ Video0/14▶
The one ideaOn Air Fitness opens a club every three weeks: 100+ clubs, 420,000+ members, ~30 openings planned this year. It wasn't built by newcomers but by a family, the Bols, who spent years inside Fitness Park as multi-club franchisees, left in 2017, turned their own club into a new brand and became franchisors in 2019. Insiders who knew the model's weak points rebuilt it leaner: lower royalties for franchisees, fewer staff per club, a 13-person head office, and clubs designed like nightclubs so that influencers advertise them for free. Result: a franchisor with a 46% operating margin and a club with roughly double a classic Fitness Park franchisee's margin. The catch: more than half the franchisor's cash comes from opening new clubs, so its spectacular profitability lasts only as long as the growth does.
A note on framing (source)

Video case (Swapn, "Pourquoi les salles de sport sont devenues ringardes," Jul 2026), from the published accounts of the franchisor and of one franchised club; figures are the video's own. Third card of the gym set with Basic-Fit vs Fitness Park (155) and Fitness Park — a franchisee's real accounts (156).

The people & the dates (references)

The father: a fitness pioneer who, inspired by Canal+, made members pay monthly by automatic direct debit — today the norm in about 95% of French clubs. The son: a former high-level athlete trained as a lawyer, who joins him. Together they develop their club under the Moving brand, then Fitness Park, becoming franchisees running several clubs in the Paris region — part of the Fitness Park ecosystem for years. 2017: no longer aligned with Fitness Park's development strategy, they leave and convert their Paris club into their own new brand: On Air. 2019: they start franchising. The trajectory: 2019, 25,000 members; March 2025, 70 clubs and 260,000 members; February 2026, the 100th club and 400,000 members — the network doubled its members in under two years, with no sign of slowing.

The model — where On Air differs

Positioning: Basic-Fit is the minimum service; Fitness Park is a notch above, still low cost but with a bit more service; On Air pushes the cursor further on experience — sport, music, design. Clubs are staged like sets, with DJ-curated ambience and ultra-"Instagrammable" spaces that work with 15–35-year-olds; it even opened France's largest gym in Paris, over 5,000 m². That staging attracts influencers who become free ambassadors — a big part of its profitability, because it lets On Air spend far less on advertising. The entry ticket: a €50,000 entry fee, a minimum personal contribution of €350,000, and a total investment of about €1,400 per m² — so ~€1.4m for a 1,000 m² club, the rest borrowed. Royalties: 7% of revenue vs 8.2% at Fitness Park — 1.2 points that look small but, on a club making €1.5m, leave almost €18,000 a year in the franchisee's pocket. The message to candidates: "you'll hand over less than elsewhere and keep more." Lean staffing: the franchise sheet announces 3 to 5 employees per club — the whole philosophy: a light structure and tight costs. "Cost killers," from head office down to the gym.

The accounts

The franchisor: revenue €12.3m; operating result (what the core business earns before interest and tax) €5.7m — a 46% operating margin, nearly €1 of margin for every €2 coming in, closer to a services or software company than a gym. Net result after tax €4m — 33% net margin, even after a €400k exceptional charge. Head office: 13 people running 100+ clubs. For comparison, the Fitness Park franchisor makes ~€66m of revenue — five times bigger — but On Air is more profitable: less structure, and above all much less advertising. Its result doubled in one year. Where the money really comes from: more than half of the cash On Air collects doesn't come from existing clubs but from opening new ones (entry fees and launch-related income). A brilliant mechanism while growth lasts, since every opening pays big immediately — and exactly why the network opens so fast. A franchised club (Maisons-Alfort): payroll at just 11.6% of revenue, vs 14.5% at the already well-optimised Fitness Park club in Rennes (card 156) — roughly double the margin of a classic Fitness Park franchisee. The founders: dividends of €753k for 2023 and nearly €1.5m for 2024, on top of any salaries — and that's only the franchisor, not counting the clubs they own directly. Those who left Fitness Park weren't wrong.

The point of vigilance

A franchisor that depends this much on new openings must keep growing to keep such impressive numbers. The day the pace of openings slows, more than half the company's engine slows with it. Solid recurring royalties will remain, but the scale will change. That's the nuance nobody sees behind the 33% margin: today it is largely a growth margin, earned on the flow of new franchisees rather than the stock of clubs already open.

And their vigilance point is yours too: build revenue that recurs, not only revenue that depends on the next new deal.

The franchisor earns a 46% operating and 33% net margin and paid ~€1.5m of dividends in 2024 — but more than half its cash comes from opening new clubs. For you: use your inside knowledge to build the leaner version, and separate growth profits from recurring ones.

Intersport vs Decathlon — The Cooperative the Giant Can't CopySwapn · Video case · 300 store owners co-owning a buying centre, desirable brands, and a real store opened up
▶ Video0/14▶
The one ideaTen years ago nobody imagined that a network of independent shop owners could worry Decathlon. Today Decathlon makes €4.73bn in France (2024) and Intersport €3.88bn — a gap of only ~€850m, after Intersport more than doubled its sales in ten years while Decathlon marked time. It did it with neither of the two usual models: not integrated stores like Decathlon, not franchising like Fitness Park, but a cooperative — 300 entrepreneurs who each own one or more stores and together co-own the buying centre that serves them. Add a bet on the brands customers actually want (Nike, Adidas, Puma, The North Face) as sneakers became fashion, and you get a challenger that has passed the giant on lifestyle sport, with store owners earning ~10% net margins and some families building empires of 27 stores.
A note on framing (source)

Video case (Swapn, "Intersport rattrape Decathlon avec un modèle interdit au géant," Sep 2026), from published accounts; figures are the video's own. The tracker's existing Decathlon (21) card covers the integrated giant; this card adds the challenger and the third ownership model after Basic-Fit (owned, 155) and Fitness Park / On Air (franchised, 156–157).

How Intersport caught up

The bet on desirable brands. Decathlon's historic model is its own brands (Domyos, Quechua, Kiprun): it designs, sells in its stores and controls the whole chain — very efficient for margins. Intersport bet the opposite: the big global brands, what it calls "desirable brands." Over ten years that won, because the sport market changed: a pair of sneakers is no longer only a technical object for running, it's a fashion object. On the sport-and-lifestyle shoes and accessories market (Kantar Worldpanel), Intersport now holds 22.1% vs Decathlon's 12.3% — nearly double. Paris. Until 2023 Intersport was everywhere in the provinces but almost absent from Paris, exactly where Nike wanted to see its products. Buying the GoSport stores filled the gap and put it in the capital.

The cooperative model

Intersport isn't a company with franchisees. It's about 300 entrepreneurs who each own one or several stores and together co-own a buying centre, officially Intersport France, whose job is to serve its own shareholders — the store owners. Concretely it does three things: it negotiates contracts with Nike, Adidas, The North Face… with 930+ stores behind it, getting terms no single store could; it runs the shared brand, logistics and support; and it returns the value to members rather than to outside shareholders. The rule that proves it's different: Jacky Rihouet, president for 14 years, led the comeback — sales from €1.2bn to €3.65bn — and orchestrated the GoSport takeover. In February 2024 he sold all his stores (31 Intersport shops, ~1,000 employees) to the Chiver group; seven months later he had to resign, because in a cooperative the president's role is tied to being an operating member — no stores, no presidency. Imagine Decathlon's CEO forced to resign for selling his personal assets: impossible. That's written in the statutes, and it's what makes the model hard to copy.

A real store opened up — Montbéliard

A trap first: a company "running an Intersport store" with €6m of sales isn't necessarily one store — many owners use one company with a head office in their home town and run several stores as secondary establishments. On Pappers, check whether you're looking at one store or five, or the ratios mean nothing. Swapn picked a genuine single store: Montbéliard Sport et Loisirs, 26 employees, 2024 accounts filed July 2025, owned by Gérard Leclerc, the current president of the Intersport France cooperative. Where each €100 goes: sales ~€7m (+3.2% in a slowing sports market); merchandise (Nike sneakers, North Face jackets, bikes) ~60% of sales; payroll €623k wages + €115k social charges = €738k, only 10.6% of sales (retail usually ~15%+) — probably because accounting, HR and logistics are pooled across the group's stores; then rent and other external charges. Net result: €710,131 — 10.2% of sales. For scale: a Burger King franchisee ~5.2% net, a McDonald's 8–12%. A well-run Intersport store isn't 5%; it's ~10% net. That profit then goes up as dividends or stays as reserves: on 28 June 2025 the sole shareholder (the Leclerc family holding) voted a €300,524 dividend; over four years this store sent up €1.87m.

The three-storey structure — how a family builds an empire inside a cooperative

Gérard Leclerc runs 27 stores (23 Intersport, 4 Black Store) from an office in Albertville; his father Guy Leclerc was president of Intersport before him. The set-up has three floors: at the top, HFL, the Leclerc family holding; below it, about ten operating companies; each runs one or several stores as secondary establishments. Three "pipes" carry value upward: cash pooling — the stores' cash is centralised on an account belonging to the holding, paid 2%; management fees for group services; and dividends — in 2024 HFL received €1.95m from its subsidiaries. In June 2025 HFL voted €1.5m of dividends to the family; over four years (2021 €1.8m, 2022 €3.9m — probably a reserve distribution, 2023 €1.5m, 2024 €1.5m) about €8.7m, all declared, certified and published — classic holding optimisation. What's unique: the man who built this empire over 34 years is now president of the whole network, elected by his peers, the other store owners.

Decathlon's counter-attack

Is the model perfect? No — and the real test is now. For its 50th anniversary in 2026 Decathlon announced a complete turn: dropping its themed brands to become one single brand like Nike or Adidas, taking a stake in Brompton to attack premium bikes, opening Decathlon City stores in town centres, and landing at the Forum des Halles in Paris — exactly where Intersport opened through GoSport. The giant has understood the threat. The match ahead: a cooperative of 300 owners obsessed with their margins versus a giant that becomes a strong brand able to talk to Nike as an equal.

Beyond the video — why this case is yours

Cooperatives and pooled platforms are common in energy. Citizen energy cooperatives, municipal utilities and buying groups for equipment all use the same logic as Intersport: many small owners gain the bargaining power and financing access of a large one without giving up ownership. And the holding structure is everyday project finance: a holding company above special-purpose companies (SPVs), each owning one asset, with cash moving up through dividends, shareholder loans and management fees. If you can read the Leclerc set-up, you can read most renewable-energy portfolios.

It more than doubled sales in ten years to €3.88bn vs Decathlon's €4.73bn and leads sport-lifestyle (22% vs 12%). A real store (Montbéliard) makes ~€7m at 10.2% net with payroll at 10.6%; its owner's family holding built 27 stores and took €8.7m of dividends in four years — and he now chairs the network. Decathlon is counter-attacking. For you: the cooperative is a third way to scale, and the holding structure is the language of project finance.

The SCI — Why the Wealthy Never Buy Property in Their Own NameSwapn · Video case · Société civile immobilière: IR vs IS, the property deficit, amortisation, and the holding-above-SCI play
▶ Video0/14▶
The one ideaSuccessful entrepreneurs, influencers and wealthy families have one thing in common when they buy property: they almost never buy in their own name. They use an SCI (société civile immobilière, a property-holding company), a simple legal tool for building, managing, passing on and growing a property portfolio. Its real power is the choice of tax regime: under income tax (IR) it lets renovation losses cut your personal tax; under corporate tax (IS) it lets the building's depreciation wipe out almost all the tax on rents, so cash can be reinvested in the next property. Used badly — for your main home, or with the wrong regime — it costs you money.
A note on framing (source)

Video case (Swapn, "Pourquoi les riches ont tous une SCI ? (et pourquoi vous devriez faire pareil)," Jun 2025); figures and rules are the video's own, French law as of 2025. Not tax or legal advice — rules change and every situation differs; check with an expert-comptable or notary. Filed in the Founder Toolkit (Legal Structure, Tax & Wealth), next to the holding structures in Intersport (158).

What an SCI is

The statutes (articles of association) run everything: the SCI's name, address, how the capital is split, what each partner contributed, and clauses governing relations between partners — e.g. a pre-emption clause, so that when one partner sells, the others have priority and an outsider can't easily get in. Managers (gérants): one or several run the SCI and represent it to third parties — useful when several people invest together and want one person to manage the properties. Accounts: as a company, it must keep accounts — depending on the tax option, a balance sheet, income statement and tax return. Creating one isn't complicated; it just demands rigour. Partners are also personally liable for the SCI's debts in proportion to their shares — a point to understand before signing.

Why use one

1 · Better than joint ownership. Buy a flat with three people without an SCI and you're in indivision: each owns a share of the property, all three must agree on everything, you can't appoint a manager, and if one wants out you go back to the notary, pay notary fees again and sometimes unfavourable tax for the others to buy him out. SCI shares transfer far more simply, and statutory clauses or a shareholders' agreement set the powers between partners. 2 · Grow the portfolio and borrowing capacity by separating your personal borrowing capacity from the SCI's, so you can multiply acquisitions more easily than in your own name. 3 · Transmission and protection of the family's assets (passing on shares rather than buildings).

The traps

Your main home in an SCI is rarely the right set-up: you become, in effect, the SCI's tenant and pay it rent — potentially taxed; bank financing can be more complex and dearer; and above all, on resale you lose the capital-gains exemption a private owner gets on a main residence. Someone who renovates their home and sells it 10–15 years later in a rising market pays no tax on the gain in their own name, but would in an SCI. Opting for VAT to recover VAT on works is rarely good: you then must charge VAT on the rent, end up with less in your pocket and few deductible expenses — get advice first.

Creating one

1) Write the statutes (online templates or a professional). 2) Deposit the share capital — legally €1 minimum, but the video advises €500–1,000; unlike a commercial company (SARL, SAS), an SCI's capital can sit in an account dedicated to the SCI and the deposit certificate is optional — no need for a notary or bank. 3) Publish the legal notice and register with the court registry: a little over €300 in total fees.

Option 1 — SCI under income tax (IR, the default)

The SCI itself pays no tax; each partner pays income tax on their share of the profit (form 2044). Example: €10,000 of rent and €5,000 of costs (management fees, loan interest, property tax, service charges) = €5,000 of profit; with two equal partners, each declares €2,500. Deductible charges are strictly regulated: management fees, improvement and maintenance works (not extensions), loan interest, service charges, landlord insurance, property tax. The big advantage — the property deficit (déficit foncier): €5,000 of rent and €15,000 of costs = a €10,000 deficit that reduces the partners' taxable income. At a 30% marginal tax rate, a €10,000 deficit saves €3,000 of tax. It's capped at €10,700 a year against your general income; any excess (e.g. €40,000 of works in year one) is carried forward to later years. Big restriction: no furnished rental — it counts as commercial activity, which an SCI under IR can't do (a small tolerance, up to ~10% of rents, exists, but a reclassification on audit could be dramatic).

Option 2 — SCI under corporate tax (IS)

The SCI becomes taxed like a company: 15% up to €42,500 of profit and 25% above. Partner's current-account contribution: lend the SCI your savings (e.g. €20,000) to buy a first property; the SCI owes you that money and can repay it later without tax. Furnished rental is allowed. The key advantage — depreciation: buy a studio for €100,000 and rent it €500/month (€6,000/year); deduct the notary fees, then depreciate the building over, say, 25 years (20–40 depending on the asset) = €4,000/year. Only €2,000 remains before other costs (property tax, insurance, management) — so almost no corporate tax. The SCI under IS is built to keep cash in the company and reinvest it. Drawbacks: taking money out personally means a second layer of tax (dividends); and on resale the gain is calculated on the book value, not the purchase price — bought €100,000, depreciated €4,000 × 10 years = €40,000, book value €60,000; sold for €120,000 → taxable gain €60,000, not €20,000. You pay back the tax you deferred. Plus full accounts (balance sheet, income statement, tax return) — use an expert-comptable.

Which one, and the holding play

IR if you want one or two flats and personal extra income (you pay income tax and social charges, but the money is yours), or if you have heavy works and want to use the property deficit. IS if you're building a portfolio for the long term and reinvesting. Why entrepreneurs put an SCI under a holding company: to invest profits from their operating business without paying personal income tax or social charges first, multiply their investing capacity, and add bank debt for leverage. With an SCI under IS paying almost no tax on rents, the first flat finances the second, then a third and fourth, until the SCI generates passive income paid out as salary or dividends. It takes 10, 15, 20 years — and the starting point is an operating business that generates cash, then a holding, then the SCI.

Beyond the video — why this case is yours

An SCI is a small SPV. In project finance each asset sits in its own special-purpose company, with its own statutes, governance, debt and tax treatment; equity comes in as share capital and shareholder loans (the current account), and cash comes back up as interest, loan repayments and dividends. The SCI under a holding is the personal-scale version of the structure you'll model on energy assets — and with your cross-border life between France and Tunisia, the question of where and how assets are held matters even more.

Make it click — similar plays

The holding above it: The holding (163). Holdings in practice: Intersport (158) — the three-storey family structure and three cash pipes; Micro, EURL or SASU (160) — the operating company first. Owners and horizons: Rolex (154), Family Businesses (84). The money books: Tax-Free Wealth (13) — the tax code as incentives; Profit First (12). Your version: build the cash engine first, then the holding, then hold assets in the wrapper that matches the goal.

How to drillChoose the wrapper for the goal: an SCI beats joint ownership on governance and transfer, and its tax option decides the rest — under IR, renovation deficits cut your personal tax (up to €10,700/yr); under IS, depreciation leaves almost no tax on rents so the cash can buy the next property, at the price of heavier tax on resale and on taking money out. Never put your main home in it, and build the operating business and holding before the SCI. Check every number with a professional.

Micro, EURL or SASU — Which Status Leaves the Most Money at Year-End?Swapn · Video case · Same consultant, same revenue, three legal statuses, three different net incomes
▶ Video0/14▶
The one ideaMost people choose their legal status at random, comparing turnover ceilings, VAT and paperwork. The only question that matters is: how much lands in your personal account after expenses, social contributions and income tax? For a solo IT consultant, the answer flips with revenue and expenses. At €30k the three statuses are within a few hundred euros, so the simplest wins. At €70k with €9k of real expenses, the EURL (single-member limited company) puts ~€600 more in your pocket than the micro-entreprise and ~€2,200 more than the SASU (single-shareholder simplified company). The SASU only shines in one case: when you are receiving unemployment benefits.
A note on framing (source)

Video case (Swapn, "Quel statut te laisse le plus d'argent à la fin de l'année ?," Feb 2026); figures are the video's simulations for a single person with no children, no unemployment benefit and no ACRE start-up relief, French rules 2026. Not tax advice — get a personalised simulation from an expert-comptable. Companion to The SCI (159): the operating company comes first, the holding and SCI later.

The three logics

Micro-entreprise: simple, fast, almost no paperwork. In exchange you can't deduct your real expenses: you're taxed on revenue minus a flat allowance set by the state, and there's a revenue ceiling (€77,700 for a consulting activity) — above it you must change status. EURL: you're a self-employed manager (TNS, travailleur non salarié) — social contributions of roughly 45% of the salary you pay yourself (€1,000 net costs the company ~€1,450). Expenses are deductible; the logic is to maximise salary because dividends are heavily taxed. SASU: you're an "assimilated employee" — better social cover but much heavier contributions, so the logic is a small salary plus dividends. Company profit pays corporate tax at 15% up to €42,500 and 25% above. The philosophy of the SASU is often "keep my unemployment benefit and build revenue in the company": pay yourself nothing, so no contributions, while the benefit covers your living costs.

Simulation 1 — €30,000 revenue, ~€8,000 of expenses

Real expenses for a consultant arrive fast: computer, phone, internet, software subscriptions (Canva, ChatGPT…), transport pass, travel to clients, meals. Micro: it can't deduct them, but the micro-entrepreneur pays them anyway — so after contributions, tax and those costs, the "super net" is about €19,122. EURL: pay yourself the whole margin as salary — €19,160 of pay plus €7,840 of contributions ≈ the €30k minus expenses; at that level a single person pays no income tax (the decote, a reduction for lightly-taxed households), so €19,160 net. The gap with micro is a few dozen euros — and the video still recommends the micro here, because there are no accounting fees. SASU: more expensive in contributions; even minimising salary and taking dividends at year-end, it leaves less.

Simulation 2 — €70,000 revenue, ~€9,000 of expenses

Swapn says €9,000 of expenses is "coherent and achievable" after 15 years advising entrepreneurs — and it can include, through the company, a share of home rent and electricity if you work from home, a coworking subscription, transport, or CESU (prepaid service vouchers) for home help. With €70k of revenue and €9k of expenses, the EURL has room to pay its manager ~€3,467 a month; the SASU at most ~€2,834 a month in salary — so in SASU the smart move is to cap salary at €1,200 a month and take ~€29,549 of gross dividends. Results: EURL ≈ €37,207 "super net" (salary ~€41,000, total pay €41,606, income tax €4,399); micro ≈ €36,615; SASU ≈ €35,000. Conclusion: the higher your expenses, the more a company makes sense; even under the micro ceiling, run a simulation — the EURL may maximise what you keep. The SASU is the choice when you're a job-seeker paid by France Travail: take everything as dividends on top of the benefit (per the video, micro income is incompatible with keeping the benefit, and EURL dividends are heavily taxed).

Why the Plumber Earns More Than You — The Best Businesses to Start in 2026Swapn · Video case · Four businesses ordinary people can launch: plumber, garden & outdoor services, AI consultant for SMEs, B2B agency
▶ Video0/14▶
The one ideaSwapn, which helps thousands of entrepreneurs create companies each year, ranked the best businesses for 2026 using the numbers it sees in its own clients: real demand, good profitability, easy to start with little money, and launchable by normal people. The surprise: the top of the list isn't a tech startup. It's a repair plumber — a job AI can't disrupt — who can bill ~€110k a year with €25k of starting investment. The rule behind the whole list: sell high-margin services people urgently need, keep fixed costs low, and organise your days well.
A note on framing (source)

Video case (Swapn, "Pourquoi le Plombier Gagne Plus que toi en 2026 ?," Mar 2026); figures are the video's own averages from its clients, not guarantees. Companion to Micro, EURL or SASU (160): once you know what to launch, choose the status.

1 · The repair plumber (top tier)

Not a big construction firm with 15 staff — a plumber focused on repairs and light renovation, alone or with an apprentice, concentrating on high-margin jobs: leaks, blocked toilets, taps, water-heater replacement. A quick leak repair ~€250 excl. VAT; bigger jobs start at ~€5,000 and go much higher. Revenue: up to 200 billable days a year (the rest is admin, buying supplies, prospecting, quotes) × ~€550/day (e.g. two taps, an unblocking and a bathroom seal = four jobs) = ~€110,000 excl. VAT. Start-up: a used van ~€20,000, tools and starting stock ~€5,000, company creation ~€1,000. Running costs: ~20,000 km a year (100 km a day — a site 50 km away, trips to Leroy Merlin, Brico Dépôt) → fuel ~€300/month; vehicle upkeep ~€500/yr; professional van insurance ~€1,000/yr; lunches on site ~€200/month (deductible in a SASU); 10-year building liability insurance (décennale) ~€2,000/yr; professional liability (RC Pro) ~€500/yr; health cover and provident insurance ~€130/month — about €14,920 a year of expenses, plus materials and depreciation.

2 · Garden maintenance & outdoor services

Services to individuals: a simple mowing €40–70; a monthly maintenance contract €100–300; hedge trimming and brush clearing; a big job €150 to ~€1,000 depending on surface; pressure-washing terraces. A well-organised solo operator averages ~€300–350 a day (a €500 terrace one day, a lawn the next) × 200 days ≈ €70,000 excl. VAT — the average Swapn sees among such clients. Low investment: a professional pressure washer ~€2,000 if you specialise in terraces, plus small gardening and cleaning kit €1,000–5,000. You start early and finish late, but you earn above the French median salary (~€1,700/month). Profitability depends on organisation: grouping three clients in the same street or zone beats spending three hours driving 100 km between two clients.

3 · The AI consultant for SMEs

A consultant or trainer in digital transition and AI for small businesses. AI and LLMs (large language models) are used more and more by individuals and professionals, but SMEs need help to implement them in their processes — that's where an outside consultant adds value, and the market is growing. More and more consultants build offers with an average daily rate above €500.

4 · The B2B service agency

Selling services to companies (B2B, business-to-business): companies pay far more easily €2,000–5,000 a month than an individual would, so a freelance consultant or small agency can reach high monthly revenue with only 5–10 clients — manageable and not too time-consuming, whereas B2C (business-to-consumer) needs many more clients at lower tickets. Better to sell few expensive services than many cheap ones. Companies seek long-term relationships, typically 3-, 6- or 12-month renewable contracts, so revenue is predictable. Example — an advertising agency taking ~10% of clients' ad spend: six advertisers spending €30,000 a month = €18,000 of revenue a month, managed by one salaried person; results drive the client's next budget, so performance is the agency's growth engine. Other angles: YouTube strategy, video editing, thumbnail design, Google Ads management, social media strategy — train, specialise, start alone, then subcontract to freelancers or hire a team of 2–4. Swapn sees service agencies at €100k–300k of revenue with only ~€10k of operating costs — intellectual services carry very low overheads.

For you: a B2B retainer practice built on an urgent problem in energy and infrastructure.

ARE or ARCE — The France Travail Mistake When You Start a CompanySwapn · Video case · Monthly unemployment benefit in a SASU vs a lump sum in an EURL: the "best combo" that isn't
▶ Video0/14▶
The one ideaAbout 1 million companies are created in France each year, roughly one founder in four while unemployed — ~250,000 people a year asking the same question: keep my monthly unemployment benefit (ARE) or take the lump sum (ARCE)? Most choose the same set-up because they were told it's best: a SASU paying no salary while France Travail keeps paying the ARE, then dividends when benefits end. Swapn's simulation of a real subscriber shows that since the April 2025 reform this "best combo" leaves almost €5,000 less than an EURL with the ARCE and a salary — and fewer pension and social rights.
A note on framing (source)

Video case (Swapn, "L'erreur fatale avec France Travail quand on crée sa boîte (Étude de cas)," Jul 2026); figures are the video's simulation, French rules as of 2026. Not legal or tax advice — get a personalised simulation. Direct follow-up to Micro, EURL or SASU (160), which flagged the SASU as the job-seeker's status: this card shows when that's no longer true.

The case and the two aids

The subscriber: an SEO consultant who just left his salaried job through a rupture conventionnelle (negotiated departure), registered with France Travail, entitled to ~€1,700 a month for 18 months = €30,600. He has a contract already signed and targets €60,000 of revenue in year one with €10,000 of expenses. His plan: SASU, keep the ARE every month, take dividends when benefits end. ARE (aide au retour à l'emploi): keep receiving the monthly benefit while you build the company — on condition you pay yourself no salary. ARCE (aide à la reprise ou à la création d'entreprise): a capital equal to 60% of remaining rights, paid in two halves — 30% at creation, 30% six months later. Here: 60% × €30,600 = €18,360, i.e. €9,180 at creation and €9,180 six months later. With the ARCE you leave the job-seeker list and can pay yourself a salary.

Why the ARE has become less attractive

A cash-flow maze: in a SASU you receive 80% of the monthly benefit during the month, then send France Travail a certificate of non-remuneration signed by your accountant to get the remaining 20% — France Travail now checks, with advances and adjustments. In an EURL it's worse: 70% monthly, the remaining 30% only after the balance sheet and tax return are filed. The 60%-of-time trap (since April 2025): you can no longer collect benefits alongside your SASU for the full 18 months. Payment in parallel is capped at 60% of the duration — 10.8 months, about 11. After that, a France Travail commission decides whether to grant the remaining 40%, and you must show you couldn't pay yourself. A freelancer billing €60,000 has the cash to pay himself, so the remaining 40% is very likely refused. Swapn has seen dozens of entrepreneurs refused for exactly that reason; the first commission decisions are "very random."

The two simulations (€60k revenue, €10k expenses)

SASU + ARE: no salary, so no social contributions — which also means the ACRE (first-year exemption from social contributions) is useless. The profit (~€50k) pays corporate tax of ~€8,250 since nothing is deducted (no salary, no contributions). Then dividends — often believed to carry "only" the flat tax — still pay ~€13,109 of flat tax. And France Travail pays only the guaranteed 60% of the time. EURL + ARCE: he takes the €18,360 lump sum, leaves the job-seeker list and pays himself a salary of €36,246. Income tax ~€2,890; social contributions only €13,752 thanks to the ACRE exemption in year one. Net in his pocket: €33,356, plus social rights (pension, health) earned through contributions. Result: the EURL with the ARCE leaves almost €5,000 more than the SASU with the ARE — for a France Travail amount that ends up identical (€18,360), because 60% of rights as a lump sum equals 60% of the time in monthly payments when the remaining 40% is refused.

Leaving a salaried role with signed advisory work already lined up is exactly the subscriber's profile — and at a senior energy/finance daily rate, revenue would arrive fast, which makes the "stay on benefits" logic even weaker. Treat it like a financing decision: compare certain vs conditional cash, timing and total net, and decide with a proper simulation — ideally before the departure is negotiated.

How to drillDon't copy the "SASU + ARE" combo: since April 2025 benefits alongside a SASU are guaranteed only for 60% of the duration, the rest is likely refused once you have revenue, the ACRE is wasted and dividends pay corporate tax plus flat tax. For a consultant with €60k of revenue, an EURL taking the ARCE lump sum (€18,360) and a salary nets €33,356 — about €5,000 more, with social rights. Simulate before you choose.

The Holding — What the Wealthy Do With Their Company's MoneyLegalPlace · Video case · Don't take the money out, make it circulate: parent-subsidiary regime, SCI at IS, investments, exit at ~3%
▶ Video0/14▶
The one ideaWhen your company makes a profit and you take it out to live or invest, the state takes up to ~56% depending on how you pay yourself. Entrepreneurs who build real wealth — the video cites Bernard Arnault and Xavier Niel — mostly don't take it out: they make it circulate. Profit moves up from the operating company to a holding at about 1% tax, then is reinvested in property (via an SCI at corporate tax), financial assets or prestige assets, and when a company is sold through the holding, the gain is taxed about ten times less than in your own name. The holding is the machine that keeps capital compounding inside the corporate world instead of being taxed at personal rates.
A note on framing (source)

Video case (LegalPlace, "Ce que les riches font avec l'argent de leur société (et que personne ne t'explique)," Jun 2026). Figures are the video's simplified examples under French rules as of 2026; the host promotes his company-formation and accounting services (promotions omitted). Not tax advice — holding structures must have real substance and be set up with an expert-comptable or lawyer. The capstone of the structuring series: status (160) → ARE/ARCE (162) → holding (163) → SCI (159).

Step 1 — Salary or dividends: what's left from €100 of profit

Dividends from a SASU/SAS: the company first pays corporate tax (15% up to €42,500 of profit, 25% above) → €85; then the flat tax of 31.4% → ~€58 in your pocket. The catch: you must wait for the year-end accounts and a profit. Salary in a SASU/SAS: ~80% social charges plus ~20% income tax → ~€44. Salary in an EURL/SARL (self-employed manager): ~45% social charges plus ~20% income tax → ~€55. Salaries are deductible from company profit, so no corporate tax on them. So financially, dividends in a SAS leave the most.

Step 2 — Why the wealthy still pay themselves a minimum salary

They don't take 100% in dividends. They pay themselves ~€1,000 a month (some 2,000–4,000) to validate pension quarters. Pension can't be seized: if everything collapses — and entrepreneurs' lives have highs and lows; plenty were rich at 30–40 and lost it — the pension remains as a safety mattress at 67–68. The same salary also gives access to a mutuelle (complementary health insurance) and prévoyance (sickness/disability/death cover). One stone, three birds. Above that fixed salary, lifestyle (restaurants, travel, gifts) is covered by dividends at ~€58 per €100.

Step 3 — The parent-subsidiary regime: moving money up at ~1%

The profit they don't need personally stays in the company, pays corporate tax, then moves up to the holding as dividends. Under the régime mère-fille (parent-subsidiary regime), those dividends are 95% exempt; only 5% is taxed at the 25% rate — about 1%. So from €100 of profit, ~€84 arrives in the holding versus €58 in your pocket — about 44% more money to invest than as a private individual.

Step 4 — Investing from the holding

Property via an SCI at corporate tax owned by the holding: it buys, rents out and invests €84 instead of €58. In your own name, rental profit is taxed ~17.2% social levies + ~20% income tax ≈ 37%; in the SCI at IS, the building's depreciation is deducted, so taxable profit is low and what remains is taxed at 15%. And protection: the property belongs to the SCI, owned by the holding — not to you personally — so in case of serious financial trouble or divorce it is, per the video, protected and outside the couple's assets (in practice this depends on how the structure was funded and set up — check with a lawyer). Financial assets: shares, ETFs (exchange-traded funds), crypto, gold — gains taxed at corporate tax (15%/25%) rather than the 31.4% flat tax. Prestige and collection assets: sports cars, paintings, watches, vineyards, châteaux, villas — anything that gains value or can be rented out (rented ~95% of the time to produce lightly taxed income). It's all money generated by a hard-working operating business — "the engine that generates cash" — but it avoids personal taxation. The video notes the proposed Zucman tax (2% on very large fortunes held through holdings) did not pass and in its view wouldn't stop the system.

Step 5 — Selling a company through the holding: ~10× less tax

If you invested €1,000 and sell for €100,000, you have a €99,000 gain. In your own name: flat tax 31.4% → ~€31,400. In the holding, on shares held as long-term participations: 88% of the gain is exempt, the remaining 12% is taxed at 15%/25% → about 3%. "37% for you, 3% for the holding — ten times less." That's where the most value is created: the day you sell your company for €100k, €500k or €1m.

Setting it up, and charity

Before your operating company exists: create the holding online with e.g. €500 of capital; once registered, use the same €500 as the capital of the operating company, with the holding as its shareholder — two companies for €500. You'll need a registered address, a business bank account and an accountant. If you already have a company: create the holding by contributing your shares to it (apport en nature, contribution in kind) — more complex, done with an adviser. The host set his up in 2008 and has used it for several operations since. Foundations and donations: the holding can make donations or create a foundation, with a tax reduction (the video says ~50%, within limits linked to the holding's revenue and a ~€20,000 floor — verify the current rules).

The key word is reinvest: the €84 is not spendable money. It's capital that stays in companies. The day you take it out personally, the flat tax applies — the holding defers and redirects tax, it doesn't erase it for consumption.

Beyond the video — why this case is yours

This is a corporate group in miniature — the language of project finance. A holding over subsidiaries, cash moving up through dividends, a separate vehicle per asset, tax depending on where profit is booked and how gains are realised: that's how sponsors hold energy portfolios (HoldCo over SPVs). Building your own small group is both a wealth tool and a hands-on way to master the structures you'll model professionally. As a value investor already, the holding is also where a future investment portfolio could compound at corporate rather than personal tax.

Make it click — similar plays

When it pays: ~€7k break-even (170). Start here: The wealth ladder (167). Why a SASU: The tax screen (166). The map: All statuses ranked by revenue (164). The structuring series: The SCI (159), Micro, EURL or SASU (160), ARE or ARCE (162). A real family holding: Intersport's Leclerc family (158) — cash pooling, fees, dividends. Owner structures: Rolex (154) — a foundation as sole shareholder. The money books: Tax-Free Wealth (13).

How to drillMake money circulate, don't take it out: of €100 of profit, ~€44–58 reaches you personally, but ~€84 reaches a holding under the parent-subsidiary regime. Pay yourself a minimum salary for pension and cover, take dividends for lifestyle, and reinvest the rest from the holding — property through an SCI at corporate tax, financial and prestige assets — and sell companies through the holding at ~3% instead of ~31%. Build the cash engine first, set the holding up early, and get proper advice.

Every Legal Status Ranked by Revenue — the Map From €0 to €150k+LegalPlace · Video case · Micro → EURL/SASU by priority → SASU + holding + SCI, in that order
▶ Video0/14▶
The one ideaAt €30k, €80k or €200k of revenue you should never be in the same legal structure. Every day accountants see founders who created a SASU to make €25k, or stayed in micro at €80k — losing thousands a year without knowing it. Their mistake isn't the status itself but the reason they chose it: image, fear, a friend's advice. The video maps revenue bands to structures: €0–40k micro, full stop; €40–60k think; €60–80k EURL or SASU depending on your priority; €80k+ build a small group in the right order — SASU, then holding, then SCI, never the reverse.
A note on framing (source)

Video case (LegalPlace, "J'ai classé TOUS les statuts juridiques selon ton chiffre d'affaires," Aug 2026); figures are the video's, French rules 2026; promotions omitted. Not tax advice. It is the master map for the structuring series — statuses (160), ARE/ARCE (162), holding (163), SCI (159). Watch the contradiction: this video calls "ARE + SASU, zero salary" the smartest combo for job-seekers; Swapn's card 162 shows that since the April 2025 reform (benefits capped at 60% of the duration alongside a company) it can leave ~€5,000 less than EURL + ARCE. Simulate your own case.

Band 1 — €0 to €40,000: micro-entreprise

2026 figures: micro revenue ceilings €203,100 for selling goods and €83,600 for services (BIC — industrial and commercial profits, e.g. hairdresser, craftsman — or BNC — non-commercial profits, intellectual services like a lawyer or nurse), on revenue cashed, not invoiced. Social contributions are a flat share of revenue: 12.3% goods resale, 21.2% BIC services, 25.6% BNC liberal professions. VAT trap: the VAT exemption thresholds are lower — €85,000 goods, €37,500 services — so you can be a micro and still have to charge VAT; many don't know, and on a tax audit lose ~20% of three years' revenue. Why micro is unbeatable here: no accountant, no balance sheet, an online revenue declaration monthly or quarterly, contributions only on what you cash, and the ACRE in year one halves contributions (the video warns the ACRE drops from 50% to 25% on 1 July — check the date). A SASU at this level costs a fortune: €1,000–1,500 a year of accounting, creation fees, ~82% contributions on pay — €2,000–4,000 a year lost on €25k of revenue, for the "president" label on an e-mail signature. Myth: "leave micro to protect my assets" — since the 2022 law on independents, professional and personal assets are automatically separated even in an individual business; your home and savings are protected. The only reason to leave before €40k: very high real expenses.

Band 2 — €40,000 to €60,000: think

You don't have to leave micro — below €83,600 (services) or €203,100 (goods) you can legally stay. Three signals to move: 1) your real expenses exceed the flat allowance; 2) you want to invest, recruit or hire — in micro nothing is deductible, in a company equipment is depreciated and salaries and their charges are deductible (a €3,000 Mac, €5,000 of equipment, a first employee at €30k gross); 3) you accumulate cash on the business account — in micro the whole profit is taxed in your income each year whether you spend it or not; in a company it can stay at 15% corporate tax. The only real argument for switching is money: do I earn more net in a company than in micro? If yes, switch; if not, stay.

Band 3 — €60,000 to €80,000: EURL or SASU, by priority

There's no best status in general — every YouTube channel says "SASU is better," every article "EURL is better." The answer depends on your personal priority, not on tax; tax is the consequence. Myth: "SAS is more flexible, SARL more protective" — false: both limit liability to contributions; the real difference is the manager's social regime. Priority 1 — maximise net now → EURL (self-employed manager, cheaper contributions); avoid big dividends in an EURL (taxed as income above 10% of capital). Priority 2 — credibility → SASU: as president you get a real payslip, which banks like for a mortgage (EURL banks look at three years of balance sheets); big B2B clients that audit suppliers; but at this revenue credibility costs ~€5,000–10,000 a year vs EURL. Priority 3 — social protection → SASU: employee-like regime; EURL's SSI (ex-RSI) pays lower daily sickness allowances and less pension — €50,000 of contributions over 20 years buys a much bigger pension in SASU. Suits future parents, those with health history, anyone who sleeps better covered. Priority 4 — build wealth → SASU: easier to put under a holding (contribution of shares with tax deferral), easier to bring in partners and to sell shares. EURL is a solo freelancer's vehicle to maximise net; SASU is an entrepreneur's vehicle to build something.

Band 4 — €80,000 to €150,000+: build the group, in order

The question is no longer which structure but how to build your small group — and the order is everything; reversing two steps can cost tens of thousands or block the set-up. Step 1: the operating SASU — it bills clients and generates revenue. Step 2: run it 2–3 years: build cash, clients, revenue. Step 3: create the holding by contributing the SASU's shares (apport en nature) — with tax deferral on the contribution gain. Step 4: for business property, an SCI owned by the holding buys your offices or rentals. Classic error: "I have a company and I created a holding" — but the holding doesn't own the first company's shares; selling them to it is taxed. It's just a second company. A holding must own the shares, ideally received as a contribution, not bought. Three levers: parent-subsidiary regime (dividends up at ~1%); SCI at corporate tax for business property but not for long-term personal property (resale on depreciated book value → big taxable gain; holding in your own name or an SCI at income tax is often better); the Dutreil pact for passing the company to your children — a 75% allowance on the value transmitted (a €1m company taxed as €250k, plus €100,000 per child per parent every 10 years) — set it up long before you're ill or retired. Offshore myth: a holding in Luxembourg or Dubai is useless in 95% of cases — you must prove economic substance (€10,000–30,000 a year minimum) or face abuse-of-law reassessments with up to 80% penalties, to save a few points on profits often stuck abroad; a French holding with the parent-subsidiary regime does the job for 99% of entrepreneurs, especially if you live in France.

Special profiles and the four costliest mistakes

Employee with a side activity: combine salary and micro up to ~€15–20k of extra revenue — but check your contract for an exclusivity clause. Job-seeker: ARE (monthly benefit) vs ARCE (60% of remaining rights in two payments) — the video favours ARE + SASU with zero salary, and calls ARE + EURL (TNS) the classic trap (see card 162 for the post-2025 counter-view). Never quit a permanent job without activating ARE or ARCE. Couple: spouse as collaborator (no pay, contributes to pension; EURL/SARL/EI only), employee, or associate (holds shares) — a SASU has no collaborator status, so a spouse helping for free is outside the law; one structure per spouse can multiply micro allowances. Future property investor: create the holding before buying — SASU → holding (via contribution) → SCI; buying first and restructuring later costs ~5.8% transfer duties each time (€17,400 on €300,000). The four mistakes: 1) leaving micro too early (a SASU at €25k "because it looks pro" = €2,000–4,000 lost a year); 2) creating the holding after the fact without contributing shares; 3) buying personal property through the wrong structure, then a costly or impossible restructuring; 4) quitting a permanent job without ARE/ARCE — resigning without a negotiated departure or registering loses 100% of benefits.

Avoid the four costly mistakes — leaving micro too early, a holding that doesn't own the shares, property in the wrong vehicle, quitting without ARE/ARCE — and simulate the ARE choice yourself.

Five Ways to Take Money Out of Your Company — From 70% Tax to 0%LegalPlace · Video case · Salary, dividends, rent, profit-sharing, expenses and pre-funded CESU, ranked by what reaches your pocket
▶ Video0/14▶
The one ideaMost founders think there are two ways to get money out of their company: salary or dividends. A well-advised entrepreneur almost never uses just one. There are several channels, each taxed differently — some cost more than 70% once charges and taxes are added, others 0%. That's why two founders with exactly the same profit can end the year tens of thousands of euros apart, legally. The question isn't "how do I pay my tax?" but "how do I keep the most money legally?" — mixing channels, each within its limits.
A note on framing (source)

Video case (LegalPlace, "Comment les entrepreneurs riches sortent l'argent de leur société," Sep 2026); figures are the video's simplified examples (income tax assumed ~20%), French rules 2026; promotions omitted. Not tax advice — several channels have strict conditions and are audit-sensitive; set them up with an expert-comptable. Completes the structuring series: status map (164), holding (163) — the holding keeps money in; this card is about money you take out.

Methods 1–2 — salary and dividends (the expensive channels)

Salary, EURL/SARL manager (self-employed, majority shareholder): contributions ~45% of net — €100 out = ~€31 to URSSAF, ~€14 of income tax → ~€55. Salary, SAS/SASU president: contributions ~75% of net — €100 out = ~€43 to URSSAF → ~€46. So salary is more efficient in an EURL; you can convert a SAS into an EURL keeping the same SIREN, name, address, contracts and bank account by amending the statutes — don't do it alone with ChatGPT. Dividends (you wear two hats: manager and shareholder): first corporate tax (15% up to €42,500 of profit, 25% above). In a SASU: €100 → €85, then flat tax → ~€58, better than SASU salary (€46). In an EURL: corporate tax + flat tax + social contributions on the dividend (the "triple penalty") → ~€36 — "forget it." Never take 100% dividends with no other income: keep a minimum salary for pension quarters, social protection, mutuelle and prévoyance. And dividends can only be paid after the first accounts close with a profit — usually 12–18 months after creation.

Method 3 — rent for your home office

If you work from home, your company can pay you rent. Simple version: the company reimburses part of your rent as an expense claim — a tolerance some inspectors accept and others don't; risky, left out. Clean version: you rent part of your home to the company and declare it as property income (revenus fonciers). The rent is deductible for the company (no corporate tax); you pay ~18.6% social levies (~€19) plus income tax (~€19) → ~€62, and it's available immediately while you wait for dividends. Boosted version: rent an equipped office (furnished), declared as BIC (industrial and commercial profits) instead of property income: you can deduct depreciation of the property (if you own) or part of your rent (if you're a tenant), offsetting ~80% of the rental income; it needs light bookkeeping, but instead of 19 + 19 you pay ~4 + 4 → ~€92, "50% more than the 62." Limits: rarely more than a third of your surface — with €1,500 monthly rent and a consulting activity, hard to justify over ~€500/month; and coherent with the rent you pay or market price. Don't pay yourself €5,000 for 7 m².

Method 4 — profit-sharing (intéressement)

A bonus paid to employees and managers under an agreement, available to companies under 250 employees. The video: ~9.7% social levies on the bonus, then ~20% income tax if taken at once → ~€72. Condition: at least one employee who isn't the manager — a spouse who really contributes, children who e.g. run the company's social media, anyone in your tax household with a real job (no fictitious employment), or regular staff. Boost: place the bonus in a company savings plan (PEE) blocked for 5 years → no income tax, only levies → ~€90; many early-release cases (marriage, PACS, a child, buying an electric car…). Ceiling: up to 20% of the beneficiary's annual salary — about two and a half months of pay. "One employee is enough." Rules are subtle, especially for the manager — get support.

Method 5 — expense reimbursements and pre-funded CESU

Expense reimbursements: €100 out, €100 in your pocket — no corporate tax, no URSSAF, no flat tax, no social levies, no income tax. Capped, of course, and only for real professional costs. Mileage allowances (indemnités kilométriques) for business travel can exceed your car's real cost, giving a legal tax-free complement if you drive a lot. Pre-funded CESU (chèque emploi service universel, a voucher for home services: cleaning, childcare, gardening…): the company buys them, deductible, up to €2,591 a year, for personal home services — the video says this lets personal spending pass through the company legally. Bonus: for employees (not the manager — a SASU president is "assimilated employee," not an employee), pre-funded CESU also give the company a 25% tax credit: it costs €100, the employee receives €125. Useful if your spouse or children are employed. (Check the eligibility rules for managers with an accountant — the conditions are specific.)

Why the Wealthy All Have a SASU — the Tax Screen Between You and Your CompanyLegalPlace · Video case · Control over when and how you are paid, salary vs dividends, the holding above, and the three mistakes
▶ Video0/14▶
The one ideaBernard Arnault, Xavier Niel, François-Henri Pinault, Martin Bouygues — very different people and sectors, one common point in their structures: not an exotic offshore set-up but the humble SAS, which anyone can create. The magic isn't the SASU itself, it's the control it gives you over the timing of your taxation. In micro you're taxed on gross revenue with no say. In a SASU you can bill €200,000 and pay yourself only what you need to live; the rest stays in the company taxed at 15% or 25%. The company earns the millions; the founder takes what he needs, when he needs it. That's the tax screen between what the activity generates and what you live on.
A note on framing (source)

Video case (LegalPlace, "SASU : Pourquoi les riches ont tous une SASU ? (et comment les copier)," May 2026); figures are the video's, French rules 2026; promotions omitted. Not tax advice. It's the "why" behind the structuring series — status map (164), taking money out (165), the holding (163).

The mechanics

What a SASU is: a simplified joint-stock company with a single shareholder. Your company pays corporate tax itself, at fixed rates: 15% up to €42,500 of profit, 25% above. The company earns money, but that money isn't directly yours — it belongs to the company and you decide when and how to take it. Option 1 — salary: as president you're "assimilated employee": same social security and pension as employees, but no unemployment insurance. Charges are ~75–80% of net salary — a €3,000 net monthly salary costs the company €5,100–5,400. Not scandalous: you're well protected and build your pension, but it's expensive. Option 2 — dividends (the SASU's main attraction): after corporate tax, remaining profit can be distributed to the shareholder — you. No social charges, but the flat tax (PFU) at 31.4% maximum in 2026 (12.8% income tax + 18.6% social levies); if you're not taxable, only the 18.6% applies.

Worked example — €100,000 of profit

Corporate tax: 15% × €42,500 = €6,375, plus 25% × €57,500 = €14,375 → €20,750. Distributable: €79,250. Flat tax 31.4% → ~€24,900. ~€54,000 net in your pocket, all through dividends. Compare a freelancer or micro-entrepreneur at the same income level: depending on marginal tax rate and contributions, €35,000–40,000 net after URSSAF and income tax. And that's before the holding.

Salary floor, then the arbitrage

Always pay yourself a minimum — about €1,000 a month — to validate pension quarters, get daily sickness allowances, maternity/paternity leave, and access to a mutuelle and prévoyance. Above that floor, do the salary/dividend arbitrage with software or your accountant. In ~90% of cases dividends are the immediate financial winner, but over the very long term salary can win because it builds pension rights more efficiently. Do the calculations; arbitrate only on the complement.

Beyond the flat tax — the holding

31.4% is still nearly a third. Those who build something long-term don't distribute personally: they create a holding above the SASU (often itself a SASU) whose purpose is to hold shares in other companies. Dividends going up to it benefit from the parent-subsidiary regime: 95% exempt, only 5% taxable at 15% or 25%. Example: €100,000 distributed. Without a holding: 31.4% → €31,400 of tax, €68,600 left to invest. With a holding: 5% taxable = €5,000 × 25% = €1,250 → €98,750 in the holding to invest. Difference: €30,150 in a single year; over 10 years with compounding, several hundred thousand euros. The money circulates in your ecosystem, not in the state's coffers — the system of Niel, Pinault and Arnault, used legally.

Is it for you? — by revenue

Below €30–35k of annual revenue: micro-entreprise is usually simpler; admin costs are lower and the SASU's tax gain is limited — don't overload yourself. €35–60k: worth real thought depending on your activity, deductible costs and real income need; if you don't need to take everything out each year, a SASU makes sense. Above €60–70k of profit, a SASU becomes clearly advantageous in most cases. Above €100k of profit, if you're not properly structured, you often throw money out of the window. It's also about credibility (banks, large accounts, partners, investors are reassured — it matters for contracts and financing) and protection (personal assets clearly separated; profits left in the company build a war chest for a downturn or a slump).

The three mistakes

1) 100% dividends, zero salary: tempting, since dividends carry no social charges (unlike in an EURL) — but no pension contributions and poor sickness cover. Balance: a salary floor, then the rest in dividends; the exact amount depends on your situation — simulate. 2) Creating a SASU purely for image: people create one because it "looks serious" while billing €15,000 a year — they pay accounting fees, a more complex admin and get almost no tax benefit. 3) A holding with no real purpose: moving dividends up with no concrete reinvestment plan behind them lets the tax authority treat it as abuse of law — a reassessment with a 40% penalty. "Not a theoretical threat, it happens." A holding is justified by a real group project — property, investments — not an empty tax safe.

This is the logic of sponsor equity. In project finance, cash stays in the SPV until the waterfall and covenants allow a distribution; sponsors decide when to take it, reinvest it or leave reserves. A SASU gives you the same control at personal scale. And the third mistake echoes your world too: structures need real economic substance, exactly as lenders and tax authorities demand of any holding above an energy asset.

Make it click — similar plays

How to drillThe SASU's power is control: profits taxed at 15%/25% inside the company, and you choose when and how to take them. On €100k of profit, dividends leave ~€54k net vs ~€35–40k as a freelancer; with a holding, €98,750 stays invested instead of €68,600. Keep a ~€1,000/month salary floor, consider a SASU from ~€35–60k and clearly above €60–70k of profit, and avoid zero-salary, image-only SASUs and holdings without a real project.

The Founder's Wealth Ladder — Why 90% of French Entrepreneurs Never Get RichSwapn · Video case · Six rungs in the right order: blind spot, separation, double reserve, arbitrage, strategy, structuring & exit
▶ Video0/14▶
The one ideaIn France, 6% of households are entrepreneurs, yet they make up 50% of the top 1% of wealth: entrepreneurship is the royal road to building wealth. And yet most founders reach 50 with less wealth than a salaried senior manager. The difference isn't talent, revenue or luck. It's a ladder of six rungs climbed in the right order, and 90% of entrepreneurs are stuck on the first three without knowing it. Your position on the ladder has nothing to do with how much you have: a founder with €3m can be stuck on rung 2 while a beginner is already on rung 4 because he built the right reflexes from the start. Getting rich comes from creating value; the ladder is what turns that income into lasting wealth.
A note on framing (source)

Video case (Swapn — Grégoire, whose firm has supported 15,000 entrepreneurs — "Pourquoi 90% des entrepreneurs français ne deviennent jamais riches," Sep 2026); figures and characters (Marc, Nadia, Sylvain) are the video's illustrations. Not financial or tax advice. This is the capstone of the structuring series: it puts cards 164, 165, 163 and 159 in order — and says most of them come late.

The summit

A founder who has climbed all six rungs: his company was sold on the best possible tax terms because everything was prepared years ahead; his holding owns an SCI that holds the walls of his former company, rented to the buyer; income that no longer depends on his daily work covers a large part of his lifestyle. He still works on a few missions he chooses. If he wants to stop tomorrow, he can. If he wants to refuse a client, he refuses. Four tests of the summit: 1) income from assets you don't operate covers your rung-2 budget without getting up in the morning; 2) your company is just one asset among others — the question isn't "what is it worth?" but "what happens if it's worth zero tomorrow?"; 3) the company runs three weeks without you without anyone noticing — team, clients and a brand that belong to the company (a profitable activity that rests on you isn't wealth, it's "an employment contract disguised as a company"); 4) you can say no — to an important client, a boring deal, a buyer offering the wrong price.

Block 1 — financial hygiene (where most founders fail)

Rung 1 — the blind spot. Three questions without looking at your bank account: How much did you pay yourself net last month, to a few hundred euros (not "between 4,000 and 6,000")? Was it the same 3, 6 and 12 months ago? Do you know exactly what it covers — housing, fixed costs, food, savings? Hesitate on one and you're on rung 1; in the video's experience 7–8 founders in 10 fail, including some making €500,000 a year and some with a holding. Rung 2 — separation (probably the most important rung). Two actions, always together: a single fixed monthly transfer from the company to your personal account, the same amount every month including good months, with the company card used only for business; and a real personal budget kept with the rigour of a company cash plan. A budget without a fixed transfer doesn't hold; a fixed transfer without a budget is arbitrary. It's not a tax lever, it's a measurement lever — without it you can't calculate optimal pay, size reserves or invest. Example: Nadia, mixed accounts, takes whatever is left; at 38 a scare and a tax audit wake her up; after 18 "boring" months she finds she needs €2,900/month to live while she was spending almost €4,000 — €1,600 a month freed to invest without earning a euro more. Rung 3 — the double reserve. Two safety pockets, distinct and quantified, on liquid risk-free supports: company side 3–6 months of fixed costs or revenue; personal side 3–6 months of the rung-2 budget (for Nadia €8,700–17,400). Most see it as defensive, born of fear; it's the opposite — it's what lets you take risk later. Without it you can't lock anything long-term, because a shock within 18 months (a client leaving, a divorce, a health problem) can force you to sell a 15-year investment at the worst moment. Don't leave it at 0%: personal side a Livret A–type savings account (liquid, risk-free, tax-free); company side term deposits or secured bond funds. Test: how many months does the company last if revenue stops tomorrow, and how many do you? (As a manager you have no unemployment cover.)

Block 2 — piloting

Rung 4 — the arbitrage. How to take money out paying the least tax and social charges — "least" meaning the total cost over your whole working life, not this year's bill. Two taps: salary, dividends, or both; depending on how you open them, the bill for the same amount can double. Set the salary/dividend split once a year at the start of the financial year with your accountant, and don't change it on the feeling of the cash balance. Status matters: in an EURL/SARL dividends above 10% of capital fall into self-employed contributions (~45%), so they open social rights but cost charges; in a SAS/SASU dividends open no social rights whatever the amount. "Pay everything in dividends to avoid charges never really works": either you build no rights, or you pay contributions anyway. A scenario that costs €3,000 more a year but builds four pension quarters and disability cover isn't necessarily worse. From here you need a real accountant, possibly a wealth adviser. Test: do you know why you're paid this amount this year? If your only answer is "to pay less tax," you're improvising. Rung 5 — the strategy (not the same as rung 4: arbitrage is how money leaves; strategy is what you do with it). Define your wealth strategy on one page — not 10, not 50 slides — with four elements: objectives ranked (e.g. retirement income, children's studies, a second home — in that order); horizon for each (retirement 25 years, studies 10, second home 5 — different horizons, different investments); allocation by support (e.g. 40% equities, 30% property, 20% secured, 10% reserve); and rules. Key danger: knowing a sector well lets you value an asset but concentrates risk — the furnished-rental expert in one town ends up with everything in one commune, one tax regime, one climate risk. The classic error: starting from a tax scheme (Malraux, PER, LMNP) instead of the strategy. LMNP was sold as magic for years; since 2025 the depreciation taken is reintegrated into the capital-gain calculation on resale, even for pre-reform properties. Test: can you write in 5 minutes on one A4 page your three ranked objectives, the horizon of each, your target allocation and your rules?

Rung 6 — structuring & exit

Strategy is what you decided; structuring is the tool to execute it — it always comes after, never before. Most founders arrive wanting "a holding to optimise because it's good" — the reflex holding, which costs a lot: a second set of accounts every year, two business property taxes, tax filings, for a gain that may be zero or negative. "The reflex holding mostly enriches your accountant and the state, not you." Real uses of a holding: financing a buyout (buying a departing partner's shares, or an OBO — owner buyout — where you sell to your own holding with a loan repaid by the operating company's dividends); and preparing sale and transmission, with three big levers — the Dutreil pact, the donation before sale, and the €500,000 allowance for a retiring manager. None of them triggers the day before the sale: Dutreil takes years, the donation must precede any agreement on price, the retirement allowance needs precise sequencing — even six months before a sale most levers are already out of reach. This rung is played 5–10 years before. And the best tax structuring in the world won't make up for a company that isn't sellable. Test: can you say in one sentence what your holding is for ("to optimise" isn't an answer), and could your company run three weeks without you?

Three founders at 55

Sylvain created his holding in 2018 for a precise use (buying out a partner), two years later put his workshop's walls in an SCI, and in 2025 started preparing his exit planned at 55 with a Dutreil pact signed three years earlier. He sold to two of his managers on the best tax terms, kept the walls he rents to the company, and his holding's rental and financial income covers most of his lifestyle — never a brilliant investment, just six rungs in the right order. Marc opened a holding five years ago "because it was good"; it holds nothing in particular and generates accounting fees. He lost two big clients and the market turned; no reserve; he should cut his pay but can't because his loans are sized on his lifestyle; nobody wants to buy his company — its goodwill is him. At 55 his wealth will be far below what he earned in 25 years. Nadia, eight years after catching up, has more modest but real, diversified wealth and a company worth something without her; she's not fully at the summit but will be at 55. "What separates rung 1 from the summit is almost never talent or income. It's a series of sometimes boring decisions taken in the right order, and 20 years of consistency."

You can climb rungs 1–3 and 5 today, as an employee. They don't need a company: a known budget, a fixed savings transfer, a double reserve and a one-page strategy apply to your salary and your existing EUR/TND portfolio right now. That's the real lesson after eight structuring cards: holdings, SCIs and exit pacts are rung 6 — the last step, not the first. And the summit test "can it run three weeks without you?" is also the test for your future consulting practice: a practice that is only you is a well-paid job, not an asset.

Make it click — similar plays

The summit: assets cover your budget, the company runs three weeks without you, and you can say no. It's not talent or income — it's boring decisions in the right order and 20 years of consistency.
