SASU → EURL → SASU — Why Successful Founders Keep Changing StatusLegalPlace · Video case · Same company, new "costume": the three-stage cycle, the EURL + holding alternative, and how a transformation works
▶ Video0/14▶
The one ideaCounter-intuitive pattern among founders who succeed: the more the company grows, the more they change legal form — sometimes several times. Start in SASU, move to EURL a few years later, then back to SASU once they really make money. It isn't indecision: each form is optimal for a different phase. A company is a legal person with an identity card (its SIREN registration); the legal form is just its costume — it can change costume without changing identity, name, address, SIRET, bank account or contracts. The question isn't "which status is best?" but "which status fits the phase I'm in right now?"
A note on framing (source)

Video case (LegalPlace, "J'ai analysé pourquoi les entrepreneurs riches changent toujours de statut," Sep 2026); figures are the video's, French rules 2026; promotions omitted. Not tax advice. It adds the time dimension to the status cards — status map (164), taking money out (165), the SASU (166) — and is rung 4 of the wealth ladder (167). Note the tension with ARE or ARCE (162) on stage 1.

Stage 1 — start in SASU (if you're on unemployment benefit)

For anyone registered with France Travail, the video calls the SASU the best status to keep unemployment rights: there's no "communicating vessels" effect between what France Travail pays you and what the company earns, as long as you don't transfer the company's money to your personal account. You can build revenue and keep profit in the company with zero social contributions as long as you pay yourself nothing — whereas an EURL pays roughly €1,500 of contributions in year one even with no pay. (Card 162 shows that since April 2025 benefits alongside a company are guaranteed only 60% of the duration — simulate before relying on this.) If you're not on unemployment benefit, skip stage 1 and start directly in EURL.

Stage 2 — switch to EURL to pay yourself

When benefits stop, the priority is to pay yourself as fast as possible at minimum cost. In SASU, a €1,000 salary costs ~€750 of contributions (~75%); in EURL ~€450 (~45%). So transform into EURL and stay there until the activity covers your target pay — what you need to live: housing, food, school, holidays, taxes. Living costs must be paid by salary, not dividends. Paying yourself entirely in dividends is "completely absurd": profit is first taxed at 15% corporate tax, then the 31.4% flat tax, it gives no pension or social protection, and dividends only exist after the first balance sheet — about a year after creation, while salary can start in month one.

Stage 3 — back to SASU for dividends

Once the activity covers your needs (consultants often bill much more than they need), the gap becomes profit. Best strategy: leave in the company what you don't need — not taken out, it bears no distribution cost, income tax or social charges and snowballs into wealth inside the company. If you do need it (e.g. to buy property or your main home, which can't be held or financed inside the professional ecosystem), there are two routes: salary (charges plus income tax, losing 50–60%) or dividends (15/25% corporate tax plus flat tax up to 31.4% in 2026). But in an EURL, dividends also carry ~45% social contributions above the threshold — "surtaxed, forget them." So the second transformation: back to SAS(U) to distribute dividends. The video's rough trigger: when you generate about €3,000 a month beyond your living needs (e.g. ~€8,000/month of activity) that you want to take out. Also, above a certain pay level some prefer to contribute more (45% → 75%) for a much better pension.

The alternative — keep the EURL, add a SASU holding

Instead of transforming a second time: keep the EURL (salary at ~45% charges) and create a holding — a SASU — that owns 100% of the EURL. The EURL's profits go up to the holding under the parent-subsidiary regime, taxed at about 1.25% ("as good as untaxed"); then the holding distributes dividends taxed at 18.6% (if not taxable) to 31.4%. This dividend cascade gives "the best of both worlds": salary at EURL rates, dividends at SASU flat-tax rates. The only constraint: two structures (two sets of accounts). For those who'd rather pay tax than manage paperwork, the single transformation is the better fit. (Card 163 and 167 add the caution: a holding needs a real purpose and substance.)

How a transformation works — and a real example

Changing form means amending the statutes — "change the costume": same name, address, SIRET and bank account; only the legal form and the statutes change. Operationally simple for you, technically complex for whoever files it: done alone, the file goes to the INPI (the French industrial-property / business registry office) and any error means starting over and paying the formalities again (~€350) plus your time. Don't ask your accountant to change status every quarter or every year — transform at phase changes. Example: a friend billing ~€7,800/month still ran out of money around the 20th of each month; asked his legal form: "SASU, for 20 years." He was short ~€1,200 a month. Transform the SASU into an EURL and his pay could rise from €3,000 to ~€4,005 the next day, at the same cost to the company — nobody had told him.

Beyond the video — why this case is yours

Structures should evolve with the asset's life cycle. In project finance the same project moves from development to construction to operation, and its financing is restructured at each phase (construction loans refinanced into long-term debt, equity recycled). Your own company can follow the same logic: the right form for launch isn't the right form for distribution. Plan the phases from day one, and keep the numbers — target pay, surplus — that tell you when to switch.

Make it click — similar plays

How to drillChoose the costume for the phase: SASU with no pay while on benefits (check the 2025 rules), EURL to pay yourself at ~45% charges until your target pay is covered, then back to SASU — or keep the EURL and add a SASU holding — once ~€3k/month of surplus needs to come out as dividends. Pay living costs by salary, leave surplus inside, and transform at phase changes, not every year.

Why the Wealthy Own Almost Nothing in Their Own NameLegalPlace · Video case · Inheritance tax, IFI and income tax vs a holding + SCI at IS + partner current account — with the caveats the video skips
▶ Video0/14▶
The one ideaThe wealthy own houses, cars, companies and investments — yet look at whose name is on them and you'll often find a company. Above a certain level of wealth the rules change, and the classic organisation is three layers: an operating company (SASU, EURL, SAS or SA) owned 100% by a holding (usually a SAS), which invests in property through one or more SCIs at corporate tax. That set-up attacks the three taxes that hit wealth — inheritance tax, the property-wealth tax (IFI) and income tax — and adds discretion and protection. The video says you don't need to be rich to start; but several of its steps are aggressive and need a lawyer, not a YouTube tutorial.
A note on framing (source)

Video case (LegalPlace — Xavier de la Barrière, expert-comptable at ComptaPlace — "Comment protéger son patrimoine comme les riches (et les copier)," Oct 2026); figures are the video's, French rules 2026; promotions omitted. Not tax or legal advice — and more audit-sensitive than the other structuring cards. It's rung 6 of the wealth ladder (167), building on the holding (163) and the SCI (159).

The problem — what you pay if you do nothing

Income tax up to 45% plus 17.2% social levies on rents — combined well above 50% at the top bracket. Inheritance tax in direct line: allowance of €100,000 per child per parent, then progressive rates up to 45% above ~€1.8m — "among the highest in the world"; Italy charges 4% above €1m. IFI (property-wealth tax): 30% allowance on the main residence, then 0.7% above €1.3m rising to 1.5% for the largest property fortunes. Since French property nets ~4–5% after charges, 1.5% of IFI can eat about a third of property income — before income tax.

Step 1 — inheritance: SCI + holding + Dutreil pact

Property goes into SCIs; the holding sets up a Dutreil pact, which gives a 75% allowance on the taxable base when the shares are donated to the children: a holding worth €1m is taxed as €250,000, then the €100,000 allowance per child per parent applies — inheritance tax typically down by at least 75%. Conditions: the holding must be an animating holding (it really runs and manages the companies below it), the heirs keep the shares for several years, and the pact is drafted with a notary. Caveat: the Dutreil pact applies to operating businesses — a holding whose value is mainly passive property (SCIs) generally doesn't qualify for the property part; get the structure checked.

Step 2 — IFI

Holding property through an SCI or a holding does not automatically take it out of the IFI base. Exception: property necessary for your professional activity — e.g. your SCI rents the building to your operating company and it's used for that activity. The video then announces a "more subtle" route, which is step 3.

Step 3 — income tax (and the IFI cap): minimum salary + SCI at IS + current account

1) Pay yourself a minimum salary, ideally from an EURL, to validate pension quarters: ~€1,000/month = €12,000/year. 2) To live on €3,000–5,000/month without dividends (31.4% flat tax), sell your property to your SCI at IS. The SCI now owns a €500,000 property; its rents are taxed at corporate tax (15%/25%), and it can depreciate ~80% of the value (€400,000) over 25–30 years — so its tax is "about four times lower" than the levies plus income tax you'd pay renting it out personally. 3) The SCI didn't pay you cash: it owes you €500,000 on your partner's current account. It repays that debt monthly from the rents — €4,000/month = €48,000/year, which is a debt repayment, not income: nothing to declare. 4) Your taxable income is now ~€12,000. IFI plus income tax is capped at 75% of your income — so at most ~€9,000 of combined tax for ~€60,000 of cash withdrawals, vs ~€15,000 of income tax alone for a single person normally. The video says it works from €500,000 to €5m.

What the video doesn't stress — read before copying

Selling to your own SCI is a taxable sale: you pay personal capital-gains tax on the property (unless it's your main home, which shouldn't go into an SCI anyway) and the SCI pays transfer duties (~5.8%) and notary fees. The current account isn't infinite: once the €500,000 is repaid, the tax-free cash stops — it's a deferral that converts your own capital back to you, not new income. Resale inside an SCI at IS is taxed on depreciated book value (card 159). The IFI-cap strategy is scrutinised: deliberately minimising taxable income to exploit the 75% cap through controlled companies can be challenged under abuse of law (penalties up to 80%). Protection claims are overstated: company assets are separate from your personal assets, but creditors can seize your shares, and in a divorce the value of shares bought with community money is generally shared. Do this only with a notary and a tax lawyer, and only with real economic substance.

The other reasons — discretion and protection

When the companies are the apparent owners, your name isn't on the deeds — more discreet; the video adds that rental and crypto gains booked in a company don't show on your personal tax return (and mentions a crypto data leak in summer 2026). It argues that what sits in the holding isn't your personal property, so it's harder to seize and better shielded in a separation — "even if we're not in the US." See the caveat above: protection is real but partial.

This is a HoldCo / PropCo / OpCo structure at family scale — the same architecture as an infrastructure sponsor separating the operating company from the asset-owning vehicle, funded partly by shareholder loans repaid before dividends. You'll recognise the shareholder-loan logic from project finance: repayments of principal are cash without profit. That fluency is valuable; the discipline is to apply it with the same legal rigour a lender would demand — substance, documentation and a clear economic purpose.

But count the sale costs, the end of the current account, the book-value gain on resale and abuse-of-law risk — and do it only with a notary and a tax lawyer.

When Does a Holding Pay? — The ~€7,000 Break-Even, Not €100,000LegalPlace · Video case · The real threshold, the cost of a holding, when to create it first, and ring-fencing investments
▶ Video0/14▶
The one idea"Wait for €100,000 of profit before creating a holding" is one of the worst pieces of advice on social media, says the video: it pushes founders to create it far too late — or sometimes far too early. A holding isn't a question of revenue, or even of profit. The real question is: from when does it actually make you money? The answer is a simple break-even: a holding costs ~€1,500–2,000 a year and saves ~30 points of tax on every euro you reinvest instead of taking out, so it pays from about €6,700–7,000 a year of profit you don't need to live on and want to reinvest.
A note on framing (source)

Video case (LegalPlace — Xavier de la Barrière — "J'ai fait le calcul : vous créez votre holding beaucoup trop tard," Sep 2026); figures are the video's, French rules 2026; promotions omitted. Not tax advice. It gives the number behind the holding (163) and the "precise purpose" test of the wealth ladder (167).

The example — a SASU making €60,000

Your SASU earns €60,000. You pay yourself €30,000, with ~€15,000 of social charges → €45,000 total cost. €15,000 of taxable profit remains; corporate tax at 15% ≈ €2,000 → ~€13,000 left that you don't need to live on. Year after year it accumulates: €13k, €26k, €39k… You'd rather invest it — in rental property, a business, financial assets, even gold — than leave it on the business account.

Two routes for the surplus

Take it out as a private individual: dividends pay the 31.4% flat tax, then you invest what's left. Move it up to a holding (usually a SAS) that owns your SASU: under the parent-subsidiary regime the dividends are taxed at ~1% — "30 times less tax" — and the holding reinvests them in rental property (possibly via an SCI), a friend's company, a new business, a buyout, crypto or financial placements, "with far more firepower" than you'd have as a shareholder taking the money out.

The break-even

Cost to create: ~€500 (more with a lawyer on the Champs-Élysées). Running cost: accountant €80–100/month, business bank account ~€20/month, CFE (local business tax) ~€20/month → ~€120–150/month, i.e. €1,500–2,000 a year. Saving: ~30 points (31.4% flat tax vs ~1%) on each euro reinvested via the holding. Threshold: €2,000 ÷ 0.30 ≈ €6,700 of distributable profit a year (net after corporate tax) that you don't need personally and want to invest. Below that, the holding costs more than it saves; above it, every euro grows the snowball faster than as a private investor.

Create it first or later?

If you're almost sure to exceed ~€7,000 of surplus in year one — e.g. a consultant billing €10,000/month who needs only €6,000 all-in to live, leaving ~€4,000/month — create the holding before the SASU (cheaper than contributing shares later, see card 164). If you're unsure of your start-up costs or have a more commercial business that may need belt-tightening, don't rush — do it later. Second condition: you must actually want to reinvest. If you don't want to bother with investments, leave the money in the company and ask your banker to place it at 2–3%.

Ring-fencing — separate your investments

You can invest directly from your SASU (property, financial placements), but then all the eggs are in one basket: if one investment fails or one asset is seized, creditors can take everything at once. Better: separate investments into compartments — a structure per investment class, each with its own business account — so an unlucky investment doesn't sink the rest, and you see clearly what each one earns or loses. "Even if you're alone, even in a SASU, even as sole shareholder, it makes sense." Conclusion: holdings aren't for when you make €100,000 or €1m — they're worth it from ~€7,000 of annual gain.

▶ Original video ↗

Read alongside

Each extra structure (holding, SCI, one company per investment) adds roughly €1,500–2,000 a year of accounts, bank and CFE — so ring-fencing has its own break-even. And remember the conditions from the other cards: the holding must really own the operating company's shares (164), have a purpose and substance (163, 166), and money moved up is reinvested capital, not spendable cash — taking it out later pays the flat tax (163).

Capture the lessons

Run the drills

Beyond the video — why this case is yours

It's a simple NPV decision. Fixed annual cost against a rate saving on a variable flow — the same break-even logic as any capex-vs-opex choice in a project. As a consultant at a senior daily rate, you'd likely clear €7,000 of surplus early, which argues for creating the holding before the operating company; and ring-fencing investments in separate vehicles is the personal version of one-SPV-per-asset.

Make it click — similar plays

The structuring series: the wealth ladder (167), the holding (163), status map (164), owning nothing in your name (169), the SCI (159).

How to drillA holding pays from ~€6,700–7,000 a year of profit you don't need and want to reinvest — not €100,000: it costs ~€1,500–2,000 a year and saves ~30 points (1% vs 31.4%) on each euro moved up. Create it first if that surplus is near-certain (e.g. a consultant billing €10k/month needing €6k), later if not, and not at all without a reinvestment plan. Ring-fence investments in separate compartments.

The Cruise Business — Floating Malls That Pay Almost No TaxSwapn · Video case · Section 883, tonnage tax, 110% occupancy, onboard spending, private islands — and MSC, the family that owns the oceans
▶ Video0/14▶
The one ideaIn November 2025 the French Senate voted a €15-per-passenger cruise tax; three weeks later, after intense lobbying, the government withdrew it. Why such resistance to €15? Because the cruise giants barely pay tax at all: Royal Caribbean made ~$18bn of revenue in 2025 and paid ~$82m of tax — under 1% — and Carnival's 2023 rate was negative. Not fraud: a 1986 US law and the European tonnage tax make it perfectly legal. Then the economics: the ticket is a loss leader to fill the ship beyond 100%, and the real profit is made once you're aboard, in a floating shopping centre designed so you spend without noticing. Behind it all sits MSC, owned by one discreet Geneva family.
A note on framing (source)

Video case (Swapn — Grégoire — "La famille qui possède secrètement les océans," May 2026), built from the annual reports (10-K) of Carnival, Royal Caribbean and Norwegian Cruise Line; figures are the video's own, sponsor segment omitted. Filed in Consumer, Retail & Luxury (leisure). Echoes the rented-edge cases Shein (152) and BCCI (148), and the private-owner logic of Rolex (154).

The tax machine

Flags of convenience. The Symphony of the Seas — over €1bn, 6,700 passengers, built in Saint-Nazaire by the Chantiers de l'Atlantique — sails under the Bahamas flag, though owner Royal Caribbean is run from Miami. Carnival registers its ships in Panama, Norwegian in Bermuda, MSC in Switzerland and Malta. None of the big ships leaving the US — the world's largest cruise market — is legally American. Section 883 (US, 1986, under Reagan): meant to avoid tax wars on international shipping by not taxing foreign shipping companies on US routes. The cruise lines structured themselves as foreign companies — Royal Caribbean is Liberian, Carnival Panamanian, Norwegian Bermudian — so their international transport income isn't taxable in the US, and almost all of it qualifies. Tonnage tax (Europe): instead of taxing real profit, the state taxes a notional profit set by the ship's size. If the Symphony were French and made €300m of profit, 25% corporate tax would be €75m; under tonnage tax its taxable base is ~€3m, so ~€7,500 of tax — "100 times less." Why do European states accept it? Because otherwise shipowners would all register elsewhere; Brussels considers it compatible state aid — "technically a tax favour, accepted because the alternative is worse." Two opposite logics, one winner. Combined with zero-tax Bahamas, Panama, Liberia and Bermuda: if the three US-listed groups paid the normal ~21% US rate, the US Treasury would collect ~$1bn more a year. Delta, United and American Airlines pay 15–25% effective tax because planes can't use Section 883.

The business model — sell the ticket at a loss, profit aboard

The cost base: a modern ship costs $1–2bn, plus 2,000–3,000 crew, fuel, maintenance and port fees — a gigantic fixed-cost structure that must be full permanently. 110% occupancy: Carnival reports occupancy of 105%, 108%, even 110%. Occupancy is calculated on two beds per cabin, but cabins have two extra fold-down beds; a family of four in a two-person cabin is 200%. So the lines will discount tickets — even sell at a loss on some campaigns — as long as the ship is physically full. Onboard spending is the real profit centre: about one-third of Carnival's revenue comes from what passengers spend after boarding (up to ~35% at Royal Caribbean): drinks, specialty restaurants, excursions, casino, shops, wifi, photos, spa. Margins aren't disclosed, but sector analyses suggest ~80% on some items: a $14 cocktail costing a few dollars of ingredients, a $90/day drinks package paid in advance, a $200 excursion bought for $20 from a local operator. "The ticket is a loss leader; the ship is a floating mall." Frictionless payment: since 2017 Carnival's Ocean Medallion, a coin-sized pendant, opens your cabin and pays for drinks, restaurants and casino with no cash or card — designed by the engineer behind Disney's MagicBand. Studies on tourism, festivals and resorts show people spend ~20% more once the act of paying disappears; Royal Caribbean and MSC copied it. Private islands: at normal port calls passengers spend in local shops and restaurants and the lines earn nothing (and pay port fees). So Carnival owns Half Moon Cay, Royal Caribbean CocoCay, MSC Ocean Cay — four private islands of the four biggest lines, all in the Bahamas — where bars, sunbeds, excursions and cabana rentals are theirs. In 2024 the Bahamas noticed and introduced a 10% tax on private-island revenue: even a tax haven started taxing "an offshore cash register."

The final boss — MSC and the Aponte family

Carnival (which owns Costa), Royal Caribbean and Norwegian are listed and pay dividends to thousands of shareholders — the wealth is diluted. MSC (Mediterranean Shipping Company) is the opposite: no board, no institutional shareholder, no fund — one family. It's #1 in world container shipping (~21% of global capacity, ahead of France's CMA CGM) and top 4 in cruises, European leader. Gianluigi Aponte, born 1940 near Sorrento into a seafaring family, merchant-marine captain, then a few years in a bank saving money; in 1970 he bought a second-hand German cargo ship on a bank loan, the Patricia, MSC's first vessel, co-founding the company 50/50 with his wife Rafaela. Fifty years later: from one cargo ship to ~700 vessels, from a Europe–Africa route to every sea — run since 1978 from Geneva, in a landlocked country. Fortune: $20–66bn depending on estimates (Forbes ranks them ~48th in the world). No transparency: the US groups file a 10-K every year (revenue by brand, margins, debt, tax rate, legal risks) — that's how this investigation was possible. MSC publishes nothing. The only real figures came from a 2022 leak in Italy's Il Messaggero: €86bn of revenue and €36bn of net profit — more than Carnival, Royal Caribbean and Norwegian combined. Swiss headquarters for attractive taxation and protective law, no listing, one family controls everything — "everything we saw at Carnival and Royal Caribbean, pushed to the maximum." April 2026: Gianluigi and Rafaela transferred ownership to their children, Diego (already running containers) and Alexa (CFO), in private and without public communication. The empire doesn't change owner, only generation.

Capture the lessons

Beyond the video — why this case is yours

Shipping and cruises are asset-heavy infrastructure finance. $1–2bn ships are financed like power plants, often with export-credit backing tied to the shipyard — Saint-Nazaire is a French industrial asset just as a nuclear plant is. The same questions you'll face in energy apply: which jurisdiction holds the asset, how is it taxed (profit, or a proxy like tonnage or capacity), what utilisation keeps the fixed costs covered, and which revenue streams sit behind the headline tariff. And the MSC story — one family, one second-hand ship bought on a loan in 1970, Geneva, 700 vessels — is the strongest argument in the tracker for patient, private, compounding ownership.

Make it click — similar plays

Rented regulatory edges: Shein (152), BCCI (148), Ireland (18). Captive spend & float: Starbucks (147), Basic-Fit (155) — ghost members. Private family empires: Rolex (154), Intersport (158), Family Businesses (84). Structuring at personal scale: the wealth ladder (167). Leisure peers: Club Med (34), Thomas Cook (138).

How to drillTwo engines, one fortress: legally, Section 883 in the US and tonnage tax in Europe, plus flags of convenience, take the cruise giants' tax below 1%; commercially, tickets are a loss leader to fill ships beyond 100%, while onboard spending (a third of revenue at ~80% margins on some items), frictionless medallions and private islands make the profit. MSC — one Geneva family, no listing, no disclosure, €36bn of profit in a leaked 2022 — pushes the model to the maximum. For you: know the tax base, fill fixed assets, capture the follow-on spend, and remember that edges built on tolerance can be clawed back.

On — The Brand That Would Rather Sell Less Than Sell CheaperEntrepreneur Mindset · Video case · Third card of the Nike story — garden-hose prototype, specialist shops, the no-discount rule, and a −20% day the founders chose
▶ Video0/14▶
The one ideaOn 14 August 2026 a co-founder of On spent ~$2m of his own money buying his company's shares. Three days earlier the stock had lost 20% in a day — the worst session in its history — and the brand had caused the fall itself, on purpose: it chose to ship fewer shoes rather than let shops discount them. A month later it took Kylian Mbappé from Nike. Even after the drop On is worth more than $11bn, less than 20 years after its creation. The stars came later. The real weapon is simple, and it's the exact opposite of what Nike did: On refuses to discount, and protects the full price even when it costs growth and stock price.
A note on framing (source)

Video case (Entrepreneur Mindset, "On, le nouveau roi de la basket choisi par Mbappé," Oct 2026); figures are the video's, sponsor segment omitted. Completes the Nike trilogy: Nike — going direct (58) explains the strategic mistake, Nike — the brutal descent (153) tells the round trip, and this card tells the story from the winner's side.

The people & the dates (references)

The garden hose: in Switzerland at the end of the 2000s, Olivier Bernard, a Swiss athlete and multiple Ironman winner, glues pieces of garden hose under the sole of a running shoe. His sponsor at the time was Nike; he showed them the idea and Nike answered it wasn't interested at all — ironic for a company whose own first invention came from a kitchen, when co-founder Bill Bowerman poured rubber into his wife's waffle iron in 1971 (the Waffle Trainer, 1974). The founding: with Caspar Coppetti and David Allemann, each founder puts in ~$150,000 and they sign a radical pact: if any of them takes another job in the first three years, he loses his shares — no plan B. The logo's top is drawn like an on/off switch. Weeks later at the big Munich sports trade show they win a prize and more than half a million Swiss francs of orders before selling a single shoe. The channel: they start in small specialist running shops, with a passionate salesperson who tells you every mountain and marathon he's done — advancing shop by shop. 2019: CHF 267m of sales; Nike the same year ~$39bn, more than 100× bigger. Nike opens the door: 25 Oct 2017, Nike CEO Mark Parker tells investors Nike will focus on 40 of its 30,000+ partner retailers — "as if Coca-Cola delivered only the 40 biggest French supermarkets." In 2020–21 Nike stops supplying Zappos, then DSW and Urban Outfitters. Nature abhors a vacuum — so do shelves. Federer joined, and on 15 Sept 2021 On listed in New York: +~50% the first evening, just under $12bn by year-end — while Nike was worth $264bn, 22× more.

The discount trap — Nike vs On

Nike, 29 Sept 2022: CFO Matthew Friend presents results; one line panics everyone — $9.7bn of inventory, +44% in a year. During Covid ships took months, so everyone over-ordered; in summer 2022 deliveries normalised and everything arrived at once. Nike cut prices and the stock fell up to 13%, its worst day since March 2020. The trap closes: discounts are like sugar — once customers taste them, they want more. Why pay full price if it'll be on sale in a few weeks? On 26 June 2025 Nike reported a 40% gross margin vs almost 45% a year earlier, explained mainly by heavier discounting, including in its own stores. On, Nov 2025, just before Black Friday: CEO Martin Hoffmann on an analyst call — "absolutely not the moment for us to drive sales through discounts," a "full-price strategy." The rule comes from luxury: Louis Vuitton never goes on sale, Bernard Arnault refuses discounts on his biggest brand because a discount admits the real price was lower; Burberry once burned over €30m of unsold goods in a year rather than sell them cheap (the video calls that absurd and wasteful). On isn't luxury, but applies the same rule: the Cloudmonster sells ~$190 vs $145 for Nike's Pegasus — a price you don't touch, in the upper range.

2026 — the founders' bet

25 March 2026: CEO Martin Hoffmann (13 years at On, ex-CFO who kept the finances even as CEO, the face for investors) announces his departure — officially planned, to take a break and pursue philanthropy, staying as adviser to March 2027; the market struggles to believe it, as the other co-CEO Marc Maurer had left in April 2025. Two leaders gone in a year, while US sales start to slow (a Jefferies analyst questions it). They don't hire outside: the insiders take over. August 2026: results below what the market hoped, for an assumed reason — the US market is flooded with promotions, and rather than follow, On deliberately limits deliveries to protect full-price integrity. If a shop has too many pairs it ends up discounting them — exactly Nike's 2022 — so On "cuts the tap" upstream: it would rather sell less than sell cheaper. The stock loses 20%; three days later Coppetti buys ~$2m of shares, the clearest founder signal: "I believe in it." They can hold out because founders hold special shares with stronger votes — with the founding team, more than half the voting rights: even when the stock collapses, they decide. A month later, Mbappé. Today On is worth roughly what it was in 2021; it's Nike that collapsed, losing more than $200bn of value.

Can On grow without becoming Nike?

On 22 Sept 2026 it promised investors at least CHF 5.6bn of sales in 2029 — almost double 2025 — with a stated goal: the most premium sports brand in the world. But doubling needs new customers. In the Americas growth already slowed to 13% in spring 2026; in Asia sales jumped over 50% in a year; and it's entering football (Mbappé) and even golf. The danger: the more people a brand sells to, the harder it is to stay exclusive — and once there's surplus to clear, the temptation of discounts returns. That's exactly the trap Nike fell into. On won the first round; the second will be to grow without becoming Nike.

Beyond the video — why this case is yours

For a consultant, the day rate is the full price. The first discount to win a mandate becomes the reference for every next one, exactly as Nike's sales taught customers to wait. Holding price and reducing scope, as On reduces deliveries, protects your positioning. And On's path — reject from the incumbent, specialist channel, then the space the giant vacated — is the classic route for an expert entering a market dominated by large advisory firms.

Make it click — similar plays

The Nike trilogy: Nike (58), Nike — the brutal descent (153). Never discount: Rolex (154), LVMH (28), Zara (149) — full-price sell-through. Founder control: Rolex (154), Intersport (158). Growth without dilution: Starbucks (147) — saturation banalises.

Follow-up: On's share price and the China backlash — Mbappé & China (191).

The next test: doubling to CHF 5.6bn without becoming Nike. For you: set a full price and protect it.

Who Really Gets Rich From F1? — Liberty Media, the Teams and the Monaco DriversSwapn · Video case · Follow-up to The Economics of Formula 1 (64) — own the rights, let others carry the risk
▶ Video0/14▶
The one ideaF1 generated more than €3.5bn of revenue in 2024 — yet the biggest winner isn't a team or a driver. It's Liberty Media, which sells no engine, car or tyre. Since buying the rights in 2017 (for more than €7bn, from an investment fund) it has turned a sport in decline into a planetary show. It owns the rights; promoters carry the event risk, teams carry the racing cost, and Liberty collects from all of them. The teams treat F1 as an advertising showcase, and the drivers optimise as personal brands — mostly from Monaco.
A note on framing (source)

Video case (Swapn — Grégoire — "Qui s'enrichit vraiment grâce à la F1 ?," Jun 2025); figures are the video's own, sponsor segments omitted. Follow-up to The Economics of Formula 1 (64). Filed in Media, Entertainment & Gaming.

The top of the pyramid — Liberty Media's four pillars

The FIA (Fédération Internationale de l'Automobile) sets the sporting rules; the business is run by Formula One Group, owned 100% by Liberty Media — an American media and entertainment giant that also owns Live Nation (which runs tours such as Lady Gaga's). "Like Disney with Star Wars, they exploit every moment of the asset." Four revenue pillars, €3.5bn+ in 2024: 1) Media rights — broadcasters pay to show the races. 2) Race hosting fees — a country that wants a Grand Prix pays: Saudi Arabia pays more than €50m to Formula One Group for the right to host. 3) Sponsors (~20% of revenue) — the Rolex banner on the finish line seen for 60 laps, Aramco, and LVMH's strategic partnership bringing Louis Vuitton, TAG Heuer and other group brands. 4) Fans (~18%) — merchandise, F1 TV subscriptions, seats and hospitality boxes; small in share but central to the asset's valuation, so Liberty's strategy is to boost the fan base. The trick: Liberty doesn't run the events. Logistics, security, ticketing staff for 6m+ spectators in 2024 — that's the promoter's job, and ticket revenue goes to the promoter. Liberty takes a big cheque each time someone wants to stage a race and avoids the inherently uncertain event business. The one exception: Las Vegas, where Liberty is the promoter itself and keeps all the event revenue (a VIP-box champagne bottle over $3,000); the CEO said it won't be repeated and promoters will keep running the other 23 races. Since 2017 Liberty has transformed the show (Netflix's Drive to Survive, the US expansion) and the accounts are clearly in profit.

The teams — F1 as a showcase

A top team (Red Bull, Ferrari, Mercedes) spends €140–200m a year. Since 2021 a cost cap — today about €123m a season, excluding driver salaries and marketing — rebalances the field and the show; it covers R&D and car parts. Ferrari (listed, so its annual report is public) has four revenue sources: 1) FOM (Formula One Management) redistribution — of the ~€3.5bn Liberty collects, ~€1.5bn goes back to the teams, partly by championship ranking (prize money) plus a historic bonus Ferrari alone receives as the only team present every season since the first Grand Prix in 1950; 2) sponsorship (e.g. Shell); 3) sale of engines and components to other teams such as Haas; 4) merchandising, from caps to scale models — every Scuderia cap pays the team. In 2024 F1 brought Ferrari €597m, plus €190m of engine and component sales = €787m. Profitable on its own? Hard to say from the report — and it doesn't matter: a winning Ferrari sells Ferrari road cars, and Ferrari beats its annual sales record every year though it hasn't won the title in a long time. "An F1 team is above all formidable advertising for the company behind it."

The drivers — brands based in Monaco

2025 pay: Lewis Hamilton 80m+, Max Verstappen ~72m, Lando Norris ~30m. Nine of the 20 drivers live in Monaco — the circuit, 300 days of sun… and taxation: since an 1869 ordinance by Prince Charles III there is no income tax for residents, and social charges are capped, so only a tiny part of a driver's income funds Monaco's social security. And drivers are brands: Hamilton sponsors and collaborates with fashion labels, Leclerc and Norris are Twitch and YouTube stars, many have big personal sponsorship deals — F1 is "an influence and personal-branding factory." What next: in 2024 Liberty bought MotoGP to repeat the recipe — the ambition is to become "the Disney of motorsport."

Givaudan — The Invisible Empire Behind What You Smell and TasteSwapn · Video case · Mastery over discovery, three locks (people, molecules, contracts), an oligopoly in the shadow, and invisibility as strategy
▶ Video0/14▶
The one ideaWhy does Nutella taste so recognisable, your toothpaste so minty, your crisps like roast chicken, your shower gel and the world's most iconic perfume smell the way they do? Much of it comes from one company most people have never heard of: Givaudan, ~€7.4bn of revenue a year. Its name appears on no label, yet it holds the formulas — and it knows what Brazil or Japan will want to smell and taste before their inhabitants do. Its obscurity isn't an accident; it's the strategy. For 130 years Givaudan has locked up the scarce resource of each era before others understood it was a resource.
A note on framing (source)

Video case (Swapn — Nils — "L'entreprise secrète qui manipule tes sens…," Apr 2026); figures are the video's own, sponsor segments omitted. Filed in Consumer, Retail & Luxury as the hidden supplier behind the brands in this shelf (Dior, Nestlé, Unilever, P&G, L'Oréal).

From synthesis to mastery (1895–1963)

The bet: brothers Léon and Xavier Givaudan (a chemist) bet on something nobody took seriously — reproducing nature's aromas and scents chemically. The industry then relied on natural raw materials: ~8,000 flowers for 1g of rose essential oil, so perfume was a luxury for the elite. In 1895 they open their first lab in Zurich; their neighbours are bakers, and in 1898 the bakery complains its bread smells of violet. Asked to leave, they move to Vernier, an industrial suburb of Geneva — still the global HQ 127 years later. Mastery rather than discovery: chemists could already make vanilla, violet or musk molecules in small batches (the first in 1868); producing tonnes, identical every time, without degrading in two weeks — nobody knew how. Givaudan's edge wasn't the discovery but the mastery: identify a molecule, understand its structure, cut its cost and above all stabilise it. A natural oil varies by season, region and weather — May rose doesn't smell like September rose — unacceptable for a detergent maker differentiating on scent; a synthetic molecule is identical every time, so manufacturers can standardise. Expansion: 1900s–1920s mass markets (cosmetics, household) emerge; in 1948 it buys Esrolko and enters food flavours — the taste of your yoghurt, biscuits, instant coffee: two industries sharing the same infrastructure (chemists, molecules, secret formulas, industrial clients demanding consistency); then Latin America. Still, in 1963 it's one player among dozens.

Under Roche — the three locks

In 1963 Hoffmann-La Roche, the Basel pharma giant, buys Givaudan — and, instead of merging everything, funds labs and research while leaving the human know-how alone. Lock 1 — people: since 1946 Givaudan has run an in-house perfumery school founded by perfumer Jean Carles: invitation-only, a few graduates a year from hundreds of candidates, no visible campus, no state diploma, no ranking — yet it trains some of the century's most influential "noses," able to identify hundreds of molecules by smell and turn a marketing brief into a sensory experience. A nose isn't hired; it's trained over years, because olfactory memory comes from repetition and accumulation, thousands of hours. Example: Calice Becker entered the school in the 1980s; a teacher told her she would never make it. In 1999 she created J'adore for Christian Dior, still a top-5 women's fragrance worldwide. But the formula belongs neither to Dior nor to her — it belongs to Givaudan. Lock 2 — molecules: patented ("captive") synthetic molecules only Givaudan may use commercially — signature longevity, projection, a trail that lingers. Competitors train chemists to identify them by nose: "industrial espionage, entirely led by smell." Lock 3 — contracts: formulas are trade secrets protected by NDAs (non-disclosure agreements) with clients — the entry rule in perfumery; no regulation forces full ingredient disclosure on the label, so Dior can't tell you what's in J'adore, not by choice but because the formula isn't theirs. "Dior sells the bottle, Givaudan holds the secret." White-label formulas: in household and mid-market cosmetics, the scent base of a €3 and a €12 shower gel may be identical — same molecule, same supplier; only dosage, packaging and price change. Exclusivity largely exists in marketing. The real barrier: competitors can buy machines, copy recipes, poach individuals, but can't recreate 20 years of excellence — the moat is the deliberate slowness of training and accumulated depth.

The dark side — Morhange and Seveso

Morhange talc (1972): French parents bought baby talc of a trusted brand; one batch was contaminated by mistake with hexachlorophene, a powerful antibacterial agent supplied by Givaudan, at an excessive concentration. Babies were injured and some died; a national scandal, a trial in 1979, convictions, compensation from Givaudan — and the Morhange name became a byword for disaster while Givaudan's faded from memory; its invisibility protected it. Seveso (10 July 1976): near Milan, the ICMESA plant — a subsidiary of Givaudan, itself owned by Roche — overheated and a reactor released for ~20 minutes a cloud containing TCDD dioxin, one of the most toxic substances ever produced. Vegetation burned, animals died, thousands of livestock were culled, 3,000+ residents evacuated; Roche/Givaudan paid ~$240m in compensation, and some zones stayed contaminated for decades. Its lasting legacy: the EU Seveso directive (1982, revised as Seveso II in 1996 and Seveso III in 2012) requiring every site handling dangerous substances to inventory risks, declare them and plan emergencies — still in force across Europe. Both crises forced Givaudan to restructure processes, retake control of production subsidiaries and build far more rigorous scientific governance.

Independence and the oligopoly (2000–today)

In 2000 Roche spins Givaudan off and lists it. 2002: Nestlé decides in-house flavours are no longer its job and sells its whole division to Givaudan — teams, labs, formulas; from then the taste of a KitKat is Givaudan's, not Nestlé's (same logic as J'adore), with Nestlé taking ~10% of Givaudan's shares. 2007: it buys Quest International, Unilever's former flavour and fragrance arm, for CHF 2.8bn — the largest acquisition in the sector's history; revenue jumps ~40% in a year, and by 2008 Givaudan is undisputed world #1 — with almost total silence: no general-press coverage, no regulator reaction. The oligopoly in the shadow: the global flavours & fragrances market is ~$30bn, with four companies holding more than 50%; Givaudan alone ~17%. And 64% of its fragrance-division revenue comes not from Chanel or Dior but from everyday products — detergent, shower gel, softener: "the €3.50 bottle you grab without reading the label is where the empire is built."

Anticipating your tastes — Customer Foresight

Givaudan sits at the centre of all the flows at once: it works simultaneously with Unilever, Nestlé, Dior, P&G and L'Oréal, in every market, category and geography. When a hair-care trend is born in Japan, it sees it before it reaches Europe; when a note starts performing in Latin America, it knows it will reach North American detergents years later — structural, not intuitive. Since 2023 its Customer Foresight platform aggregates years of olfactory and taste preferences from hundreds of markets and thousands of client interactions into AI, to model not what people want today but what they'll want in ten years: weak signals invisible in sales data, and synthetic profiles (e.g. a sustainability-minded Gen Z segment in Southeast Asia) that simulate a segment's future desires before it clearly exists. A brand asking for "a perfume that represents femininity" gets not a formula but a trajectory: what your consumer will want to smell in five years and how to get there. Invisibility as strategy: Givaudan could have built a consumer brand; it chose the shadows so clients keep the illusion of exclusivity — there'd be no Chanel No. 5 mystique if everyone knew who made the recipe. Its business depends on long-term contracts and a position clients can't leave without rebuilding everything — which is why it's still there 130 years later. "The best place to rule is in the shadows."

An expert who masters critical supply, contracts and risk across several energy developers can occupy the same seat: indispensable, hard to replace, seeing patterns no single client sees. And Seveso connects straight to your world: the European framework for industrial hazard came from one reactor's 20 minutes — the same logic as nuclear safety culture, where one event reshapes regulation for a whole continent.

It bought clients' flavour arms (Nestlé 2002, Quest 2007) to become #1 with ~17% of a market four firms control, earns most from everyday products, and now uses cross-client data and AI to predict tastes. Morhange and Seveso were its dark side — and gave Europe its industrial-safety law. For you: own the know-how, layer your locks, and sit where many clients' information meets.

Visa & Mastercard — The Toll Road Nobody Has Managed to ReplaceSwapn · Video case · 50% net margins, a four-party network, three locks (network effect, bank switching cost, data), and a sovereignty problem
▶ Video0/14▶
The one ideaVisa made ~$40bn of revenue last year and Mastercard ~$28bn — and the most surprising number isn't revenue, it's margin: Visa keeps ~50% as net profit ($20bn), Mastercard ~46% on a ten-year average, with fewer employees than a small French town. They don't make cards and they aren't banks: they run the toll road that carries every card payment between banks, and take a tiny fee on each one. Billions have been spent trying to replace them; nobody has, because the road isn't a technology — it's a 60-year network of trust.
A note on framing (source)

Video case (Swapn, "Pourquoi personne n'a réussi à remplacer Visa & Mastercard," May 2026); figures are the video's own. Filed in Finance, Banking & Fraud. Sibling of the other "own the toll" cases: Liberty Media / F1 (173) and Givaudan (174).

What they actually do — and who earns what

Most people think Visa and Mastercard make cards, or are banks. Neither. Every card payment involves four parties: you (the cardholder), your bank (the issuer), the merchant's bank (the acquirer) and the merchant. Visa or Mastercard are the "trusted messengers" in the middle: they check the transaction is legitimate and the funds exist, and pass the authorisation and settlement between the banks in a few hundred milliseconds. The money: each card payment costs the merchant ~1–3%; most of it — the interchange — goes to the issuing bank. Visa/Mastercard take only a fraction: ~€0.30 on a €100 purchase. But Visa processes ~257 billion transactions a year: €0.30 × 257bn ≈ $40bn of revenue, ~$20bn of net profit. Why the margin is so high: an asset-light network built over ~60 years, long since amortised — each extra transaction costs almost nothing (near-zero marginal cost). Going from 257 to 300 billion transactions is almost pure profit, with no proportional investment. On top, value-added services — tokenisation, AI fraud prevention, data analytics, cybersecurity — now ~40% of Mastercard's revenue, bought even by their would-be competitors. Visa's table in the video: operating margin ~80% every year 2021–2025.

How the network was born

1958: Bank of America launches BankAmericard. No internet: the merchant phoned your bank to check funds; transactions were printed on paper slips with a roller machine, couriered to the bank each evening, added up by hand and transferred to the merchant's account. Other banks wanted in, and BankAmericard became Visa; in parallel, rival banks formed an association that became Master Charge, then Mastercard in 1979 — same logic, more independent governance. The duopoly was born, not as a technology but as a network of trust between thousands of banks, convinced brick by brick over decades. Technology changed completely — paper, terminals, real time, contactless — but the network stayed; they only updated processes, never had to rebuild relationships.

The three locks

1) The network effect. The more Visa cardholders, the more merchants accept Visa; the more merchants, the more consumers want Visa — a loop running since 1958. Result: billions of cards and ~150 million merchants in 200+ countries. A rival must create an equally large circle of merchants and consumers simultaneously, with no initial value for either side — "the most formidable barrier to entry in economics." 2) Bank switching cost. Even if a challenger won consumers, banks must migrate: months or years of IT overhaul and massive operational risk. Banks keep what works — not passivity, a rational calculation: the cost of change can exceed the gain, even with better redistribution. 3) Data. VisaNet handles hundreds of millions of transactions a day; 60 years of buying behaviour across hundreds of countries and every type of merchant isn't an asset you can buy — impossible to rebuild without those years. This "economic fortress" — a moat — comes from the trust network, not from the best technology.

Russia, sovereignty and the challengers

24 Feb 2022 Russia invades Ukraine; five days later Visa and Mastercard suspend operations there: ~143 million users cut off from international payments within 48 hours — the first time the world grasped what depending on payment infrastructure controlled by private US companies means. In Europe, ~61% of transactions go through US networks and 18 EU countries have no credible domestic alternative; France has CB (Carte Bleue), but most cards are co-badged and often route through Visa. Meanwhile, 2018–2022, their average fees rose ~34% — pricing power despite political pressure. Not real competitors: PayPal mostly debits your card (so Visa/Mastercard behind it); Apple Pay and Google Pay are a software layer on your Visa/Mastercard; Stripe connects e-merchants to banks — the payment still rides the card networks. Crypto: Visa settled ~$225m on blockchain in 2025 and its blockchain-related volume rose 525% — they absorb it rather than die. Real alternatives are national and domestic: UPI in India (16bn+ transactions a month, instant account-to-account transfers, government-run), Pix in Brazil (central bank, 2020, free, instant, 200m+ users), Europe's Wero (EPI, led by major banks) and the ECB's digital euro. They work — but stay domestic; as soon as a payment crosses a border, Visa and Mastercard take over again. Cashless growth is their biggest tailwind: each contactless, online or subscription payment is one more transaction; Visa's cross-border payments grow 18–21% a year at high margin. Markets aren't worried: Visa ~$550bn, Mastercard ~$440bn — ~$1tn for fewer than 60,000 employees; each Visa employee generates over $1m of revenue a year.

How to drillBe the road everyone must use: Visa and Mastercard take ~€0.30 per €100 on hundreds of billions of transactions over a 60-year, amortised trust network — ~50% net margins, ~$1tn of value, fewer than 60,000 staff. Three locks protect them (two-sided network effect, bank switching cost, decades of data); wallets and crypto run on their rails; only state-backed domestic systems (UPI, Pix, Wero) truly compete, and not across borders. Their real risk is sovereignty, not competition. For you: find the toll roads in energy and price your work as a small fee on a large flow.

Tetra Pak — The Little Logo on Your Milk Carton and the Machine-Plus-Consumable LockSwapn · Video case · Sell the line, sell the cartons forever: Nespresso logic at industrial scale, an antitrust fight, and how SIG broke in
▶ Video0/14▶
The one ideaLook at a milk or orange-juice carton in your fridge: next to the brand, a strange mention — "Tetra Pak, protects what's good." Behind that small logo is a Swedish company that sold 174 billion packages in 2025 and makes more than €12.35bn of revenue — yet produces neither your milk nor your juice. It does better: it creates dependence, exactly like Nespresso with its capsules or HP with its ink cartridges. Tetra Pak locks industrial clients in with its machines to sell them its consumable — so effectively that several competition authorities opened cases against it. Fifty years later it still dominates.
A note on framing (source)

Video case (Swapn, "Ce mini logo sur vos briques de lait cache un empire tentaculaire," Oct 2026); figures are the video's own, sponsor segment omitted. Filed in Consumer, Retail & Luxury, next to the other invisible suppliers behind famous brands: Givaudan (174) and Visa & Mastercard (175).

From a folded cylinder to a sterile carton (1929–1961)

1929: Ruben Rausing co-founds a packaging company; so convinced he's found a great idea, he buys out his partner four years later. He wants to replace glass bottles with something lighter and cheaper to produce — and for over ten years the solution escapes him. 1943: a young lab assistant, Erik Wallenberg, folds a cardboard cylinder into a tetrahedron — the future "berlingot": little material, easy to assemble. But an invention on paper isn't a market: it must be made and filled by the thousands every day without interruption. Rausing's wife imagines the answer: form and fill the package continuously from a roll of carton under an uninterrupted flow of liquid, avoiding contact with air before sealing. 1951: engineer Harry Järund builds the first machine; the following year it is delivered to a Swedish dairy to package cream. 1961: the aseptic technology — milk sterilised at very high temperature, then packed without air contact, so without bacteria: it keeps for months at room temperature with no cold chain. Glass bottles become old-fashioned: lighter containers, cheaper trucking, no empties to collect, return and wash. The last problem — tetrahedrons stacked badly on pallets — led to the rectangular brick.

The business model — the line and the consumable

Tetra Pak doesn't just sell cartons. At a dairy it installs the machines that form and fill the bricks, and supplies the material: big flat rolls of carton the machine unwinds, forms, fills and seals continuously. Each new carton uses a roll bought from Tetra Pak — the consumable. The carton is multilayer: cardboard for rigidity, plastic for sealing, and an aluminium layer protecting the milk from light and oxygen. Machine and material must work together: a bad weld can compromise sealing and preservation, so for a dairy the price of the packaging is only part of the calculation — it buys the reliability of a system only Tetra Pak can provide. The relationship goes further: at the start of 2026 more than 8,600 Tetra Pak fillers run in factories worldwide, with 330,000+ spare-part references; Tetra Pak trains the operators and offers multi-year service contracts — up to guaranteeing a production result, billed on the volume actually produced rather than per part. And the system now spans beyond the packaging line. The idea: sell a machine and everything that makes it run. The switching cost: replacing a coffee machine is easy; replacing a packaging line means redesigning the production line, hundreds of thousands of euros at stake or more, and stopping production during the change. A dairy could still try to put just the rolls out to tender — except some contracts signed with Tetra Pak forbid it, and companies can't even decide when to end the collaboration.

The antitrust fight

In the early 2000s, authorities established that Tetra Pak controlled 70–80% of the market for aseptic machines and cartons in the European Economic Area, and nearly 90% in the 1980s–90s. Being dominant isn't illegal in itself; competition law sanctions how a firm uses that position, and dependence on one supplier only becomes a legal problem if it's organised abusively. Before the judges Tetra Pak defended its clauses on technical and food-safety grounds — no wish to control the market, only to guarantee quality. The judges rejected it: demanding a precise quality is one thing; contractually forbidding any alternative supplier is another. The case also revealed other practices on packaging for fresh products: Tetra Pak sometimes sold machines and cartons at a loss to oust rivals like Elopak from tenders, funding those losses with very comfortable margins in aseptic, where it led — and kept price gaps between European countries to stop a client buying cheaper in another country. It locked by contract what could have stayed open to competition. (Historical note: the European Commission's 1991 decision fined Tetra Pak ECU 75m, then a record, upheld by the European courts in 1996.) But a fine doesn't free a dairy: the day after the ruling, it still needs Tetra Pak machines to fill its cartons.

How challengers got in — and the logo

A rival can't convince a dairy to scrap a running line overnight. The first strategy is timing: arrive when the manufacturer launches, or when it invests to renew a line. SIG and Elopak sell their own machines and packaging — and to beat Tetra Pak they had to bring new solutions: SIG solved a problem Tetra Pak didn't handle well at first, packaging juice with pulp and fruit pieces without compromising the seal, by injecting a sterile inert gas at the top of the brick before sealing (Tetra Pak later adopted the method). SIG Combibloc is no marginal player; the gap remains large, but competition has gained ground. The logo: the name visible on the carton is the drinks brand's — but the second name belongs to the company that designed the system. "It's as if a bottling company forced Coca-Cola to put its own name next to theirs." Placing its logo everywhere gets Tetra Pak into the minds of consumers and industrials alike — a mark of renown and quality — which it can afford because it offers a unique solution: a light, sterile package transportable at scale.

In nuclear and power plants, the vendor of a critical system often controls spare parts, qualified services and upgrades for the asset's whole life — the Tetra Pak model at 60-year scale. Knowing how the lock is built (installed base, integration, service contracts billed on availability, restrictive clauses) is exactly what lets an owner negotiate it — and what a lender looks at when assessing O&M (operations and maintenance) risk. It's also a model you could flip: a recurring service attached to the asset you advise on.

Make it click — similar plays

How to drillInstall the line, sell the rolls forever: from Wallenberg's 1943 tetrahedron and continuous aseptic filling (1961), Tetra Pak built a system — 8,600+ fillers, 330,000 parts, outcome-based service — where machine and carton only work together, making switching a production-stopping, six-figure decision. It reached 70–90% of European aseptic packaging, crossed the antitrust line with exclusive clauses and predatory pricing, and still dominates, while SIG got in at renewal moments with better tech. For you: map the OEM lock-ins on your assets, negotiate them at renewal, and design recurring services of your own.

The Real Business of Ski Resorts — Where Your €70 Lift Pass GoesSwapn · Video case · Plan Neige 1964, La Plagne's €5bn concession, the DSP model, the state as 43% shareholder, and Tignes taking the keys back
▶ Video0/14▶
The one ideaAt the end of 2025 the Compagnie des Alpes signed a contract worth €5bn of cumulative revenue to run one ski resort for 25 years: La Plagne, the most visited ski resort in the world — ~2.7m skier-days and ~€100m of revenue a year, from an empty mountain pasture in the 1950s. The engine behind it is not the snow but a contract: the DSP (délégation de service public, public-service concession). The commune owns the domain; a specialist operator invests, runs it, takes the commercial risk and is paid by lift passes — and when the contract ends, everything returns to the commune. That's project finance on a mountain.
A note on framing (source)

Video case (Swapn, "Le vrai business des stations de ski (et où part ton forfait)," Mar 2026), from the Compagnie des Alpes' financial reports, Pappers accounts and the Cour des comptes; figures are the video's own, sponsor segment omitted. Filed in Energy, Infrastructure & Resources because the DSP is a concession model — the same family as Vinci (142). Leisure peer of the cruise business (171).

From misery to Plan Neige (1950s–1970s)

In the 1950s the French Alps were no ski paradise but a poor territory: villages emptying, young people leaving for cities, an economy of livestock, farming and — for La Plagne — lead, zinc and silver mines in the valley. Pierre Josserand, founder of Val Thorens: "the villages were in ruins and Savoie was a land of misery." In 1964 de Gaulle and Pompidou launched the Plan Neige: the state would create ski resorts from nothing on virgin high-altitude pastures, to capture emerging demand and stop the French spending their money in Switzerland and Austria (the same logic as the Mediterranean resorts built against Spain's Costa Brava). In about 15 years, ~150,000 beds were built in 40 resorts, 20 created from scratch — La Plagne, Les Arcs, Les Menuires, Val Thorens, Avoriaz. Farmers who owned the pastures were expropriated so communes could take the land, and the integrated resort was born: leave your flat in ski boots and you're on the slopes — roads, car parks, buildings, lifts all designed for skiing. Today France sells ~51–54m skier-days a year, among the top three countries alongside the US and Austria (51.8m). La Plagne: opened December 1961, boomed from 1964, the M2000 "paquebot" building in 1969, the bobsleigh event of the 1992 Albertville Olympics, the Vanoise Express linking it to Les Arcs in 2003 to form Paradiski — today 11 villages, 225 km of slopes, 76 lifts.

The numbers — 37% operating margin

La Plagne is run by the SAP (Société d'Aménagement de La Plagne), 98% owned by the Compagnie des Alpes — a listed group running La Plagne, Les Arcs, Val d'Isère, Méribel, Serre Chevalier… and leisure parks (Parc Astérix, Futuroscope, Walibi): ~€1.4bn of revenue in total. Ski division 2024–25: €594m revenue, +7.5% (€489m in 2022–23 — +€100m in three years), ~€59m average per resort, but very unequal; La Plagne alone ~€104m (Pappers). EBITDA (operating cash profit, before depreciation and tax) of the ski division: €219m, a 36.9% margin — €37 of every €100 — up from 31% three years earlier. Two drivers: energy (lifts and grooming machines all night are among the heaviest costs) and price — lift-pass prices rose sharply on top of volume. "Closer to a tech company or a service business than to typical capital-heavy tourism."

Where your €70 goes — three beneficiaries

1) The operator (SAP / Compagnie des Alpes) collects all lift-pass revenue and pays staff, lifts, patrollers, seasonal workers, energy, maintenance, groomers and investment (€106m invested in 2024–25 in new lifts at Les Arcs, La Plagne, Tignes, Méribel). What's left is profit, paid as dividends: €1.10 per share in 2024–25, +10%. And the surprise: no US fund or billionaire — the largest shareholder is the Caisse des Dépôts, the French state's financial arm, with 43%; then Crédit Agricole des Savoie ~7%, the Auvergne-Rhône-Alpes region and Savoie department ~6%, local banks (Banque Populaire, Caisse d'Épargne Auvergne-Rhône-Alpes). The dividends come back to the Alpine territory and the state. 2) The communes: ski lifts are a public service, like waste collection or public transport; under the Loi Montagne (1985) 3% of lift gross receipts go to the commune and 2% to the department — ~€5m a year at La Plagne — and the communes remain owners of the installations. 3) The valley — the biggest: Domaines Skiables de France measures that every €1 spent on a lift pass brings ~€6 more spent in the resort (accommodation, restaurants, ski hire, ESF ski lessons). Nationally, winter mountain tourism is ~€10bn of economic impact a year, ~15% of national tourism revenue on a much shorter season, 120,000 direct and up to 360,000 indirect jobs; above a certain altitude, 55%+ of the local economy depends on skiing.

The DSP — and the €5bn contract

The commune owns the ski domain but lacks the skills and resources to run it; it won't tender lift construction and hire staff itself. Instead the commune (or several together) launches a call for tenders and grants a concession of 20–30 years to a specialist like the Compagnie des Alpes, which invests, maintains and runs the resort and is paid by lift passes. The operator takes the commercial risk: no snow, it suffers; Covid closures, it suffers. The French specificity: at the end of the contract everything — installations, investments, improvements — returns to the commune. La Plagne, Nov 2025: renewed for 25 years (2027–2052) for €5bn of cumulative revenue, lifting the Compagnie des Alpes' backlog (future revenue guaranteed by contract) from €5.8bn to €10.7bn — "visibility tech companies would dream of." The risk — Tignes: renewal isn't guaranteed. The commune declined to renew and takes over operations through a local public company; at the end of May 2026 the Compagnie des Alpes loses Tignes, compensated ~€103m for non-amortised installations, while already-amortised lifts become the commune's property — a big loss after 25 years of tens of millions of revenue. "They're not owners; they only have the right to operate temporarily."

The Cour des comptes warning and diversification

In February 2024 the Cour des comptes audited 42 resorts across all French massifs: the model is running out of breath for small and mid-size resorts — in some, 23% of lift revenue comes from public subsidies, not viable long term — and by 2050 all resorts will be "more or less affected" by global warming. A two-speed ski industry: high-altitude giants like La Plagne (79% of the domain above 2,000 m) with decades ahead, and mid-mountain resorts suffering more and more from lack of snow. The Compagnie des Alpes diversifies: leisure parks now weigh €678m, more than skiing; it bought a park in Germany to make a new Parc Astérix; four-season resorts (MTB, hiking, trail) — summer revenue doubled in four years. Bottom line for La Plagne: ~€100m of revenue, 37% margin, ~€37m of EBITDA, a €5bn 25-year contract — and €1 of lift pass puts ~€7 into the local economy.

Beyond the video — why this case is yours

This is concession finance in your own backyard. A ski DSP has every element of a project-finance deal: a grantor, a long tenor, capex by the operator, revenue risk, fees to the authority, and handback at the end — Tignes is a live example of termination and compensation terms. Living near the Alps, you can study these contracts first-hand, and the climate split between high and mid-altitude resorts is exactly the physical-risk analysis lenders now require on energy assets. A natural niche: advising communes and operators on concession renewals, energy costs of lifts and snowmaking, and four-season transition investments.

Make it click — similar plays

Concessions & toll assets: Vinci (142), Kinder (116), Visa & Mastercard (175). Leisure & fixed assets: the cruise business (171), F1 / Liberty Media (173) — owning rights while others carry event risk. State as shareholder: the wealth ladder (167) — patient capital; Rolex (154).

Same parent: the Compagnie des Alpes' theme-park side — Parc Astérix (181).

How to drillRead a resort as a concession: born from the 1964 Plan Neige, La Plagne went from empty pastures to ~€100m of revenue at ~37% margin, run by the Compagnie des Alpes (43% owned by the state's Caisse des Dépôts) under a DSP — the commune owns, the operator invests and takes the snow risk, pays 3% + 2% of receipts, and hands everything back at the end. The €5bn 25-year renewal doubled the backlog; Tignes shows the renewal cliff; the Cour des comptes and climate split the sector in two. For you: this is project finance on a mountain — study the contract terms, especially the end of term.

The Real Business of Casinos — The House Always Wins, but the State Wins MoreSwapn · Video case · Gross gaming revenue, 55%+ to the state, slot machines as the real engine, and Partouche's renovation playbook (Annemasse +20%)
▶ Video0/14▶
The one ideaYou put €100 on a blackjack table. Who wins it — you, the casino, the dealer? The hidden winner is the state. French casinos are a ~€3bn-a-year activity with 31 million visits in 2024, but of the €2.7bn of gross gaming revenue they keep after paying winners, about €1.5bn — more than 55% — goes to the state and local authorities before a single salary, electricity bill or rent is paid. The casino lives on a thin slice, and the real engine isn't the green table: it's the slot machine.
A note on framing (source)

Video case (Swapn, "Le vrai business des casinos (ce que personne ne voit)," Feb 2026), from Groupe Partouche's annual reports and Cour des comptes reports; figures are the video's own, sponsor segment omitted. One figure is corrected: the video says €926,000 staked per day across Partouche's slots, but its own maths (€3.62bn ÷ 365) gives ~€9.9m a day, consistent with its €2,048 per machine per day. Filed in Media, Entertainment & Gaming. Sibling of the other tax-and-concession cases: ski resorts (177), cruises (171).

The house edge and gross gaming revenue

Every game is designed so the casino wins statistically over the long run — the house edge. At French roulette, on €100 staked the casino keeps on average ~€2.70. What the casino really earns is the produit brut des jeux (PBJ, gross gaming revenue): stakes minus winnings paid back — e.g. coins inserted into a slot minus payouts. It isn't revenue in the usual sense. In 2024 France's ~200 casinos generated €2.7bn of PBJ. Casinos also run restaurants, bars, hotels, shows, sometimes spas — but at Partouche, the largest French group with 44 casinos, gaming is still 77% of revenue.

Where the money goes — €100 at a table

The player gets back ~€95 on average; the casino's PBJ is €5. Of that, ~€2.80 goes in compulsory levies, leaving €2.20 — before the dealer, staff, electricity (lights everywhere), machine maintenance, rent, property charges and security. The margin on €100 staked is a few cents. Of the ~€1.5bn of levies: the state takes ~77% (general budget — roads, hospitals, schools); communes 15–20%; social security 5–8% (~€100m via the CSG, the general social contribution). Only certain towns may host a casino — seaside resorts, spa towns, some mountain towns — and for them it's a golden goose: a mid-size town whose casino makes €30m of PBJ collects €3–4m a year, sometimes 20–30% of the municipal budget. Per the Cour des comptes, French casino taxation is ~20 points higher than neighbouring countries — and France has ~30% of Europe's casinos. July 2025: the government raised CSG levies again, created a new tax on slot machines and a 15% tax on casino advertising (to fight gambling addiction) — ~€90m a year more for the state; the casinos protested, the law passed.

Partouche's accounts — and the two levers

Partouche (listed): 44 casinos, 41 in France; PBJ €748.3m in 2024 (+5.1%); after levies, net gaming revenue €352.4m (+4%) — i.e. ~€395.9m paid in gaming levies, more than half the gross staying out of the company. Group operating margin (EBITDA) ~18% of revenue — relatively flat. Lever 1 — renovate: a renovated casino attracts more players; in 2025 the recently renovated Annemasse casino grew PBJ by more than 20%, and Divonne-les-Bains by more than 17%. Lever 2 — slot machines, "the secret few people know": 72% of Partouche's PBJ (€522.6m in 2024), while traditional table games are only ~5%. By law slots must return at least 85% to players, so PBJ can't exceed 15% of stakes. 2025 slot PBJ €543.5m ÷ 0.15 = €3.62bn staked in a year — ~€9.9m a day across 4,847 machines, about €2,048 staked per machine per day.

Threats and signals

1) Tax: every finance law brings new taxes, and casinos are an easy political target — "who will defend gambling merchants?" 2) Online: regulated casinos can't offer everything online, while illegal offshore sites capture customers outside the legal, taxed circuit. 3) Habits: young generations play on mobile rather than in physical halls — does the old model with dress codes and chips have a future? Positive signals: attendance in France rose 4.9% in 2025; renovations prove a modern casino can thrive; online is a growth avenue; Partouche's net income jumped ~80% in the first half of 2025. "Even in a hostile environment where taxes capture more than half your activity, a good strategy can prosper." So who really wins at the casino? The state.

Capture the lessons

Beyond the video — why this case is yours

It's on your doorstep, and it's a lesson in revenue-based levies. The Annemasse casino — renovated, +20% in 2025 — is a live example of capex driving revenue in a regulated, licensed asset. And the casino waterfall is the same question you'll ask in energy finance: does the state tax gross revenue (like casino levies, or windfall-revenue caps imposed on generators in 2022) or profit? Revenue-based levies hit before costs and debt service, and can wipe out coverage ratios — exactly what a lender must model.

Make it click — similar plays

Who really gets paid: ski resorts (177) — communes and the state as beneficiaries; cruises (171) — the opposite, almost no tax. Regulated, licensed assets: Visa & Mastercard (175), Vinci (142). Captive spend: Basic-Fit (155) — ghost members, the gym's "house edge".

How to drillFollow the €100: the player gets ~€95, the casino's gross gaming revenue is ~€5, levies take ~€2.80 before any cost — over €1.5bn a year, 55%+ of French casinos' €2.7bn PBJ, mostly to the state, 15–20% to host towns. Partouche lives on slots (72% of PBJ, €2,048 staked per machine per day) and renovations (Annemasse +20%), with taxes rising every year and offshore online competition. The house always wins; the state wins more. For you: always find where the state takes its cut in the revenue waterfall.
