Tencent — The Chinese Giant That Quietly Bought Global GamingSwapn · Video case · Copy-and-adapt, the shark-tank culture, WeChat as everything-app, buy-without-controlling studios — and a founder who isn't free
▶ Video0/14▶
The one ideaIn 2015 a Chinese giant bought 100% of Riot Games, publisher of League of Legends (67m monthly players, $1.6bn a year). The same company owns ~40% of Epic Games (Fortnite), 84% of Supercell (Clash of Clans, Clash Royale, Brawl Stars) and stakes in 740+ tech companies worldwide. Yet abroad Tencent is mostly known for WeChat, the super-app through which 1.3bn Chinese message, pay, bank, shop and book doctors. Two empires: one in China that made it rich but subject to the Party, one in the West that protects it — "an empire that rules billions of lives but doesn't control its own."
A note on framing (source)

Video case (Swapn, "Le géant chinois qui rachète le gaming mondial (mais personne n'en parle)," Jan 2026); figures are the video's own, sponsor segment omitted. Filed in Technology, Semiconductors & AI. Echoes the sovereignty theme of Visa & Mastercard (175) and the China cluster (Huawei, Anta, Luxshare).

Copy, adapt, survive (1998–2004)

1998: Pony Ma (Ma Huateng), a 27-year-old developer, sees the internet arrive in China and, with four friends, founds Tencent. He discovers ICQ, the first instant messenger — English interface, US servers, slow and unstable in China. He copies the concept, adapts it to Chinese language, networks and culture: OICQ, later QQ. "Pure plagiarism," but a fundamental rule: being first in a market is useless if you're not the best for the local user. Early on the founder chats with the rare users himself — even posing as a woman to keep people connected. It catches on, but servers cost a fortune: every new user means more hardware and brings no revenue. Then AOL, owner of ICQ, sues for IP violation. 1999: near bankruptcy, nobody wants to buy. Pitching investors, instead of "invest now and get rich," he says: "if you don't fund us now, OICQ will probably disappear — and even if you do, we may not survive." Investors are won over by his transparency; IDG Capital puts in $2.2m for 40% — just before the 2000 dot-com crash. Monetisation: he copies an idea again and launches QQ Show, customisable avatars users can dress and accessorise — no manufacturing, stock or logistics, "pixels sold by the chain," a few cents each times millions of young users. Tencent becomes profitable. (He meets his wife on the app: "I'm the papa penguin.")

Beating Microsoft and the shark tank (2004–2013)

2004: Microsoft arrives in China with MSN Messenger to crush the "little Chinese clone" — billions, global brand, teams everywhere. Its fatal error: arrogance and distance — every decision went up to US headquarters, taking weeks or months; Tencent shipped features in days. MSN loses. Pony's trait: constructive paranoia — in tech, if you don't evolve fast, you die. 2009: he knows smartphones will change everything and QQ was built for PCs; WhatsApp, Kik and Line are emerging; he remembers AOL and Yahoo, desktop giants who missed mobile. Radical decision: three teams with the same objective — build a mobile messenger — competing with each other and with QQ itself. Tencent calls it the "shark-tank culture": baby sharks devouring each other in the womb; only the strongest survives. January 2011: WeChat is born — and crushes rivals like Talkbox with colossal resources. End of 2012: 100m users in 433 days (Facebook needed almost five years); 2013: 300m; today ~1.32bn, used by ~95% of Chinese.

The everything-app (2014–2017)

The real revolution came by accident: for Lunar New Year, the tradition is red envelopes filled with money. Tencent let users send them in WeChat for the 2014 festival — 75m+ red envelopes exchanged in a few days. Tencent understood the future was mobile payment: WeChat Pay was born. It also invested hundreds of millions in gaming studios and sport — including a $1.5bn, 5-year deal to stream NBA games in China. January 2017: mini-programs — instead of downloading apps from a store, access tens of thousands of apps inside WeChat: order a taxi, book a hotel, shop, pay your doctor. Revenue reaches tens of billions of dollars; it becomes almost impossible to live in urban China without the app — a de facto monopoly on daily life, and the holy grail for the Chinese Communist Party.

The trap closes (2017–2021)

2017: a new cybersecurity law forces all Chinese tech companies to share data with the government; overnight WeChat becomes officially a tool of mass surveillance — every message, payment and movement potentially accessible to the Party. Dissidents see accounts blocked without notice: unable to pay or communicate — instant digital death. Tencent cannot refuse: obey or be dismantled. Pony Ma chooses absolute silence — no more public statements or interviews, applying every directive without a word. 2020 onward the screws tighten: a wave of regulation against tech giants (antitrust, data, gaming time limits for minors).

The Western empire — buy without controlling

Abroad, studios hit the same wall: how to distribute League of Legends or Clash of Clans in China? Impossible without a local partner — the Great Firewall blocks Facebook, Google, YouTube; for games, same rule. Pony's answer: become the indispensable gateway, by buying stakes. 2012: ~40% of Epic Games (Unreal Engine, then Fortnite, a planetary free-to-play phenomenon). 2015: 100% of Riot Games — LoL then $1.6bn of revenue, 67m monthly players, free with microtransactions for skins, "Tencent's DNA." And remarkably, Tencent touches nothing: no Chinese directives, no interference; Riot stays 100% autonomous — Tencent brings capital and opens China, but doesn't run it. "Counter-intuitive: buy without controlling." 2016: the biggest: 84% of Supercell for $8.6bn — same strategy, full team autonomy; the studios keep thriving. Why? These studios generate billions of dollars outside China — cash the Chinese government can't block by decree: Pony's lifeline. And a second, subtler advantage: they employ thousands in the US, Europe and Finland and serve hundreds of millions of Western players. Destroying Tencent would no longer be a Chinese problem — it would hit LoL, Fortnite and Clash players, funding and jobs worldwide: "too tentacular to be destroyed, too big to fall" — geopolitics through gaming. It also worries the West: some see a Trojan horse; Trump threatened to ban WeChat in the US in 2020; India banned it.

Beyond the video — why this case is yours

Sovereign and political risk is core to project finance in emerging markets. Between France and Tunisia, you'll assess projects where the host state can change rules overnight; Tencent's answer — revenue and stakeholders spread across jurisdictions, cash the state can't block — is the corporate version of offshore accounts, political-risk insurance and multilateral co-lenders. And "copy, adapt to local conditions" is a legitimate entry route: proven energy-finance practices adapted to North African markets, where you speak the languages and know the culture.

Make it click — similar plays

Sovereignty & sanctions: Visa & Mastercard (175), Danone & Carlsberg (140). Owner who doesn't control: Liberty Media (173), the holding (163). Speed & self-cannibalisation: Zara (149), Nokia (129). Captive digital spend: cruises (171).

How to drillCopy, adapt, outrun, then spread out: Pony Ma cloned ICQ as QQ, survived on $2.2m from IDG and QQ Show avatars, beat Microsoft on speed, used a shark-tank of internal teams to build WeChat (100m users in 433 days, now 1.32bn), turned red envelopes into WeChat Pay and mini-programs — then, as Beijing turned WeChat into a surveillance tool, built a Western shield by buying Riot, Supercell and 40% of Epic without controlling them. Rich and powerful, but not free. For you: adapt proven models locally, and price political risk before anything else.

Ferrero — From a Shortage of Cocoa to a Fortress Built on HazelnutsSwapn · Video case · Emotional engineering, one brand per segment, vertical integration, a family that answers to no one — and the price of opacity
▶ Video0/14▶
The one ideaFerrero, Kinder, Nutella — everyday classics, all from one family group that owns dozens more. A line of Italian artisan chocolatiers from the 19th century turned into a dynasty of chocolate and hazelnut. Michele Ferrero spent 50 years creating iconic products, building an industrial empire and preparing his succession; his designated heir died tragically, and the younger son who was never meant to rule turned the group into a cold, opaque global financial machine. Shaken by environmental, health and tax scandals, the fortress still looks impregnable — because it is built on four locks: emotions, the supply chain, money and silence.
A note on framing (source)

Video case (Swapn — Nils — "Vous ne verrez plus jamais FERRERO de la même façon," Dec 2025); figures and characterisations are the video's own (several from press investigations), sponsor segment omitted. Filed in Consumer, Retail & Luxury. The family-empire sibling of MSC (171), Rolex (154) and Givaudan (174).

Turning shortage into genius (1946–1964)

1946: Italy comes out of the war in ruins; the population is hungry and cocoa — a luxury import from Africa — is rare and unaffordable. In Alba, a small town in Piedmont, pastry maker Pietro Ferrero has a problem: customers want chocolate, but cocoa costs a fortune. His idea: instead of importing scarce cocoa, use what's at hand — Piedmont produces Europe's best hazelnuts, abundant and cheap. He mixes hazelnuts, a little cocoa and sugar into a paste that is cheap, filling and tasty (the Giandujot, then the spreadable Supercrema). His son Michele sees beyond a local Piedmont product: something all of Europe could eat. To be number one, good chocolate isn't enough. 1964: he perfects Supercrema, improves the recipe, puts it in a recognisable glass jar and renames it Nutella — an immediate success in Italy; Germany in 1965, France in 1966; by 1970 Europe's #1 spread.

Lock 1 — emotional engineering and one brand per moment

What makes Michele different isn't the product but his grasp of marketing: he doesn't want to sell chocolate but emotions. Nutella isn't a spread — it's childhood, the after-school snack, Sunday-morning comfort, the slice your mother made. Ferrero ads never talk about ingredients; they talk about family, happiness, shared moments. "People don't buy chocolate, they buy a moment of happiness." Each brand targets one emotion and one moment of life. Kinder for children: Kinder Surprise (1974) with a toy inside, traded in school playgrounds and collected for years — 30 billion sold since 1974. It was banned in the US (hidden toys in food are considered a choking hazard); Ferrero simply separated chocolate and toy in a double package. Families with Nutella; then in 1982 Ferrero Rocher for the last segment — a whole hazelnut in a crisp wafer, coated with chocolate and chopped hazelnuts, wrapped in gold foil; ads show elegant receptions ("the Ambassador's"); priced high but not too high — not €50 a box, not €5, "just enough luxury for the middle classes." Son Giovanni: "Tradition is like a bow — the tighter you draw the string, the further you can shoot the arrows of modernity and innovation."

Lock 2 — control the whole chain

While Mars, Nestlé and Lindt depend on outside suppliers for raw materials, Michele bets the opposite: control everything. First target, hazelnuts: Turkey produces ~70% of the world's hazelnuts. In the 1980s Michele buys whole plantations, signs long-term contracts with Turkish cooperatives and builds processing plants on site — hazelnuts become paste in Turkey, then ship to Ferrero's European factories. In 2015 a dedicated division, Ferrero Hazelnut Company: processing plants, 10 experimental farms, 3,000 employees just for hazelnuts, working with ~55,000 producers. It controls the purchase of about a quarter of world hazelnut production: when a harvest is bad, Ferrero is protected while competitors suffer shortages and price rises; Ferrero sets prices and guarantees quality — dependent on no one. He doesn't stop there: own packaging plants (the Rocher's gold foil, the clear plastic boxes, the cartons), long-term contracts on cocoa.

Locks 3 and 4 — money, power and silence

Money: Ferrero is 100% owned by the family, never listed, accountable only to the family. Opacity is a weapon: profits routed through Luxembourg, strategic decisions without pressure, scandals survived without a collapsing share price. Power: Michele "doesn't do politics, he does lobbying" on every front that threatens the model. Palm oil (~20% of Nutella — cheaper than cocoa butter, gives the creamy texture, but an environmental disaster: deforestation, CO₂): fierce defence of "sustainable palm oil," funding favourable studies, intensive lobbying in Brussels — no ban, no really binding regulation. Sugar: lobbying to keep the EU quotas that guaranteed low, stable prices (kept until 2017). Locally in Alba Michele becomes a living legend — funding schools, hospitals, infrastructure; the local press never criticises Ferrero. Image: also among the companies most engaged on sustainable palm oil — real efforts that coexist with a tax strategy depriving states of billions and lobbying that avoids binding rules: "pioneer of environmental sustainability, champion of tax avoidance." Michele spent 30 years building it: industrial, fiscal, political, green.

Succession — the heir dies, the younger son executes the plan

Michele is 84; Pietro, the heir trained by his father, admires his creativity and marketing but reproaches him for not eliminating competitors, and proposes an aggressive acquisition plan — Michele refuses: he wants organic growth, new products, innovation. On 18 April 2011 Pietro dies in a cycling accident (per the video: on a business trip in South Africa) at 47. Giovanni inherits at 51 — a fortress and two ghosts — and in 2015 takes command and executes his brother's plan: 2015 Thorntons (historic British chocolatier); 2017 Nestlé's US confectionery (Butterfinger, Baby Ruth, Crunch); 2018 Fannie May (Chicago); 2019 part of Kellogg's biscuits; 2022 Wells Enterprises (ice cream). More than $4bn of acquisitions in seven years; Ferrero now controls ~35 brands in 170 countries with ~47,000 employees. Michele spent 50 years building brands; Giovanni transformed the empire in 7 through aggressive external growth.

The fortress tested

Test 1 — palm oil: NGO and media pressure; sales continue as before; Ferrero's presence in Brussels may have helped. Test 2 — February 2019: a French journalistic investigation exposes the Luxembourg system: between 2006 and 2024 the Ferrero family reportedly received €7.3bn of dividends and paid only €66m of tax — ~0.8%. Media scandal; France and Italy investigate; in 2021 a French tax reassessment claims €185m. Ferrero's reaction: pays cash, no public comment, no explanation, total silence — "if that's the price of peace, keep going and pay." The Luxembourg system keeps working; no shareholder to answer to. The pattern: almost unlimited money absorbs fines, lobbying prevents binding rules, communication stays minimal and opacity maximal. "Giovanni didn't betray his father's legacy; he extended it."

▶ Original video ↗

Two generations, two growth models
Michele (to 2015)Giovanni (2015 →)
GrowthOrganic: invent products (Nutella, Kinder, Rocher)External: $4bn+ of acquisitions in 7 years
EdgeEmotional brands + vertical integrationScale: 35 brands, 170 countries, 47,000 staff
Constant100% family ownership, opacity, lobbying, silence in crises

Capture the lessons

Run the drills

Beyond the video — why this case is yours

Supply-chain security is the energy transition's central question. Ferrero's hazelnut strategy — long-term contracts, owned processing, a quarter of world purchases — is exactly what utilities and states now do for uranium, critical minerals, transformers and turbines. In critical-equipment contracting, the lesson is the same: lock the scarce input upstream before a bad "harvest" hits. And the Luxembourg episode is a reminder that structures without substance eventually meet the tax authority.

Make it click — similar plays

Family fortresses: MSC (171), Rolex (154), Intersport (158), Family Businesses (84). Owning the input: Givaudan (174), Tetra Pak (176). Tax structures: owning nothing in your name (169), the holding (163). Shrinking a giant's brands: Danone / Faber (38).

How to drillFour locks built a fortress: emotions (Nutella sells childhood, one brand per moment — Kinder, Nutella, Rocher), the supply chain (~25% of world hazelnut purchases, own plants and packaging), money (100% family, Luxembourg, €7.3bn of dividends taxed at ~0.8%) and silence (lobbying, cash settlements like the €185m French reassessment, no comment). Michele built by invention over 50 years; after the heir's death, Giovanni bought $4bn+ of brands in 7. For you: turn constraints into products, secure your critical input upstream, and remember opacity has a price.

Parc Astérix — Where Your €75 Goes, and Why Record Revenue Means Lower ProfitSwapn · Video case · Pricing power, captive spend, the licence royalty, intragroup debt, depreciation vs cash, and a €250m bet on long-term value
▶ Video0/14▶
The one ideaA family day at Parc Astérix costs ~€300 (~€75 each). Of that, less than €20 stays with the park. Last year it took a record €216m of revenue from a record ~2.9m visitors — yet its net profit halved in three years, to €14.7m (6.8% of revenue; under 7 cents per euro). Is the park in danger? No: it's run to maximise long-term asset value, not net profit. It throws off ~€51m of operating cash a year, sends most of it up to its parent, the Compagnie des Alpes, and reinvests massively — which, through depreciation, crushes the accounting result while building an asset worth more and more.
A note on framing (source)

Video case (Swapn, "Le Parc Astérix : l'envers du décor financier que personne ne montre," Apr 2026), from the filed accounts of Grévin et Compagnie, the company that operates the park; figures are the video's own, sponsor segment omitted. Filed in Media, Entertainment & Gaming. Same parent as the ski resorts (177) — the Compagnie des Alpes, whose reference shareholder is the state's Caisse des Dépôts. Best read with casinos (178) and cruises (171) — three "follow the €100" cases.

Revenue — pricing power and captive spend

~2.9m visitors spend on average €74.60 each (ticket ~€62, plus a Gaulish kebab, an Idéfix plush, a fast pass). In 2019 the average spend was €54: +38% in six years, while cumulative inflation was barely 20% — the park raised prices almost twice as fast as inflation. That's pricing power: the ability to raise prices without losing customers. Where the €216m comes from: tickets €106m (half); food & drink €34m — you eat on site, you have no choice, a captive customer, like an airport sandwich; shops €15m (your child wants the €25 legionnaire helmet); hotels €26.5m, +13% in a year — growing ~2.5× faster than ticketing: stay at Les Quais de Lutèce, the Cité Suspendue or Les Trois Hiboux and you stay two days instead of one, eat dinner in the park, buy the €18 Gaulish breakfast; occupancy exceeds 90% in summer — hence a fourth hotel of 300 rooms in the plan, "each room is a cash machine." Then €20m of "other services" — mostly fast passes: €30, 40, sometimes €50 on top of the ticket not to queue. "The park has literally monetised waiting."

Where the €216m goes — who helps themselves on the way

1) Staff: €67.4m — the first beneficiaries; no them, no park. 2) The Astérix licence: ~€10m a year to Éditions Albert René (named after Albert Uderzo and René Goscinny, Astérix's creators), owned by the Hachette group, for the right to use the name, characters and universe — almost as much as the park's net profit; every Obélix plush and photo with Panoramix sends part of the money up to the rights holder: "the price of intellectual property," the equivalent of 150 extra employees, "except it's a transfer, not people running the park." 3) Debt: €92.5m, not borrowed from banks but from its parent, the Compagnie des Alpes, at 4% — €4.8m of interest a year; the money passes from one pocket of the group to the other. 4) The state: corporate tax €4.9m. Add €30m of purchases and raw materials (burger meat, maintenance parts, electricity) and €25.6m of subcontracting and fees: over €200m of the €216m are gone. 5) Wear over time — depreciation: a roller coaster doesn't last forever; structures are depreciated over 20–40 years, mechanisms over 10–15. In 2025 depreciation reached €24.7m — not money leaving, just an accounting entry recording that a €30m ride is worth a bit less each year. Before depreciation the park makes €51.2m of EBITDA (operating cash profit): "the park is not in difficulty; it invests massively, and in accounting terms that reduces its net result."

A subsidiary inside a bigger machine

Grévin et Compagnie is 100% owned by the Compagnie des Alpes — not 51%, not 80% — a listed group that also runs Futuroscope, Walibi, the Musée Grévin and about ten Alpine ski areas, with the Caisse des Dépôts (the French state) as reference shareholder. The AGM of 5 January 2026 voted €8.85m of dividends to the parent: a 60% payout, three years running. After tax and dividends the park keeps €5.8m — for annual capex of ~€44m. It can't finance itself alone: it sends cash up to the Compagnie des Alpes, which refinances it through intragroup credit lines — a closed circuit.

The €250m plan — and how it's financed

The biggest investment programme in the park's history: €250m over three years — an Egypt zone in 2026 with the attraction Senet Automati, an extension of the Greek zone, the fourth hotel L'Odyssée (300+ rooms, ~€80m), and in 2027–2028 Londinium, an €88m indoor zone with an interactive dark ride. The goal: enter Europe's top 5 parks and reach 270 opening days a year vs 218 today — indoor means open in winter, rain or hail. Financing: ~35% by bank credit; the hotel off the park's balance sheet through a leasing structure; the rest from operating self-financing (the ~€51m of pre-dividend EBITDA) and the Compagnie des Alpes' financial support. The hotel should add €15–20m of annual revenue if it performs like the existing ones, and Londinium lengthens the season and attracts a new public — "not irrational, but clearly enormous." The number that sums up the risk: today the park needs under 2 years of cash to repay its debt; with the plan, almost 4 — "and 4, in finance, is where bankers start to grit their teeth."

Long-term value, not net profit

Of €216m: €67.4m to staff, €30m purchases, €10.1m licence, €25.6m external services and fees, €24.7m depreciation, €4.8m interest, €4.9m tax, €2.1m profit-sharing to employees; of the €14.7m left, €8.85m to the shareholder and €5.8m — 2.7% — in reserve, the safety cushion. "And 2.7% is probably exactly what's planned." Every euro reinvested in a new attraction, hotel or longer season raises the park's value in 10, 20, 30 years — the logic of all the great theme parks, Disney and Europa-Park alike: invest massively, crush short-term net profit, build an ever more valuable asset. The park's real-estate assets — attractions, buildings, hotels — stand at €233m net on the balance sheet; with the €250m plan, close to half a billion. "That's the real wealth."

The key skill it trains: separating cash from accounting, and reading a "falling profit" as either a warning or an investment cycle.

Its ~€51m of EBITDA and intragroup refinancing fund a €250m plan that lifts leverage from <2 to ~4 years. Run for long-term asset value, not annual profit. For you: read EBITDA, capex and leverage before judging any result.

Why Sanofi Let Go of Doliprane — a National Icon That Wasn't a Cash MachineSwapn · Video case · 453m boxes, ~75 cents a box, the safeguard clause, a €16bn LBO by CD&R, and the sovereignty question nobody asked in 2008
▶ Video0/14▶
The one ideaIn France a box of Doliprane sells every 7 seconds — 453 million boxes a year; virtually every French person has taken it. On paper, a cash machine for Sanofi. Yet in October 2024 Sanofi announced the sale to the American fund CD&R (Clayton, Dubilier & Rice) for €16bn — called a national scandal, "a stab in the back" (former health minister François Braun), a betrayal of pharmaceutical sovereignty (unions). The twist: even at that volume, Doliprane is barely profitable — "rather a financial millstone." The sale isn't a scandal; it's an economics lesson.
A note on framing (source)

Video case (Swapn — Grégoire — "Pourquoi Sanofi s'est débarrassé de Doliprane ?," Nov 2025); figures are the video's own, sponsor segment omitted. Precision: technically Sanofi sold a controlling stake (~50%) in Opella, its consumer-health division that owns Doliprane, valued at about €16bn; Bpifrance (the French public investment bank) took a small stake and the state obtained commitments on French sites and jobs. Filed in Healthcare, Pharma & Health-Tech, next to Big Pharma (80).

Where your €2.15 goes

Medicine is regulated: each actor's share is fixed by decree. The pharmacist takes ~80–85 cents (margin, dispensing fee, advice fees); the wholesaler who stocks and delivers ~30 cents; the state ~5 cents of reduced-rate VAT. The laboratory receives ~€1.30, not the 95 cents a simple subtraction suggests, because pharmacist and wholesaler margins are calculated on the manufacturer's price, not the final price. From that €1.30 come sector-specific contributions no other industry pays — leaving Sanofi ~75 cents a box, ~35% of the public price. Is that profitable? Sanofi doesn't publish the cost of a box (molecule, tableting, packaging, transport, regulatory compliance, raw materials) — and since production of the molecule was moved to China, the figures are even more opaque. The video's estimate: a very thin operating margin.

The tax that punishes selling more

A unique French system — "incredible for us French, problematic for manufacturers." About 55–60 cents of taxes per box, including the safeguard clause (clause de sauvegarde): if laboratories' revenue on reimbursable medicines grows too fast, they pay back 70% of the excess to the national health insurance. The more Doliprane they sell, the more tax they pay; in 2024 the clause brought €1.6bn to the state for the whole sector. Put yourself in Sanofi's place: a low-price, mass-volume drug whose price is regulated (you can't raise it), with compulsory taxes you can't reduce, and the more you sell the more you pay — "caught in a vice." France is the European country with the highest taxation on medicines. Meanwhile Sanofi remains a scientific and industrial flagship whose future lies in developing innovative treatments — immunology therapies at several thousand euros — and its share price has been mediocre versus European peers who bet on high-margin innovation; it cut ~14,000 jobs in France in recent years. The Doliprane sale is "not the cause but the symptom" of a long erosion of margins. "It's not Sanofi abandoning Doliprane, it's the tax system pushing it out" — a rational choice: sell it to invest elsewhere, like Apple killing the iPod for the iPhone.

The silence of 2008

In 2008 Europe's last paracetamol plant, Rhodia's Roussillon site, closed: the active ingredient's production went entirely to China. Economically logical: 1 kg of paracetamol cost €4 to make in France vs €3 in China — €1/kg, about 2% of the final box price. For 2% a European plant closed, and nobody moved: no scandal, no minister crying treason, no sovereignty debate. Why? The offshoring was invisible — Doliprane still looked French, because Sanofi's plants at Lisieux and Compiègne kept tableting, packaging and boxing it. The real loss of control happened then, not in 2024.

CD&R's bet

Clayton, Dubilier & Rice: a US private-equity giant founded in 1978, managing tens of billions of dollars, in France since 2004 (Rexel, SPIE, Socotec, B&M, Conforama). Its particularity: long holding periods, typically 8–9 years on French deals — not vulture funds selling companies in pieces, but buy, develop, exit with a capital gain. €16bn is potentially the largest LBO (leveraged buyout: an acquisition financed largely with debt repaid by the target's cash flows) in French history. Four levers: 1) Internationalisation — the US is 24% of Opella's revenue, France only 10%; Doliprane barely exists outside France, and CD&R has the network to replicate it in the US and Asia, a multi-billion paracetamol market dominated locally by Tylenol. 2) Operational optimisation — the classic PE playbook: compress costs, rationalise production, shrink the structure; unpopular but effective for margins, raising EBITDA and therefore valuation. 3) Price pressure — lobbying the French government to raise regulated prices, politically risky but possible, especially with the threat of complete relocation in the background. 4) Exit — in 5–7 years, sell Opella to another pharma player or float it; the bet is that a buyer pays more than €16bn. Why couldn't Sanofi do it? Internationalising Doliprane would take billions of marketing and distribution — every euro of which is one euro less for the next cancer treatment, not Sanofi's job. CD&R is the reverse: no R&D, it optimises and internationalises — a dedicated, lighter structure without a pharma giant's costs, with all energy on one mission: make Opella a global consumer-health leader.

Consequences and the three lessons

Price: regulated, so it shouldn't change — but will dosages change, are there other levers? Jobs: Opella still employs ~1,000 people at Lisieux and Compiègne; CD&R commits to keep them but without binding guarantees, and private equity's track record on job promises isn't reassuring. Sovereignty: Covid showed it — when Chinese borders closed, France came close to a paracetamol shortage; it hasn't controlled the supply chain for 16 years. The real question isn't who owns the brand but whether we can produce in a crisis, and whether CD&R might serve the US first — on that, the sale changes nothing: France was dependent before and will remain so. Lesson 1: volume doesn't guarantee profitability — 453m boxes but ~75 cents after tax; when costs eat almost everything, commercial success is an illusion. Lesson 2: emotional attachment isn't a strategy — Kodak died clinging to film; Apple killed the iPod for the iPhone. If you have a "Doliprane" you keep out of nostalgia while it costs more than it brings, you know what to do. Lesson 3: understand the system before judging — the problem isn't Sanofi but a tax system that makes structurally unprofitable the medicines we need most.

Capture the lessons

Beyond the video — why this case is yours

Regulated prices, clawbacks and sovereignty — the same triangle as energy. Nuclear output in France has its own regulated-price and clawback history (ARENH), CfDs (contracts for difference) pay back above a strike price, and 2022 brought revenue caps on generators. Doliprane shows how such rules can make a high-volume asset unattractive to its owner and attractive to a buyer with a different plan. And the 2008 Roussillon closure is the supply-chain lesson for critical equipment: sovereignty is lost quietly, upstream, long before anyone argues about the brand.

How to drillLook under the volume: of a €2.15 Doliprane box, the lab nets ~75 cents after pharmacist, wholesaler, VAT and sector taxes — and the safeguard clause taxes it more the more it sells. The real sovereignty loss came quietly in 2008, when paracetamol production left for China over 2% of the price. For you: compute unit margins, map where critical inputs are made, and judge the system before the actor.

Castel — The World Wine Emperor Nobody KnowsSwapn · Video case · Everyday wine at scale, the African bet, full vertical integration, many brands and no family name — and the growers' anger
▶ Video0/14▶
The one ideaIn France, one bottle in six sold in supermarkets comes from the same group — more than €5.6bn of revenue in 2024 — and almost nobody has heard of it. Roche Mazet, Baron de Lestac, Listel, La Villageoise; Château Beychevelle (a Saint-Julien grand cru classé), Château Beaumont, Château Ferrande; France's largest wine-shop chain; breweries across Africa. From €3 table wine to €50+ bottles, it all belongs to Pierre Castel, son of Spanish immigrants, 98, ~9th French fortune (~€14bn). While Bolloré and Arnault make headlines, the "baron of wine" dominates in the shadow — same weight, zero noise. His name appears on no label, and that's no accident.
A note on framing (source)

Video case (Swapn — Nils — "L'empereur mondial du vin que personne ne connaît," Nov 2025); figures and characterisations are the video's own, sponsor segment omitted. Filed in Consumer, Retail & Luxury, next to the other discreet family empires Ferrero (180) and MSC (171). Also directly relevant to you: Castel has vineyards in Morocco and Tunisia.

Scale and contrast

Pernod Ricard, the king of spirits (~€12bn of revenue), cultivates and celebrates its brand. Castel does the opposite: dozens of brands, none carrying the family name. It's the world's #3 wine producer; of the ~3bn bottles of wine drunk in France a year, Castel produces ~8% of the volume and ~16% of wine sold in supermarkets. It owns 21 châteaux in France, the 565 Nicolas wine shops, the e-commerce site Vinatis, and sells 4.6bn bottles a year all drinks combined, in 22 countries from Europe to Asia — but above all in Africa.

The bet against the market (1949–1950s)

Pierre Castel, born 1926 to Spanish immigrants, works in the vines from 12; at 20 he's a docker. In 1949, at 23, he founds with his brothers and sisters a small wine-trading business, Castel Frères — nothing exceptional among hundreds of négociants. In the 1950s wine was everyday currency: everyone had small artisanal production, wine moved in barrels and was sold in bulk to bistros and grocers, a bottle on the table at every meal — the French drank 138 litres per person per year. The industry wanted to move upmarket — grands crus, excellence, prestigious appellations: "that's where the money is." Castel bets the opposite: keep everyday wine and take it from craft to industry — standardise, bottle at scale, export. Exports generate cash; with it he buys French wine estates that lack the means to modernise (e.g. a château in 1957) and builds his own bottling lines. By the end of the 1950s the system works — and the timing is perfect: France gets richer, the middle class explodes, supermarkets spread, and wine becomes a mass market.

The African bet (1960s →)

In the 1960s the former colonies have just gained independence; new states are unstable and uncertain, and big French groups look elsewhere — too risky. Castel sees an opportunity ("a wind of freedom") and changes strategy: from exporting French wine to the continent to setting up there. He builds relationships with heads of state — Omar Bongo, future president of Gabon, encourages his projects — and builds breweries on site to produce locally, plants and infrastructure, investing for the long term. In countries where industrial jobs are rare, Castel employs massively, trains technicians, pays salaries — the bet ends up paying. In 2011, at Alassane Ouattara's inauguration as president of Côte d'Ivoire, Vincent Bolloré and Martin Bouygues are present but on the sides; Pierre Castel has the place of honour between the president and his wife. That proximity to power creates grey areas: in 2021 an investigation targeted a Castel sugar subsidiary in the Central African Republic for opaque practices, notably on working conditions; the group is criticised for lack of transparency and the means used to keep its dominant position — it has locked its markets so tightly that nobody can really compete.

Strategy 1 — own the whole chain

Vertical integration: from production to distribution, Castel controls everything. 21 châteaux, 3,000 hectares of vines (1,400 in France, 1,600 in Africa and the Mediterranean — Morocco, Tunisia, Ethiopia), its own industrial bottling lines, then distribution — the Nicolas shops, Vinatis online — plus its African distribution network. It controls costs, margins, logistics and shelf presence.

Strategy 2 — many brands, no family name

French consumers are attached to the idea of small independent producers. So, from entry-level to the most expensive bottle, each brand keeps its own identity and story — everyone suspects La Villageoise in a box isn't artisanal, but the strategy breaks consumer resistance to an industrial giant. Fun detail: "Baron de Lestac" is an anagram of Castel — "the farmer's son bought himself nobility in the supermarket."

Layer 3 — influence (the controversial part)

While Pierre Castel stays invisible to the public, the wine industry discreetly influences the political environment. The Loi Évin has regulated alcohol advertising since 1990 and notably prevented promotion of wine tourism; in 2015 the wine lobby Vin & Société ran a campaign to loosen it, triggering a vote in the Assemblée — 102 for, 29 against: a win for the industry, and wine-tourism advertising now runs on TV. What creates debate: the lobby's delegate later became Emmanuel Macron's agriculture adviser, and the following year the president almost repeated their slogan on camera ("we must stop pestering the French about wine consumption"). The video stresses it isn't saying Castel is directly involved in this lobby, but admits the group benefits.

The growers' anger

Bordeaux winegrowers protest against purchase prices that are too low: the cost of producing a bottle often exceeds the price Castel pays for their grapes or wine, so they lose money every harvest. A Gironde grower: "We can't live from our work any more. The négociants break prices and Castel is the biggest." Castel sues the organisers for commercial disruption and damage to its image; the growers answer they're defending their survival; Castel says it respects the law and contracts. Not the first time: in the 1970s Languedoc growers already protested against Castel's imports of foreign wine — commando operations, blocked trucks, physical threats. Pierre Castel invited the protest leader to a chic Bordeaux restaurant, listened, promised to stop the imports, everyone shook hands — then he quietly resumed elsewhere through other routes. Fifty years later, the empire still inspires fear among independent and mid-size growers. Does Castel make French wine accessible, or has it built a system where only giants survive? "The question is open."

▶ Original video ↗

Capture the lessons

Run the drills

Beyond the video — why this case is yours

Castel is the long-game African and Maghreb investor. It entered post-independence markets others found too risky, produced locally, built infrastructure and political relationships, and has dominated for 60 years — the same playbook infrastructure and energy investors use in Africa, with the same governance risks. With vineyards in Tunisia and a France–Africa footprint, it's a model (and a cautionary tale) for anyone building a France–North Africa practice: patient local presence wins, but proximity to power must be managed with clean governance.

Make it click — similar plays

Discreet family empires: Ferrero (180), MSC (171), Intersport (158). Integration: Tetra Pak (176), Rolex (154). Africa & political risk: Tencent (179), Danone & Carlsberg (140). Supplier squeeze: E.Leclerc (22).

How to drillWin where nobody looks: Pierre Castel bet on everyday wine when the trade chased grands crus, recycled export cash into estates and bottling, bet on post-independence Africa with local breweries and presidential relationships, then integrated soil to shelf (3,000 ha, 21 châteaux, Nicolas, Vinatis) behind dozens of brands with no family name — one supermarket bottle in six, €5.6bn of revenue. The cost: grey areas in Africa and growers paid below production cost. For you: find the neglected volume market, enter risky regions early and locally, and keep governance clean.

The Five Luxury Playbooks — Louis Vuitton, Gucci, Rolex, Chanel, HermèsSwapn · Video case · Same velvet boutiques, five opposite strategies: visibility, dilution, organised frustration, price inflation, absolute rarity — and who really buys luxury now
▶ Video0/14▶
The one ideaWalk into Chanel, Louis Vuitton or Rolex: the same muted décor, discreet music, subtle scent — you're meant to feel like a monarch. All luxury brands share the same codes. So why is Louis Vuitton the most powerful (valued at ~$300bn), why do some spend billions on advertising while others don't need to, and how does a bag sell for €200,000 at auction? Because behind the uniformity hides an invisible war: each house built a precise heritage over decades or centuries, and that positioning dictates five completely different psychological strategies — all generating tens of billions.
A note on framing (source)

Video case (Swapn — Nils — "L'étrange héritage des marques de luxe," Sep 2025); figures are the video's own, sponsor segment omitted. Small corrections: Rolex's Oyster (1926) is the first widely recognised waterproof wristwatch; the Chanel 2.55 rise from ~€4,500 (2019) to €7,500+ is closer to +65% than the video's 55%. Filed in Consumer, Retail & Luxury; overview card for LVMH (28), Gucci / Kering (19) and Rolex (154).

1 · Louis Vuitton — accessible dream, maximum visibility

1854: a simple trunk maker who seduces Parisian aristocracy with flat, stackable trunks; craftsmanship serving the elite. 170 years later it produces millions of items a year and makes €20bn+ of revenue. How to go from royal craft to industrial empire without losing its soul? Inject ~€1bn of advertising a year — celebrities, artistic collaborations, massive presence on every continent — to democratise access to the dream. The ladder: a perfume at ~€150 is the entry door (the client tastes prestige and belonging), then entry leather goods ~€800, then the icons at €2,000–3,000 — each step a higher level of commitment, a logic of progressive accessibility. LV did what many thought impossible: reach millions while keeping its prestige.

2 · Gucci — when heritage isn't enough

1921: Guccio Gucci opens a leather-goods shop in Florence, specialised in high-end equestrian goods, inspired by the English high society he served as a groom at London's Savoy. It becomes the reference for riders and Italian aristocracy; in the 1950s the American jet set adopts it from Hollywood to New York — the first Italian luxury brand in the US. The horse-bit becomes its icon, the green-red stripes its signature: the discreet luxury of the Italian upper bourgeoisie. Then strategic errors nearly killed it: it rushed its transformation without respecting the codes that made its strength. From the late 1970s, under financial pressure, Gucci multiplied licences for every imaginable product — Gucci whisky, Gucci coffee cups, Gucci office chairs. That proliferation diluted the brand and opened the door to massive counterfeiting. Lesson: legend and heritage aren't enough if the marketing isn't up to it.

3 · Rolex — organised frustration

The DNA is technical: 1910, the first chronometer certificate ever granted to a wristwatch; 1926, the waterproof Oyster. A Rolex is more than jewellery — a precision instrument, each movement needing months of adjustment, so production must be limited… Except the numbers tell a slightly different story: ~1m watches a year, €10.1bn of revenue — far from confidential craft. The "absolute rarity" is an impression: Rolex turned frustration into desire. It controls distribution drop by drop — no online sales, only carefully chosen authorised dealers who receive quotas deliberately too small for demand; the most wanted models (Daytona, Submariner) are always out of stock, with endless waiting lists. "That's exactly what they sell": the prohibition creates desire, and the watch becomes desirable precisely because it's impossible to buy. See the full story in card 154.

4 · Chanel — perpetual price increases

Another rarity technique, just as formidable: raise prices perpetually. Every ~6 months Chanel raises its prices — not 2–3% to follow inflation, but 10–15%. A 2.55 bag cost ~€4,500 in 2019 and exceeds €7,500 today. The systematic inflation is orchestrated, and rests on the heritage: in 1910 Paris, Gabrielle Chanel revolutionised women's fashion — no more corsets, ornate hats and constricting dresses; the Chanel suit, No. 5, the little black dress, all symbols of emancipation; a political revolution too — the independent woman who works, travels, decides; elegance without ostentation, comfort without vulgarity. That philosophy still shapes every boutique (velvet welcome, golden light, precious materials). "Today the bags aren't more expensive — they've simply taken value." Chanel announces increases weeks in advance, and clients rush to buy before the rise: the price hike itself becomes a sales event.

5 · Hermès — absolute rarity, no compromise

It combines rarity, price and conditioning in a perfect alchemy of ultra-luxury. The story starts on a plane in 1984: actress Jane Birkin sits next to Hermès CEO Jean-Louis Dumas and complains her bag lacks pockets; Dumas sketches a few drawings and creates the Birkin — the most desired bag in the world, sold up to €200,000 at auction, carrying the name of the celebrity it was made for. The heritage goes back to 1837: Thierry Hermès opens a saddlery workshop in Paris making harnesses and saddles for the aristocracy, each piece unique, handmade, built to last generations — when you equip thoroughbreds for royal families, you don't mass-produce. That 19th-century philosophy still governs the empire, and the numbers defy classic commercial logic: Hermès produces ~120,000 such bags a year against a world demand that could easily absorb ten times more, with margins above 40%. Owning one means a social status, belonging, a myth. Hermès solved the impossible equation of contemporary luxury: while LV juggles mass and prestige, Rolex organises frustration and Chanel manipulates inflation, Hermès makes no compromise — ultra-luxury can never become accessible; it will stay minority, elitist, frustrating. "That's the condition of its superiority."

Who really buys luxury now

Not only the heiress or the rich kid — the market has flipped. In ultra-luxury, 20% of clients make 70% of revenue: on one side an ultra-wealthy elite collecting exceptional pieces; on the other a mass of new buyers who now represent half of the global luxury market — and they aren't rich, they're the middle and working classes. In highly unequal regions, Google searches for luxury brands explode: the wider the gap between classes, the more social pressure pushes people to buy luxury to look successful; during Covid many used government aid to buy luxury. Gen Z starts buying luxury around 15, vs 18–20 for millennials. Second engine: wealthy Asian millennials — between 2015 and 2019 they alone tripled Gucci's revenue, and 300m new Asian buyers are expected by 2030. This generation discovers luxury through social networks, not discreet word of mouth: 38% of luxury consumers discover brands and products via social media; 15% of TikTok users bought a luxury item right after seeing it there — TikTok has become a more powerful prescriber than Vogue; creators decode and compare products, and for 59% of luxury buyers on TikTok the goal is no longer status but self-indulgence. This generation wants proof.

Capture the lessons

Run the drills

Beyond the video — why this case is yours

Positioning is a choice of model, then consistency. An expert practice faces the same choice as a luxury house: be scarce and expensive with few clients (Hermès), build visibility with an entry offer that leads to bigger mandates (LV), or raise your rate steadily as demand grows (Chanel). The Gucci warning is the most useful: accepting every adjacent request for cash dilutes the expertise that justified your price. Your "only person who can" sentence is your heritage — the rest follows from it.

Make it click — similar plays

Single-house deep dives: Rolex (154), LVMH (28), Gucci / Kering (19). Never discount: On (172). Pricing power: Parc Astérix (181). Emotional brands: Ferrero (180).

How to drillSame codes, five strategies: Louis Vuitton spends ~€1bn a year on visibility and an entry ladder (€150 perfume → €3,000 icons); Gucci nearly died from licences that diluted its equestrian heritage; Rolex organises frustration with quotas while making ~1m watches; Chanel raises prices 10–15% twice a year and turns hikes into events; Hermès refuses to meet demand (~120,000 bags vs 10× demand, 40%+ margins). The buyers are now half aspirational middle class, Gen Z and Asian millennials discovering luxury on TikTok. For you: anchor positioning in a true heritage, choose one model, and refuse the "licences" that dilute it.

Alphabet — The Ad Machine That Funds the MoonshotsSwapn · Video case · PageRank, the ad auction, ~75–80% of revenue from ads, the 2015 holding, cloud diversification, $50bn+ capex — and the AI and antitrust threats
▶ Video0/14▶
The one ideaEveryone uses Google daily — search, Maps, YouTube — an extension of our digital life. Behind that omnipresence sits a simple reality: ~80% of revenue comes from one activity, advertising. The fortune of Google — or rather its parent Alphabet — rests on companies paying to appear on your screen at every search and every video. Alphabet is an ultra-profitable ad agency that funds futuristic projects and diversifies into cloud and AI. The open question: in 10 years, will it still be an ad machine, or the leader in AI and health — will the moonshots have paid off?
A note on framing (source)

Video case (Swapn, "La vérité derrière le Vrai géant qui contrôle Google !," Aug 2025); figures are the video's own (FY2024 and H1 2025), sponsor segment omitted. Precision: Google acquired Android in 2005 and YouTube in 2006, as the video says. Filed in Technology, Semiconductors & AI, next to Amazon / AWS (11), Microsoft Copilot (13) and Waze (51).

From BackRub to an indispensable company (1996–2014)

1996, Stanford: two students, Larry Page and Sergey Brin, work on a search engine called BackRub. The idea is simple but revolutionary: rank web pages by their incoming links — what will later be called PageRank. In the early internet, pages were hard to find unless you had the exact address, and searching a topic was difficult. The mission is clear: organise the world's information and make it universally accessible and useful. Within months Google becomes the most used search engine in the world. In the 2000s it diversifies: Gmail (2004), Google Maps (2005), YouTube bought in 2006 (now one of the world's most visited sites) and Android bought in 2005 — the most used smartphone OS, putting Google in the pockets of billions. In under ten years, a student project became indispensable.

2015 — Alphabet: separate the cash machine from the moonshots

By 2015 Google is a giant — search, YouTube, Android, Chrome, Maps — plus ambitious, lesser-known projects like Waymo self-driving taxis and the biotech lab Calico. The problem: everything was mixed in the accounts, and investors struggled to separate the activities. Page and Brin create Alphabet, a holding that separates the Google cash machine from the futuristic projects called "moonshots".

How the ad machine works

Search alone generates $198bn of revenue. Type "cheap plumber Paris" or "holidays in Greece" and you see sponsored links: a company pays to be placed at the top, there's an auction, and the company pays per click. Google's genius: letting businesses in every sector and of every budget advertise online — web giants with budgets of tens or hundreds of millions, and a Toulouse hairdresser who wants his salon featured as a sponsored link on Google Maps. Revenue from virtually every sector and company in the world. Plus YouTube: $36bn of ad revenue in 2024 (before, during, after videos, or site-based). And the Google Network: ads displayed on partner sites. Advertising is ~75–80% of total revenue — which makes Alphabet dependent on it.

Diversification — cloud and subscriptions

Google Cloud, sold only to businesses: $43.2bn of revenue in 2024, +31% vs 2023 — and above all, for the first time, profitable: $6.1bn of profit, a 14% margin; in H1 2025 already $13bn+ of profit at a 20%+ margin. The colossal investments start paying off; cloud becomes a growth engine and is strategic, since Google wants to compete with Microsoft's Azure and Amazon's AWS, the leader in enterprise cloud infrastructure. Subscriptions and hardware: YouTube Premium and YouTube Music passed 125m subscribers; Google One storage; Pixel phones, Nest thermostats and the connected home — $40.3bn in 2024, still small next to advertising but growing year after year.

Profit, capex and culture

Once taxes, depreciation of all the buildings, salaries — everything — are paid, Google's net profit is $100bn for 2024, +36% vs 2023. Few companies in the world have such financial power. It's mostly reinvested: Google is one of the world's biggest investors — 2024 capex (capital expenditure) of more than $50bn, mainly to innovate and build data centres and the AI of tomorrow (Gemini): staying ahead to keep a near-hegemonic position on the web. It also funds employee perks: ~180,000 employees, average annual pay estimated at ~$250,000 (pulled up by engineers and stock bonuses) — among the highest in the world; the counterpart may be very long hours, pressure to ship and frequent reorganisations. Google pioneered quality of life at work through magnificent facilities.

The threats — AI and antitrust

CEO Sundar Pichai calls AI the most important technological revolution of our time — more than the internet or the smartphone. It's a real challenge: OpenAI with ChatGPT took a lead over Gemini, and players like Anthropic's Claude, Perplexity and France's Mistral offer what could become alternatives to Google. If young generations prefer to ask an LLM (large language model) like ChatGPT for a structured answer rather than run a Google search that sends them to several websites, the search engine's hegemony could be challenged. And the law: antitrust cases in the US and Europe against Google's near-monopoly on search could force it to divest assets — e.g. Chrome, which drew an unsolicited purchase offer from Perplexity should Google be forced to sell. (Update from the record: in September 2025 a US judge ruled Google need not divest Chrome, though remedies on data-sharing and exclusive deals apply; EU cases continue.)

Alphabet's capex is your market. The $50bn+ a year going into data centres and AI is the demand side of your target intersection — energy transition, AI infrastructure and project finance: every new data centre needs firm power, grid connection, cooling and long-term energy contracts. The case also mirrors your situation: a reliable cash machine (your role at EDF) funding a moonshot (your independent practice) — the discipline is to keep them separate, give the moonshot a budget and a deadline, and measure it.

Alphabet (2015) ring-fences the moonshots; cloud ($43.2bn, now 14–20%+ margins) and subscriptions diversify; $50bn+ of capex funds data centres and AI. Threats: AI chat replacing search, and antitrust. For you: their capex is your market — and keep your cash machine and your moonshot separate.

Divain vs Adopt vs Equivalenza — Three Ways to Sell Affordable PerfumeResearch case · Equivalence (smell like a famous bottle) vs original creation (own identity) — channels, structures, legal edges and lessons
◆ Research0/14▶
The one ideaA designer perfume costs €100–150, but the juice inside is a small part of that price: most of it pays for the brand, the licence, advertising, the bottle and distribution. That gap created a European market for affordable fragrance, and two opposite models fight over it. Equivalence brands (Divain, Equivalenza) promise "the smell of a famous perfume for a fraction of the price" and sell a reference number. Original-creation brands (Adopt) sell their own named fragrances at a low price. Same price range, opposite strategy: the first borrows someone else's demand; the second builds its own.
A note on framing (sources)

Research case built from company and trade-press sources (Premium Beauty News, Modaes, Journal des Entreprises, Cosmeticobs, Alimarket) rather than a single video; figures are as reported at the dates given and some are partial — notably Divain, a private Spanish company that publishes little. The legal points are general context, not legal advice. Filed in Consumer, Retail & Luxury, next to Givaudan (174) — the supplier side of every perfume — and the five luxury playbooks (184) — the brands being imitated.

Divain — equivalence, online-first (Spain)

Concept: openly sells "equivalence" perfumes — fragrances formulated to smell like well-known designer scents. Each is identified by a three-digit number (e.g. DIVAIN 001, DIVAIN 086) rather than a name, and its site offers a search engine where you type the perfume you like to get the matching Divain reference. Range: a very wide catalogue — reported at 800–900+ references (men, women, unisex, children), organised by olfactory family. Channel: built online (free shipping, easy returns, free samples), with a strong performance-marketing and press presence in Spain; it has since started opening physical stores, beginning in the Barcelona area. Price: typically ~€15–30 depending on size and promotions. What we don't know: Divain doesn't publish founding details or revenue in sources we could verify — treat it as a fast-growing private company whose economics are inferred, not disclosed.

Equivalenza — equivalence, franchised stores (Spain)

Founded in 2011 in Barcelona by Francisco Morán, Miguel Aznar and Jaime Berdejo. Same equivalence idea as Divain, but built through physical stores, mostly franchised: 400 stores by its expansion years, now 500+ points of sale in ~20 countries (Spain ~95, of which 14 company-owned; Italy its biggest market at ~54% of sales; recent entries in Romania, Moldova, Poland, Congo via a master franchise). Reported revenue: €26.6m for the year to June 2024 (company level). Ownership: ~70% French capital, ~30% founders (Berdejo sold in 2015). Legal friction: its low-cost replica positioning led to disputes with major perfume groups; in 2015 French justice placed it under investigation for counterfeiting brand perfumes (Modaes). The lesson: equivalence grows fast but lives close to the legal line.

Adopt — original creations, own factories (France)

History: born in 1986 as Réserve Naturelle, founded by a Bordeaux entrepreneur who opened ~60 shops; bought by an investment fund in 2015, renamed Adopt and expanded to 135 stores, then 170+ in France (about 200 targeted). Concept: not copies but signature fragrances with names (Hot One, Moonlight…), reworked with perfumers from the big houses (Firmenich, Symrise, Robertet, Givaudan) under an in-house creation director — creation can take up to 12 months. The economics: most of the budget goes into the juice; a single 30 ml tube format, decorated label, no secondary packaging, very little advertising — the stores are the media. Price from ~€10.95–11.95 per 30 ml; 150+ fragrances. Volume: 6 million bottles sold in France in 2022 (+35% the year before); "a perfume sold every 5 seconds" worldwide. Structure and capital: €26m raised in May 2022 (NextStage AM, Pépites & Territoires by AXA France, Trocadéro Capital); a second factory at Château-Renard (Loiret), on a former Pierre Fabre site — €15m over five years, ~100 jobs at full capacity — on top of production near Bordeaux. Network: company-owned and franchised stores in France, ~2,000 points of sale in ~40 countries, owned shops in Barcelona and Madrid (2023), and expansion into Canada.

Other European reference points

Zara and high-street fashion sell low-price fragrances under their own brand, sometimes with well-known perfumers credited — "affordable but original," like Adopt, distributed through existing fashion stores. Discount supermarkets periodically launch "inspired by" scents as traffic drivers. Outside Europe, Middle-Eastern houses (Lattafa, Armaf) and US online brands (Dossier) have made the "smells like" category global through social media. None of these change the core split: borrow a famous reference, or build your own name.

The legal edge — why equivalence is a narrow road

A smell itself is hard to protect: perfume formulas are usually guarded as trade secrets rather than by copyright, so making a similar scent is not, by itself, illegal. The risk is in how you sell it. Using a famous brand name to promote the copy — comparison lists, "smells like X," look-alike bottles — can be treated as counterfeiting, misleading advertising or taking unfair advantage of a reputation. The reference case is the EU Court of Justice ruling L'Oréal v Bellure (2009), which held that comparison lists linking cheap imitations to famous perfumes could infringe trade marks. That's why equivalence brands use numbers, keep brand names off packaging, and push the matching to search tools and word of mouth — and why they face recurring lawsuits.

The three models side by side

IdentityNumbers + search engineNumbers, in-store matchingNames (Hot One, Moonlight)
Who creates demandThe luxury brands' advertisingThe luxury brands' advertisingAdopt's own stores
ChannelOnline first, stores recently500+ mostly franchised storesOwned + franchised stores, 40 countries
ProductionSpain (details undisclosed)SpainOwn French factories
Price~€15–30LowFrom ~€11 / 30 ml
Main riskLegal (trade marks), ad costsLegal (2015 French case)Fixed costs of stores and factories

Capture the lessons

Beyond the case — why it's yours

It's the positioning choice in miniature. As an expert you can be an "equivalence" — "a cheaper version of a big consulting firm" — which borrows their credibility but competes on price and lives in their shadow; or an "Adopt" — your own named method, built on deep know-how (the juice), with low overheads and a direct relationship. The first is faster to sell; the second builds an asset only you own. Your positioning sentence should make clear which one you are.

Make it click — similar plays

The supplier behind every perfume: Givaudan (174). The brands being copied: the five luxury playbooks (184), LVMH (28). Fast copy vs own identity: Zara vs H&M (149), Shein (152) — copying and the legal edge. Franchise vs owned: Basic-Fit vs Fitness Park (155), Intersport (158).

How to drillTwo answers to the same price gap: Divain and Equivalenza sell numbered "equivalents" of famous perfumes, riding the luxury houses' advertising — fast to grow (Divain online, Equivalenza through 500+ mostly franchised stores) but close to the trade-mark line; Adopt (ex-Réserve Naturelle, relaunched by a fund in 2015) sells its own named fragrances from ~€11, spends on the juice not the packaging, uses stores as media and owns French factories. For you: decide whether you're a cheaper version of someone else's name, or the owner of your own.

Mr. Bricolage — When the Central Depends on Weakening ShopsCorentin Mercadal · Video case · A buying central of independents, the owned-store trap, the Covid boom and four years of decline — read through real store accounts
▶ Video0/14▶
The one ideaOnly four years ago Mr. Bricolage and its network of independent retailers reached €2.37bn of business volume with 900+ points of sale, all federated around one central buying office and a simple promise: neighbourhood DIY for everyone. Since then, €260m of sales have evaporated, the group's net profit has been divided by four, and network volume has fallen for the fourth year in a row. The cause isn't one bad decision: it's a model where the central earns from its members' activity, so when the shops weaken, the central weakens with them — and shops without cash can no longer invest to stop the slide.
A note on framing (source)

Video case (Corentin Mercadal, "La chute brutale de Mr. Bricolage," Apr 2026), built from the group's accounts and the filed accounts of member stores; figures are the video's own, sponsor segment omitted, and some passages weren't visible in the transcript screenshots, so the card sticks to the figures shown. Filed in Consumer, Retail & Luxury as the counter-example to Intersport (158) — a federation of independents that is growing.

What was built (1965 →)

In 1965, 13 hardware dealers from the Orléans region signed the statutes of an association, the ANPF. The founding rule: pooling purchases creates negotiating power and margin — as long as volumes grow, everyone wins. But the model has an Achilles' heel: Mr. Bricolage was never an integrated retailer like Leroy Merlin or Castorama. It doesn't control the till of each shop; its economics rest on royalties, commissions and services billed to members. The central's health depends directly on the shops': if members falter, the central weakens.

The owned-store trap (2009–2015)

For a long time the model coexisted with a less visible reality: Mr. Bricolage also ran stores it owned and operated itself. In 2012 it owned about 81 stores, mainly from the 2009 acquisition of Briconaute and Jardinoute — two-thirds of consolidated revenue (€373.6m of €560m). Problem: those stores lost money. The retail division's operating result was negative year after year — −€14.8m (2013), −€11.4m (2014), −€12m (2015): an ageing concept, weak competitiveness against the big integrated chains, and a central distracted by running shops instead of serving its members.

The Covid boom — and the hangover

Then the unexpected: in 2020, while whole sectors of the economy collapsed, neighbourhood DIY exploded — French people stuck at home painted, repaired and gardened, and the network reached its peak (~€2.37bn of volume). But it was an exceptional demand, not a new normal. Since then volume has declined four years in a row; the central earns less and less each year — operating result down to ~€24.9m (8.7% margin) in 2025 — and net profit fell from €34m in 2021 to €8.4m in 2025, divided by four in four years.

Inside the shops — the real accounts

Mr. Bricolage is above all independent retailers: over a thousand in the network, about 400 under the Mr. Bricolage banner — people who invested their savings, borrowed, hired staff and carry the brand locally. Do they make a living? The video analysed the filed accounts of 67 member stores (2023–2024): average revenue ~€3.25m in 2024 vs €3.35m in 2023; gross margin ~39% — in line with the sector — but the picture darkens further down the income statement. In a 2025 sample of 22 stores: average revenue €2.92m (−7.4%), gross margin slightly lower, 21 of 22 saw sales fall, 9 saw EBITDA deteriorate, 13 saw net profit decline and 9 were loss-making. Not a clear rebound: a network under pressure with local improvements but no overall normalisation. Cash is the real problem: renovating a shop, installing click-and-collect, changing the till system all need profitability, available cash and a banker who follows. Average cash per store fell from €355,000 (end 2023) to €232,000 (end 2024), while working capital stays heavy — ~€72,000 tied up on average, with a large share of the business sitting in stock. At that level the capacity to invest disappears: shops can't modernise, so they age, and customers go elsewhere — a vicious circle.

The fight back (2025–2026)

Logistics: the main logistics platform was enlarged and robotised, roughly doubling its surface; the L'Hospitalet warehouse was closed to pool volumes. The aim: prepare smaller, more frequent orders suited to neighbourhood shops and click-and-collect. IT: almost all Mr. Bricolage stores in France adopted a unified commercial-management system — before, each member managed stock with its own, often heterogeneous tools; now the central steers the data in real time, spots anomalies and helps members calibrate orders. Formats: a City format for town centres, and Mr. Bricolage Relais, a lighter version for rural areas where a big store isn't viable — 45 Relais stores were operating in early 2026. Plan: a new strategic plan, "Puissance 1000", launched for 2026, financed by a new credit line secured in March 2026. "The will is there, the financing is there, the plans are there" — the open question is whether shops with thin cash can follow.

Capture the lessons

Beyond the video — why this case is yours

Counterparty health is project-finance basics. A central living on royalties from weakening shops is like a lender exposed to offtakers or contractors in decline: the contract looks fine until the counterparty's cash runs out. Reading member accounts — cash, stock, debt capacity — is exactly how you'd assess an offtaker or a supplier on a critical-equipment contract. And the 2020 spike is a reminder to normalise exceptional years before sizing any debt.

Make it click — similar plays

How to drillFollow the members' cash: born in 1965 as a pooling association of 13 hardware dealers, Mr. Bricolage earns royalties and commissions from independent shops, wasted years on loss-making owned stores (81 in 2012, −€11–15m a year), rode the 2020 DIY boom to €2.37bn of volume, then lost €260m of sales while its net profit fell from €34m to €8.4m. Member stores show falling sales, 39% gross margin but shrinking cash (€355k → €232k) and stock-heavy working capital — no room to modernise. The fight back: robotised logistics, unified IT, City and Relais formats, "Puissance 1000." For you: a central is only as strong as its members — read their accounts.

Modular Construction — The Little-Known Business Behind the Site Hut (and EDF's 5,600 Modules)Les Echos · Video case · From the 1851 Crystal Palace to factory-built buildings: a rental business at heart, a factory that must keep running, and a nuclear-scale order
▶ Video0/14▶
The one ideaThe big boxes you see on every construction site are site huts — and almost everyone remembers a prefab classroom or temporary office. That's only the tip: prefab now means student residences, hotels, public buildings, and contracts worth more than €100m. In the trade it's called modular construction: complete modules built in a factory, then assembled on site "like Lego." It's a small, little-known market (~€1.5bn in France in 2025, ~7,000 direct jobs) — but it's mainly a rental business (71.8% of revenue), it runs on factories that must stay busy, and one of its biggest clients is EDF, which ordered 5,600+ modules for its new reactors.
A note on framing (source)

Video case (Les Echos — Olivier Harmant — "Le business méconnu des préfabriqués," 2026, series "Business méconnus"); figures are the video's own. The Vendée manufacturer visited is transcribed as "Kuno" — most likely Cougnaud, the Vendée-based leader alongside Algeco. Filed in Energy, Infrastructure & Resources because of the EPR2 order and its project-delivery logic.

Where it started — the Crystal Palace (1851)

On 1 May 1851, Queen Victoria opened the first-ever World's Fair in London's Hyde Park, in the Crystal Palace: 39 m high, 70,000 m² of floor, then the largest glass building in the world. The other feat was speed: the decision to build came only 11 months earlier, after 250+ abandoned projects, and it was built in 190 days — thanks to prefabrication: standardised glass and metal components made in series and assembled on site.

Three things called "prefab"

Prefab has a thousand faces — site huts and classrooms, but also prefabricated lodges at the Futuroscope, hotels, a building for the Paris 2024 Olympic village since converted into a student residence, and a state tender for 1,500 prison places. Three different things: 1) prefabrication and off-site construction — single elements made in a factory (a wall, a door, a façade) and assembled on site later; 2) modular construction — complete assemblies built in the factory: the modules, the subject here. Purchase prices: ~€2,000/m² for a permanent building at Les Sables-d'Olonne, ~€1,700/m² for another. Still marginal in France: ~€1.5bn of revenue in 2025 — "a drop of water next to the building sector's billions."

A rental business

Modular is above all rental: 71.8% of 2025 revenue, often with or without a purchase option; sales of new or used modules are just over 28%. The same module earns rent many times over, site after site.

The factory — construction meets industry

At La Roche-sur-Yon in Vendée, one of the two French heavyweights of modular construction (with Algeco) runs a 20,000 m² site with 300 people, where up to 100 modules for sale can be assembled at once. Apart from masons, every building trade is there — welders, waterproofers, plasterers, electricians, plumbers, joiners, painters — but instead of working on a site, everyone is in the same factory at the same time: "a radically different model, at the crossroads of the building site, public works and industry." Output: about 1,000 m² of modular buildings a day. Process: chassis made in a neighbouring plant; the module's frame (usually steel or wood) assembled on it; then walls with insulation, electrical cables… Constraint: modules travel by road, so size is capped by bridges and road gauge — up to 13 m long and 3.5 m high.

Keep the factory running — EDF and the cycle

Modular is gaining ground on traditional building and tenders are more and more ambitious. EDF is the example: to build France's future nuclear reactors it ordered 5,600+ temporary or permanent modules for 90,000 m² — offices, rest rooms, even infirmaries — to house 10,000+ workers; a contract of about €100m over 7–8 years. Spectacular, but above all vital, because unlike traditional construction, modular works with factories that must keep running. The risk: production overcapacity. And the sector is sensitive to the economic cycle: in 2026 growth sectors — defence, energy, aeronautics — pull orders up, while many SMEs and mid-size firms are in difficulty and postpone investment. Result: margins are much higher in rental than in permanent construction, where they're far tighter — sometimes just break-even. "The site hut for hire hasn't said its last word."

This is literally your programme. The 5,600 modules for 10,000+ EPR2 workers are part of the site you work on, and modularisation is one of the big levers new nuclear builds use to cut schedule and cost — moving work from a congested site to controlled factories (as SMR — small modular reactor — designs push further). You're unusually well placed to understand both the supplier economics (factory loading, rental fleet, reuse) and the owner's view (rent vs buy, interfaces, schedule) — a concrete niche where nuclear delivery meets industrial finance.

Make it click — similar plays

A ~€1.5bn niche in France, 71.8% rental with higher margins than tight-margin permanent sales, it depends on keeping factories loaded through the cycle — which makes EDF's €100m, 7–8-year order of 5,600+ modules for 10,000+ EPR2 workers vital. For you: this is your site's support economy, and modularisation is a nuclear-delivery lever you can advise on.
