Exaion — Why EDF Is Selling Its Computing Start-up to a US Bitcoin MinerLes Echos · Video case · A corporate spin-off, a capital increase that looks like a sale, sovereignty, the Cloud Act, and a political storm
▶ Video0/14▶
The one idea"Prime Minister, I ask you solemnly: are you going to sell off a new champion born of national genius?" Few people had heard of Exaion until mid-August 2025, when EDF announced the sale of control of this start-up to MARA, a US leader in bitcoin mining. A deal that could have gone unnoticed became a national affair for three reasons: crypto, sovereignty, and a report to the national financial prosecutor (PNF). It's a case study in how a corporate venture is born from internal assets, why a big group divests what isn't core, and how "who buys" can matter as much as "for how much."
A note on framing (source)

Video case (Les Echos — "Cryptos : pourquoi EDF vend sa pépite aux Américains ?," Jan 2026); figures and statements are the video's own. The legal points are allegations in a parliamentary report to the prosecutor, not charges or findings, and the outcome after the video isn't covered here. Filed in Energy, Infrastructure & Resources — it's about EDF's assets, data centres and the energy–compute intersection. Note for the reader: this concerns your own employer, so treat it as a public case, read through public sources.

Born inside EDF (2018–2024)

Exaion's story begins in 2018 when two EDF employees meet: one is responsible for EDF's data centres, the other an investment director at the group's incubator, EDF Pulse. Together they look for a way to recycle EDF's supercomputers — the group has peak-computing machines deployed to manage its generation fleet. Exaion officially starts in 2020 within EDF. Using that computing power, the start-up does mainly three things: 1) renting computing power for 3D data processing (video games, cinema, animation); 2) over time its core became private cloud for AI and high-performance computing, with sovereignty as the key argument — data hosted in data centres in France or Canada, where Exaion is also established; 3) blockchain and crypto-asset services — since 2021 Société Générale's crypto subsidiary uses Exaion's infrastructure to secure its crypto-asset issuance, and at the end of 2024 the start-up obtained registration as a digital-asset service provider (PSAN). The stated ambition: a kind of digital safe for banks and financial institutions.

The deal (August 2025)

EDF's CEO since May 2025, reputed to be a cost-cutter, was given a mission to refocus EDF on its core businesses. "Selling Exaion doesn't mean the project is bad for EDF — it means it isn't a priority." On 11 August 2025, EDF Pulse Ventures announced an investment agreement with MARA: MARA acquires 64% of Exaion for about $168m, of which roughly €30m goes to EDF and the rest is injected directly into Exaion to fund its development — "not really a sale, rather a capital increase." MARA can go up to 75% by 2027 for $127m more; EDF stays a minority shareholder and a client of Exaion. On paper, a good deal for EDF and growth capital for Exaion.

Why it blew up — three fronts

1) Cloud Act and sovereignty. MARA Holdings is a US company based in Florida; under the US Cloud Act, US authorities can in some cases require US companies to hand over data they control, even stored abroad — awkward for a business selling "sovereign" cloud. In parliament the question was put directly ("are we going to sell off sovereign nuggets growing in France?"). Days after the announcement, the economy ministry asked EDF to reopen the file. The key question: are Exaion's activities strategic for France? The Treasury (Direction générale du Trésor) decides, through foreign-investment screening, and can impose conditions or block the deal only if the activity falls in a sensitive sector. The grey zone: blockchain and high-performance computing weren't explicitly listed as strategic — emerging activities not yet at critical size in France. The minister argued Exaion doesn't weigh heavily in tomorrow's tech stakes, as it doesn't mine bitcoin; per the video, the Treasury was about to authorise the sale with conditions. 2) Bitcoin mining. Exaion doesn't mine bitcoin, and MARA categorically denies wanting to mine in France with it — but French competitors aren't convinced. Mining in France isn't banned, but has never had a regulatory green light from the state or big utilities like EDF for large-scale deployment. French crypto players fear MARA will capture this activity (access to cheap, low-carbon power); a French consortium even made a counter-offer, unsuccessfully. A critic: "MARA buys this empty shell for $170m… only ~€29m comes back to EDF, the rest stays in the capital to build mining farms." 3) The judicial front. In mid-December, two parliamentarians filed a report under Article 40 to the PNF on the conditions of the sale, citing suspicions including misuse of corporate assets, organised fraud, illegal taking of interest and influence peddling — notably free-share allocations and the potential personal enrichment of Exaion's two managers, which could reach €33m if the deal closes. One of them, Senator Dany Wattebled: "two EDF people invest €126,000 and could get several million euros…" These are allegations; nothing in the video establishes wrongdoing.

Primark — The Retailer That Refused Everything, Now Forced to ChangeCorentin Mercadal · Video case · No ads, no online, no sales — volume, big stores and a patient sugar-and-tea parent; then falling like-for-likes, delivery and a demerger
▶ Video0/14▶
The one ideaPrimark is an anomaly in ready-to-wear. For 50+ years it did no advertising, never sold online, never ran sales, and its founder never gave an interview in 40 years — everything Zara, H&M and Shein do to exist, Primark refused. Yet it became a world leader in low-price clothing: 500 stores, 20 countries, 80,000+ employees, and in its last year £9.5bn of revenue and £1.1bn of operating profit — a record. Now it's in its biggest strategic turn: like-for-like sales are falling, margin lost two points in a half-year, and for the first time in 57 years it says yes to delivery; its CEO left overnight, and it's preparing to separate from its parent. Can a model built on store visits survive making buying more convenient?
A note on framing (source)

Video case (Corentin Mercadal, "La chute inévitable de Primark," Oct 2026); figures are the video's own, sponsor segment omitted; some passages weren't in the screenshots, so the card sticks to what was shown. Filed in Consumer, Retail & Luxury with the fast-fashion set: Zara vs H&M (149), Uniqlo (151), Shein (152).

Origins — Penneys and a patient parent (1969 →)

June 1969, 47 Mary Street, Dublin: above the door another name, Penneys — still the name of the Irish stores. The first Saturday, not a single customer; Arthur Ryan, 34, stands on the doorstep all day. He's a former buyer at Dunnes, the big Irish chain, with one wish: make fashion accessible to people watching their budget. He lacks the money for stock, premises and openings — and the backing comes from an unexpected player: Associated British Foods (ABF), a bread, sugar and tea group controlled by the Weston family (owner of Twinings). ABF brings two things: money and patience. In 1974 the chain crosses the Irish Sea to open in Derby, England — but an American company, JC Penney, already owns the name in the UK, so it needs a new one: Primark.

How a €2 T-shirt makes money

Its cost is decided before manufacture: fabric, cut, finishes, number of seams — each choice adds cost. Primark owns no factories; it orders from independent suppliers, and quantity changes everything: in 2014 its development director called it a volume company selling 150 million T-shirts a year. Long runs cut the cost per garment and give Primark negotiating weight — "the exact inverse of Zara, which pays a high price for reactivity." Primark places long orders planned months ahead on a huge base of basics — socks, pyjamas, underwear that don't go out of fashion in three weeks. The easiest saving to see is yours: you do the logistics — you find the aisle, your size, choose, carry it home; a delivered order means picking, packing, transport to the door. And the store makes your basket grow: you come for jeans and on the way see children's clothes, socks, an accessory — at a few euros, an extra item takes little thought. That's how low prices and profitability coexist: in 2025 Primark's operating margin reached 11.9% — almost €12 of profit per €100 of sales. Condition: sell a lot. A Primark store is a huge surface, a team and a rent — costs paid every month even when customers are fewer.

Expansion — the big-store bet

In the 1990s British high-street retail went into crisis; BHS, C&A gave up huge spaces in the best streets, and Arthur Ryan, opportunistic, picked them up one by one. The big coup: July 2005, ABF signs its biggest cheque — £409m for 120 Littlewoods stores; Primark then had only 122 and kept about 40, the biggest and best placed. Revenue doubled in only four years — but, a surprising detail, Littlewoods' mail-order catalogue business wasn't taken over: Primark wanted walls and footfall. Continental Europe: Madrid 2006, Germany 2009, then Portugal, Belgium, Austria, Italy. On 16 December 2013 it arrived in France at the Grand Littoral mall in northern Marseille — not Paris, not the Champs-Élysées, but a popular, high-traffic mall — then Paris region, Lyon, Lille, Toulouse, Bordeaux: today 30 stores in France, just over €1bn of revenue, and still no address inside Paris, where 5,000 m² at a bearable rent doesn't exist.

Rana Plaza and Covid — the parent as shield

Behind the low prices, who actually makes the clothes? On 24 April 2013 the Rana Plaza building collapsed in Bangladesh; more than 1,100 people died. Among the workshops in the building, one with 580 workers made products for Primark. Primark reacted fast: compensation for workers and families, help to other victims, signing the Bangladesh building-safety accord — $14m over two years. But a company that never explained itself now had to answer. Then Covid: lockdowns closed stores, and a retailer with no online sales had nothing to sell; historic UK high-street names (Debenhams, Topshop, Arcadia) disappeared within months. Primark survived thanks to its parent: ABF's food and agricultural businesses (Twinings tea, Jordans cereals, Silver Spoon sugar) sold in supermarkets that stayed open, some brands even grew, and in spring 2020, while Primark burned cash behind closed shutters, ABF's food side generated about £300m of cash — time to get through. Then a historic rebound: £7.7bn (2022), £9bn (2023), £9.5bn (2025), with the highest profit in its existence. So when people ask why Primark didn't deliver earlier: it had just proven its model in the hardest possible test.

The cracks

The big-store logic — the bigger the store, the more you sell and the better you spread costs — had a second half that never happened: sales per m² fell even before Covid, and an oversized store doesn't shrink on its own. In 2022 ABF booked a £206m impairment on German stores: hoped-for profits no longer justified their value, while rents continued; between 2022 and 2025 the German network went from 32 to 27 stores and lost a quarter of its selling space. On 1 September 2026 Primark opened its 500th store — expansion continues. But there are two ways to grow revenue: open new shops, or sell more in existing ones (like-for-like sales), and the two curves have split: in 2025 sales +1%, like-for-like −2.3%; 2026 similar, about −2%. Customers have more options with new arrivals every day (Shein): Primark must now defend not just its prices but the reason to come. In July 2026 it cut prices permanently on hundreds of items, up to −25%, raised marketing spend for the first time in its history, and accepted a margin around 10% for 2026 vs 11.9% the year before — and expects volumes to follow.

New leadership, delivery and the demerger

On 31 March 2025, at the London open, ABF published a short statement: Paul Marchant, Arthur Ryan's successor, had resigned with immediate effect after 16 years in which revenue went from £2.3bn to £9.5bn — following an inquiry into his behaviour towards a woman. The interim went the same day to the group's finance director, ready to take decisions the chain always refused. First, click & collect: order online, collect in store — the last mile is still you; tested from November 2022 in 25 stores in northern England, rolled out from May 2025. Then home delivery. Investors had long asked: why buy a sugar maker to own Primark? On 21 April 2026 the answer came: Primark will be listed alone in London before the end of 2027; the Weston family stays majority on both sides. The split doesn't end the empire, but changes the light in which each decision is read.

Delivery: added sale or replaced visit?

Same basket: say €6 of margin left in store, €2 in delivery (after product, average returns, packing, preparation, transport); in both cases fixed costs still need funding. Nina lives too far and would never have set foot in a Primark: delivery creates €2 that didn't exist — a created sale. Léa came every Saturday; now she orders from her sofa: her parcel brings €2 but her visit would have brought €6 — €4 less. Sarah wanted to order from home and, without delivery, would have gone elsewhere: a kept customer. The mix of these profiles reveals the activity needed to break even — the trap: even if every parcel is profitable alone, the total result can fall. For 57 years your visit was part of the economics: huge-volume buying, stores that concentrate sales, a patient shareholder through crises. Now Primark adds a channel built on the opposite of what it knew; delivery's success will be judged on what it adds to Primark as a whole. The real question: can it make buying more convenient without breaking the economics that make its prices possible?

Capture the lessons

Run the drills

Beyond the video — why this case is yours

Fixed assets, utilisation and patient owners — your world. A Primark store works like a power plant: big fixed cost, profitable only at high utilisation; oversized assets get impaired when demand disappoints. ABF's role (cash from stable food businesses carrying a cyclical one) is the logic of diversified sponsors and patient capital in infrastructure. And Rana Plaza is a reminder that supply-chain safety and labour conditions are now part of every contract's risk — exactly what you manage on critical equipment.

Make it click — similar plays

Fast-fashion set: Zara vs H&M (149), H&M (150), Uniqlo (151) — basics too, different strategy; Shein (152). Patient owners: Rolex (154), Ferrero (180). Retail under pressure: Mr. Bricolage (187).

How to drillPrimark refused everything — ads, online, sales, interviews — and won on volume basics (150m T-shirts a year), big stores where customers do the logistics, and a patient parent (ABF) that funded the 1969 Dublin start, the £409m Littlewoods deal and survival through Covid; it reached £9.5bn and 11.9% margin. Now like-for-likes fall (−2.3%), German stores were impaired, prices are cut up to 25%, margin is guided to ~10%, the CEO left, click & collect and delivery arrive, and Primark will list alone by 2027. For you: model cannibalisation, read like-for-like, and size fixed assets to proven demand.

Mbappé and China — How One Old Clip Became a Business Crisis OvernightEntrepreneur Mindset · Video case · A personal brand as a company, market concentration, sponsors' exit speed, and who really pays (La Liga, Real Madrid, On)
▶ Video0/14▶
The one ideaA few seconds of video, filmed six months earlier and deleted in under two hours, were enough to trigger an international business crisis. On the night of the Ballon d'Or (Monday 26 October 2026), a clip of Kylian Mbappé laughing at a meme that put his face on Mao Zedong's body spread on Chinese platforms. Within 48 hours, per the video: three Chinese-market sponsors dropped him, his Chinese social accounts were frozen, Chinese state TV cut the entire Spanish league, Real Madrid apologised, the share price of his new kit sponsor fell, and a US congressional committee weighed in. The lesson isn't about football: at global scale, an individual is a company, and a company exposed to one big market lives by that market's red lines.
A note on framing (source)

Video case (Entrepreneur Mindset, "Comment la CHINE a effacé MBAPPÉ en une nuit," 27–28 Oct 2026) about events of the previous 48 hours; everything here is as reported by the video, not independently verified, and the story was still developing (no sanctions lifted at the time). Some names were unclear in the transcript. Filed in Media, Entertainment & Gaming, next to F1 / Liberty Media (173); direct follow-up to On (172).

What happened, per the video

The clip came from an April shoot with the French programme The Bridge: Mbappé laughing at a meme pasting his face onto Mao Zedong (the internet had also turned him into Kim Jong-un, Stalin, Mobutu — teammate Dembélé reportedly called him "Mobu" to mock his supposed influence in the dressing room). The video slept six months, then The Bridge published it on Ballon d'Or night, reportedly with his entourage's agreement (per RMC Sport); deleted in under two hours, but already on Chinese platforms. In France calling Mao a dictator shocks few people; in China, Mao founded the People's Republic in 1949, and while historians associate his rule with tens of millions of deaths (notably the Great Leap Forward famine), for the Party his achievements weigh more. The cascade: 2m+ followers lost on Chinese accounts; per Chinese media, two more sponsors — a luxury house and the Swiss watchmaker Hublot — removed content featuring him from their Chinese accounts; in Beijing, at Adidas's flagship (Real's kit supplier), AFP found no shirt with his name. Only unofficial sellers on Taobao still sold his merchandise. Why so fast? In China, keeping someone accused of hurting the country risks being boycotted in their place — the video recalls H&M in 2021: an old statement about not buying Xinjiang cotton over forced-labour suspicions resurfaced, triggered a huge boycott, and its China sales fell 23% in a quarter.

The real losers

On Ballon d'Or night Chinese state TV didn't only cut Real Madrid matches — it cut the whole Spanish league. According to Spanish daily AS, China brings La Liga about €50m a year in TV rights alone, possibly up to €100m a season with partnerships; in August La Liga had signed with Migu, China Mobile's streaming platform, to broadcast all its matches in China until 2030. La Liga's president Javier Tebas apologised to China on behalf of the league and all its clubs, met China's ambassador to Spain the same day, and posted that China "is and will remain a strategic partner." Imagine being president of a small Spanish club: none of your players spoke of Mao, and you vanish from Chinese TV because of a French show's backstage. US politics stepped in too: a House select committee (the video's description) criticised the pressure. Chinese TV indicated that until Real Madrid apologised, all other discussion was suspended — and within hours Real Madrid reversed: on Wednesday an official statement apologised to the Chinese people "for the inconvenience caused by the recent remarks of our player," with a letter passed to Chinese TV via La Liga. Real claims nearly 100m supporters in China and has Chinese sponsors such as Hisense. Chinese TV confirmed receipt and said: "We will listen to their words, but watch their actions even more" — La Liga still wasn't back on air. Another company sweating: On, the Swiss sports-shoe brand Mbappé had joined in September as ambassador and shareholder after leaving Nike — on Tuesday its share price lost up to 6% on Wall Street; China weighs about 10% of its sales. Beijing said it took seriously "the apologies presented by the person concerned" — note, the person concerned — but said nothing about lifting sanctions. The state-backed Global Times concluded that Mbappé paid the price and his case should be a red line for all foreign celebrities who want to sell in China.

Political risk is a line item in project finance. Lenders model sovereign and political events (sanctions, expropriation, market closures) with insurance, multilateral lenders and diversified offtake — this case shows how fast such an event moves when one market holds the switch. It's also a reminder for a France–Tunisia professional building a public profile: in sensitive industries like nuclear, what you say publicly is part of your bankability.

At global scale a person is a company, concentration in one market is political exposure, and partners' risks are yours. For you: map political red lines and concentration in every plan with foreign exposure.

Tunisia's Top 5 Business Leaders — Five Ways a Tunisian Builds BigResearch case · Ben-Gacem (BlueFive), Lazaar (Swicorp), Zouari (Picard), Seddiki (Movepayment), Neifar (Groupe Neifar) — backgrounds, how they won, the mechanisms, lessons for founders and investors
◆ Research0/14▶
The one ideaFour of the five built their fortune outside Tunisia's domestic market, by plugging Tunisian talent into a bigger capital pool: Gulf money (Ben-Gacem, Lazaar), the French retail system (Zouari), the German–Maghreb diaspora corridor (Seddiki). Only Neifar grew from home, as a construction conglomerate with a Libyan wing. The lesson isn't "be Tunisian and succeed abroad" — it's find the bridge between two pools and own the toll on it.
A note on the source

The list comes from a poster by Success Story (it calls itself the "#1 MENA (Middle East and North Africa) online business media"). I couldn't find the article behind it, so the ranking is the publisher's choice, not a measured one — and the five are on very different scales (a ~$15bn investment firm next to an early-stage fintech). The facts below come from press and company sources listed at the bottom; where sources disagree, I say so.

1 · Hazem Ben-Gacem — the dealmaker who spun out his own firm (BlueFive Capital)

Background: Tunisian; Harvard bachelor's degree; M&A (mergers and acquisitions) at Credit Suisse First Boston, New York. Joined Investcorp (the Bahrain-based alternative-asset manager, $50bn+ under management) in 1993/94, ran European private equity, then global technology private equity, and became co-CEO in 2018. Involved in 40+ of its private-equity deals over ~30 years.
How he won: left Investcorp in September 2024 and launched BlueFive Capital in November 2024 in ADGM (Abu Dhabi Global Market, the emirate's financial free zone) with 15 founding shareholders and two arms: BlueFive Financial (buying and merging financial-services firms) and BlueFive Asset Management (private equity and infrastructure). By July 2026 it reportedly managed about $15bn, with offices from London to Beijing. Reported funds: a $2bn GCC (Gulf Cooperation Council) private-equity fund and a $3bn technology/growth fund.
2026 deal run: lead investor in the HOF Capital consortium that bought Porsche's stake in Bugatti Rimac; 49% of Massar Solutions (fleet services, 8,500+ vehicles) from TAQA; led a $250m raise for CargoX (autonomous delivery); 49% of LeasePlan Emirates; merger forming BlueFiveSidra (Islamic finance, $3.8bn+).
Beyond money: founded the Harvard office in Tunisia (2017), Harvard's first in the Arab world; former member of Tunisia's national shooting team (bronze, 2017 African championships).
Mechanisms: the GP spin-out (a senior partner leaves a big firm and raises his own funds on his record); Gulf sovereign and family-office money as the LP (limited partner, the fund's investors) base; minority stakes beside state-linked partners; buy-and-build consolidation in financial services.

2 · Kamel Lazaar — the pioneer who built a Gulf investment bank (Swicorp)

Background: born 1952 in Tunisia; economics in Tunis; Vice-President at Citibank in North Africa, Europe and Saudi Arabia (sources differ on the exact posting); on the founding team of Samba (Saudi American Bank), the Saudi bank formed from Citibank's Saudi branches.
How he won: founded Swicorp in 1987 — one of the first investment banks in MENA. Headquartered in Riyadh, offices in Tunis, Dubai and Geneva; investment banking, private equity and asset management, $1bn+ in assets. Swicorp also invests in infrastructure — e.g. three solar plants in Egypt built with Spain's Acciona (2019).
Beyond money: the Kamel Lazaar Foundation (2005), one of the largest modern and contemporary art collections in the region; the Ibraaz platform; helped bring Tunisia back to the Venice Biennale after ~60 years; the Maghreb Economic Forum (2011).
Mechanisms: the cross-border bridge — Swiss banking standards, Saudi capital, Maghreb deal flow; moving from advisory fees to principal investing; culture as soft power and network.

3 · Moez-Alexandre Zouari — the franchisee who became the brand owner (Picard)

Background: French, of Tunisian origin; Dauphine business studies. Built the group with his wife Soraya (she runs finance and administration, he runs stores and acquisitions). Started in 1998 with Paris convenience stores (group: Imanes).
How he won: became one of the largest franchisees of Casino-group banners — Franprix, Monoprix, Monop', Leader Price — about 500 stores by 2018 (sold 198 Leader Price stores back to Casino that year). Then the jump from operator to owner:
• 2019: 43% of Picard (frozen food, ~1,100 stores, €1.4bn sales) from Aryzta for ~€156m, backed by ICG (Intermediate Capital Group, a debt and private-equity firm).
• 2021–22: discount chains Maxi Bazar and Stokomani.
• 2023: bid for Casino with Xavier Niel and Matthieu Pigasse — lost to Daniel Křetínský (the trio later got a settlement from fund Attestor).
• 2024: bought out Lion Capital — the family vehicle (IGZ) now holds 100% of Picard, valued at about €2.2–2.4bn (≈9–10× EBITDA, earnings before interest, taxes, depreciation and amortisation). Sources differ on whether closing was Dec 2024 or early 2025.
• 2025: 27 Monop' stores into a franchise joint venture with Monoprix.
Challenges magazine put the couple's wealth at ~€1.25bn in 2025 (104th in France). See Picard (20).
Mechanisms: franchise cash flow → minority stake with a financial partner → control buyout (a family-owned LBO, leveraged buyout); buying discount retail; a family holding as the acquisition vehicle.

4 · Mohamed Seddiki — the nomad who builds on the corridor he lives (Movepayment)

Background: ~40, school in Tunisia, computer science in Hanover, 8 years at Volkswagen (engineer → product manager). First business: a language school for the diaspora — 6 branches in Tunisia, 3 in Algeria, a presence in India, approved for ÖSD and ECL German-language exams (i.e. it feeds the Germany-migration pipeline).
How he's building: Move Payment GmbH (Braunschweig, Germany; founded 2023 or 2024 depending on source). "Pay by Bank" via open banking — the customer pays straight from their bank account, no card: instant payouts, no chargebacks, 1% fee, 3,000+ European banks, aimed at small online shops. Plus low-cost transfers to Tunisia, Morocco and others, and a planned "Global Account" for Tunisian freelancers. It runs through a licensed gateway partner rather than its own payment licence.
Mechanisms: the diaspora corridor (people go north, money comes back south); undercutting the card toll — see Visa & Mastercard (175) and Neobanks / Revolut (52); licence-light via a partner; the first business funds and informs the second.
Honest scale check: no public funding, volumes or revenue. On this list he is the promise, not yet the proof.

5 · Fathi Neifar — the home-grown conglomerate builder (Groupe Neifar)

Background and business (from the group's own website; little independent coverage): founded in 1980 as a construction company — buildings, infrastructure, civil engineering (hotels, housing, offices, hospitals). Head office Les Berges du Lac (Tunis), a site in Sfax, and a Libyan arm (office in Tripoli, company LTC, projects there).
How he won: used construction cash flow to diversify — Super Mousse (foam and spring mattresses), wooden furniture, electrical wiring harnesses (Sidilec), olive-oil exports (Royal Oil Company), hotels, real estate. Nine subsidiaries listed.
Mechanisms: the classic family conglomerate — one cash engine funding adjacent businesses; Libya as a high-risk, high-margin neighbouring market.
Caution: in March 2025 Africa Intelligence ran a headline that Neifar was "taking shelter in Dubai" — the reasons aren't public (paywalled). Not a finding of wrongdoing, but an open question worth checking before treating him as a model.

Side by side
LeaderBaseEngineWhose capitalKey moveMoat
Ben-GacemAbu Dhabi / LondonPrivate equity, financial servicesGulf sovereign & family officesSpin-out from Investcorp → BlueFive30-year deal record + Gulf trust
LazaarRiyadh / Geneva / TunisInvestment bank, PE, infraSaudi & Gulf investorsFounded Swicorp (1987)First-mover bridge Gulf–Maghreb–Swiss
ZouariParisConvenience & frozen-food retailOwn cash flow + ICGFranchisee → 100% Picard ownerOperator knowledge + family speed
SeddikiBraunschweig / TunisiaOpen-banking payments, remittancesOwn (no public round)Language school → fintechLives the corridor he serves
NeifarTunis / Sfax / TripoliConstruction + diversified industryOwn cash flowConstruction → conglomerateLocal networks, Libya access
Three archetypes

The capital bridge (Ben-Gacem, Lazaar): earn trust inside a big institution, then take the relationships out and connect Gulf money to deals elsewhere. Scales furthest; requires decades of record.
The diaspora operator (Zouari, Seddiki): grow inside a host-country system (French franchises, German payments) and use cash flow or corridor knowledge to move up the value chain.
The home conglomerate (Neifar): dominate one local trade, diversify around it, expand to the neighbour. Strong locally, exposed to political and key-man (founder-dependence) risk.

Lessons for the investor

Back the spin-out, not the brochure: a first-time fund from a 30-year veteran (BlueFive) is underwritten by a visible record. Operator-owners buy cheaper and run better: Zouari knew Picard's customers before he owned it. Corridor fintech is a regulation bet: a partner licence can be withdrawn. Conglomerates hide risk: limited disclosure, founder dependence, cross-border political exposure — price it or skip it. Media rankings are marketing: verify independently.

Beyond the list — why this case is yours

You are a Franco-Tunisian with a project-finance toolkit — the exact profile of the bridge archetype. Lazaar's Swicorp co-invested in Egyptian solar with Acciona; Ben-Gacem's BlueFive buys infrastructure with Gulf money. The open seat: someone who speaks EPC (engineering, procurement and construction) contracts, nuclear and grid delivery, French and Arabic, and can bring Gulf or European capital to Maghreb and French energy/AI-infrastructure projects. Ben-Gacem's path also says the record comes first: your EPR2 years are your Investcorp years — make them legible.

How to drillFive Tunisians, three playbooks: the capital bridge (Ben-Gacem's BlueFive, ~$15bn; Lazaar's Swicorp, since 1987), the diaspora operator (Zouari, from Paris franchisee to 100% owner of Picard; Seddiki, from language school to open-banking payments), and the home conglomerate (Neifar, construction to mattresses and olive oil, with a Libyan arm). The common thread: plug talent into a bigger capital pool and own the toll on the bridge. Your version: Gulf/European capital ↔ French and Maghreb energy infrastructure.

On Screen ▶The entrepreneurship curriculum on film — dramatizations & documentaries, ranked by lesson density.

The best entrepreneurship films aren't highlight reels — they dramatize a real, transferable strategic lesson. The Founder's lesson isn't "work hard," it's own the real estate, not the burgers. This library is the exhaustive shelf, each title tagged to the lesson it teaches and, where relevant, to the case file it brings to life. Read the case, then watch the dramatization. Titles marked [case] correspond to a card in Library 09.
